Taiwan hosts WITSA Global AI Summit for second year, launches global AI index
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:13:44 UTC
19:13:44 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan hosted the WITSA Global AI Summit for the second consecutive year Tuesday, bringing technology leaders, government officials, and industry representatives from around the world together to discuss AI development and the launch of a new framework for evaluating national AI ecosystems.
The two-day summit at the Grand Hotel was organized by the World Innovation, Technology and Services Alliance and hosted by the Taiwan Innovative Software and Services Association. The event was held under the theme “AI Alive, Beyond the Future.”
WITSA, founded in 1978, is an alliance of technology industry associations from more than 80 economies. Its members represent more than 90% of the global ICT market, according to the organization. A major focus of this year's summit was the launch of the WITSA Global AI Index, described by WITSA as the first industry-led benchmark of national AI ecosystem maturity.
The summit also marked the launch of the inaugural WITSA Global AI Awards, recognizing achievements in seven categories: AI infrastructure, talent, entrepreneurship, use cases, data, public policy, and investment.
Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), in a video message, said the summit's focus on sovereign AI, hardware-software integration, and intelligent robotics is closely aligned with Taiwan's AI development strategy. She said the government is implementing the Ten AI Initiatives Promotion Plan approved by the Cabinet in January.
Hsiao said Taiwan is expanding computing capacity and strengthening data governance as part of efforts to develop sovereign AI. The government is also working to build traditional Mandarin AI training data that reflects Taiwan's cultural characteristics and can support domestic AI model development.
She also highlighted Taiwan's efforts to integrate AI with hardware and develop intelligent robotics for applications including health care, hospitality, logistics, and disaster response. At the same time, Hsiao said Taiwan needs to ensure that AI development is accompanied by digital equity and strong governance, including privacy protections under the AI Basic Act.
WITSA Chairman Dato' Dr. Sean Seah said the new index is intended to change how economies assess their AI development. “The index is not just a benchmark but a map,” Seah said, describing it as a tool that can help governments, businesses, investors, and other stakeholders identify gaps and determine how to move forward.
Seah said economies have plenty of narratives about their AI ambitions but need a standardized assessment of what they have actually built. The index provides an “honest mirror” for governments, he said, showing their current AI capabilities rather than simply measuring their aspirations.
Seah also emphasized that the index is intended to go beyond measurement. “A diagnosis without a prescription is only half” of the solution, he said, explaining that WITSA wants the framework to help member economies move from identifying weaknesses to developing practical strategies for improvement.
WITSA describes the index as an industry-led initiative rather than one developed by a single government or technology vendor. The organization says the framework is supported by practitioner input from its member associations and an independent expert panel.
Moving from AI hardware to complete solutions
TISSA Chairman Dr. Brian Shen (沈柏延) said Taiwan's greatest advantage remains its highly integrated technology supply chain, but the economy needs to use that foundation to develop stronger software capabilities.
“Taiwan's greatest strength is its world-class supply chain in semiconductors, servers, networking, and ICT hardware,” Shen said in an interview on the sidelines of the summit. “The next step is to go beyond hardware manufacturing and turn those strengths into competitive advantages in AI software, industry applications, and integrated solutions.”
Shen said Taiwan does not need to compete with the largest US technology companies across every area of AI but should focus on sectors where it has established expertise and global connections. “This is a turning point. Technology is creating new opportunities, and we need to change with it.”
One of Taiwan's biggest challenges is turning individual AI projects into scalable products, Shen said. “AI implementation in Taiwan is very diversified, but many applications are still not mature products,” he said. “We have many proof-of-concept projects, but a proof of concept is not a product.”
The next step, he said, is to transform successful AI use cases into repeatable products and services that can be marketed internationally. “We need to help Taiwan's software companies move from one project experience to products and solutions that can compete globally,” Shen said.
Shen also pointed to Taiwan's strong showing in the inaugural WITSA Global AI Awards as evidence that Taiwan’s AI capabilities extend beyond hardware. “The recognition shows that the world increasingly sees Taiwan not only as a major supplier of AI hardware, but also as an important partner in AI technology, applications, and industry innovation,” he said.
“Taiwan has a unique advantage because we can integrate semiconductors, computing infrastructure, cloud services, cybersecurity, software, and deep industry knowledge into a comprehensive AI ecosystem.” Shen said the awards also demonstrate the need to move successful AI applications toward commercialization.
“The seven WITSA awards we previously earned are important because they show what Taiwan has already achieved,” he said. “But many of these are government use cases. Our next goal is for software companies to turn these successful use cases into products.”
He said TISSA plans to use WITSA's international network to help Taiwanese companies gain exposure in overseas markets and exchange experience with AI developers worldwide. “We need to use the WITSA network to show Taiwan's talent, products, and successful AI use cases globally, while also learning from international experiences and best practices,” Shen said.
WITSA's broader agenda reflects the same shift from AI potential to implementation. The 2026 summit's program includes discussions on sovereign AI, AI hardware-software integration, intelligent robotics, policy, investment, and talent.
For Taiwan, the discussions underscore a broader challenge: how to turn its central role in the global semiconductor and AI hardware supply chain into a stronger position in AI software, applications, and services.
Shen said the objective is ultimately to move Taiwan beyond supplying components and toward developing complete AI solutions for global markets. “Taiwan's opportunity is to build world-class AI software and industry solutions on top of its world-class hardware foundation,” he said.

Taipei's fire department develops bleeding control training kit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:13:30 UTC
19:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taipei City Fire Department said Wednesday that its firefighters have developed a cheaper emergency training set.
The fire department said in a press release that its first responders came up with the idea by applying field experience. It noted that the device costs NT$860 (US$27) per set compared to commercial versions sold at NT$4,000 (US$126).
The department said severe bleeding remains the leading cause of trauma-related deaths, especially in the armpit and groin where tourniquets cannot be applied. It added that timely wound-packing and pressure can stop bleeding, buying valuable time. A tourniquet is a tight strip wrapped around a limb to stop blood flow.
The department said traditional training used raw pork with fake vessels, which is unsanitary, while commercial models are expensive and had to be shared between trainees. It instead used non-toxic silicone to cut unit costs. The increased accessibility has sped up training 30-fold.
The department said the kit features fake wounds and uses a pressurized blood bottle to simulate continuous bleeding, requiring trainees to master correct packing position, depth, and force to stop the blood flow. It said the device can be reused thousands of times.
The department said the real benefit is that frontline personnel receive more frequent training so the injured can be treated more quickly. It aims to expand the training to the general public so that help is available before the ambulance arrives.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taiwan is using its technological prowess to link up with the world, not to dominate the world, Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu (吳志中) said at Semicon Taiwan on Wednesday.
Wu visited several of the record 18 national pavilions at the international semiconductor show on its opening day, per CNA. The former Taiwan envoy in Paris praised France’s pavilion as an expression of bilateral cooperation able to create a better future.
Newly appointed French representative Frederic Laplanche said his country’s presence was proof of excellent relations. French enterprises and research bodies enjoyed a stable interest in Taiwan, while also showing the depth of France’s semiconductor industry, he said.

The US and the Netherlands also featured prominently at the Sept. 2-4 event, while Sweden and Finland opened a shared pavilion for the first time.

Unknown Publisher

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The foreign ministry on Tuesday condemned statements issued by China and Kyrgyzstan that it said denigrate Taiwan’s sovereignty, urging Bishkek not to endorse Beijing’s claims.
China’s foreign ministry on Monday released a joint declaration on a comprehensive strategic partnership in which Kyrgyzstan reiterated its support for the “one-China” principle and opposition to “Taiwan independence,” per China's state-run Xinhua. The foreign ministry accused Beijing of repeatedly using international engagements to promote its ”one-China" narrative.
The ministry said Taiwan is a sovereign and independent country and is not subordinate to China. It said statements intended to undermine sovereignty cannot change that reality.
It also urged the international community to take China’s use of coercion and inducements seriously, as it seeks to influence other governments’ sovereign decisions. Such actions constitute not only pressure on Taiwan but also a major challenge to democratic systems and the international rule of law, the ministry said.
The ministry called on Kyrgyzstan not to follow China in promoting what it described as distorted and false claims. It said Taiwan will continue to deepen cooperation with like-minded countries, uphold democratic values, and resist economic coercion and diplomatic bullying.

Sotheby’s and Christie’s unveil masterpieces in Taipei previews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:12:53 UTC
19:12:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – International auction powerhouses Sotheby’s and Christie’s will bring their autumn auction previews to Taiwan in September.
Sotheby’s expands its regional footprint with stops in Taipei and Taichung, while Christie’s hosts a focused exhibition at Dopeness Art Lab in Taipei's Daan District.
Sotheby’s preview is led by Nara Yoshitomo’s immersive installation “Drawing Room in Crate Reykjavik,” making its global auction and local debut with an estimate of NT$182 million to NT$263 million.
Created for a 2009 exhibition at the Reykjavik Art Museum, it stands as the largest and most complex masterpiece within the artist’s rare “Crate Series.” “Drawing Room in Crate Reykjavik” transforms shipping crates into a private, peek-in studio.
The interior houses 97 unique paintings, a large acrylic work on wood, two small chairs, a CD player, and hanging light bulbs.
Viewers peer through flaps and apertures to discover Nara’s iconic motifs — children, houses, and mountains.
By shifting between viewer and voyeur, visitors experience the artist’s solitary creative process, blurring the boundaries between logistics, storage, and finished art. The work also represents the pinnacle of Nara’s collaboration with the Japanese design collective Graf, under the moniker "YNG."
Sotheby’s also highlights Nara’s 1994 full-body portrait “Present,” alongside Bada Shanren’s historic “Album of Miscellaneous Paintings.”
Marking the artist's 400th birth anniversary, the album showcases expressive inkwork and features the earliest known seal impression of the name "Bada Shanren."
Zhang Daqian’s (張大千) 1938 landscape “Pine Trees and Clouds on Mount Huang” and a rare Yongle blue-and-white jar round out the offering.
Christie’s is anchored by Jean-Michel Basquiat’s 1984 canvas “Ancient Scientist,” featuring a towering skull-like figure infused with African sculpture, Renaissance art, and pop culture elements.
Kusama Yayoi’s 2011 painting ”A-Pumpkin” makes its auction debut, rendered in her signature yellow-and-black dots. Abstract works by Zao Wou-Ki (趙無極) and Gerhard Richter further bolster the showcase.
Preview Details
- Sotheby’s Taichung: Sept. 5–6 | Funee G Tower
- Sotheby’s Taipei: Sept. 12–13 | Hwa Nan Bank International Convention Center
- Christie’s Taipei: Sept. 12–13 | Dopeness Art Lab

UAE travel from Estonia plunges as airlines cut Dubai flights
The number of people traveling to the United Arab Emirates has fallen dramatically since the start of the military conflict between the United States and Iran, said travel agent Mauri Saarend.
"The number of travelers has certainly fallen dramatically. At Estravel, the number of travelers who have purchased some form of service for the United Arab Emirates this year has fallen 77 percent compared with the same period last year, essentially reaching levels last seen during the COVID-19 pandemic," Saarend told ERR.
Several airlines, including Finnair, SAS and Norwegian, have announced that they will not operate flights to Dubai this winter season.
Saarend acknowledged that European airlines have indeed canceled flights to Dubai. At the same time, he said Qatar Airways has already begun operating its own flights from Helsinki to Doha, the capital of the UAE's neighboring country Qatar, while Emirates flights from Helsinki to Dubai are on sale from October.
"Flydubai is also expected to return to both Riga and Vilnius in December. AirBaltic's flights from Riga also remain on the schedule for now. Turkish Airlines, the airline most commonly used by Estonian travelers flying to the Middle East, resumed its routes to both Abu Dhabi and Dubai some time ago," Saarend said.
According to Saarend, charter flights from Estonia to the United Arab Emirates have not been a significant factor in recent years, while the few package tours available have generally used scheduled flights with connections.
He added that sales of package tours to the United Arab Emirates at Estravel have been negligible compared with sales of tickets for scheduled flights.
Among tour operators, Tez Tour is offering package tours to Dubai for the winter, he said, and those packages are also available through Estravel.
"But in general, when it comes to Dubai, buying flights and accommodations separately offers significant savings and much greater flexibility in travel dates. This is especially true now, as several hotels there are offering substantial discounts to attract customers.
"We can also put together a customized trip for independent travelers without any difficulty," Saarend said.
"I would also point out that undoubtedly the most affordable way to visit the United Arab Emirates is to make a stopover of several days or longer in Dubai or Abu Dhabi when flying with Emirates or Etihad, respectively, to Southeast Asia or Oceania. This adds very little to the price of the ticket to the long-haul destination, while making the trip more interesting and less tiring," Saarend said.

The hackers protecting America’s water supply
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:10:28 UTC
19:10:28 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
Last month we talked briefly about how and why cyberattackers are targeting municipal water utilities throughout the United States. Today we’re taking a closer look at that story—why we’re so vulnerable to these attacks but also how volunteer hackers are working to protect our access to clean, safe water. Our guest today is Eric Geller, a senior reporter at Cybersecurity Dive, who focuses on federal cybersecurity policy and critical infrastructure protection.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Feltman: Thanks so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Eric Geller: Thanks for having me.
Feltman: So I wanna start with a very basic question. When we talk about cyberattacks, what is it we’re actually talking about? What’s under that umbrella?
Geller: Well, it’s a wide range of things. It can be everything from guessing somebody’s password or tricking them into handing it over and then just logging in like a real authorized user and messing with the computer system. Or it can be essentially fooling the computer system itself, taking advantage of a vulnerability in the software to get access to something that you shouldn’t be able to access. And then you can, sort of, layer on top of that the supply chain aspect, which is: all these companies are interrelated. So if you can get into one company, you might be able to then jump from there into another company’s systems, either by, again, pretending to be an employee of that first company or by taking advantage of actual connections between the computer systems and moving between them, like a burglar going from one room of a house to another. So there’s really a wide range of technical and social things that are involved here.
Feltman: So we recently talked on the show about water utilities, you know, being vulnerable to cyberattacks. Could you tell us a little bit more about why water is so vulnerable when it comes to cybersecurity?
Geller: We’re really talking about a combination of factors. First of all, many of these are very small. A lot of them are in rural areas. Even the ones that aren’t don’t have a lot of employees; they certainly don’t have a lot of people who are dedicated to security. They know water systems, they don’t necessarily know cyberdefense. There’s not a lot of money to upgrade the technology, and the technology is often old. Some of this equipment is running very early versions of Windows, and there’s not a lot you can do to harden that kind of technology. You can really just bolt security on top of it, and that’s not gonna be as effective as booting up a brand-new machine running the latest version of Windows. So we’re talking about old equipment.
We’re also talking about equipment that is not standard off-the-shelf commercial stuff like an iPhone or a version of Windows on your laptop. These are devices that have bespoke software on them. It’s not always easy for the employees at these water stations to understand the security implications, and they’re not easy to upgrade, and oftentimes they’re not designed with security in mind. So recently we saw a lot of attacks where once the hackers found a device that was accessible from the Internet, which is already something you’re not supposed to allow, they discovered that the login system used a default password, and that’s a second thing you’re not supposed to allow. So that’s a combination right there of two problems that really should not exist, but they do exist because a lot of these utilities are not ready to, sort of, be looking for those problems.
Feltman: So let’s talk about DEF CON Franklin. How did it start, and what’s the goal here?
Geller: Well, DEF CON Franklin grew out of the DEF CON Hacker Conference in 2024. It was sort of a spin-off effort that was designed to bring together people who are experts in cybersecurity and wanna improve and protect their communities with infrastructure operators that don’t have cybersecurity expertise and don’t have a lot of money.
So the system connects volunteers with infrastructure operators that want help making specific changes in their networks. The initiative that I wrote about recently for Cybersecurity Dive was focused on pairing up utilities with experts who could basically make a series of targeted improvements, whether that is helping them understand all the devices on their network—that sounds so simple, but oftentimes these utilities don’t know what they’re running—or whether it’s things like setting up multifactor authentication that you don’t just need a password to log in—these very basic things. DEF CON Franklin sort of connected experts with water systems that wanted this kind of help.
Feltman: I have friends who go to DEF CON, because I’m a nerd, but I think maybe some listeners—their idea of a hacker crystallized when Hackers came out, which unfortunately, I’m so sorry to say, was 30 years ago. Really shocking stuff. But can you tell us a little bit more about who people are who go to DEF CON, who self-identify as hackers these days? What kind of crowd are we talking about?
Geller: It’s a really interesting conference. I was just there at the beginning of August. Of course, it’s gotten a little more corporate over the years, but it does still try to maintain that independent streak, that sense of, you know, we’re the wild fringes of the community. Of course, in reality, a lot of these people are longtime professionals. They’re working in mid-level or senior-level roles inside companies. They are the security people for their companies. You also have a lot of enthusiasts, people who maybe don’t work in cybersecurity but really care a lot about it, want to understand the state of the technology.
Maybe they work at an accounting firm or they work at a hospital. One thing we’ve seen recently is a real significant expansion of the critical infrastructure community, so that’s power plants, water systems, hospitals. They are more and more realizing that they’re vulnerable to hackers and sending people to DEF CON. And so you see folks from hospital systems. You see folks from municipalities showing up to learn from the cybersecurity community about what they can do.
Feltman: Yeah. So in the piece you reported recently, what did you hear from folks about how this is going? You know, what kind of support people are getting?
Geller: Well, I talked to one woman who is the public works director in a very rural community—Wilder, Idaho—and she was telling me about how, you know, she understands that there is a threat out there, but until she started working with a volunteer from DEF CON Franklin, it’s sort of like the expression “you don’t know what you don’t know.” There was a whole world that she just didn’t understand the contours of, and as she started to learn more about it, that crystallized for her where the risks were in her own network, and she started to make these changes so that she was more secure. And then actually one thing I really appreciated hearing from her, and was a little bit surprising in a good way, was she would go out to these meetings with other public works people from the community, from other areas in Idaho, who were also struggling with cybersecurity, and she would tell them what she had learned and try to spread that knowledge so that other communities can start making those changes.
Some of this stuff is so basic that if we were to be told, “You need to go make this change,” we would probably say, “Oh, of course, I already do that. Obviously, I’m gonna use multifactor authentication,” right? But these are not standard Windows logins. These are very complicated systems. It’s not always easy to set up this kind of technology with them. But once you do set it up, she was saying there’s this peace of mind that the entire town has now because they know that, at the very least, they’ve made it a lot harder for people to break into their systems.
Feltman: What do you think that the future looks like here? Do you think this kind of, like, grassroots mitigation is our best way forward? Or are we maybe learning lessons from this that municipalities are gonna take on more broadly?
Geller: Well, one thing that the organizers of this initiative are very clear on is: this is not a substitute for dedicated government funding in the same way that the government gives out grants to harden sports stadiums and other facilities against terrorist attacks, in the same way that major transit systems like the New York City subway are focusing on preventing bombings. These organizations, from the smallest water utilities up to the largest hospital systems, need some sort of sustained focus on cybersecurity. And for most of them, they’re not gonna be able to come up with that money on their own. It’s gonna have to be federal funding. If you talk to folks in the community, that’s their hope for the future of this project, is that it’s not gonna be a volunteer initiative. It’s going to be federal government funding and perhaps some state government funding to give these organizations the support they need to make these changes. But in the meantime, yes, there’s a significant effort to set up what you could think of as cyber civil defense in the same way that, during the Cold War, there was this focus on people helping each other make their communities resilient against some sort of nuclear attack.
We’re seeing a similar concept at play here where universities creating clinics, philanthropists are donating money to organizations that are sending volunteers out into the community. Oftentimes these students going out to work with the local hospital, the local water system to help them make basic changes.
Feltman: And what about the people on the DEF CON Franklin side? What gets them excited about doing this work? You know, are they coming back to keep helping people repeatedly?
Geller: I talked to Jake Braun, who is a former White House and DHS official who runs DEF CON Franklin, and he was telling me that originally he didn’t expect volunteers to keep coming back after they had finished a particular stint working with a water utility. But he was saying it’s really inspiring that the volunteers want to keep getting sent out to other utilities to work on more projects. And part of that is a lot of these folks either grew up in rural areas or they live in rural areas, and they know firsthand that it is threadbare budgeting in these utilities. You know, they’re struggling sometimes just to be able to afford the treatment chemicals they need. So paying for some kind of expensive cybersecurity monitoring system, that’s out of the budget for sure. They’re not even thinking about that. And so when somebody shows up and says, “I can help you make basic changes, and I’m not gonna charge you any money,” once you get through the, sort of, “Who are you, how can I trust you?” which was a very real obstacle that this program had to overcome, for the utilities, it’s a godsend. And I think for the volunteers, knowing that they can make this kind of difference in their community, it’s a significant boost for them. And so that’s what Jake Braun from DEF CON Franklin was telling me, that he’s really been impressed by the commitment of the volunteers.
Feltman: Yeah. And how did they make those inroads? What did it take for them to get the trust of these utility companies?
Geller: Well, a big thing for Franklin was partnering with the association that represents rural water systems. That’s a group that has affiliates in every state. Those state affiliates talk very closely with the utilities themselves, so there’s a trust relationship there. The utilities trust this group, so when the group comes to them and says, “Would you be interested in being part of this program? We can vouch for the program itself.” They’re gonna vet the participants on their end—that’s a real signal to the utilities that this is not some fly-by-night initiative, but this is really something that’s been thought out and planned carefully. And I can imagine being a water system operator and not wanting to let somebody sit down at my keyboard and make changes on my network. I would be very worried about what I was getting myself into. But once you have that association coming to you and saying, “Trust us, we’ve done our due diligence,” that really opened a lot of doors, and from there it was a question of getting everybody to sit down and get on the same page, because the volunteers had these grand ideas about what they could accomplish. The utilities had, in some cases, unrealistic expectations about how secure they already were, and they were saying, “Come in here and do a test on us and you’ll see that we’re secure.” And the volunteers would say, “How about we make some basic changes first so that this test is a little bit more useful?” And so connecting the two sides in a way where they had the same expectations, that was a big part of the setup for the program.
Feltman: Well, I know it’s kind of an aside, but I really loved the story behind the name of the project. I would love if you could tell our listeners a little bit about that?
Geller: Sure. The name for the program comes from Benjamin Franklin, who created the first volunteer fire department in the U.S., and the idea behind that is it was a time when a lot of systems for what is the government gonna be doing, what do we owe each other as members of this new community, had not yet been created. The rules had not yet been written. And this was the first step toward a sense of civic participation in keeping our community safe, at least in the United States. And DEF CON Franklin, is trying to bring that same spirit forward of saying that while we obviously need government funding to do any kind of uniform improvements to cybersecurity across the country, we wanna live up to that same spirit of civic participation and civic engagement.
One thing I’ll add is that DEF CON Franklin did an interesting study where they talked to utilities about all these offers they were getting from big technology companies to say, you know, “We’ll gift you this product. You can have it for free, and it will help you with cybersecurity.” And what Franklin found is in most cases, these really small utilities can’t take advantage of those offerings because either they don’t have staff on hand to monitor whatever this product is and read and analyze the data that they’re getting, or the companies are saying, “You can have this expensive device.You gotta buy it from us, but then we’ll give you the licenses to use it.” So the devil is in the details there, and I think that’s really interesting because a lot of this conversation often comes down to “ Well, just have the big tech companies give away their products to the water utilities. That will solve the problem.” And the reality is it doesn’t solve the problem because these things are, as Jake Braun told me, free like a puppy, meaning, you know, they hand you the technology, but then there’s a lot of costs on the back end that you actually need to pay to make use of the technology.
Feltman: Yeah. They’re not cleaning up the pee for you, so.
Geller: Exactly.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much for coming on to talk us through this.
Geller: Thank you so much for having me. I enjoyed it.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to kick off the long weekend with a chat about a new piece of genre-bending fiction about online dating.

Ukraine Crushes FSB Assassination Plot Against Russian Opposition Leader

Ukraine Crushes FSB Assassination Plot Against Russian Opposition Leader
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) and military intelligence agency (HUR) foiled an assassination plot organized by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) against a Russian opposition figure who had traveled to Ukraine for Independence Day, the agencies announced on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The SBU said the intended target was “one of the leaders of the Russian opposition political national movement,” who arrived in Ukraine for the country’s Independence Day celebrations on August 24. Ukrainian authorities have not officially disclosed the person’s identity or details of how the attack was intended to be carried out.
“Ukraine’s Security Service, jointly with the HUR of the Ministry of Defense, prevented a terrorist attack that Russia’s FSB was preparing against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition political national movement, who arrived in Ukraine on the occasion of our country’s Independence Day,” the SBU said.
HUR also confirmed the joint operation, saying investigative measures were continuing. Neither agency disclosed whether suspects had been detained or provided additional information about the preparation of the attack.
Ukrainian media have identified the possible target as Stepan Kaplunov, a Russian national and deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), a formation of Russian citizens fighting on Ukraine’s side.
RBC-Ukraine reported on September 2, citing unnamed sources, that Kaplunov was the opposition figure targeted in the alleged FSB operation. The SBU and HUR have not officially confirmed his identity as the intended target.
The announcement comes amid questions surrounding Kaplunov’s whereabouts. The RDK previously reported that he had disappeared near his home several days before the Ukrainian security services announced that they had foiled the FSB operation.
RDK chief of staff Oleksandr Fortuna said the group contacted HUR, the SBU, and Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation after Kaplunov went missing.
Separately, Ukrainian media and Telegram channels reported an overnight confrontation involving armed personnel in Kyiv. Videos circulating online showed several groups of men in military-style clothing, while recordings from the area appeared to capture gunfire.
Kaplunov’s lawyer, Taras Borovskyi, claimed that law enforcement officers had arrived at Kaplunov’s residence before fellow servicemen later appeared at the location. He also alleged that Kaplunov had been detained by the SBU.
Ukrainian authorities have not confirmed those claims or publicly established a connection between the reported confrontation in Kyiv and the FSB assassination plot announced by the SBU and HUR. The Ukrainian security agencies said operational and investigative measures remain underway.
Earlier, the SBU dismantled a Russian military intelligence network that had been preparing targeted killings of prominent figures in Ukraine, detaining more than 10 operatives and killing one armed suspect who resisted arrest.

US and Iran exchange strikes as lull in fighting ends

Breadcrumb
US and Iran exchange strikes as months-long lull in fighting ends
The United States and Iran exchanged intense strikes across the Middle East overnight, abruptly ending a months-long lull in hostilities.
US strikes hit sites across Iran late on Tuesday and into Wednesday morning, with Iranian authorities reporting at least 11 people killed. The US military claimed that the latest round of attacks targeted Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications facilities, despite Iranian officials reporting multiple civilian casualties.
Search and rescue operations were underway on Wednesday after Iran accused the US of striking a house hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a coastal city near the Strait of Hormuz in Sirik County, Hormozgan province.
Iranian officials said at least four people, including a four-year-old child, were killed and dozens injured in the attack. US Central Command said it was aware of reports that a wedding had been hit, but insisted that US forces do not target civilians.
The incident has prompted outrage and could become a significant case of civilian casualties in the escalating conflict.
In a letter to the International Criminal Court, Iran’s Red Crescent Society (IRCS) called for immediate legal action following last night’s US strike on the wedding ceremony in Kuhestak.
“Given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” the IRCS said.
“Intentionally launching an attack in the knowledge that such attack will cause incidental loss of civilian life or injury to civilians that would be clearly excessive in relation to the concrete and direct overall military advantage anticipated may, subject to the conditions and elements prescribed by the Rome Statute, give rise to individual criminal responsibility under international criminal law,” the statement added.
Iran said US strikes also hit telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan, with repair crews working to restore services.
Elsewhere, Iranian media reported that at least three members of the Basij paramilitary force were killed in a strike on Lavan Island in the Gulf. Four other soldiers were reported killed in Kermanshah province, near the Iraqi border.
In Khuzestan province, attacks on three locations killed at least seven people and wounded eight others, according to the province’s deputy governor. Explosions were also reported in Chabahar and elsewhere in Sistan and Baluchestan province.
Axios, citing US officials, reported that US forces struck two Iranian tankers during the latest wave of attacks. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, however, said on Wednesday that two of its oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
"I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing," US President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?"
Iran’s joint military command responded with a warning that any country supporting the US military campaign in the region would face "heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses".
Iran retaliates across Gulf
Iran launched retaliatory missile and drone attacks across the Gulf as well as Jordan and northern Iraq, ending a relative quiet period in which Iranian strikes and regional air raid alerts had largely subsided.
Tehran said it targeted US military installations in Kuwait, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, including Al Dhafra and Al Minhad air bases in the UAE. Authorities in the UAE had not publicly acknowledged any damage or casualties by Wednesday morning.
Kuwaiti authorities said they extinguished a fire in Kuwait City after what they described as an Iranian drone attack on a residential building. No injuries were reported. Iran claimed that it had targeted Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base, though Kuwaiti officials did not confirm that the base had been struck.
In Bahrain, air raid sirens sounded across the kingdom overnight and into Wednesday morning. The Bahraini military said its air defences were responding to multiple Iranian attacks. While Iran claimed to have struck with drones the Sheikh Isa Air Base, which hosts US troops, Bahraini authorities had not commented on the claim or reported any damage.
Jordan’s military said it intercepted 10 Iranian missiles, while the remaining projectiles landed in unpopulated areas, adding that there had been no casualties or damage to infrastructure.
Iran also claimed responsibility for attacks in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, saying it had targeted US facilities in Erbil in a "coordinated missile and drone attack", according to the state news agency IRNA.
In a statement on Wednesday morning, the US consulate in Erbil urged Americans to "exercise heightened vigilance" amid renewed attacks. The Kurdistan Democratic Party said two of its sites northeast of Erbil had been hit by Iranian strikes, without giving details on damage or casualties, as residents reported explosions across the city overnight.
The renewed escalation follows months of limited direct confrontation since July, during which both sides largely held fire but failed to make progress in negotiations. US-Iran talks have stalled in recent weeks, while Washington has threatened further sanctions aimed at weakening Iran’s economy.
Pakistan, which has sought to mediate between the two sides, said it remained committed to efforts to end the conflict.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said on Wednesday that Islamabad remained hopeful the two sides would "return to the table for dialogue". He said Pakistan had seen "considerable momentum" on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz during an official delegation’s visit to Tehran last month.

Cadet force expansion target pushed back to 2035
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
11:00:58 BST
19:00:58 KST

The Ministry of Defence has pushed back its target for expanding the UK’s cadet forces by 30% from 2030 to 2035, while confirming that the funding required to support the planned increase has yet to be finalised, the department has said.
The change was disclosed in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked the Defence Secretary what target had been set for the size of the cadet forces by 2030 and what funding had been allocated to achieve it.
Veterans and People Minister Calvin Bailey said the original target came from the Strategic Defence Review published in June 2025. He said: “The Strategic Defence Review, published in June 2025, recommended that MOD should expand in-school and community-based Cadet Forces across the country by 30% by 2030. This timeline has recently been re-set in the Defence Investment Plan to 2035 as one of the measures required to increase the rate of Armed Forces transformation.”
The MOD currently supports just over 137,000 cadets alongside around 28,000 adult volunteers. Bailey said achieving the planned 30% expansion would mean recruiting around 40,000 additional cadets, taking the overall number to roughly 177,000, while also requiring a substantial increase in the number of adults supporting cadet units.
He said: “There are currently just over 137,000 cadets supported by 28,000 adult volunteers. An increase of 30% in cadet numbers equates to an additional 40,000 cadets, an expansion that would also require approximately 8,000 more adult volunteers. Details of the funding necessary to support this level of growth are yet to be finalised.”
The department is therefore working towards an expansion of both cadet numbers and the volunteer workforce needed to support them, but has not yet set out the final financial requirement for delivering the programme. On the figures provided by the minister, the adult volunteer population would need to rise from around 28,000 to approximately 36,000 if the planned increase is delivered.
Bailey said work was already underway on how the expansion would be carried out. “Work is currently underway to set the foundations for sustainable growth and to determine how the 30% increase in cadet numbers will be delivered.”
The MOD is also preparing a new Cadet Action Plan, which Bailey said would be announced in October during the first National Cadets Week. The plan will cover both cadets and the adults who support them, including recruitment, retention and the resources available to individual units.
Bailey said: “And we are developing a new Cadet Action Plan, to be announced in October during the first National Cadets Week. The Plan will focus on modernising the cadet experience, providing an attractive offer to retain and recruit adult volunteers, and ensuring that cadets and volunteers have the right resources and support.”

For fibromyalgia, gentle and enjoyable exercise seems to works better than pushing through pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:46 UTC
19:00:46 KST

A tailored, low-intensity exercise program provides evidence of lasting relief and improved quality of life for people with fibromyalgia. Brain scans indicate that these benefits are linked to changes in the cerebellum, a brain region involved in movement and pain processing. The research was published in Scientific Reports.
Fibromyalgia is a chronic disorder characterized by widespread pain, fatigue, poor sleep, and a nervous system that is overly sensitive to physical sensations. It often severely impacts a person’s daily life and functional independence. Adapted physical activity involves physical exercises customized to an individual’s specific capabilities, needs, and health limitations.
“When I came to this chronic pain center in 2015, after working in supportive and palliative care, sports medicine, and emergency medicine, I really did not understand this disease,” lead author Stéphanie Ranque-Garnier, a pain medicine physician at Timone Hospital’s Pain Assessment and Treatment Centre in Marseille, France, told PsyPost.
“I often heard that it was ‘not a real disease’ because it was not dangerous in terms of survival, and that people with fibromyalgia ‘would not heal,'” she continued. “This seemed very paradoxical to me.”
A 2019 review gathered earlier clinical trials to show that combining different types of exercise can help people manage fibromyalgia. Additionally, a 2020 review explains the biology behind why working out can provide both immediate and long-term pain relief.
Despite exercise being a recommended treatment, many patients with fibromyalgia remain sedentary because typical workouts tend to trigger symptom flare-ups. Standard exercise guidelines can be vague, leaving patients unsure of how often, how long, or how intensely they should be active.
“In my clinical practice, I was struck by how difficult it was for many patients, especially with fibromyalgia, to become physically active, even when they knew that physical activity could be beneficial,” Ranque-Garnier noted. “I realized that simply telling patients to ‘exercise more’ was not only insufficient, but could even be counterproductive.”
For the current study, the authors wanted to see if a highly structured, supervised, and well-tolerated exercise routine could bring sustained relief. They also sought to understand the brain mechanisms involved by using neuroimaging.
The research, led by Ranque-Garnier and her colleagues, involved 79 adults with moderate to severe fibromyalgia. The scientists randomly assigned the participants into two groups. Thirty-nine patients received the supervised adapted physical activity program alongside standard care, while 40 patients received only standard care. The researchers followed both groups for a total of 12 months.
The exercise intervention lasted for six months and consisted of three two-hour sessions per week. These sessions included a mix of pool and land-based activities kept at a very low intensity. The exercises were broken up into small bursts based on each person’s tolerance limits to avoid exacerbating their pain.
“The activity had to be adapted not only to their physical capacity and symptoms, but also, and importantly, to their tastes,” Ranque-Garnier said. “Motivation cannot come from cycling like a laboratory rat, especially if you do not like cycling!”
The research team used questionnaires to measure the patients’ quality of life, pain levels, sleep quality, and fatigue. They also used pedometers to track daily steps and conducted aerobic fitness tests. A subset of 33 patients underwent positron emission tomography, or PET, scans to track changes in brain metabolism.
The findings showed that quality of life improved for the exercise group. At the six-month mark, the exercise group showed a 14.5 percent better score on a standardized fibromyalgia impact questionnaire compared to the standard care group. Patients in the exercise program reported less average pain, better sleep, and greater flexibility. They also reported immediate symptom relief after individual sessions.
The team carefully monitored this immediate impact. “Our simplest tool for knowing whether a session was appropriate was the patient’s own evaluation before and after the session,” Ranque-Garnier explained. “The session should leave the patient at least as well as, and ideally better than, before — in terms of pain, mood, fatigue, and concentration.”
The exercise group also became more active outside the program. At three months, they added an average of 1,619 daily steps to their baseline of about 4,185 steps, while the standard care group experienced a slight decrease in their daily steps.
These physical and emotional benefits occurred even though the patients did not show improvements in maximum aerobic capacity. This suggests that people with fibromyalgia do not need to endure high-intensity, exhaustion-inducing workouts to experience real health benefits.
“The main message is that physical activity is a major therapeutic approach in fibromyalgia, but more is not better,” Ranque-Garnier told PsyPost. “Quality of life and fibromyalgia symptoms improved even though we did not observe a major improvement in the shuttle walking test.”
In fact, focusing on performance can backfire. “Some patients in the control group became physically more active but experienced worsening symptoms and eventually abandoned their activity because they had pushed themselves too hard,” she noted. “We think that some had been motivated by the title of the study and applied the familiar ‘no pain, no gain’ principle.”
This led to a crucial realization for the research team. “In fibromyalgia, an activity that is physically possible is not necessarily an activity that is therapeutically appropriate,” Ranque-Garnier added.
The brain scans indicated an increase in metabolism in the right cerebellum of the exercise group. The cerebellum is a structure located at the back of the brain that traditionally helps coordinate movement, but it also plays a role in regulating pain and emotion. This metabolic increase was directly correlated with the patients’ increased daily step counts.
“The increase in cerebellar metabolism after six months of the program is particularly interesting in this regard and raises the possibility of changes in neural networks involved in cognitive, movement, and pain processing,” Ranque-Garnier said.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2017, which similarly found that lighter forms of physical activity improve quality of life and reduce pain. The 2017 study evaluated natural daily activity levels across healthy adults rather than a structured low-intensity exercise intervention in fibromyalgia patients.
The results also parallel a 2023 study covered by PsyPost, which found that physical activity provides pain-relieving benefits. However, that previous research evaluated experimental pain tolerance in the general population rather than clinical pain reduction and quality of life in fibromyalgia patients following a structured exercise intervention.
Additionally, the current results echo research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that structured exercise improved sleep and modulated cerebellar brain activity. That 2024 work examined brain functional connectivity in older adults with insomnia rather than cerebellar metabolism in fibromyalgia patients.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The patients in this study were recruited from a specialized pain center and had already participated in therapeutic education workshops. This specific background means they might have been more motivated and ready to adopt new habits than the average person with fibromyalgia.
“Our study does not mean that any form of exercise will improve fibromyalgia, nor that patients should simply push through their pain,” Ranque-Garnier cautioned. She emphasized that the intervention was closely supervised by professionals specifically trained to adapt exercises for chronic pain.
The brain imaging findings are based on a small subset of the total participants. The researchers note that these mechanistic conclusions should be interpreted cautiously until they are confirmed in larger groups.
“The neuroimaging findings should also be considered as mechanistic clues rather than proof of causality,” Ranque-Garnier said. “We therefore cannot conclude that we have identified a single brain mechanism or a universal exercise prescription for fibromyalgia.”
Spontaneous physical activity in the control group could not be fully controlled, and wearing a pedometer might have influenced the behavior of the participants.
Looking ahead, the team hopes to identify predictive factors that lead to long-term remission in chronic pain. The ultimate goal is to help patients regain confidence in their bodies and become more active in their everyday lives.
“One of the most beautiful things I hear from patients in remission is: ‘I stopped passively enduring my symptoms and started being active with the resources I have,'” Ranque-Garnier said.
The study, “Efficacy and mechanism of supervised adapted physical activity on quality of life for patients with fibromyalgia: single-center, prospective, randomised clinical and neuroimaging study,” was authored by Stéphanie Ranque, Jérôme Laurin, Marius George Linguraru, Zhifan Jiang, Anderson Loundou, Laurent Boyer, Régis Guieu, José Boucraut, Caroline Sault, Jeremy Simon, Fanny Barthelemy, Anne Donnet, and Eric Guedj.

====================================================================================================

DLR Group on translating urban density into intimate neighborhoods in the middle east
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:24 UTC
19:00:24 KST

SHAPING MIDDLE EASTERN URBANISM FROM MASTERPLAN TO MICRO-MOMENT
‘When you have the same types of buildings and spaces replicated everywhere, you lose any sense of place,’ states Henrique Dias, Middle East Hospitality & Mixed-Use Director at DLR Group, in an interview with designboom. Across the Middle East, cities are building at an unprecedented speed and monumental scale. As sprawling block footprints and towering verticality dominate the landscape, urban density is often viewed as an environmental and psychological challenge. In our conversation with DLR Group, it becomes clear that the key challenge of modern urbanism is not high density itself, but how that density is designed, experienced, and rooted in place. Key decisions about scale, walkability, and sensory environment determine how millions of people experience life for generations.
‘Density isn’t the problem — repetitive, overwhelming design is. In our design process, we create spaces that allow users to connect with the environment and navigate a complex plan while recognizing that every location and design is distinct,’ continues Dias. ‘From a landscape perspective at the ground level, it’s about creating distinct moments within dense environments, giving people choices, whether for gathering, socializing, or finding quiet spaces. It comes down to sensory richness and variety rather than repetition,’ adds Stefan du Toit, Design Director, Landscape. For DLR Group’s work in the Middle East, that philosophy plays out differently depending on terrain, climate, and cultural context, from mountain masterplans in Makkah to heritage-driven interiors in Abha.
DLR Group creates for human scale by integrating porosity and organic flow into what otherwise might be one large mixed-use block | all images courtesy of DLR Group
HOW DLR GROUP BRINGS SPATIAL CALM TO DENSE URBAN ENVIRONMENTS
By shifting the lens from megaproject massing to human-scale perception, DLR Group’s multidisciplinary team aligns master planning, architecture, landscape, and interior design to translate massive urban footprints into legible, approachable, and deeply authentic communities. Humans require environments that feel intuitive, welcoming, and responsive to maintain a sense of emotional security. When developments become overly uniform or monumental, individuals lose their bearings and lack a clear pathway to connect with the surrounding space.
‘Architecture can sometimes suffer from designer ego, where architects try to scream louder than one another with flashy, contextless sculptures,’ reflects Dias. ‘There is no room for architectural ego in designing for the greater good of the project and end user. The design must be humble, meaningful, and aligned with the user experience while meeting client expectations.’ To counter this alienation, DLR Group prioritizes spatial clarity and cognitive ease over visual spectacle, embedding tactile materials, balanced spatial hierarchies, and central civic anchors to foster daily social encounters and a genuine resonance with nature.
rooted in Makkah’s spiritual and natural identity, MAAD’s mixed-use masterplan is designed to balance seasonal pilgrim flows with permanent urban livability
DECONSTRUCTING SCALE AT FOR SENSORY-RICH AND WALKABLE COMMUNITIES
A human-scale experience is primarily won or lost at the horizontal surface where people actually stand and move. Rather than allowing high-rise structures to plunge abruptly into hard paving, landscape architecture acts as a vital calibration tool, stepping down massive architectural volumes into digestible foregrounds.
‘We view landscape as an interface between the scale of architecture and the human scale,’ explains Stefan du Toit, Design Director, Landscape. ‘Instead of creating an abrupt transition between a high-rise building and the ground level, we step it down using curated topography and layered experiences. As a user approaches a building, we break down that mass using plants, shade structures, and artistic features. Working hand-in-hand with architects allows us to introduce new amenities at multiple vertical levels, breaking the sheer scale into digestible human experiences.’
EMAAR – The Heights in Dubai, UAE, breaks down a large development into places that feel local, walkable, and centered around family life
In hot, arid climates, outdoor spaces are often abandoned unless thermal comfort and sensory engagement are actively designed. Whether people choose to walk depends on more than basic street proportions, as a route is walked when it is continuously shaded, comfortable underfoot, and rewarding to move along. This first-principles approach to walkability is vividly illustrated at EMAAR – The Heights in Dubai, a vast 750-hectare masterplan where DLR Group translates thoughtful master planning into everyday family living. Rather than allowing the development’s scale to overwhelm residents, the plan organizes over 7,500 homes into an array of intimate neighborhood clusters, each anchored by a central Wellness Club directly sited amid a polycentric open space network spanning 1.9 million square meters. Curvilinear villa layouts, green noise-filtering buffers, neighborhood pockets for dwell or play, and shaded pedestrian routes work alongside continuous blue/green systems to maintain neighborhood intimacy at scale and make wellness feel tangible.
SUMOU in Al Khobar is organized as a live-work-play ecosystem, reducing the need for long-distance movement
Similarly, in mixed-use developments like SUMOU in Al Khobar and LIWAN Najd in Riyadh, DLR Group weaves continuous pedestrian networks and central car-free wadis using tree canopies, vegetated groundcover, water features, and lighter paving surfaces to lower radiant temperatures. To balance density with daily well-being, the team structures these developments around central civic nodes such as schools, mosques, workplaces, and retail destinations, wrapping residential clusters around them so essential daily life sits within a comfortable walk. Elevated green terraces, subtle level changes, and shifting planting densities create a natural gradient between active public plazas and tranquil home environments. By sequencing shade, seating, and framed views, distance across both developments is measured in spatial experience rather than physical exertion, creating places where people naturally want to slow down and linger.
‘In this climate, streets must be both functional and beautiful. We have to push back against the obsolete thinking that it’s simply too hot to walk here,’ notes Shawn Meyers, Middle East Master Planning Director at DLR Group. ‘If people have a tree canopy, a place to rest, or a reason to linger, they’re willing to walk further and engage more fully with their neighborhood — and, more importantly, with their neighbors,’ adds du Toit.
conceived as a car-free, green pedestrian spine, LIWAN Najd in Riyadh’s Granada District connects hospitality, housing, commerce, worship, and community life
TERRAIN, CULTURAL ROOTS, AND REGIONAL AUTHENTICITY
Modulating the monumental scale also demands deference to terrain and local context. At MAAD in Makkah, a mixed-use masterplan designed to balance seasonal pilgrim flows with permanent urban livability, DLR Group used the site’s steep mountainous terrain as an organizing framework rather than flattening the landscape. By concentrating high-density development at lower elevations and tapering massing as the topography rises, built forms merge naturally into the mountain through stepped terraces and landscape-led transitions.
Where developments touch deeply personal or spiritual journeys, architecture must yield to quiet humility. ‘For destinations such as Makkah, the interior design is never intended to become the focal point of the experience — it exists to support the journey taking place within the guest,’ explains Vaida Buchrotaite, Middle East Director of Interior Design at DLR Group. ‘As the architecture merges into the mountains, the interiors continue that story through restrained materiality, gentle spatial layering, and carefully choreographed arrival sequences that encourage moments of reflection and calm.’
natural features such as the surrounding mountains and wadis define movement, density, and urban form
forms, textures, patterns, materials are an extension of the physical terrain and create a continuum of the land’s cultural significance
A similar sensitivity defines how regional heritage is expressed across DLR Group’s projects. At The Point in Abha, traditional Al-Qatt Al-Asiri wall art is not applied as superficial decoration, but distilled into custom textiles, geometric textures, and warm, mineral-toned palettes. Rather than recreating historical styles, the design team abstracts regional patterns and local crafts into modern, bold lifestyle destinations that feel authentic, warm, and deeply rooted in place.
‘We celebrate local culture by infusing our interiors with subtle echoes of regional patterns, craftsmanship, textures, and art rather than applying them literally,’ continues Buchrotaite. ‘These references are paired with contemporary styling, refined detailing, and sometimes even bespoke patterns developed specifically for each project.’
The Point is a vibrant mixed-use development situated in southwestern Saudi Arabia, within the Asir Region, which is well known for its cultural heritage and natural landscapes
THE INTEGRATED STUDIO WORKFLOW
Ensuring that a macro-scale urban vision successfully translates into micro-level sensory touchpoints requires breaking down traditional design silos. ‘For us, integrated design is an active, iterative workflow rather than a passive collaboration,’ notes Shawn Meyers, Middle East Master Planning Director at DLR Group. ‘We can achieve far greater value when the master planners, architects, landscape architects, and interior designers shape the vision together from day one, rather than working in a sequential hand-off.’
By embedding this holistic workflow across every phase, DLR Group proves that even the most ambitious megaprojects can be crafted as intimate, legible spaces where human experience remains the ultimate priority. ‘Bringing all key decision-makers together at project inception creates alignment around a common vision from the outset,’ adds Buchrotaite. ‘Maintaining open dialogue and actively inviting input from every discipline throughout the design process leads to stronger decisions, a more cohesive outcome, and a more collaborative experience for both the team and the client.’
all food and beverage patios and terraces have a clear line of sight toward the central entertainment space
project info:
brand: DLR Group
 projects: EMAAR – The Heights (Dubai), MAAD (Makkah), The Point (Abha), SUMOU (Al Khobar) and LIWAN Najd (Riyadh)
 interviewees: Shawn Meyers (Middle East Master Planning Director),  Vaida Buchrotaite (Middle East Director of Interior Design), Henrique Dias (Middle East Hospitality & Mixed-Use Director) and Stefan du Toit (Design Director, Landscape)

Walmart’s Sam’s Club accelerates expansion in China as membership passes 10.7 million
Company to open 13 new stores this year, bringing total to 76, as value prices and exclusive goods prove to be a winning formula
US membership-only retailer Sam’s Club has sped up its expansion in China this year, with the launch of its sixth Beijing location on Monday drawing long queues of eager shoppers.
The Walmart-owned warehouse retailer has found a winning formula in China, with its value pricing and exclusive goods attracting middle-class consumers even as some foreign brands shut down stores or pull out of the country.
Sam’s Club said last month that it had 10.7 million paid members in China as of June. Its total annual membership revenue could hit 3 billion yuan (US$450 million) this year, with its basic and premium memberships priced at 260 yuan and 680 yuan a year, respectively.
“The appeal of Sam’s Club is the breadth and quality of goods offered along with wholesale pricing,” said Cathy Chao, senior director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “Many goods are unique and cannot be found through alternate channels, and consumers hold a general impression of consistently high-quality goods at a reasonable price, which can justify the membership pricing.”
In addition, the membership model encouraged frequent visits by consumers seeking to maximise the value of the annual fee, Chao added.
The company said that it planned to open 13 new Sam’s Club stores nationwide this year, including in several lower-tier cities, bringing the total to 76.

Recently, a social media creator filmed their story, which went viral, garnering over 18 million views and significant public support. As reported by Fengmian News, online fundraising efforts approached 100,000 yuan, bringing He closer to her surgery goals.

The Hidden Value of Back-to-School Shopping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:00:02 UTC
19:00:02 KST

One of my first school memories comes from the first day of first grade, when my German mother dropped me off with a blue paper cone stuffed with fresh school supplies and a brand-new, boxy green backpack. Peering into the cone, inside at a Staedtler eraser and a pack of gummy bears, I felt like an alien about to make first contact with my classmates at Blessed Sacrament in Johnson City, N.Y.
Even without a Trapper Keeper, I blended in.
Americans were agog over back-to-school shopping then, as they are now. This year, the average family is projected to spend $489 per child on stationery, devices, clothing, shoes, and the latest technology for packing organic strawberries.
It's easy to dismiss our collective consumer ritual as another marketing season. Yes, it was invented by department stores selling school uniforms in the 1800s, and then turbocharged with seasonal catalogs and sales by retailers like Montgomery Ward and Sears in the century that followed. And it is a sort of pre-Halloween ritual in which we all foist new costumes on our children.
But all those new backpacks, sneakers, pencil cases, and lunch boxes do something else. They help turn our children back into students.
For two glorious summer months, we released our children from the routines and identities of school. They've spent a culturally sanctioned rumspringa at pools, beaches, and camps, in the woods, or on a Nintendo. Then, almost overnight, we thrust them back into desks, routines, homework, and a social world that is often new and uncertain.
A handful of new pencils can help.
Others are more aspirational. A set of cleats doesn't make you a soccer player, and a graphing calculator doesn't teach you calculus. But these objects signal the roles we are stepping into—to the people around us and to ourselves. Possessions can help us become someone new.
That's why transitions are so often linked to new possessions. We wear funny hats and robes when we graduate from college. Wedding rings, dresses, and tuxedos mark our transition from singlehood to married life. We furnish nurseries before our babies arrive. A suit, scrubs, or a desk can make a new professional identity feel real.
Possessions can be the bridges we need to new identities before we feel entirely comfortable inhabiting them. Having a first child is a psychedelic experience. You're handed a fragile infant and sent off to do your best. A first-year medical student is a long way from being a physician. Possessions associated with these roles help cement identities as we grow into them.
Our children often face no less dramatic transitions.
My son, who was just a giant in the familiar melee of daycare, will become a kindergartner this week in an enormous building filled with children much bigger than him. Your sixth grader is becoming a middle schooler. Or your ninth grader is starting high school. They may not yet know what role we and their peers expect them to play.
Practically, their old backpack works. And, yes, buying what you already own is expensive and wasteful. A replacement will not kindle new friendships and a sudden capacity for algebra. Teaching our children about waste and having enough are important lessons.
But the mistake is assuming that we buy possessions purely for function. An old backpack can still carry books. Shoes that fit in June may miraculously survive until September. They may also carry an old identity. To a child, they may feel like a younger self.
A transition doesn't require us to replace everything. One or two new possessions may be enough to construct the new identity. A new ring is enough for many married couples.
A new backpack, sneakers, pencil case, lunchbox, or graphing calculator is a prop for this new identity. It tells classmates and teachers, “I belong.” More importantly, it can help our children say this to themselves.
