====================================================================================================

What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:00:27 UTC
17:00:27 KST

Breadcrumb
What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Ukrainian drones struck Russian cargo ships carrying stolen Ukrainian grain in the Sea of Azov in April.
Since then, drone attacks by both sides have intensified in the Black Sea region, continuing throughout the summer months.
"For Ukraine, targeting Russia’s oil revenues - and particularly the so-called shadow fleet that enables Moscow to circumvent sanctions - is an important part of increasing the economic cost of the war and degrading Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its military operations," Dr Yevgeniya Gaber, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Turkey Program, told The New Arab.
In August, two Turkish-owned civilian ships, the Yaşar and the Nadezhda, were struck by drones after departing from the Russian port of Novorossiysk. In response, Turkey’s Foreign Ministry called for the safe passage of commercial shipping through the Black Sea.
“Russia has fewer sea drones, but it is using both planes and drones to track the Ukrainian navy. For Russia, the Black Sea is now mainly used to strike southern Ukraine and protect their own commercial shipping, since their fleet is now hidden in ports,” Clément Molin, an open-source analyst following the Ukraine conflict, told The New Arab.
“Ukraine’s UAVs are being constantly used to track Russian ships, and more than 200 commercial ships have been targeted, mainly from [Russia’s] ghost fleet,” he said. “Ukraine has barely any navy but managed to create a new dimension of the war at sea with drones.”
No ceasefire in sight
On 13 August, Ukrainian drones hit the Russian port facility of Novorossiysk, damaging two grain export terminals. It wasn’t long before Russia carried out a wave of strikes in Ukraine’s Odesa Oblast, hitting food storage infrastructure.
“Russian forces have targeted Ukrainian ports, grain terminals, silos and export infrastructure throughout the war. What has changed is the scale and intensity of the pressure, including more attacks on civilian commercial vessels, warehouses and food-related infrastructure,” Gaber said.
“The consequences are particularly serious for agricultural exports and, therefore, for food security well beyond Ukraine. Between 1 and 26 August, Ukraine exported only 822,000 tonnes of grain - around 21 percent of what it could normally have exported with functioning logistics," she added.
"Total agricultural exports, including grain, oilseeds, oils and meals, amounted to approximately 1.4 million tonnes, only around one-third of Ukraine’s potential export capacity during this period, according to the Ukrainian government."
On 27 August, The Wall Street Journal reported that wheat prices had reached a three-year high as the Black Sea fighting disrupted grain exports, with Odesa and Novorossiysk losing export capacity.
In late August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia was not ready for a ceasefire on grain shipments in the Black Sea. Moscow reportedly sought to include an end to attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in the agreement.
The Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have been a key way for Kyiv to bring the war back home to Russia after four and a half years of the full-scale invasion.
“The problem is not limited to attacks on ships themselves. Russia is targeting the infrastructure that makes maritime trade possible: ports, grain silos, warehouses, railway connections and other logistical nodes,” Gaber told The New Arab.
“In July alone, Russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian seaport infrastructure, 35 attacks on civilian vessels in ports, and 22 attacks on vessels operating through the Ukrainian maritime corridor.”
The attacks come as both Russia and Ukraine are in peak harvest season, and the grain will go to waste unless it is exported soon. Major commercial shipping firms are suspending operations due to the threat of drones in the Black Sea.
“This creates longer-term economic damage as well. Ukrainian farmers lose revenue from exports and face higher logistical costs, reducing the capital available to invest in the next planting season,” Gaber said.
Diplomatic tensions
The Turkish Foreign Ministry warned that the attacks could have “multifaceted negative repercussions”, including for food security.
“We therefore reiterate our call to all relevant actors, particularly the warring parties, to urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea.”
The collapse of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkey had helped facilitate, effectively ended in the summer of 2023. However, Ukraine and Russia were still able to ship their agricultural products to the international market by staying close to the coastlines.
To mitigate any diplomatic blowback, Scott Lucas, Professor of International Politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told The New Arab that Ukraine could signal that “we don’t want to be in this situation…of having to counter-attack against the Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Russians put us in this situation”.
The politics surrounding grain shipments from the Black Sea to the Middle East have become an increasingly sensitive issue. The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry noted that stolen grain exported by Russia was reaching Turkey, Egypt, and Algeria.
In April, Ukraine and Israel exchanged accusations over a Russian shadow fleet vessel that arrived in Israel carrying grain from the occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Diplomatically, Ukraine has limited means to stop these attacks as long as Russia is unwilling to respond to calls for de-escalation. Kyiv has repeatedly called for a ceasefire and negotiations to end the war, while Moscow has continued to intensify attacks on critical infrastructure," Gaber said.
"This is why Ukraine argues that diplomacy has to be backed by greater economic, political and military pressure on Russia. Middle Eastern countries also have an interest in making this message clear.”
Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping are not simply a bilateral Russian-Ukrainian issue, she said, as they directly affect the reliability and cost of food imports and therefore regional food security.
Syria and Egypt's food security
Over 90 percent of Ukraine’s agricultural exports are shipped through seaports, with countries in the Middle East especially vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the global food supplies. Many have taken steps to mitigate these risks. In the spring, for example, Egypt reached a deal to receive grain shipments from Russia.
“In the case of Egypt, [it depends on] how much backstop they have from the Gulf States. Do they have alternative sources for supply?” Lucas told The New Arab.
Roughly 80 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports came from Black Sea ports in the first half of 2026.
The Emirati company Al Dahra Agriculture Trading and Egypt’s General Authority for Supply Commodities recently signed a five-year, $500 million wheat supply agreement. Egypt’s government has also imposed price controls on unsubsidised bread since March. In mid-August, Egypt expanded a cash subsidy scheme to cover more food items.
“Anytime you get a disruption to grain supplies, especially in countries that are already in a tenuous economic situation, you have to run it on a case-by-case basis on how well these countries prepared for such a shock. 2010 is a reminder of what can happen quickly,” Lucas added.
A poor harvest and high food prices in 2010 contributed to the uprising against the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad in Syria, which lasted nearly 14 years.
“A lot of countries don’t want Syria to fail,” Lucas said, explaining that Syria could likely rely on Turkish and US assistance since the Trump Administration is interested in maintaining Syrian stability.
Likewise, Ukraine has sought to build up its own avenues of cooperation with the new Syrian government.
“During President Zelensky’s visit to Damascus in April, food security was one of the issues discussed with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, alongside broader security and trade cooperation. Ukraine has offered to support Syria through initiatives such as Grain from Ukraine,” Gaber told The New Arab.
Syria has made progress in increasing its own domestic production of wheat. Benjamin Fève, a Senior Consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory Limited, told The New Arab that for now, Syria’s food supply was relatively safe.
“Syria had a very successful harvest. Its strategic reserves have been replenished, and Syria will be much less dependent on imports. Even if the food supplies are secure in the short term, in the medium and long term, they are not, given the huge variability in harvests and wheat production overall,” he said.
“In order to make Arabic flat bread, a staple food in Syria, you need 80 percent of soft wheat and 20 percent of hard wheat,” Fève added.
“Syria exports its surplus of hard wheat at a premium and imports less expensive soft wheat. Depending on where Syria sources its soft wheat, disruptions could cause food insecurity.”
Restarting negotiations
Changing weather patterns, conflicts, and high fuel prices are still significant concerns and could affect the food security of tens of millions of people dependent on the international grain trade. Still, the possibility of talks or a new Black Sea Grain Initiative between Russia and Ukraine appears distant.
“While Ukraine is offering additional grain supplies to countries that need them, Russia is attacking the ports, storage facilities and logistical infrastructure required to produce, store and export that grain,” Gaber told The New Arab.
The risk for the countries in the Mediterranean region and beyond remains present as long as the conflict shuts down the grain transits through the Black Sea.
“For Ukraine to play a stabilising role in food security across the Middle East and Africa, it first needs to be able to maintain production and secure access to the Black Sea. At present, Russia remains the principal obstacle to both," Gaber added.
Lucas noted that Ukraine has to find a way to get Russia to the negotiating table. “That hand was played very well by the Turks in supporting Ukraine in 2022. Can you do the same thing here?”
But while Ukraine has indicated that it wants to negotiate, Russia continues to pursue maximum demands.
The United States and the international community would have to put more pressure on Russia to reach an agreement. “If you can get that type of political strategy, you can put the onus on the Russians,” Lucas said.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
September 2, 2026
The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month.
Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August.
Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism'
"We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said.
The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added."
France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response.
"I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest, Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships.
Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks.
Germany's Wadephul says 'pressure on Russia is being stepped up'
German Foreign Minsiter Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks."
"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Urkaine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said.
The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences."
He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict."
What did Germany say about its investigations?
Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack.
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics.
Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine."
Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events.
Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city.

The Verkhovna Rada is testing voting by MPs in a shelter
Kyiv • UNN
The Rada is testing a backup electronic voting system using MPs’ personal phones during prolonged air-raid alerts. Workstations have been set up in the shelter.
Members of Parliament began testing the voting system in the shelter of the Verkhovna Rada, reports UNN.
Details
Dear colleagues, an air raid alert has been declared in Kyiv. I ask everyone to proceed to safe places in accordance with the shelter plans posted at your seats. The plenary session will resume 15 minutes after the end of the air raid alert. I also ask those who wish to try the new system in the shelters
On Tuesday, September 1, Stefanchuk reported on his Facebook page that "together with the head and employees of the Secretariat of the Verkhovna Rada, we presented parliamentary journalists with an IT solution that will ensure the continuity of the plenary process even under such conditions."
Mobile workstations for all members of Parliament have already been set up in the shelter of the Parliament building. A backup system for electronic voting using personal mobile devices has been developed, and MPs will test it this week. Work on it began at the start of the full-scale invasion, without any expenditure of budget funds. This voting format will be used only during prolonged air raid alerts. In other cases, the Verkhovna Rada will work as usual in the session hall. Russian attacks must not paralyze Ukrainian state institutions. Parliament must remain capable of making decisions on which the country's defense, economy, and stable operation depend
MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak showed what voting in the shelter looks like.
Reminder
Due to the persistent air raid alerts in the capital, the Secretariat of the Verkhovna Rada is working on measures to ensure the uninterrupted operation of Parliament. In particular, there is an idea to vote through an app, but a final decision has not yet been made.
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine also demonstrated an alternative format for working during air raid alerts.

BP appoints new chair after contentious ousting of Albert Manifold in May
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:59:04 UTC
16:59:04 KST

BP has appointed a new chair after a months-long search following the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold, seeking to draw a line under the boardroom turmoil at the oil and gas company.
Ian Tyler, who has served as the interim chair and sat on the BP board as a non-executive director since April 2025, is assuming the role on a permanent basis immediately.
His appointment comes after Manifold’s shock removal in late May after only eight months in the role, with BP citing concerns about governance oversight and conduct.
Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director who led the search for a new chair and also runs the insurer Aviva as chief executive, announced on Wednesday she would stand down at next year’s annual meeting.
She was criticised after Manifold’s short tenure as chair, as she had led the process that resulted in his appointment to replace Helge Lund. When Manifold exited, Blanc said that while he had helped drive BP’s transformation, there were “governance oversight and conduct issues it [the board] deems unacceptable”.
Reports claimed senior colleagues had felt belittled by Manifold, while he was also accused of trying to exert control as if he were an executive rather than a chair.
Manifold responded by accusing the oil company of firing him without warning and disputed reports about his conduct.
Tyler is a former chief executive of the construction company Balfour Beatty, he chairs the builders merchants Grafton Group and is senior independent director of the mining company Anglo American. In the past he chaired Cairn Energy and the housebuilder Vistry Group and served as a non-executive director of the defence contractor BAE Systems.
He is tasked with overseeing a shift in BP’s strategy to refocus on fossil fuel extraction and ditch renewable energy investments. Meg O’Neill, the BP chief executive, last month urged Andy Burnham to make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even though the oil company wants to sell its North Sea business.
However, she said North Sea investments were “not competitive” within BP’s portfolio, as the company reported its highest quarterly profits since the first year of Russia’s war on Ukraine, boosted by rising oil and gas prices caused by the Middle East crisis.
Blanc said on Wednesday: “I am delighted that the board has unanimously appointed Ian Tyler as chair of BP. Ian brings significant experience providing challenge and support to executive teams, while maintaining strong governance and oversight on behalf of shareholders.”
Tyler said: “I will lead the board’s evolution, ensuring we have the depth, experience and capabilities needed to support the company’s strategic priorities and long-term value creation. I am committed to establishing regular and transparent engagement with our shareholders.”

FT: Russia secretly helped Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:58:51 UTC
16:58:51 KST

Russia has secretly been helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles since 2023 under a program code-named C430L, the Financial Times reports.
The program continued even after the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran, according to an FT investigation based on leaked Russian correspondence, travel records, and an analysis of military patents.
The program’s main goal, the journalists say, was to help Iran develop a ramjet engine capable of sustaining cruise missile flight at several times the speed of sound.
Rosoboronexport ran the program on the Russian side, coordinating the project with NPO Mashinostroyeniya and bringing in leading Russian missile designers to work on C430L.
Missile weapons experts say the technology being developed is intended for anti-ship missiles and weapons capable of striking ground targets. “This is the transfer of a highly strategically sensitive military technology from Russia that the Iranians have wanted to acquire for decades,” said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at the British organization Conflict Armament Research. “A program like this would require political clearance from the very top in Russia.”
Iran has already built the ramjet engine and conducted flight tests, the FT reports, though there is so far no evidence that the supersonic cruise missile developed with Russian assistance has entered service.
In June 2024, Vladimir Putin threatened, at a meeting with representatives of international news agencies, that Moscow would supply “similar weapons” to regions of the world “where strikes will be carried out on sensitive facilities of those countries that do this to Russia” in response to strikes on Russian territory with Western weapons, the FT reports. The C430L program was already underway at the time, according to the outlet.

Xi calls on SCO to work toward more just global governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:58:46 UTC
16:58:46 KST

Xi made the remarks in his speech at the "SCO Plus" meeting in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
"The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO's commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times," Xi said.
"Currently, major changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism and protectionism are resurging against historical trends. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of the world do not condone power politics, conflict and confrontation, or isolation and backwardness," he added.
What they want instead, Xi said, is to hold a place on the world stage through national development and international cooperation.
Xi noted that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power, adding that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible.
"What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How are countries going to take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history," Xi said.
Noting that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, Xi said sovereign equality and mutual respect are fundamental principles; balance, order and the rule of law are inherent requirements; multilateralism, dialogue and consultation are essential pathways; mutual benefit, win-win and inclusiveness are the way forward for development.
"We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth," Xi said, adding that "as an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs."
He called on various parties to promote the common values of humanity, reject double standards, exceptionalism, foreign interference, bullying and the law of the jungle, and advance the rule of law in international relations.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," he added.
Xi also said that world affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all.
"The authority and vitality of the United Nations need to be restored. Multilateral mechanisms, global and regional, should enhance their coordination and improve their efficiency," he said.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi added.
Xi noted that after a 25-year journey, the SCO has successfully set a stellar example in conducting relations among big countries, among neighbors, and among countries of different sizes.
The SCO, Xi said, has successfully brought together half of the world's population and a quarter of the global economy, generating strong driving forces for development, adding that a more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to a multipolar world.
"It is important that SCO member states and partners ride the trend of history and shoulder the responsibility of our times. Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said.
To further enhance the SCO's role, Xi called for advancing common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength.
"We should continue to leverage our strengths, unlock our potential, and connect the multiple growth poles across the continent through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. We should empower each other, help each other succeed, and work together to create new opportunities and promote shared prosperity," Xi said.
"We should promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom," Xi said, calling on various parties to "carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the SCO Plus partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes."
Xi also proposed that the SCO countries should guide the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action.
"We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
Xi also called for sticking to the principle of "planning together, building together and benefiting together" to encourage equal participation in global governance by all countries and ensure all will benefit from it.

Northern Sea Route freight traffic may reach 100 mln tons by 2030-2032
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:58:18 UTC
16:58:18 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 2. /TASS/. Rosatom aims to bring freight traffic along the Northern Sea Route to 100 mln metric tons by 2030-2032, CEO of the state corporation Alexey Likhachev told reporters at the Eastern Economic Forum.
"Acting on instructions from the president and the government, we have indeed prepared a model that has been agreed with virtually all government agencies and approved by the government. It is a major financial plan with two key parameters. There are many different details, but two are the most important. The first and fundamental one is freight traffic. We are, of course, working on a fairly optimistic scenario under which we will surpass the 100 mln metric ton mark sometime around 2030-2032," Likhachev said.

U.S. Army delegation visits Korea’s K9 howitzer production line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:56:45 UTC
16:56:45 KST

- A U.S. Army delegation led by Brent G. Ingraham toured Hanwha Aerospace's Changwon production facilities on August 26.
- The visit included demonstrations of the K9MH, K9A1 and Chunmoo systems as Hanwha expands U.S.-based howitzer production in Opelika, Alabama.
A senior U.S. Army acquisition delegation toured Hanwha Aerospace’s production facilities in Changwon, South Korea, on August 26 to review the company’s manufacturing capabilities across artillery, rocket systems and other land defense platforms.
The delegation was led by Brent G. Ingraham, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology. The visit included a tour of the K9 self-propelled howitzer production line, where K9MH systems are currently in production, along with a look at automated manufacturing processes including robotic welding that Hanwha uses to support high-volume output.
The delegation also watched live mobility demonstrations of the K9MH and K9A1 howitzer variants, along with a demonstration of Hanwha’s Chunmoo multiple rocket launch system, before viewing the company’s broader land systems portfolio. The visit ended with discussions between Hanwha and the delegation on the company’s manufacturing capabilities and the Army’s modernization priorities.
“Hanwha brings proven manufacturing capabilities and global production experience that will strengthen deterrence and support the U.S. industrial base,” said Michael Coulter, CEO of Hanwha Defense USA. “For more than seven decades, the U.S.-Korea alliance has been a cornerstone of peace and security, and defense industrial cooperation is an increasingly important pillar of that alliance.”
The Changwon complex serves as the production base for Hanwha’s K9 family of howitzers, supplying concurrent production programs for South Korea, Poland, Australia, Egypt and other allied nations. Hanwha said the manufacturing capacity built through those programs will inform how the company scales up its U.S. operations.
Hanwha is expanding its U.S.-based production of the K9MH variant as part of what the company calls a phased localization strategy. Hanwha Defense USA’s integration and test facility in Opelika, Alabama, currently serves as the company’s U.S. artillery manufacturing hub, with additional production phases under evaluation as the company works to scale output to meet Army requirements.
Hanwha’s Changwon visit follows the company’s recent K9 export agreement with Spain, signed with Indra Sistemas on August 31, which made Spain the 11th country to operate the howitzer.

The shifting ties in Australia's backyard as 'deep pockets' beckon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:56:09 UTC
16:56:09 KST

in brief
- Geopolitical tensions over Taiwan are hanging over the annual Pacific Islands Forum in Palau.
- However, island leaders insist local climate threats and rising drug crime take priority.
China and Taiwan's diplomatic tug-of-war is casting a shadow over the ongoing Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) as a handful of national leaders declined to attend — however, experts on the ground caution that a geopolitical focus risks ignoring the core priorities of Australia's neighbours.
The annual 18-member gathering in the Taiwanese-allied nation of Palau opened on Monday with climate change, economic security, and the rising influence of the transnational drug trade top of the agenda.
China has said it has "serious concerns" that Taiwan was invited to attend in its own right, while questions have been raised about whether China has influenced five of 18 national leaders from the forum (those of Kiribati, Fiji, Vanuatu, Samoa and Solomon Island) not to attend.
The cornerstone regional political forum began this year with a pointed message from Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr, who urged nations to adhere to this year's theme of unity and reminded outside partners that they "do not choose our destination".
This year's PIF takes place as Kiribati moves to constitutionally restrict diplomatic recognition to UN member states only — thus excluding Taiwan — while China actively seeks to strip Taiwan of its 'development partner' status in the forum. This comes nearly two months after a Chinese ballistic missile test in the Pacific Ocean.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Taiwan, a self-governing democracy, broke away from mainland China in 1949. China views it as Chinese territory that must be brought under its control by force if necessary.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has made strengthening regional ties a key focus of his administration's foreign policy, signing multiple bilateral agreements with countries like Fiji, Vanuatu, and Tuvalu.
But despite the noise around China, "leaders have made it clear they're here to work" Tess Newton Cain, principal consultant at Asia-Pacific strategic firm Sustineo, told SBS News from Koror.
"The issue of the China-Taiwan tussle is largely a distraction, and one that they try to minimise."
On Wednesday, $600 million in Australian funding was announced to tackle transnational drug smuggling from South America that is increasingly causing harm across the Pacific.
Cautions against Pacific chess games
China has made the PIF something of a battleground, maintaining that Taiwan ought to be sidelined during talks, as it is not technically a "dialogue partner" due to a difficult compromise that PIF members have reached over its status for the past three decades.
Palau, one of the few nations that maintains official diplomatic ties with Taiwan, has accused China of running a coercion campaign against it after travel warnings were issued to Chinese citizens looking to visit Palau.
Australia, which maintains a flexible approach to the 'One China' policy by recognising Beijing and maintaining informal economic and security ties with Taiwan, is better able to weather such geopolitical storms in part owing to its size.
Yet, as Pacific island nations increasingly turn to China for economic support, experts caution that for Australia to treat the Pacific as a geostrategic game would be a mistake, as that is "certainly not" how Pacific leaders see their own relationships.
"It's not appropriate that Australian officials or politicians are shaking hands with members of the Pacific while looking past them to see what China may or may not be doing," Newton Cain said.
Professor Dave Peebles, director of the Pacific Security College at the Australian National University, agrees that the Taiwan question is not the focus of relations in the Pacific.
Issues of Taiwanese sovereignty are "not something" Australia is seeking to influence in its dealings with island nations, he told SBS News, as those decisions are for democratically elected governments of Pacific Island countries to make.
"Some Pacific Island countries do have similar relationships with Taiwan as Australia does," Newton Cain said. "Others are possibly just too small to be able to justify that and to have to wear the tussle and competition that comes with that."
However, she dismissed fears that Kiribati's current domestic push to change its constitution in a way favourable to China — making it far more difficult for successive governments to switch alliances back — is a blueprint for a wider Pacific pressure campaign.
Whether a country recognises Taiwan can have significant domestic impact on small island nations.
In 2024, after decades of support, the Pacific Island nation of Naoero (formerly Nauru) abruptly severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan and formally recognised the People's Republic of China as "the only legitimate government of China and Taiwan" — leaving the latter with just a handful of diplomatic partners, including just three in the Pacific.
Diplomats and technical staff were forced to rapidly leave the country as it moved to deepen economic ties with the economic superpower, which has developed a "very strong portfolio" of investment in regional countries that do make the switch.
"It's often quite evident to see at a fairly early stage the impacts of having a partner that comes with deeper pockets than Taiwan," Newton Cain said.
Bigger issues at hand
While the threat of a hostile takeover of the region that the Chinese Communist Party views as an "inalienable part of China" simmers in the minds of policymakers across the globe, the threat of regional intervention from the United States and its allies has thus far kept the cross-strait conflict tense but cool.
As such, analysts argue that, while military conflict in the region and its impact on the economy is a genuine concern for Pacific nations, there are more immediate problems to deal with.
"There's no getting around the fact that the global and regional order is changing and the Pacific isn't immune from that," Peebles said. "But I think too that the Pacific is confronting this poly-crisis and geopolitics, though very important, is but one of the issues."
The PIF is expected to produce a joint shared position from all members, including Australia, on climate, which will be taken to the pre-Conference of the Parties meeting in Fiji in October before COP31 in Türkiye in November.
For low-lying Pacific nations, rising sea levels are considered an existential threat, one that Australia recognised with the landmark 2023 Falepili Union treaty that would allow a third of the 11,000 people living in Tuvalu to immigrate and escape increasing flooding.
"This is a serious gathering of serious people to discuss serious issues," Peebles said, also speaking from the forum in Koror. "There is a lot going on at this meeting, happily, that has nothing to do with geopolitics and is setting the region up for success."

What really helps Europe deal with drought

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

What really helps Europe deal with drought
September 2, 2026
Europe is in drought. As the burning of fossil fuels pushes up temperatures that are making summers hotter and drier, the continent's soils, lakes and rivers are struggling to recover. Southern and Western European countries are particularly affected. But they're not the only ones.
"We've seen drought risks expanding northward during the last decade", says Gisela Elsner, Climate and Sustainability Policy Officer at the German Konrad Adenauer Foundation, who has followed EU water management efforts for years.
"Central and Western Europe, but also southeastern European countries, are increasingly vulnerable due to climate change."
For the month of August this year, satellite data shows areas as far north as Denmark and Sweden experiencing extremely dry conditions more often seen in regions such as the Sub-Saharan Sahel.
The impact is palpable. Some of the continent's longest rivers like the Rhine or the Danube have reached historic lows, disrupting inland shipping routes. Farmers from Germany to Ukraine are reporting below-average harvests, and areas from the United Kingdom to Switzerland to Germany have announced restrictions on household water use.
To make matters worse, this year's El Niño event — a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures — is set to be one of the strongest on record. Experts predict that 2027 will be even hotter and drier as a result.
Europe will have to adapt to this reality, says Gisela Elsner. "It is not yet a matter of not having water in our taps anymore. But we need to prioritize and use our water resources efficiently."
So, how can countries across the continent set about doing this? DW analyzed water usage in European nations and reviewed the evidence to find out which measures have the most impact.
Which European countries use the most water?
Private households in Europe account for a relatively small share of water usage. Depending on the country, they consume a daily per capita average of between 50 and 300 liters, which equates to less than 20% of all use.
Two thirds of water withdrawn continent-wide is for agriculture — mostly for irrigation — as well as electricity cooling for nuclear and fossil fuel power plants.
In already drought-prone countries like Greece, Turkey and Spain, agriculture accounts for most of the near 2000 liters of water withdrawn per person each day.
Electricity cooling is the biggest factor in Eastern European countries like Bulgaria or Hungary, but also in the Netherlands or Estonia, which use between 1000 and 2000 liters per capita daily in total.
Where Europe can save the most water
"There is no single solution that is sufficient to solve this challenge," says Gisela Elsner. "It has to be a combined bundle of measures."
And they exist. A recent report published by the European Environmental Agency (EEA) found that EU countries could save between 10 and 40% of water annually by implementing targeted strategies.
For states in Western and Eastern Europe, shifting to clean energy would make a big difference. While nuclear, and planet-heating oil, gas and coal need huge amounts of water for cooling, wind and solar do not.
Electricity cooling: renewables to the rescue
So besides becoming the cheapest forms of energy, the renewables that are increasingly replacing fossil fuels are also helping countries to save water. Over the past two decades, Europe has reduced its water usage by around a quarter — mostly because of more efficient electrical cooling.
Even with nuclear plants still requiring water in countries like France, Spain or Sweden, the potential savings are massive. The EEA estimates that EU countries could make significant further savings of between 45 and 95% — equal to hundreds of liters per person each day — by expanding renewables and improving cooling systems.
Better irrigation can help in agriculture
In Southern Europe, agriculture is the big-ticket item. The EEA report recommends, for instance, replacing open water transport channels with closed pipes to avoid evaporation during heatwaves, switching from surface irrigation to sprinklers or drip irrigation, and opting for less water-intensive crops whereever possible.
Public water supply: leaky pipes lose lots of water
In EU countries, around one in four liters of drinkable water from the public supply is lost to leaky pipes and evaporation before it ever reaches its destination — according to estimates by the European association of water providers EurEau.
In Romania and Italy, the share is more than 40%. According to the EEA report, avoiding these losses would account for most of the potential savings in the EU's public water supply.
Once drinking water reaches households and businesses, individual behavior has an impact as well. The EEA report lists extensive recommendations for savings in daily life, from low-flow toilets and efficient washing machines and dishwashers, to harvesting rainwater. Yet even if every citizen in Europe did all they could, it would only reduce the daily per person household water use by between 10 and 40%.
Citizens could also contribute through more responsible consumer decisions, such as considering the water footprint of the products they buy or support, says Alexander Psomas, water resources expert at the Greek consultancy Brilliant Solutions, who co-authored the EEA report.
"Citizens can also push our governments to be more accountable on their energy policy and the impact it has on water."
What Europe can learn
Drought and heat waves are not just a European problem. Many parts in the world are even more severely affected by the climate crisis. And data from the United Nations shows regions in Northern Africa, the Middle East and Asia have been dealing with much higher levels of water stress for a long time.
This also means that Europe can collaborate with, and learn from, the rest of the world on how to adapt to water scarcity. "The UN World Food Program and the FAO are all working on similar questions in the Global South," said Giriraj Armanath, Research Group Leader at the International Water Management Institute.
Gisela Elsner recounts, for instance, chip manufacturers in the German state of Saxony recently looking to expertise from Singapore on how to reuse wastewater to cool their factories.
"We can definitely learn from those countries which already have all the knowledge and the technologies that can be used in our context as well," she said.
Public and politics are paying more attention to water use
Both Gisela Elsner and Alexander Psomas say they have noticed both politics and the public becoming more aware in recent years.
"The water scarcity and droughts topic did not have a relevant EU working group until 2022", Psomas told DW. "Today, it's one of the working groups with the highest participation. There is a growing interest and concern on this issue."
What he would like to see more of, he says, is public debates about water strategies, especially during election periods.
"If a country runs low on water, it affects everyone," he says. "I would like to see politicians discuss what kind of solutions they're offering for making their countries more water resilient in 10, 20 years from now."
Edited by Tamsin Walker and Gianna Grün

Chevron set to expand in Venezuela as US energy secretary lands in Caracas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:55:38 UTC
16:55:38 KST

Chevron is expected to announce an expansion of its Venezuelan operations on Wednesday, hours after the country's parliament approved handing Washington control of a fifth of its oil reserves and as US Energy Secretary Chris Wright arrives to sign the agreement.
America's second-largest oil company is preparing to deepen its presence in a country most of its rivals abandoned two decades ago.
An unnamed US official briefed reporters and said Chevron executives would appear alongside US Energy Secretary Chris Wright in Venezuela to unveil fresh investment, which would be the first corporate move to follow the agreement that just cleared Venezuela's National Assembly.
Wright landed in Caracas late on Tuesday after the Venezuelan vote, with the signing set for Wednesday.
Chevron is the only major American producer to have stayed in Venezuela since Hugo Chávez completed the nationalisation of the industry in 2007, a move that drove Exxon and ConocoPhillips out.
A vote and an argument about the fine print
Speaking in Spanish for an interview posted online on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the arrangement in blunt terms.
"Essentially, this is now an agreement with the US government, specifically involving the Defense Department, which holds a special account allowing it to take possession of a certain percentage of these assets," Rubio said, adding that American backing would help the company attract the private investment needed to develop the fields.
The "vast majority" of the 17 fields had been in Chinese and Russian hands, Rubio pointed out as the White House has also cast the agreement as a reassertion of the Monroe Doctrine.
Those fields come with 100-year rights for North American Blue Energy Partners and hold 65 billion barrels. A new company will be created in which the US Department of War's Office of Strategic Capital takes a 35% stake, with the US State Department entitled to buy 20% of output at production cost.
US citizens must form a majority of the board, and Washington holds a veto over appointments.
Venezuelan lawmakers approved the agreement by a show of hands, though some opposition members abstained, saying they had not seen the terms.
"We need and are obliged to know what is written in the fine print," said opposition lawmaker Luis Emilio Rondón.
"Who benefits from this oil if it stays underground?" argued the National Assembly chief Jorge Rodríguez in return.
NABEP is owned by Alejandro Betancourt, who has faced investigations over alleged money laundering in Spain and Switzerland without charges being filed and has been accused of involvement in a corruption scheme at state producer PDVSA.
An unnamed US official called him a "proven operator" while conceding that geopolitics sometimes means dealing with imperfect figures.
"I'm not nominating anyone for sainthood here," the official said. "What I am telling you is that this is a person that, in the past, has been helpful to the United States government."
What the deal has not settled
Analysts remain sceptical that output can be revived quickly, with estimates ranging from one to ten years before new barrels reach the market. Washington is not investing money in the venture, officials say, arguing its backing alone will attract the capital needed.
US President Donald Trump suggested on Monday that others would follow Chevron.
"We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in," Trump stated.
However, Exxon's position appears unchanged as a spokesman said on Tuesday that "nothing has changed" after CEO Darren Woods also called Venezuela "uninvestable" earlier this year.
For the US administration, the urgency is domestic.
US President Donald Trump just met oil executives at the White House on Tuesday as petrol prices climbed because of new US strikes on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, posting afterwards that "we are unleashing American Energy Dominance!"
Cheaper fuel is a priority before November's midterm elections, in which Republicans could lose control of both the House and the Senate.

At least two people sustained minor injuries in an explosion at a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg, police reported on Wednesday.
The station building and Track 1 are currently closed, a police spokesperson told daily Bild on Wednesday morning.
Train services have also been disrupted and are being rerouted to other tracks.
Augsburg is a regional transport hub and is around 55 kilometres from the Bavarian capital Munich.
Explosives experts from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office are on the scene, according to police. The cause of the explosion is still unknown.
Police are also investigating suspected sabotage at an Amprion power substation in Bergheim, in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, public broadcaster WDR reported.
A short circuit knocked several power lines out of operation, but the wider electricity supply was unaffected.
Police suspect the incident was deliberate rather than the result of a technical fault. Investigators are examining whether it could be connected to suspected sabotage in Brandenburg.
Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant
The incident in Bergheim came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant.
“We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said.
Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded.
Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated.
Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations.

Van Weel rejected the suggestion that the Netherlands had become a “narco-state”, where drugs gangs have free rein, but acknowledged that criminal networks such as those of Leijdekkers and the convicted crime boss Ridouan Taghi had taken root in the country and are benefiting from Dutch financial and logistical facilities.

German Navy tests Israeli LORA ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:52:55 UTC
16:52:55 KST

- Germany's Navy conducted a successful dual firing trial of IAI's Naval LORA ballistic missile under its OPEX testing program.
- Germany is reportedly moving forward with plans to procure the missile system, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers.
The German Navy successfully completed a dual firing trial of Israel Aerospace Industries’ Naval LORA ballistic missile, launching the weapon from an operational German vessel and hitting its target with precision in both test scenarios, IAI said.
The trial was conducted as part of the German Navy’s Operational Experimentation program, known as OPEX, a testing initiative the service launched to support its “Marine 2035 and Beyond” plan. IAI said the missile was launched from a configuration comprising a command trailer and a launcher aboard the German vessel, and that the weapon system met all the trial’s objectives in both scenarios.
Separately, Reuters reported that a German frigate tested the Lora system in the North Atlantic, between Ireland and Iceland, in a previously undisclosed operation. According to that report, Germany now plans to move forward with preparations to procure the missile, which has a range of more than 500 kilometers (311 miles).
LORA, short for Long Range Artillery, is a quasi-ballistic missile developed by IAI’s MLM Division that can be launched from land-based mobile launchers or naval vessels. The missile has a publicly listed operational range of 90 to 430 kilometers (56 to 267 miles) and uses a combination of GPS and inertial navigation for guidance, with a circular error probable of 10 meters (33 feet), according to IAI’s own published specifications. It is unclear whether the range Reuters cited reflects an upgraded or export-specific configuration.
The missile has seen combat use by Azerbaijan, which deployed the system during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh conflict against Armenia.
“This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense,” said Boaz Levy, IAI’s Chairman. “The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany, the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed. This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
“Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany,” said Guy Bar Lev, IAI’s CEO. “This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
Germany separately fields IAI’s Arrow 3 missile defense system, which has been operational on German soil as part of the country’s broader air and missile defense buildup.

Andy Burnham to face first PMQs as borrowing costs rise – UK politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:52:55 UTC
16:52:55 KST

Burnham to take PMQs as borrowing costs rise, and thinktank says higher defence spending not 'realistic' without tax rise
Good morning. Andy Burnham will face PMQs for the first time as PM today but he already has a fairly good idea of the questions he might get from Kemi Badenoch because she rehearsed them all yesterday. Here is an excerpt from the press release the Conservatives put out yesterday summarising those questions – and their take on how Burnham responded.
Kemi Badenoch asked if Burnham would:
-Set out a plan to get defence spending to 3% of GDP;
-Confirm whether Labour will use a Rwanda-style deal to secure our borders;
-Set out a timeline to get foreign-born prisoners out of British prisons;
-Pledge no new taxes at the forthcoming budget; and
-Stand up to his own backbenchers and cut benefits.
In response, Burnham floundered and couldn’t give straight answers to clear, straight questions.
Today Badenoch may well ask again about tax, benefit cuts and the economy.
And that is because, while Westminster was focused on Burnham’s impressive debut in the Commons yesterday afternoon, the more significant story may have been happening elsewhere, on the financial markets. The Telegraph sums it up like this.
Not for the first time, the Telegraph’s headline was not entirely fair to a Labour prime minister. As Heather Stewart explains in her Guardian story, the government’s long-term borrowing costs did jump “to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds” – but this was mainly the result of international factors.
As Graeme Wearden reports in his business live blog today, the UK is not the only country where government borrowing costs are soaring; Graeme says Australia, India and Germany are among other states facing similar problems.
But, just because the UK is not alone, that does not mean the problem is not real; as Heather reports in her story, the rise in borrowing costs means the Treasury has lost £12bn from its fiscal safety net. She quotes an economist saying “based on Tuesday’s yields, [the Treasury’s] headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.”
When Badenoch challenged Burnham over tax yesterday, he pointed out that in his first week in office he made two tax-cutting announcements. But he refused to oblige her by ruling out tax rises in the budget.
Today the Resolution Foundation thinktank (whose former chief executive, Torsten Bell, is now a Treasury minister) has published a report saying that, if Burnham wants to raise defence spending, as he proposes, taxes will probably have to rise for ordinary workers. It says:
International data shows that the rise in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) last year and frozen tax thresholds in the UK have led to the largest annual rise in taxes on average workers across 33 comparable OECD rich countries. Strikingly, however, this was from a very low base – lower than the US, for example. The UK remains in the bottom third of such countries for the level of tax on an average worker, and the effective tax rate on a typical earner is still lower than it was before the financial crisis. Indeed, no country raises more in total tax as a proportion of GDP without also asking more of single average earners.
This analysis strongly suggests that any politician promising a bigger state and lower taxes on middle earners is not being realistic. So if we want to increase defence spending, then there is a clear case for paying for this through broad-based tax rises that include typical earners paying more.
With all this on the table, PMQs is likely to be dominated by questions about tax and borrowing.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.15am: Michael Shanks, the energy minister, Ofgem officials and other energy experts give evidence to the Commons energy committee about the electricity market.
9.30am: Stephen Timms, the social security and disability minister, gives evidence to the Commons work and pensions committee.
Morning: Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, holds a press conference in Cardiff ahead of the start of the Senedd year.
After 12.30pm: MPs debate the remaining stages of the representation of the people bill.
Afternoon: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is doing an interview with Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, ahead of the party’s conference that starts on Friday.
Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state and Cabinet Office minister, will make a Commons statement after PMQs on “rewiring the state”. This will cover the ambitious devolution plans published by the government during the summer recess.
Alexandra Topping has written a good preview of the challenge Kemi Badenoch faces at PMQs today. As she puts it, “early indications suggest [Badenoch] understands that Burnham’s folksy Hovis advert charm may require a different approach.”
Burnham faces an even bigger challenge. He became Labour leader and PM arguing that the Westminster political model functions in a way that is holding Britain back, and he has pledged to shake it up. He has said that he views PMQs as part of the problem, and suggested he would like to change the way it is conducted. But he has not properly explained how. According to a BBC report, this might mean a “tonal shift”, more jokes and less reliance on notes.
To older readers, some of this may sound familiar. Previous incoming prime ministers have tried to change PMQs – and failed. David Cameron said that he wanted to “end Punch and Judy politics” at PMQs. Keir Starmer said that, as part of his approach to PMQs in opposition, he would focus on “constructive criticism”. Trying to make PMQs gentle and civilised never seems to work because the dynamics of the event institutionalise conflict. Cameron explained it like this in an interview in 2013 explaining why Punch and Judy were still alive and well.
People don’t believe it but MPs do work hard and for 30mins each Wednesday they go effectively to the Colosseum and [what] they see are the Christians going to be eaten by the lions. And you’ve got a choice - are you going to be a Christian or a lion? It pays to get stuck in. When we’ve tested this. The public expects PMQs to be robust.
Historically, trying to make PMQs more dignified has been a bit like saying that boxing matches would be better if contestants didn’t actually hit each other.
But PMQs can change. In its modern form, it only started in the 1960s. Blair failed to change the tone of PMQs, but as soon as he won the 1997 election he changed it from being a twice-weekly event (two sessions of 15 minutes, on Tuesdays and Thursdays) to being a once-a-week event (half on hour on Wednesdays). If Burnham really hates PMQs, he could consider further reform along those lines, but he has expressed no interest in doing that.
Polanski says Greens will make Holborn and St Pancras byelection 'referendum on ending rip-off Britain'

The Holborn and St Pancras by election will be a referendum on ending rip-off Britain. Only the Greens have a real plan for real hope and change.
We will announce our candidate in due course and they will set out an exciting agenda for the deep change our country needs.
I am proud of what I have achieved in the first year of my leadership of the Green party but it is just the start.
I am very excited for the next chapter for myself, for the Greens and for people across the country.

According Politico, Polanski has already started campaigning. In their London Playbook briefing, Andrew McDonald and Megan McElroy report:
Polanski hasn’t confirmed he intends to run in Keir Starmer’s Holborn and St Pancras seat, but … Green officials put out an afternoon statement saying “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP,” he was knocking doors in Camden last night and he sent out a quote saying “I am very excited for the next chapter for myself.” See if you can decipher that one. One person in the party said they expect him to put himself forward for selection this week.
But my POLITICO colleague Isabel Loubser (formerly of the Islington Tribune) hears from two Green figures that one of Polanski’s two deputy leaders, Mothin Ali, is also interested in running. One person says he would potentially gain the backing of two key leftie groups in the constituency: the Camden People’s Alliance and a local Muslim alliance too. The seat has a big Bengali and Muslim community.
Scottish government accused of 'slash and burn' approach to health boards
Patrick Greenfield
Patrick Greenfield is a Guardian reporter covering Scotland.
Reaction to Scottish first minister John Swinney’s programme for government is still coming in this morning after he unveiled the SNP’s plans for the next five years in Holyrood yesterday. A major restructuring of local government and NHS health boards, and a new misogyny bill to crack down on violence against women and girls were among the most eye-catching announcements.
Swinney also insisted that his administration will move forward with plans to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items despite strong opposition from farming and business groups.
The Scottish Greens’ co-leader, Ross Greer, said it was a “disappointing” programme that Nicola Sturgeon would not have backed, urging the SNP to roll out a £2 bus fare cap in the Highlands and west Scotland to the entire country. He also criticised Swinney for “throwing open the doors to tech billionaires by encouraging more applications to build hyperscale data centres in Scotland”.
In his speech, the first minister said there would be a strategic approach to green data centres “with clear expectations” around environmental and community benefits, something which was cautiously welcomed by campaign groups, but there was no suggestions of an outright moratorium.
On the health board overhaul, the union Unite criticised the programme for government as a “slash and burn” agenda, warning that it was likely to result in job losses. “Reducing health boards does not reduce workload or staffing pressures. Unite will not stand by and allow workers and services to be attacked,” said Unite regional coordinator James O’Connell.
Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson rejects suggestions government does not have firm control of spending
Sally Jameson, a Cabinet Office minister, was the No 10 voice on TV and radio this morning. In interviews, she insisted that Andy Burnham did take fiscal responsibility seriously.
Asked about Jim O’Neill’s claim that Burnham’s tone in the comments yesterday would have concerned investors, (see 9.36am) she told Sky News she did not agree. She explained:
I think it’s important we don’t over-read into individual comments people make, because I think Andy Burnham has been really clear that we are going to stick to those fiscal rules rigidly, and that fiscal responsibility is absolutely imperative.
We’ve got to have controls on spending, and I don’t think Andy or anyone else has said any different to that.
And on the Today programme she said Burnham was “absolutely clear that we will be sticking to the fiscal rules and making sure that we’re controlling public spending”.
Former bank chief Howard Davies joins O'Neill in urging Burnham to scrap pensions triple lock
Sir Howard Davies, a former chair of NatWest and a former chair of the Financial Services Authority, echoed Jim O’Neill’s comments (see 9.36am) this morning. In an interview on the Today programme, he said Andy Burnham’s stance on economics was causing some concern in the markets.
Davies said the rise in long-term UK government borrowing costs yesterday was not “a major crisis of confidence in the UK government”.
But, asked if Burnham’s approach to public spending was causing “some market jitters”, he replied:
Yes, I think it is.
Unfortunately, we do have a circus built around our budgets, which actually does not happen in many other countries. There is a whole industry of people … to create expectations and then dash those expectations, and I think we are going to face a very dicky period between now and the budget.
I think we’re going to see a very uncertain period for the next three or four weeks, and it would be helpful if the government could make some signs about their overall approach to the fiscal balance, which I think could calm things down a bit.
Davies, like O’Neill, also said the government should get rid of the pensions triple lock. “If a government does not grasp that nettle at some point, then I think its credibility is going to be on the rack.”
Burnham has committed to keeping the pensions triple lock for the duration of this parliament, saying he has to because that is what Labour promised in its manifesto.
He has not said anything about his plans for the triple lock in the next parliament. But with Reform UK, the Conservatives and the Lib Dems all in favour of keeping the triple lock, it is not hard to see why he does not want to break ranks and suggest it could go after 2029.
Burnham's Commons speech 'last thing' bond market wanted to hear because it implied more spending, Jim O'Neill says
Andy Burnham’s speech to MPs yesterday was “the last thing” that investors wanted to hear, according to Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist who served as a Treasury minister under David Cameron.
O’Neill, who sits in the Lords as a crossbencher, is not a regular Burnham basher; he is a big supporter of Burnham’s devolution agenda and he has been an informal adviser to the PM. There were even discussions about his taking a job in the No 10 team, which floundered because he did not want a formal role.
But potential policy disagreements also seem to have been a factor, and in an interview on LBC last night O’Neill said investors would be worried by the fact that Burnham seemed to express no interest in cutting spending. He said:
Andy made his first big speech in parliament since after the recess … and the tone of it, implying a lot more government spending to take control of X, Y, and Z, is the last thing that investors want to hear on a day where all of this is going on in the background.
And so yes, they’re like, ‘Who’s going to get real in this country about the challenges of getting our debt down and controlling spending?’
O’Neill also said it had been a tough day for government borrowing.
‘It is a tough day. Ten-year gilt yields or 10-year interest rates have risen by a quarter of a percent, which in one day is a lot. We’ve not had that since Liz Truss days …
If your country, whether it be ours or others, is under the focus of ‘Can they come up with a sensible fiscal strategy?’ on a day where the markets think ‘Well, no you’re not showing any signs of it’, they’re going to have a bad day.
O’Neill followed this up with an interview to the BBC where he said Burnham should end the pensions triple lock and cut welfare spending “in a credible manner”. He said these were “golden opportunities” because they would lead to a “significant decline” in government borrowing costs.
Burnham to take PMQs as borrowing costs rise, and thinktank says higher defence spending not 'realistic' without tax rise
Good morning. Andy Burnham will face PMQs for the first time as PM today but he already has a fairly good idea of the questions he might get from Kemi Badenoch because she rehearsed them all yesterday. Here is an excerpt from the press release the Conservatives put out yesterday summarising those questions – and their take on how Burnham responded.
Kemi Badenoch asked if Burnham would:
-Set out a plan to get defence spending to 3% of GDP;
-Confirm whether Labour will use a Rwanda-style deal to secure our borders;
-Set out a timeline to get foreign-born prisoners out of British prisons;
-Pledge no new taxes at the forthcoming budget; and
-Stand up to his own backbenchers and cut benefits.
In response, Burnham floundered and couldn’t give straight answers to clear, straight questions.
Today Badenoch may well ask again about tax, benefit cuts and the economy.
And that is because, while Westminster was focused on Burnham’s impressive debut in the Commons yesterday afternoon, the more significant story may have been happening elsewhere, on the financial markets. The Telegraph sums it up like this.
Not for the first time, the Telegraph’s headline was not entirely fair to a Labour prime minister. As Heather Stewart explains in her Guardian story, the government’s long-term borrowing costs did jump “to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds” – but this was mainly the result of international factors.
As Graeme Wearden reports in his business live blog today, the UK is not the only country where government borrowing costs are soaring; Graeme says Australia, India and Germany are among other states facing similar problems.
But, just because the UK is not alone, that does not mean the problem is not real; as Heather reports in her story, the rise in borrowing costs means the Treasury has lost £12bn from its fiscal safety net. She quotes an economist saying “based on Tuesday’s yields, [the Treasury’s] headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans.”
When Badenoch challenged Burnham over tax yesterday, he pointed out that in his first week in office he made two tax-cutting announcements. But he refused to oblige her by ruling out tax rises in the budget.
Today the Resolution Foundation thinktank (whose former chief executive, Torsten Bell, is now a Treasury minister) has published a report saying that, if Burnham wants to raise defence spending, as he proposes, taxes will probably have to rise for ordinary workers. It says:
International data shows that the rise in employer national insurance contributions (NICs) last year and frozen tax thresholds in the UK have led to the largest annual rise in taxes on average workers across 33 comparable OECD rich countries. Strikingly, however, this was from a very low base – lower than the US, for example. The UK remains in the bottom third of such countries for the level of tax on an average worker, and the effective tax rate on a typical earner is still lower than it was before the financial crisis. Indeed, no country raises more in total tax as a proportion of GDP without also asking more of single average earners.
This analysis strongly suggests that any politician promising a bigger state and lower taxes on middle earners is not being realistic. So if we want to increase defence spending, then there is a clear case for paying for this through broad-based tax rises that include typical earners paying more.
With all this on the table, PMQs is likely to be dominated by questions about tax and borrowing.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.15am: Michael Shanks, the energy minister, Ofgem officials and other energy experts give evidence to the Commons energy committee about the electricity market.
9.30am: Stephen Timms, the social security and disability minister, gives evidence to the Commons work and pensions committee.
Morning: Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Welsh first minister, holds a press conference in Cardiff ahead of the start of the Senedd year.
After 12.30pm: MPs debate the remaining stages of the representation of the people bill.
Afternoon: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, is doing an interview with Chris Mason, the BBC’s political editor, ahead of the party’s conference that starts on Friday.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines and insurance companies on Tuesday that the presence of Ukrainian drones had made Russian skies dangerous to use and that they were effectively closed.
"Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports: the Russian sky is becoming completely dangerous," Zelensky said in his nightly video address.
Ukraine poses no threat to civil aviation, he said, "but there will be drones in Russia's skies and due notice must be taken."
"Although Russian authorities are not properly announcing it, Russian airspace will effectively be closing. The war started by Russia is closing its own skies," Zelensky added.
The full risk of Ukrainian drones to aviation over Russia is not clear, but there have been deadly incidents of civilian aircraft being mistakenly targeted in the region.
Aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions said in an alert to clients that while the majority of Ukraine's drone and missile strikes were likely to occur within 300 kilometers (186 miles) of the border, daily attacks deeper inside Russia were near-certain through 2026, including near Moscow and St Petersburg.
"There is also a realistic possibility that the frequency of Ukrainian strikes will continue to increase in the short term deep inside Russian territory," the alert said. "It is assessed that miscalculation and/or misidentification is likely in areas related to the Ukraine conflict."

Ireland foreign minister dodges question over Russian-owned alumina plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:51:17 UTC
16:51:17 KST

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee would not commit to including Ireland's alumina plant, whose products reportedly ended up in Russian weapons in Ukraine, in an upcoming EU sanctions list, during remarks made ahead of a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers on Sept. 2.
The Irish Times published data in May showing that the Aughinish Alumina plant, owned by Russian company Rusal, exports overwhelmingly to Russia, with the material reportedly being found in weapons Moscow uses against Ukraine.
The Irish government initially argued that sanctioning the plant would cause more harm to the EU than to Russia. However, Dublin later agreed to an investigation, which "has not found concrete or definitive evidence linking the alumina to a weapons manufacturer in Russia," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin.
"Look, you'll know that the report was recently provided to the (European) Commission in relation to Alumina," the Irish foreign minister said when asked about sanctions against the plant ahead of a ministerial meeting in Wicklow, Ireland.
"We've also provided it to our colleagues in Ukraine and we will work with them."
Ukraine has not recently commented on the Aughinish Alumina plant, but Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously said that Russia must be "deprived of access" to alumina.
The topic is back on the table because the EU is considering its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, which is set to include some 1,600 listings, the highest number ever.
"Ireland has supported every single package of sanctions that has been put forward. We have worked over the last number of months with colleagues to ensure that the 21st (package passes)," McEntee said.
However, Estonia's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna revealed that he had proposed the inclusion of alumina in the 21st package of sanctions, passed in July.
It did not feature, meaning an EU member state had vetoed its inclusion. All EU sanctions require unanimity among the 27 member states.
Ireland has never admitted to vetoing the plant's inclusion, but it is the only country with an obvious interest in doing so.
Just after McEntee spoke, her Finnish counterpart Elina Valtonen said Finland remains "open to sanctioning aluminum."
"Russia is a war economy... everything is going directly or indirectly towards the war," Valtonen said.
"I think we really need to explore all the options on the table."
