Russia attacked energy infrastructure: the situation is most difficult in Odesa Oblast, a large part is without electricity
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
10:49:54 EEST
16:49:54 KST

Russia attacked energy infrastructure: the situation is most difficult in Odesa Oblast, a large part is without electricity
Kyiv • UNN
Russia struck Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The most difficult situation arose in Odesa Oblast.
Russia attacked Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the night of September 2. The situation is most difficult in Odesa region, where a large portion of consumers are without electricity. Power outages are also reported in four other regions. UNN writes about this, citing data from the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo as of September 2.
What is the situation in Odesa region?
"At night, the enemy carried out a massive missile-and-drone attack on Odesa region's energy infrastructure," Ukrenergo reported.
"The situation is most difficult in Odesa region. There, as a result of the enemy's massive attack on energy infrastructure, a large number of consumers have been left without power," the Ministry of Energy noted.
Emergency repair and restoration work in the region, as noted, began as soon as the security situation allowed. Energy workers are working to restore the damaged equipment as quickly as possible, the Ministry of Energy emphasized.
As Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper reported, eight people, including a 5-year-old child, were injured in Odesa region on September 2 as a result of a combined enemy attack. The Russians targeted civilian and energy infrastructure.
In Odesa, a 24-story residential building was damaged in Russia's September 2 attack. Office buildings and two educational institutions were also damaged, Odesa City Military Administration head Serhii Lysak stated. Due to damage to a number of educational institutions, classes there have temporarily been organized remotely, the regional administration head added.
"Due to a shortage of capacity," public electric transport in Odesa is temporarily suspending operations. "Trams and trolleybuses are not running," the Odesa City Council reported.
Where else are there power outages due to enemy attacks
"As a result of hostilities and shelling of energy facilities, some consumers in Sumy, Kharkiv, Chernihiv and Kherson regions were without power as of this morning," the Ministry of Energy reported.
As stated, restoration work is ongoing everywhere the security situation permits.
Will there be power outages across Ukraine?
The ministry reported that restrictions are not expected to be imposed today.
It also urged people today, September 2, where possible, to shift active energy consumption to daytime hours—from 10:00 to 16:00—and limit the use of powerful electrical appliances from 18:00 to 22:00. This helps reduce the load on the power system.
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption has decreased. Today, September 2, as of 09:30, it was 6.8% lower than at the same time the previous day—Tuesday. The reason for the change is clear weather across nearly all of Ukraine, which contributes to the high efficiency of household solar power plants and a corresponding decrease in the amount of electricity consumed from the grid. Another factor is the significant number of consumers experiencing emergency outages due to the effects of the nighttime missile-and-drone attack on energy infrastructure.
Yesterday, September 1, the daily consumption maximum was recorded in the evening. It was 3.4% lower than the maximum of the previous day—Monday, August 31. The reason was the easing of heat in most regions of Ukraine and a reduced need for widespread use of air conditioners.
What preceded this
Kremlin head Vladimir Putin ordered the Russian armed forces to prepare massive strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure .

On Tuesday, illegal settlers burned another two Palestinian vehicles and spray-painted racist slogans during a raid on the village of Umm Safa in the central occupied West Bank.
Since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, attacks by Israeli forces against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have intensified, while illegal settler violence has also increased.
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said settlers carried out 628 attacks against Palestinians, their land and property during August.
The commission said the attacks directly harmed 164 Palestinians, including 20 children and 17 women. It added that illegal settlers also targeted 21,508 trees, including 19,375 olive trees.
About 750,000 Israeli settlers live in 141 illegal settlements and 224 outposts in the occupied West Bank, with 250,000 living in 15 illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem, according to Palestinian figures.

Charlie Kirk murder suspect to face potential death penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:46:00 UTC
16:46:00 KST

Charlie Kirk murder suspect to face potential death penalty
September 2, 2026
The murder case against Tyler R., the man accused of fatally shooting conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, is headed to trial, and he could face the death penalty if convicted, under a new ruling.
Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled late on Tuesday that prosecutors had presented sufficient evidence to proceed, ordering that the defendant be set for trial.
The 23-year-old suspect pleaded not guilty to all seven charges, including aggravated murder, following the ruling. A hearing to schedule the trial date is set for October 23.
What did the prosecutors say?
Prosecutors say Tyler R. fired a single shot from a rooftop more than 400 feet (~122 meters) away, striking 31-year-old Kirk in the neck as he addressed a crowd of more than 3,000 people at Utah Valley University.
A strong supporter of President Donald Trump, Kirk has been credited with motivating young voters to turn out for him in the 2024 US presidential election.
Utah County prosecutor Ryan McBride told the court the defendant "lay down in a prone position, and he would have seen this mass of people, of 3,000-plus people there for the event, took aim, put his crosshairs on Charlie Kirk and fired."
McBride argued the shooting "created a great risk of death that anyone would know about."
Prosecutors also pointed to the rifle's additional unfired rounds as evidence that the suspect "came prepared to shoot again," and presented DNA evidence they say ties him to the weapon and to a tool allegedly used to engrave one of the cartridges with the words "Hey Fascist! CATCH!"
What did the defense say?
The defendant's attorneys have argued the case does not meet Utah's legal threshold for aggravated murder, which requires showing that others faced a high probability, not just a possibility, of harm.
Defense attorney Staci Visser told the court, "There is one act. There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," adding that there was "zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."
The defense also challenged the reliability of the prosecution's DNA testing.
Court hears argument for political motive
Prosecutors say the defendant targeted Kirk over his political views, citing a text message in which he allegedly wrote to his roommate, "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."
A handwritten note he reportedly wrote the roommate, who he was romantically involved with, read: "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."
However, defense attorney Richard Novak countered that Kirk had spoken "hatefully" about LGBTQ people and that the wording of the message didn't necessarily indicate a political motive.
Kirk family welcomes 'important step' for justice
Kirk's parents and widow, Erika Kirk, who now leads his organization Turning Point USA, attended the hearing. In a statement, the Kirk family said the ruling "marks an important step in our family's pursuit of justice for him."
"Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father," read the statement posted by Erika Kirk on social media.
Legal analyst Seth Zuckerman told Reuters he expects the case to go to trial rather than end in a plea deal, saying prosecutors "may not be willing to take the death penalty off the table, and that would probably require a trial."

Fake 10 Downing Street listing on Booking.com highlights security failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:45:12 UTC
16:45:12 KST

Successive politicians have clawed their way past colleagues over the years to call the residence home. Yet in an offer that probably seemed too good to be true, the property site Booking.com has been accused of “systemic security failures” after it was able to set up and accept payment for a fake listing for 10 Downing Street.
A property listed as a “1 bedroom apartment in the heart of London” – with the exact address and a picture of the prime minister’s home – was listed on 18 June by researchers from the consumer watchdog Which?.
The listing, which promised a four-minute walk to the Houses of Parliament, was set up so that users had to request a stay and were unable to reserve and pay automatically.
The booking window opened briefly and closed so that a test could be carried out by a researcher from Which?. The consumer watchdog said a payment for a week-long stay had been processed by the digital travel site that enables users to book hotels and other accommodation as well as flights and car rentals.
The money had still not been refunded more than six weeks after it had been set up, according to Which?, which is associated with the Consumers Association charity.
A fake review was also uploaded to the site, describing the stay as “exceptional” and enjoying the experience of “hanging out with Larry the cat”, in a reference to Downing Street’s resident feline.
Despite Booking.com sending a message saying the review would be checked by a team of moderators, the consumer watchdog said it had been added almost immediately.
The team of researchers were also said to have used Booking.com’s mailing system to send an external URL asking the representative for credit card details to confirm the booking, Which? said.
The watchdog claimed the travel site had told them it had the ability to block URLs being sent through the messaging system if it suspected fraudulent activity, but it had not done so.
The listing was finally removed on 27 August, six weeks after it went live.
Rory Boland, the editor of Which? Travel, said: “If Booking.com’s so-called sophisticated AI systems can’t spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it’s no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily.”
The watchdog said its investigation had “uncovered systemic security failures across the platform” and urged Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, to investigate.
A Booking.com spokesperson said: “This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings on our platform. The property added by Which? was not visible to customers or ‘live’ for the time period referenced.
“We use a range of checks, verification measures and artificial intelligence, which help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours.”
It said that as the property was not open and bookable, some of its automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the fraud listing.
An Ofcom spokesperson said platforms have legal duties obliging them to take down illegal content generated by users once it is known. “Booking.com is not in scope of future rules that will apply to paid-for fraudulent advertising, and any change to that would be a matter for government,” they said.

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Europe imported one of its lowest volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) for the month of August in the past five years amid intense competition with Asia for available supplies on the market due to the Middle East crisis, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
In August, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system totaled only around 9.1 billion cubic meters, up 8% from July but down 6% from August 2025. Over the past five years, Europe purchased a lower volume of LNG in August only in 2024, when imports totaled 7.3 bln cubic meters.
In January-August 2026, LNG flows from terminals into Europe's gas transmission system slowed to around 90.3 bln cubic meters, already 2.8% lower than in the same period of 2025.
LNG supplies accounted for the largest share of Europe's gas supply sources in January-August at 42.5%, according to data from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG) as of August 28. Supplies from the North Sea, primarily Norwegian gas, ranked second with a 37.5% share, followed by supplies from North Africa at 9.2% and supplies from the east at 6%, including Russian gas, gas supplied from Ukraine, as well as withdrawals by European companies of their own gas from Ukrainian underground storage facilities.
This exceeded the share of withdrawals from underground gas storage facilities, which stood at 1.5%. Gas supplies from Azerbaijan accounted for 3.4%.

New photo shows Wolf XM30 hidden under tarp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:43:53 UTC
16:43:53 KST

- General Dynamics Land Systems released the first photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype, shown wrapped in a tarp during transport following its August 21 delivery to the U.S. Army.
- The vehicle's design remains concealed as it competes against American Rheinmetall's Lynx XM30, with the Army expected to select a winner in 2027.
General Dynamics Land Systems released the first publicly available photo of its Wolf XM30 prototype in transit this week, showing the vehicle wrapped entirely in a black tarp and strapped to a flatbed trailer.
The image follows the company’s confirmation that it delivered the prototype to the U.S. Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, on August 21, a delivery The Defence Blog previously reported based on a social media post from Geoffrey Norman, a retired Army brigadier general who now serves as director of strategy at General Dynamics Land Systems.
The tarp keeps the vehicle’s actual shape and design details concealed. General Dynamics has not released an uncovered photo of the Wolf XM30 or said when the vehicle’s full appearance will be shown publicly. The transport photo is the closest look the public has gotten so far at the physical hardware behind the program.
Norman, who spent 30 years in the Army as a tanker and cavalryman before joining General Dynamics two years ago, worked on the Next Generation Combat Vehicle Cross Functional Team at Detroit Arsenal before leaving the service. In his earlier post announcing the delivery, he said the Wolf uses what the company calls a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new software and hardware be added to the vehicle without a full redesign, a “born-digital” approach he said was built specifically for future upgrades.
Norman said the August 21 delivery is the first of several Wolf XM30 prototypes General Dynamics plans to complete and hand over to the Army. Additional vehicles are expected to go to Fort Hood, Texas, where the Army will run them through an evaluation process that could lead to a full-rate production decision. General Dynamics has credited teams across six sites, Sterling Heights, Lima, Scranton, Tallahassee, Grand Rapids and London, with building the vehicle.
The Wolf XM30 is one of two competing designs in the Army’s program to replace the M2 Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, which has been in continuous service for more than 40 years. American Rheinmetall Vehicles is building the program’s other entrant, the Lynx XM30, and delivered the first of eight Lynx prototypes to the Army within days of General Dynamics’ Wolf delivery. That delivery put the Lynx into government-led developmental and performance testing under the program’s Phase 3/4 Engineering and Manufacturing Development contract, worth approximately $764 million. Rheinmetall has said it will deliver its remaining seven prototypes later this year for use in operational unit training, running in parallel with technical evaluation as part of the Army’s Transformation in Contact 2.0 initiative.
Both companies are developing and testing their prototypes in Michigan, drawing on the state’s concentration of Army ground-vehicle expertise centered on Detroit Arsenal, home to the Army’s Tank-automotive and Armaments Command and the Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center.
The Army is expected to select a winning XM30 design in 2027, with the design and prototype phase of the program alone valued at $1.6 billion.

Arctic route saves time and costs for Indian shippers – CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:42:22 UTC
16:42:22 KST

Arctic route saves time and costs for Indian shippers – CEO
The absence of Western sanctions and the shorter distance make the Northern Sea Route along Russia’s Arctic coast attractive to India, the CEO of a logistics company has said.
”The key factor is the absence of problems related to sanctions restrictions, which allows us to insure cargo against transport risks at very favorable rates,” Y&H Cargo CEO Rakesh Mishra said at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Tuesday.
The four-day annual event is being attended by officials, businessmen, experts, and researchers from 80 countries.
Mishra said the Arctic route is shorter for Indian shippers and will also provide a boost to trade with Southeast Asia, the world’s largest manufacturing hub. “Overall, this trade route is more efficient than the western route,” TASS cited him as saying.
The 5,600 km Northern Sea Route (NSR) from Vladivostok to Murmansk runs off Russia’s Arctic coastline and is the shortest shipping route between East Asia and Europe. For India, the route can save up to 40% in distance and around two weeks in travel time to most European ports.
Mishra added that the Middle East conflict leaves India, which has traditionally relied on the Suez Canal route, with “no choice but to develop the eastern route.” India is the second-largest importer of Russian oil and the two countries have set a bilateral trade target of $100 billion by 2030.
India plans to send its first commercial ship along the NSR next year, an official said at the Arctic-Regions Forum in Arkhangelsk last month.
State-owned conglomerate Rosatom is the designated operator and coordinator of the NSR and also manages Russia’s nuclear-powered icebreaker fleet, which is keeps the shipping lane navigable.
Shipping traffic along the Chennai-Vladivostok corridor – also known as the Eastern Maritime Corridor – has seen a 70% jump in cargo movement.

Surge in attacks on mosques

Photos: Santa Zukker's solo exhibition opens at Artius Gallery in Tallinn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

Photos: Santa Zukker's solo exhibition opens at Artius Gallery in Tallinn
On 28 August, Santa Zukker's solo exhibition "Mööda maastikke" (Along the Landscapes) opened at the Artius Gallery in Tallinn, bringing together the artist's work from the past year along with earlier cityscapes featuring naïvist and futuristic elements.
"Along the Landscapes" views landscape not only as a real place but above all as an inner and perceptual space. Santa Zukker combines realism with naïvist and surreal elements, creating places that feel recognizable to the viewer yet do not exist in reality.
"Nature brought me to painting and also keeps me doing it. I perceive a cognitive horizon in everything and everyone I see," Zukker said.
At the exhibition, central focus is placed on locations that do not exist in real life but nonetheless feel familiar. These are landscapes somewhere between memory and imagination — places a viewer may be seeing for the first time yet may still recognize as personally familiar.
Santa Zukker is a cultural and art scholar as well as an artist. Her work centers on conveying memories, moods, and inner experiences. She has exhibited her works in numerous Estonian galleries and art institutions, including Haus Gallery, Kunstiruum, Staapli3 Gallery, Teachers' House, Metropol Gallery, Artstac Gallery, Stockmann Gallery, the Pärnu Museum of New Art, the Eduard Vilde Museum / Kastellaanimaja, Kadriorg Gallery, Nõmme Cultural Center, Põhjala Studio Gallery, the Office of the Chancellor of Justice, Altos in Telliskivi Creative City, and others.
"Along the Landscapes" will remain open at Artius Gallery until 28 October.

Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:36:52 UTC
16:36:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's fishermen face shrinking fishing grounds and repeated arrests by Israel
For fishermen in the Gaza Strip, the sea has become increasingly difficult and dangerous to access, as Israeli naval forces continue to restrict their movement, open fire on fishing boats, and arrest fishermen, according to local fishermen's representatives.
On Tuesday, Israeli naval forces arrested 10 fishermen off the coast of al-Zawayda in central Gaza and Sheikh Ajlin, southwest of Gaza City, according to the Union of Fishermen's Committees.
In a press statement, the union said Israeli forces opened fire on the fishermen's boats before taking the detainees to the Israeli port of Ashdod.
Seven of the fishermen were later released, while three remained detained at an unknown location at the time of reporting, the union added.
"The arrest of these 10 fishermen adds to a series of daily violations, including killing, arrest, and the destruction of fishing boats and equipment, in addition to preventing fishermen from accessing the sea for more than three years," Zakaria Bakr, an official with the Fishermen's Committees, told The New Arab.
"The arrests were part of broader restrictions and violations affecting Gaza's fishing sector, including the destruction of boats and fishing equipment and restrictions on access to fishing areas," he said.
The number of Palestinian fishermen arrested by Israel since the Israeli genocidal war began on October 2023 had reached about 150, he explained.
Under constant fear
For fishermen who continue to venture into the sea, each trip has become a source of uncertainty.
"We go to sea not knowing if we will return," Salim Hamouda, a Gaza-based fisherman who has worked in the profession for years, told TNA.
Hamouda said the sea had previously provided his family with a stable source of income but had now become associated with fear and insecurity.
"We go out to sea not knowing what will happen to us. We might return with some fish, or we might lose our nets or boats, or we might be shot at or arrested. The sea has become a path to death for us, not a path to livelihood," he added.
Hamouda noted that the decline in fish stocks, rising fuel prices, and the high cost of fishing equipment had further undermined the profession.
Many fishermen and their families were now dependent on debt and humanitarian assistance, according to Hamouda.
"No one asks about us. Organisations talk about farmers, displaced people and workers, but fishermen have been forgotten," Hamouda lamented. "We have families and children who need food, medicine and education, and we have no other source of income."
Mohammed Saadallah, another fisherman from Gaza, said the fishing community had been living under a constant sense of fear and uncertainty, while many fishermen had lost their boats and nets during the war.
"We used to live off the sea, but today we cannot work," Saadallah told TNA, "A boat that used to support an entire family can be destroyed in minutes, while nets that we buy at great expense can be lost in an instant."
"We are not asking for the impossible. We simply want to work safely and return to our families. But even this right has been denied to us," he said.
Heavy losses
The restrictions have affected not only fishermen but also thousands of people who depend directly or indirectly on fishing for their livelihoods.
According to the Union of Fishermen's Committees, around 4,000 fishermen in Gaza work on more than 700 boats, while around 70,000 people rely on fishing and the sale of fish for income.
Bakr estimated that the fishing sector had suffered direct losses of about 120 million US dollars, with around 95 per cent of its infrastructure damaged or destroyed through bombardment, fires and the destruction of fishing equipment.
He estimated indirect losses at approximately 7 million dollars per month, as the fishing catch has fallen to about 2 per cent of its pre-war level.
Bakr described the restrictions and attacks on fishermen as violations of international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention.
He also said the ceasefire had failed to provide meaningful protection for fishermen, as restrictions and attacks continued.
He called on the international community and relevant countries to pressure Israel to halt violations against fishermen, ensure safe access to fishing areas and support the rehabilitation of Gaza's fishing sector.

Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:56 UTC
16:35:56 KST

For the first time, we are spending more than an hour each day travelling to and from work. This emerged in an international study by HR services provider SD Worx, the findings of which appeared in Flemish daily Het Laatste Nieuws. The average Belgian worker’s commute takes 61 minutes a day, which is well above the European average of 48 minutes.
Belgians’ commute to work longer than an hour a day for the first time
With an average commute of 61 minutes a day, Belgians are Europe’s commuting champions. Sweden (57 minutes) and Ireland (56 minutes) complete the top three.
Part of the explanation lies with ‘long-distance commuters’, says SD Worx. More than one in eight Belgian workers (13 per cent) commute for two hours or more a day – the highest proportion of all the countries surveyed. This group often travels more than 120 kilometres a day. The international average is 8 per cent.
“Belgians live quite a long way from work, but traffic jams undoubtedly play a role too,” says Veerle Michiels, a mobility expert at SD Worx. The majority of Belgian commuters travel to work by (company) car.
The study reveals that public transport remains an area for concern: only 25 per cent of women and 28 per cent of men find public transport convenient, reliable and easily accessible. This is lower than the European average of 36 per cent across the countries surveyed.
A symbolic threshold crossed
“The one-hour mark is more than just a symbolic threshold,” emphasises Michiels. “It crosses the line that employees themselves still consider acceptable.”
Nevertheless, Belgians seem to have largely accepted long journey times as part of the job. One in three Belgian employees (34 per cent) say that their commute takes up a significant amount of their working time, which is barely above the average of 32 per cent across the countries surveyed.
Men’s commute longer, women prefer to work from home
The SD Worx study reveals clear differences between men and women. For instance, men spend longer travelling to work (65 minutes) than women (56 minutes). There are also twice as many men (23 per cent) as women (12 per cent) who commute more than 100 kilometres a day.
Women live closer to work, and they also have a lower threshold for acceptable commuting time (47 minutes) than men (67 minutes). They are also more likely to say they would prefer to work from home more often (35 per cent compared with 28 per cent of men).

Apple joins Google in renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:37 UTC
16:35:37 KST

Apple Maps now shows Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for US users, following Google's lead in complying with US President Donald Trump's order as trade talks with Canada sour.
Apple has become the latest company to adopt US President Donald Trump's new name for Lake Ontario — Lake America — on its Apple Maps platform.
The move came less than a week after Trump formally ordered the change in an executive order. Lake Ontario is one of North America's five Great Lakes, alongside Superior, Michigan, Huron and Erie.
The name change was driven largely by the collapse of trade talks between the US and Canada at the end of August, after the US imposed new 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€17.3bn) worth of Canadian goods.
Apple Maps users based in the US will see the lake as Lake America, while those in Canada will still see the original Lake Ontario. According to US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Trump personally approached Apple and urged it to implement the change on its navigation platform.
Trump has since posted a number of AI-generated social media videos, including one showing him kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with one reading "Welcome to Lake America".
At the lake itself, however, Canada has installed a new sign reading "Lake Ontario. Now and Always."
"Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. Long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario," Ontario Premier Doug Ford said, according to the BBC.
Canada has also said it will implement "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs in response to Trump's new levies.
Google under fire
Google made the same move over the weekend, drawing significant criticism on social media, with users accusing the tech giant of capitulating to the Trump administration.
This is despite the fact that while the US president can dictate how the federal government refers to geographic features, he has no authority to force private companies, foreign governments or even US states to do the same.
"The US Geographical Names Information System has formally changed the name for 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in the United States," Google said in a blog post.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using maps in the US will see 'Lake America', those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario', and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names."
However, other map services such as MapQuest have refused to change the lake's name. Last year, MapQuest also declined to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
The latest stand has driven MapQuest to the number one spot on the US Apple App Store's top charts, as of 1 September, ahead of even long-time favourite ChatGPT.

Why Greece is betting on Israel’s Achilles Shield
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:35:08 UTC
16:35:08 KST

Why Greece is betting on Israel’s Achilles Shield
The defence deal between the two countries fits into a larger shift in regional alliances amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
On Monday, Greece and Israel signed a $3.5bn defence deal to build an integrated, multilayered defence network to protect Greek territory dubbed the Achilles Shield. The package brings together the David’s Sling and Spyder interceptors, the Barak air and missile defence system and multimission radars, alongside a separate deal adding Drone Dome systems to protect strategic sites from UAVs.
It is the largest defence deal ever concluded between the two countries. It is also one of the most significant export agreements in Israel’s recent history.
What makes the agreement particularly striking is that it comes as Israel’s global standing is at one of its lowest points in decades. And Greece is no outlier, given that 65 percent of its citizens now view Israel unfavourably. Why, then, has Athens now chosen to openly deepen its ties with Israel in the most politically sensitive of areas: defence and military technology?
Firstly, the shadow of Israel’s conflict with Iran looms large. In early March, an Iranian drone struck Cyprus, Greece’s neighbour and close partner. This likely reinforced anxieties that were already visible in 2024. After Israel, with the help of the United States, downed approximately 300 Iranian drones and missiles, Greek Defence Minister Nikos Dendias called on Athens to develop its own antidrone “dome”.
The deal is therefore partly the product of pragmatic necessity as countries scramble for military solutions to growing drone threats. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, for example, are acquiring antidrone technology from Ukraine, another country able to market its products as battle-tested.
Despite its political disadvantage, Israel has a practical head start, given that it has long practised “arms diplomacy”, using its defence industry as a springboard to cultivate deeper bilateral ties with prospective buyers.
The second factor driving the Achilles Shield deal is another longstanding tenet of Israeli grand strategy: the “periphery doctrine”. This advocates that Israel develop ties with non-Arab states and peoples on the periphery of the Levant to counter the hostility between Israel and its immediate neighbours. It is a recognition that shared threats can produce strategic partnerships. And in the case of Israel and Greece, that shared threat is Turkiye.
The irony is that Turkiye – as a non-Arab state and the gateway between the Middle East and Europe – was Israel’s close partner in the early days of the periphery doctrine. In 1949, Turkiye was the first Muslim country to recognise Israel. In subsequent years, Ankara and Tel Aviv developed robust but clandestine security ties.
This worked as Israel intended in that it opened the door to increasingly public and broader bilateral relations, which continued even after the Islamist-oriented AK Party, or Justice and Development Party, came to power in Turkiye in 2002.
But both sides fell out in late 2008 after Israel launched an offensive on the Gaza Strip. Subsequent divergences over Israeli policies towards the occupied Palestinian territory have gradually unravelled their deep ties.
Bilateral trade has collapsed since Ankara imposed an embargo on Israel in 2024. There are no longer direct flights between the two countries. In June, US President Donald Trump claimed that US pressure stopped Turkiye from joining the war on Iran, on Tehran’s side. This may sound far-fetched, yet it illustrates how Israel and Turkiye not only disagree on many geopolitical issues, but increasingly see each other as rivals and even threats.
What is remarkable is how quickly Greece has filled the void. In previous years, Tel Aviv’s partnership with Ankara precluded closer ties with Athens. But no more: in late 2025, Israel, Cyprus and Greece signed a “Joint Action Plan” that mandates enhanced military cooperation.
Energy has reinforced this strategic convergence. The discovery of substantial gas reserves in the eastern Mediterranean encouraged Israel, Greece and Cyprus to cooperate on pipelines and maritime security.
And, as was the case with Turkiye, more extensive bilateral ties followed security cooperation: some 744,000 Israelis visited Greece in 2025, compared with the peak of 558,000 Israeli tourists who travelled to Turkiye in 2008.
The increasing regional division into competing blocs has also driven the burgeoning Israel-Greece relationship. In February, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu floated a “hexagon alliance” of Israel, Greece, Cyprus, India and unnamed Arab and African countries.
Six months later, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. This alliance broadly overlaps with what commentators earlier labelled the “Islamic coalition”.
This is an evolving dynamic and inter-bloc collaboration is as common as intra-bloc divergences. But it demonstrates that the crisis of confidence in the US as a security guarantor extends beyond the Gulf states and predates the recent war on Iran. It also portends headaches for Washington’s policymakers, given that these increasingly competing states are all US allies.
The Achilles Shield deal is therefore the new manifestation of an old Israeli strategy that has been accelerated by the US-Israel war on Iran. Public scepticism may complicate Greece-Israel relations, but Israeli-Turkish ties deepened for decades despite similarly unfavourable public attitudes.
In short, in the eastern Mediterranean and elsewhere, growing popular outrage at Israel’s policies will continue to coexist uneasily with deepening security cooperation at an elite level. The irony is that the same conflicts that have damaged Israel’s international standing have also increased the value of its military experience and defence technology.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

- The U.S. Air Force added $11.2 million to BlueHalo's Aiman Improved Readiness contract, bringing its total value to $41.2 million.
- Work is being performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, under Air Force Research Laboratory management, with completion expected by February 2028.
The U.S. Air Force has added $11.2 million to a contract with BlueHalo LLC for a program called Aiman Improved Readiness, bringing the deal’s total value to $41.2 million, up from $30 million, according to a Department of War contract announcement.
The modification adds scope to a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract Air Force Research Laboratory originally awarded to BlueHalo. Work will be performed in Beavercreek, Ohio, near the lab’s headquarters at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base. The contract is expected to be completed by February 13, 2028.
Fiscal 2026 research, development, test and evaluation funds totaling $32,147 will be obligated at the time of this modification. Air Force Research Laboratory at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, is the contracting activity managing the award.
BlueHalo, based in Huntsville, Alabama, and Arlington, Virginia, is a defense technology company that works across space superiority, directed energy, counter-drone systems, autonomy, radio frequency and signals intelligence programs. The company has held multiple prior contracts tied to the Wright-Patterson research ecosystem.
In February 2026, the Department of War awarded BlueHalo a separate sole-source contract worth up to $19.95 million to develop AI-enabled frameworks for human biological modeling, work performed in nearby Dayton, Ohio, and managed through the same Wright-Patterson contracting activity. That program focuses on integrating large-scale biological data with artificial intelligence to support monitoring of warfighter health, performance and exposure risks, with work running through February 2029 and options extending to 2031.
BlueHalo has separately built up a portfolio of space technology work. In March 2025, the company said it successfully demonstrated a long-haul, two-terminal laser communication system designed to simulate conditions across low-Earth, medium-Earth and geosynchronous orbit, advancing the technology to Technology Readiness Level 6, a designation indicating the system has been proven in a relevant environment and is ready for accelerated development.
The Air Force has not disclosed the specific technical scope of the Aiman Improved Readiness program, what capability or system it supports, or how this funding increase changes the program’s objectives beyond the added dollar value.

Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.

Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.

Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA,,, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges. REUTERS

Pearl Liang brings Hong Kong dining memories to Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:30:19 UTC
16:30:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — From baskets of dim sum to steamed fish for the family table, some of Hong Kong’s most familiar food memories have made their way to Taipei.
Pearl Liang is bringing them to life through Sept. 30 with a 10-dish selection created with guest chef Chan Hon Cheong (陳漢章), executive Chinese chef of Michelin-recommended One Harbour Road. The offerings draw on three sides of Hong Kong’s food culture — tea-house dim sum, banquet cuisine, and home-style cooking.
The journey starts with dim sum, a dining tradition that took root in Hong Kong after spreading from Guangzhou during the late Qing Dynasty (1850 to 1910). Tea houses became gathering places for generations of diners, who came together over tea and small dishes, with siu mai and fun guo becoming staples of the Cantonese table.
One dumpling takes inspiration from the Qing Dynasty dish “scrambled crab.” Instead of crab, it combines egg white with grass shrimp, atrina, carrot, coriander and scallions, wrapped in pumpkin and red rice powder that turns translucent when steamed and finished with flying fish roe.
Another dish puts a different spin on traditional fun guo. Coriander is incorporated into the wrapper, while the filling combines deep-sea Chilean seabass, shrimp and water chestnut. The dumpling is steamed and finished with flying fish roe.
The menu then moves from the everyday tea house to the more elaborate world of banquet dining, which became increasingly popular in Hong Kong from the 1950s onward. Such dishes are traditionally judged not only by flavor but also by the skill and preparation behind them.
The four-treasure soup is served inside a hollowed-out papaya filled with a broth made from Jinhua ham and chicken, along with crab meat, roast duck, bamboo fungus and Chinese violet. The filled papaya is then steamed, allowing its natural sweetness to blend into the rich broth.
Another banquet-style dish, stuffed crab shell, is a classic Cantonese preparation. It combines crab meat with coconut milk and onion before being fried. The result pairs the sweetness of crab with the creamy aroma of coconut.
Wok hei takes center stage in the fried rice with duck liver, beef and mushrooms. The term refers to the smoky aroma that develops when ingredients are quickly cooked over high heat in a wok.
The dish combines Thai rice, beef, egg and Yunnan termite mushrooms with duck liver. Unlike the goose liver traditionally used in Hong Kong, the lower-fat duck liver is used to better suit local tastes, with crispy garlic added on top.
The final part of the menu turns to the family table, where steamed fish has long been a familiar Cantonese staple. Rather than relying on elaborate sauces, the preparation centers on fresh fish and a handful of ingredients.
The fish is marinated for 24 hours before being steamed with preserved mustard greens, scallions and lotus leaf. It is finished with a sauce made from soy sauce, fish sauce, and rock sugar.
Dessert brings the meal back to another set of familiar Hong Kong flavors. The almond tart takes inspiration from almond tea and steamed milk custard, combining almond paste, egg white and milk in a flaky tart shell.

For the heathens amongst you, the Vulcan salute is the gesture made famous by Leonard Nimoy's character Spock. It involves raising your hand, palm forward, with the middle and ring fingers parted. Europe ends summer with lowest gas inventories on record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:30:01 UTC
16:30:01 KST

MOSCOW, September 2. /TASS/. Gas inventories in European underground storage facilities (UGS) are at their lowest level since records began in 2011, with one month to go before the traditional start of the heating season, posing a risk to gas supplies in the region, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Gas withdrawals from European storage facilities in August were the highest in five years at 771 mln cubic meters, up 11% from last year. At the same time, injections into UGS facilities fell by 8% to 10 billion cubic meters. As a result, total net injections, the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes, were 9% lower in August than a year earlier and among the lowest in 12 years at just 9.2 bln cubic meters.
At the end of August 2026, European UGS facilities were 65.39% full, 16.76 percentage points below the average for that date over the past five years, compared with 77.7% a year earlier. This was the lowest level for that date since records began in 2011. At the end of the month, EU storage facilities held around 71.5 bln cubic meters of gas, 14 bln cubic meters less than a year earlier and the lowest level since 2013. Gazprom forecast that gas inventories in European UGS facilities might not even reach 75% by the next heating season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas inventories. The average pace of replenishment at EU storage facilities in July was among the lowest since records began in 2011 and accelerated only slightly in August. At the current pace, Europe may have its storage facilities only 70-75% full by the start of the fall-winter period, which would be the lowest level ever recorded at the beginning of a heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU countries must ensure that their gas storage facilities are 90% full at some point between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% flexibility margin is allowed in the event of difficult storage-filling conditions. Accordingly, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 billion cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 fall-winter period to meet the storage target. So far, Europe has injected only 60% of the volume needed for the coming winter, or 41 bln cubic meters.
The pace of storage filling this year has been significantly affected by Europe's loss to Asia in the competition for available LNG supplies during the Middle East conflict, higher fuel prices and extreme heat in June and July. During such hot summer periods, demand for electricity to power cooling and air-conditioning systems rises sharply. Gas is one of the main sources of electricity generation, alongside nuclear, wind and solar power.
LNG supplies to Europe
Europe imported one of its lowest volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) for the month of August in the past five years amid intense competition with Asia for available supplies on the market due to the Middle East crisis.
In August, LNG flows from European terminals into the EU gas transmission system totaled only around 9.1 billion cubic meters, up 8% from July but down 6% from August 2025. Over the past five years, Europe purchased a lower volume of LNG in August only in 2024, when imports totaled 7.3 bln cubic meters.
In January-August 2026, LNG flows from terminals into Europe's gas transmission system slowed to around 90.3 billion cubic meters, already 2.8% lower than in the same period of 2025.

Minister sent death threats over plans to shoot “problem wolves”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:29:43 UTC
16:29:43 KST

Minister sent death threats over plans to shoot “problem wolves”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Junior agriculture minister Silvio Erkens says he has has received death threats after bringing new rules making it easier for provincial and local governments to shoot wolves that pose a danger to people.
Erkens told MPs that local authorities needed more powers to drive away wolves that had lost their fear of humans, with shooting a last resort to deal with so-called “problem wolves”.
He faced criticism in parliament on Tuesday for announcing the measures in July before they could be debated, as well as for his comments in an interview about the shooting of a wolf known as Bram in December 2025.
“The world is on fire, all sorts of things are going on and at the same time people in our country are organising funerals for Bram the wolf. Totally out of touch with the world,” Erkens told the Telegraaf.
Bram, officially designated wolf GW3237m, became a cause célèbre for animal welfare campaigners after Utrecht province gave a local hunting organisation a licence to kill him last July.
It followed a number of incidents in which the wolf had approached humans, including an attack on a child. Bram was shot dead last December after campaigners lost a court battle to have the permit revoked.
14 packs
Erkens also criticised a report by scientists at Wageningen University, who said the Netherlands’ wolf population should be allowed to grow both for legal reasons and to benefit the ecosystem.
He said there was “not a single realistic scenario in which you’d want 56 wolf packs”. Currently there are 14 packs established in the country, with more than 100 wolves altogether.
The return of the animals to the Netherlands a decade ago has sharply divided opinions, with right-wing and rural parties calling for stronger measures to cull their numbers while progressive parties have said they should be protected.
Under Erkens’ rules, a wolf becomes a “problem wolf” if they attack people, react aggressively rather than running away, or attack horses or cattle more than once in a two-week period.
Local authorities then have a range of options to drive off the wolf, including shooting them with paintball guns, with killing them as a last resort. “I would hope that all of us would draw a red line if a child is attacked by a wolf,” he said.

AFL boss backflips by scrapping controversial 'Opening Round' experiment

The 2027 AFL season will begin with all 18 teams in action in a traditional nine-game first week.
AFL boss Andrew Dillon confirmed the end of the three-season "Opening Round" experiment designed to grow the game in Queensland and New South Wales.
The decision comes after Dillon previously defended the concept, saying it was "key" to growing Australian rules football in the northern states.
The AFL has scrapped the Opening Round experiment after three seasons and will return to a traditional nine-game first week.
League boss Andrew Dillon today confirmed the demise of the much-criticised concept that featured four games played exclusively in Queensland and New South Wales between only a selection of eight clubs.
Designed to build a foothold in rugby league heartland, it instead drew criticism given the fixturing created a staggered start and early-season byes.
Defending it in March, Dillon said Opening Round was "key" to growing the sport north of Victoria, citing record attendances and membership rises.
"What we've found in the last couple of years is that focus on NSW and Queensland is helping to grow awareness in NSW and Queensland and at the same time it hasn't taken away from our round one," Dillon said at the time.
But, with the season to begin a week later next year due to the MCG hosting the 150th anniversary cricket Test between Australia and England, it has been taken out with the trash.
"We have been working through alternative options to deliver the start of the AFL season," Dillon said in a statement.
"After important feedback from fans and stakeholders, and consultation with clubs and broadcasters, round one will see the return of a traditional nine-game round played across the country."
The first round will be played from Wednesday or Thursday, March 17 or 18, just days after the final day of the historic Ashes Test.
The 24-round home-and-away season will conclude on Sunday, August 30, with the five-week finals series beginning with two wildcard finals in the first week of September.
The grand final will be held on Saturday, October 2 and Gather Round in South Australia is locked in for April 8-11.

U.S. Navy awards GE $2.87 billion for F/A-18 engines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:27:18 UTC
16:27:18 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded GE Aerospace a $2.87 billion sole-source contract for F414 engine component logistics support tied to its F/A-18 E/F/G fleet.
- The five-year contract runs through August 2031, building on nearly two decades of Navy performance-based logistics agreements for the F414 program.
The U.S. Navy has awarded GE Aerospace a five-year contract worth up to $2.87 billion to keep the engines powering its F/A-18 E/F Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler fleet running, one of the largest single logistics contracts the Navy has issued for the program.
The performance-based logistics contract covers support for 17 components of the F414 engine. Work will be performed primarily in Lynn, Massachusetts, GE’s longtime home for the F414 program, which will handle 90 percent of the effort. The remaining 10 percent will be performed at the Navy’s Fleet Readiness Center Southeast in Jacksonville, Florida, where GE has partnered with the Navy on depot-level repair work for nearly two decades. The contract runs through August 2031 and includes no option periods.
The award was made on a sole-source basis, with only one company solicited and one offer received, under authority set out in federal procurement law. Naval Supply Systems Command Weapon Systems Support in Philadelphia is managing the contract.
Fiscal 2026 Navy working capital funds totaling $198.2 million will be committed at the time of award to fund an initial delivery order, with $148.7 million of that amount obligated concurrently as an undefinitized contract action. Those funds will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year. Subsequent delivery orders issued under the contract will draw on future fiscal year working capital funds, which similarly will not expire.
Performance-based logistics contracts work differently from traditional parts purchasing. Rather than the Navy buying individual components as needed, GE is paid to guarantee the availability and readiness of the F414 components covered under the deal, shifting responsibility for inventory management and repair turnaround onto the contractor. The Navy first moved to this model for the F414 engine in 2006, when GE won its original four-year F414 PBL contract covering more than 600 engines already in the fleet.
The F414 is a derivative of GE’s earlier F404 engine, the powerplant that flew the original F/A-18 Hornet, enlarged and improved to power the newer Super Hornet and Growler. The Navy’s long-range procurement plan has called for more than 1,000 F414 engines across its history, and GE has delivered more than 725 of them to date, according to the company. The engine has logged more than 750,000 flight hours across the fleet and has consistently exceeded the Navy’s reliability targets, according to GE.
The F414 also powers Australia’s fleet of F/A-18F Super Hornets, which became the aircraft’s first international customer in 2007, and the engine has separately been adapted to power Saab’s Gripen fighter under the designation F414G.

German police report sabotage attack on power grid near Cologne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:26:56 UTC
16:26:56 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
An electric substation near Cologne was the target of a sabotage attack, police said Wednesday.
“Based on the current state of the investigation, we do not believe this was a technical malfunction, but rather a deliberate act— a criminal offense,” a police spokesperson for the western city of Essen told the German Press Agency.
The cause and circumstances of the incident in the Rhein-Erft district remain unclear. The investigation is in full swing.
According to the spokesperson, the police were called to the substation in the Rheidt district of Bergheim around 8 pm local time (1800GMT) on Tuesday evening due to a technical malfunction.
A short circuit caused several power lines to fail. Based on current information, there was no outage of the general power supply.
 
- Energy provider confirms incident
The facility belongs to the energy provider Amprion, which confirmed the incident.
“An incident occurred on Tuesday evening in the vicinity of Amprion’s Rommerskirchen substation in the Rhineland that affected the operation of power plant feeders,” the company stated early Wednesday morning. This reportedly led to equipment failures at RWE Power.
The Dortmund-based company added: “The general power supply was not affected at any time, and system stability was always ensured.”
Experts from Amprion are working with the relevant safety authorities to clarify the facts as quickly as possible and assess the impact.
The latest incident comes only a day after a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg.
 
- Explosion at Augsburg station
Meanwhile, at least two people sustained minor blast injuries in an explosion at a train station in the southern city of Augsburg on Wednesday.
The station building and Track 1 were closed, while trains were rerouted and local public transportation was disrupted.
Several windowpanes were also damaged.
Explosives experts from the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office were dispatched to the scene. The cause of the explosion remains unknown.
 
-  Suspected sabotage at Brandenburg power plant
The incidents came after unidentified suspects carried out a sabotage attack on an electrical facility at a major power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday, according to authorities.
Brandenburg Interior Minister Jan Redmann said the suspects used projectile devices to cause a short circuit in an extra-high-voltage line near the Jaenschwalde power plant.
“We cannot currently confirm that an explosive device detonated there or anything of that sort,” Redmann said.
Police earlier said devices apparently made from pyrotechnics had been found at an electrical substation, although reports differed over whether any of them exploded.
Bild reported that police had confirmed an explosion and discovered several improvised incendiary and explosive devices, not all of which detonated.
Public broadcaster RBB, however, quoted police spokesperson Stefanie Pilz as saying that no explosion had occurred.
Grid operator 50Hertz said unknown perpetrators damaged several transmission lines, briefly interrupting operations. All lines were later restored, and the public electricity supply was unaffected.
The Jaenschwalde facility near the Polish border is one of Germany’s largest lignite-fired power stations.

The German government said on Tuesday that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russian cultural center in Berlin.

Lufthansa Chair: collaboration with SWISS key to airline success
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02

Lufthansa Chair: collaboration with SWISS key to airline success
For Johannes Teyssen, Chairman of the Lufthansa Supervisory Board, the future of Swiss International Airlines (SWISS) lies in collaboration within the Lufthansa Group, he said in a newspaper interview.
“If we spend our time discussing how the various brands under the Lufthansa umbrella differ from one another, we are on the wrong track,” he said in an interview with the Swiss paper Neue Zürcher Zeitung on Wednesday.
SWISS is independent, but also part of a group. “There’s no other way. Or do you know of any other airline in Europe or North America with a good hundred aircraft that can survive on its own?” Flying, he explained, is simply a business of economies of scale. For the future, there is “only cooperation, not an either/or situation”. Anything else is mere nostalgia.
He does understand the concerns in Switzerland about SWISS, however. “But sometimes they strike me as phantom pains that you still feel years after an amputation – rather than focusing on how we can improve together in the future.”
‘Tackling weaknesses’
His most important task, he said, is to ensure that Central Europe continues to have a large, efficient airline in Lufthansa. “We have seen during the financial crisis and the Covid-19 crisis just how dangerous it is when international players suddenly drop out. We must be capable of operating core infrastructure ourselves – whether in finance, energy or, indeed, logistics.” Europe must not allow itself to become dependent on the Chinese, the Americans or others.
The entire group must return to a position of strength, said Teyssen when asked about the fact that SWISS is Lufthansa’s cash cow, while other airlines such as Austrian, Brussels Airlines or the core Lufthansa brand are making little profit or even incurring losses. He wants to “tackle” the weak spots.
However, it was still too early to announce any specific measures. “The group is enormously complex. It has over 100,000 employees and is responsible for 3,000 flights a day. It hasn’t just turned 100 because it’s incapable of anything. I approach my task with great respect.”
Teyssen has been Chairman of the Supervisory Board at Lufthansa in Germany since May.

Xi calls for SCO to strive for higher quality development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:26:29 UTC
16:26:29 KST

Xi made the remarks in his speeches at the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the "SCO Plus" meeting held in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
China stands ready to work with all parties to implement the Global Civilization Initiative, Xi said, adding that China will host SCO forums on innovation and sustainable development, on people-to-people friendship and on friendship cities, as well as establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation center.
The SCO should always advocate that all countries, regardless of their size, are equal, and that regional affairs should be discussed by all countries to bridge differences and build consensus, properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, and meet common challenges through multilateral collaboration, Xi said.
ADVANCING GLOBAL GOVERNANCE
At the "SCO Plus" meeting, Xi called on the SCO to shoulder the responsibility of the times and work together to advance a more just and equitable global governance system, as well as an equal and orderly multipolar world.
In his address, Xi noted that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible, and multipolarity, independent choice of development paths, and greater democracy in international relations are the right way forward.
Xi said that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power. As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs, he said.
Xi said that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, in which sovereign equality and mutual respect should be upheld as fundamental principles, balance, order and the rule of law as essential requirements, multipolarism, dialogue and consultation as key pathways, and mutual benefit, win-win cooperation and universally beneficial and inclusive development as the way forward.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," Xi said.
China, as a major country, has set an example in this regard and played a leading role, said Seun Sam, a policy analyst at the Royal Academy of Cambodia.
"Major countries taking the lead in abiding by international law can have a demonstrative effect, help safeguard the sovereignty and interests of small countries like Cambodia, promote mutual trust among countries, and achieve peaceful coexistence," he said.
Xi called on countries to promote the common values of humanity, advance the rule of law in international relations, restore the authority and vitality of the United Nations, and improve the coordination and efficiency of global and regional multilateral mechanisms.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi said.
Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, said that with its deep experience in multilateral cooperation, the SCO has developed mature practices for transcending differences, building consensus and fostering cooperation.
It enables countries with different political systems, cultural traditions and interests to engage in equal dialogue and practical cooperation, precisely what is needed to build a more just and equitable global governance system, Ulmasov said.
Highlighting the role of the SCO, Xi put forward three proposals for the organization to advance common prosperity, promote the development and rise of the Global South, and guide the reform and improvement of global governance, to make greater contributions to an equal and orderly multipolar world.
As an important pillar of South-South cooperation, the SCO should carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the "SCO Plus" partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes, Xi said.
"Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said.

Economic Watch: Five years on, China's youngest stock exchange carves out a niche for small innovators
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:26:01 CST
16:26:01 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- An artificial intelligence (AI) model in training or a complex scientific simulation needs computing power. The less visible challenge is matching each job with suitable computing resources across a nationwide network.
Beijing Paratera Tech Corp., Ltd. has built its business around that task. Once a computing job is submitted, its scheduling system matches the workload with suitable resources, while its self-developed platform manages and dynamically allocates computing resources nationwide.
The company was still in a phase of rapid expansion and heavy research spending when it listed on the Beijing Stock Exchange, or BSE, on Nov. 1, 2023. It listed under the exchange's second set of standards, centered on market value, revenue growth and operating cash flow, and raised 290 million yuan (about 43 million U.S. dollars) in its IPO. The proceeds have since gone toward core computing-resource scheduling technology and building a nationwide integrated computing network.
Paratera fits the profile the BSE was designed to serve: a smaller, innovation-led business seeking public-market capital while scaling its technology and operations. China announced the exchange on Sept. 2, 2021, as part of efforts to support innovation by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), saying it would be built as the primary platform serving innovation-oriented SMEs.
Five years later, the exchange has grown from 81 companies at the start of trading to 339. More than 60 percent are national-level "little giant" firms, a designation for specialized and innovative SMEs, and the share among companies newly listed in 2026 is close to 90 percent. Companies in strategic emerging industries and advanced manufacturing account for more than 80 percent of listed companies.
The BSE works in tandem with the National Equities Exchange and Quotations, or NEEQ, in a tiered cultivation system for smaller businesses. The NEEQ has served 14,000 SMEs, and nearly 850 companies cultivated through the market have gone on to list in Beijing, Shanghai or Shenzhen. More than 80 percent received funding support while quoted on the NEEQ.
Its rules reflect that role. The BSE uses four sets of listing standards that take into account market value, revenue, net profit and R&D investment, accommodating companies at different stages of growth. Over its first five years, it has helped SMEs raise about 80 billion yuan, with more than 80 percent of the funds raised going to green and low-carbon development, the digital economy, high-end equipment manufacturing and new materials.
For Hubei Kait Automotive Electronic & Electrical Systems Co., Ltd., or KAIT, a maker of automotive sensors and actuators, that financing model has translated into new products. The company moved from the NEEQ to its Innovation Layer and then to the BSE. In its 2023 IPO, KAIT initially earmarked proceeds mainly for controllers and temperature sensors, but later redirected some funds toward automotive actuators as demand surged amid rapid advances in vehicle intelligence across China's new energy vehicle sector.
Its active-grille-shutter actuators have since been installed at scale in new vehicles, expanding the availability of domestically produced alternatives in a segment supplied largely by overseas manufacturers. KAIT has also used equity incentives to attract and retain R&D and management talent and has expanded into areas including data-center liquid cooling and embodied intelligence.
The same pattern appears in very different industries. Beijing Tri-Prime Gene Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. has brought a digitalized production facility fully online and is leading a Beijing municipal key laboratory focused on long-acting targeted delivery technologies for peptide and nucleic-acid drugs.
Chairman Cheng Yongqing said listing brought changes beyond financing. Ongoing regulatory requirements, he said, had also pushed the company to strengthen corporate governance, information disclosure, internal controls, R&D and branding.
Across the exchange, R&D intensity and the number of invention patents are both more than twice the average for enterprises above the designated size in China. Eighteen BSE companies have been recognized as manufacturing "single champions," a designation for manufacturers that lead in specialized market segments, while 17 have received national science and technology awards.
Trading activity has grown alongside the market. Average daily turnover has risen from less than 1 billion yuan in the BSE's early days to more than 20 billion yuan so far in 2026, while the number of qualified investors has climbed from about 4 million to more than 11 million. Institutional investors now account for 24 percent of trading, up from 9 percent at the market's launch.
International market advisers have also taken note. A midyear review by KPMG, a global organization of independent professional services firms, said the BSE "stood out" in the first half of 2026, with 36 new listings raising 11.4 billion yuan. Both the number of listings and funds raised were five times their year-earlier levels.
The BSE also sits within a much larger SME economy. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said in its 2026 review of SME financing that SMEs contribute roughly 70 percent of China's technological innovation, 60 percent of GDP and 80 percent of urban employment. The report tracks SME equity fundraising on the BSE alongside Shanghai's STAR Market and Shenzhen's ChiNext.
China has continued to broaden capital-market channels for innovative companies. Shanghai's STAR Market supports companies in high-tech and strategic emerging sectors, while Shenzhen's ChiNext mainly serves growth-oriented innovative and entrepreneurial companies. Regulators have also expanded listing standards and introduced measures to make refinancing, equity incentives and mergers and acquisitions more flexible.
Within that broader system, the BSE focuses on innovative SMEs. It operates with the NEEQ in an integrated, tiered structure, creating a progression from NEEQ cultivation to a BSE listing for qualifying companies.
At the larger end of China's technology-financing landscape, 2026 has also brought major listings. Memory-chip maker CXMT Corporation raised about 66.6 billion yuan in gross proceeds in its Shanghai STAR Market offering, making it the largest-ever IPO on the board. Humanoid-robot maker Yushu Technology Co., Ltd., known as Unitree Robotics, raised about 6.1 billion yuan in gross proceeds in its August STAR Market offering.
Beyond the public markets, the Hurun Global Unicorn Index 2026 counted 381 unicorns in China, the world's second-largest total and 38 more than a year earlier. Separately, China ranked first among countries and territories in the Nature Index 2026 Research Leaders, based on 2025 publication data from 178 selected high-quality publications.
For Paratera, that wider story comes back to computing power: matching demand with resources across a nationwide network. Five years after the exchange was announced, the task is different but the logic is familiar -- matching a growing group of smaller innovators with public-market capital. ■

Kenyan editor found safe after abduction, Standard Group says
NAIROBI, Sept 2 - An editor of one of Kenya's largest news outlets was abducted by armed men and released hours later at the edge of a dam more than 200 km (124 miles) away, his employer said on Wednesday.
Alex Kiprotich, an associate editor for Standard Group, was taken from a car near the city of Nakuru shortly before 9:20 p.m. on Tuesday, the company said in a statement.
Dashcam footage shared by Standard Group appeared to show four armed and masked men emerging from a vehicle parked on a busy road. Screams could be heard from the car carrying Kiprotich.
He was dumped near the Masinga Dam more than 200 km southeast of Nakuru, where he was found safe, the company said in a statement, without providing further details of his condition or the circumstances of his release.
Kenyan police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the incident.
Dozens of government critics and activists have been reported abducted or missing in Kenya since anti-government demonstrations in June 2024.
Human rights groups have accused state security agencies of being responsible. Government officials have denied those allegations, although President William Ruto acknowledged in June that there had been instances of excessive and extrajudicial action by members of the security services.
The Standard newspaper, which is owned by Standard Group, has been critical of Ruto's government, accusing it of enabling corruption and police brutality. Ruto has accused The Standard of running "extortionist propaganda headlines".
Standard Group CEO Chaacha Mwita said Kiprotich had escaped an earlier attempt by armed men to seize him in June and that both incidents were linked to his work as a journalist.
"This is a really sad thing to happen in a country like Kenya that says it is free and respects the freedom of the media and journalists to do their work," Mwita said.
Ruto's spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

New tool uncovers thousands of potential cancer targets in "junk DNA"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
15:25:36 CST
16:25:36 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed a new tool to explore the mysterious workings of the vast region of the human genome once dismissed as "junk DNA," identifying thousands of potential targets for precision cancer treatments.
The breakthrough marks a major advance for the pioneering field of RNA-based medicine by providing a way to detect the hidden molecules, known as long non-coding RNA (lncRNA), and determine the likely role each is playing in the growth of different cancers, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute.
The QIMR Berghofer-led team used single-cell and spatial tissue analysis, combined with computational and mathematical modelling, to develop the new tool, with the findings published in Nature Methods.
Using tissue samples from 13 types of cancer, including breast, brain, bowel and skin cancers, researchers identified 219,442 potential lncRNA molecules, including 94,795 that had never been documented before, many of which emerged as top potential functional candidates.
The team mapped the precise three-dimensional location of each lncRNA in cancer tissue and cells, as well as its interactions with other cells, genes and molecules and where that activity was occurring in the tumor.
The findings have been combined into a publicly accessible interactive atlas called SPanC-Lnc, described by the researchers as the most comprehensive resource of its kind.
The study's lead author, QIMR Berghofer Associate Professor Quan Nguyen, said the atlas and the tool are being shared with the global research community to help accelerate the discovery of new cancer biomarkers and therapeutics.
The next step is to validate each lncRNA discovery through functional experiments to identify the most promising candidates for potential diagnostics and treatments, according to the study. ■

Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities' move to increase defense spending

BEIJING, Sept. 2 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the decision of Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te to raise the island's defense budget in 2027, saying it would only bring grave disaster to the people in Taiwan.
Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks in response to a question about the island's defense budget of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars (about 31 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, which Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te said was aimed at strengthening its defense capabilities and demonstrating its resolve to defend itself.
Zhang said Taiwan authorities led by Lai Ching-te have stubbornly adhered to their separatist stance of seeking "Taiwan independence," disregarding the mainstream public opinion on the island that calls for "peace, development, cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation."
They have instead stoked confrontation across the Taiwan Strait and squandered public funds in pursuit of their independence agenda, Zhang said, adding that such efforts are "simply beyond their capabilities" and will only have serious consequences for the people of Taiwan.
"We are unwavering in our resolve and formidable in our ability to safeguard national sovereignty and territorial integrity, and will never leave any room for separatist activities seeking 'Taiwan independence' in any form," Zhang noted.
She called on people in Taiwan to recognize the dangers of "Taiwan independence" separatism, firmly oppose such activities, and safeguard the common home of the Chinese nation.
Taiwan's executive authorities approved the island's 2027 general budget on Aug. 20, with defense spending rising sharply to over 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars for the first time.
The defense budget accounts for roughly 29 percent of total government expenditure, meaning that about 29 out of every 100 New Taiwan dollars in government spending would go toward defense. ■
