One year on, has Swiss AI model Apertus lived up to the hype?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

One year on, has Swiss AI model Apertus lived up to the hype?
One year after its launch, Switzerland’s fully open AI model has passed four million downloads and found real-world uses. Now on version 1.5, Apertus is closing the gap with its rivals, but weaknesses on key tasks still make it difficult for the Swiss model to compete in the fast-moving AI race.
The news arrived with much fanfare: Switzerland finally had its own fully open, transparent and multilingual artificial intelligence (AI) model, designed with data protection rules and the European AI Act in mind. Yet just weeks after its launch, Apertus was attracting harsh criticism. Some usersExternal link went as far as calling it “unusable” and “unable to correctly answer even the most basic questions”.
One year on, the numbers look encouraging. Apertus has surpassed four million downloads on the AI platform Hugging Face – a figure Apertus community lead Oleg Lavrovsky considers representative of global interest in open-source AI projects.
Download figures, however, do not necessarily correspond to real-world usage. Lavrovsky says he is aware of at least 70 external deployments and more than one hundred derivative versions of the Swiss model. That includes Singapore’s SEA-LION projectExternal link, which independently adapted Apertus and other AI models to work across multiple Southeast Asian languages.
For Lavrovsky, this is important validation. “We wanted to create a foundation model,” he says. “When people optimise or adapt Apertus, that’s exactly what’s happening.”
In July, the team released Apertus 1.5, which introduced image understanding and improved reasoning capabilities, among other features. The official roadmapExternal link foresees the release of Apertus 2.0 in 2027.
For those who remain disappointed, Lavrovsky has a clear message: Apertus was not designed to rival ChatGPT. It is not a finished commercial product, but a foundation that companies, institutions and researchers can adapt to their own needs. He acknowledges, though, that questions remain about to what extent the Swiss model’s potential is translating into actual use and tangible value.
AI models can be developed and released with different levels of openness:
Open source: The model’s trained parameters, or “weights”, training code and information about the training data are publicly available, allowing others to inspect, modify and reproduce it. Examples include Apertus and OLMo.
Open weight: The model’s weights are publicly released and can be downloaded and adapted, but the full training code and datasets are not necessarily disclosed. Examples include Meta’s Llama and Alibaba’s Qwen.
Closed/proprietary: The model’s weights, training code and datasets are not publicly released. This is the case for most commercial models, including OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude.
Multilingualism and data safeguards have paid off
Some firms have found uses for Apertus. Ticino-based Artificialy, which specialises in AI solutions, says it works extensively with Apertus.
“We’re not doing charity. We don’t use Apertus because we have to, but because it’s a good model,” says Damiano Binaghi, the company’s head of deep learning.
According to Artificialy, Apertus is already mature enough for some industrial and public-sector applications. The company’s internal tests show particularly good results in translation and multilingual conversations.
“We often prefer Apertus to other models for our clients’ translation tasks, especially when they involve Switzerland’s four national languages or sensitive documents,” Binaghi says.
One example is the southern Swiss canton of Ticino, which has decided to migrate to Apertus for the automated translation of administrative documents. The cantonal migration office benefits the most, as it deals with personal documents in multiple languages and requires both accuracy and strong data protection guarantees.
“The needs of Ticino’s migration office are almost the perfect embodiment of the model’s strengths,” Binaghi says.
Multilingualism is one of the areas in which Apertus’s developers invested most heavily. Around 40% of its training data is in languages other than English, and the corpus includes more than 1,800 languages, including under-represented ones such as Romansh and dialects of Swiss-German. By comparison, estimatesExternal link suggest that current AI models use only around 10% of non-English data.
>> Does Apertus really speak more than 1,800 languages? We’ve analysed the facts and myths surrounding the Swiss AI model:
More
Fact and fiction about the Swiss AI model Apertus
Full openness was one of the reasons AI Singapore chose Apertus as the foundation for a version of its SEA-LION project. “We chose Apertus because it is one of the few truly open-source models in the world and that’s important for research, especially when you need to know exactly what data was used and how it was trained,” Leslie Teo of AI Singapore told Swissinfo by email.
For the same reasons, Apertus has also found applications in medicine. In June, the Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL) presented MeditronFOExternal link, a fully open framework for building clinical AI models based also on Apertus.
The performance gap remains
While Artificialy considers Apertus 1.5 to have improved significantly in translation, vision and reasoning, the company sees room for improvement.
“When it comes to agentic capabilities, despite considerable progress, Apertus is not yet at the level of other open-weight models,” Binaghi says. Agentic AI models are able to independently execute actions involving several steps, such as comparing and booking flights.
The gap is also visible in benchmarks published by the Apertus team itself. The original and largest model, with 70 billion parameters, remains well behindExternal link similarly sized open-weight models, particularly in programming, mathematics and reasoning tasks.
Liip, a Zurich-based digital agency that tested Apertus in ZüriCityGPT, its AI-search tool for answering citizens’ questions, also sees Apertus lagging behind commercial models, although the release of Apertus 1.5 has narrowed the gap.
Josef Kruckenberg, head of generative AI projects at Liip, says Apertus 1.5 produces more useful answers, follows instructions better and is more likely to refuse to answer when it lacks sufficient information. But it lags behind in what Liip considers its most important criterion: faithfulness, or the extent to which every part of an answer is supported by the available sources.
“So far, we haven’t used Apertus in client projects. We felt it wasn’t ready yet,” Kruckenberg says. With Apertus 1.5, it is still too early to determine concrete ways of using it with clients, he adds.
>> AI models have biases? Switzerland’s Apertus is no exception:
More
Swiss AI shows bias despite transparency efforts
The price of openness
Developing competitive fully open models remains a difficult undertaking and involves inevitable trade-offs. “Being truly open-source means being unlikely to use some data, and this has consequences on performance and general capabilities,” Leslie Teo of AI Singapore says.
Artificialy’s Binaghi agrees: Apertus relies on transparent and verifiable public data in line with copyright requirements, unlike proprietary developers that often use licensed or undisclosed datasets. This can lead to a slight quality gap, but it also strengthens digital sovereignty, he points out.
Federico Magnolfi, head of Natural Language Processing at Artificialy, estimates that Apertus 1.0 was already around two years behind the best US models when it launched. “Two years is enormous in a sector that advances every three months,” he says. Closing that gap requires new training cycles, computing capacity and investment. As the flagship project of the Swiss AI Initiative, Apertus already uses a significant share of the public computing resources available. Lavrovsky acknowledges that the allocation of those resources is not without debate.
Not all of Apertus’s shortcomings necessarily stem from the model itself. An AI model is only one component of a wider system. Software for tasks such as retrieving and ranking information relevant to a user’s request also matters. 
 
Kruckenberg of Liip thinks that software components surrounding Apertus still have to be adjusted to work optimally. In Liip’s tests, for example, an inaccurate answer about Zurich’s population was not solely due to Apertus: the retrieval system had failed to select the most up-to-date source. 
For Kruckenberg, this shows that a good AI model alone is not enough to be competitive. “The whole ecosystem around it also needs to be up to the task,” he says.
In its second year, Apertus will have two major challenges: improving the model itself and strengthening the ecosystem on which it depends. Both will be essential if the Swiss AI model wants to remain competitive and achieve broader real-world adoption.

Separately, sirens warning of a suspected hostile aircraft infiltration sounded overnight in several communities in Israel's Upper Galilee. The IDF initially said the alerts were triggered by a suspected aircraft infiltration, but later said interceptors had been launched following a false identification.
Sirens sounded in Kfar Yuval, Ma'ayan Baruch, Dafna and HaGoshrim. It was the first time since June that communities in northern Israel received warnings of a suspected drone infiltration from Lebanon.
Last week, Hezbollah also launched two explosive drones at Israeli troops operating in the Ali Taher Ridge area, according to the military.
The IDF said troops opened fire and downed one of the drones, while contact was lost with the second. No injuries were reported.
"The IDF will not allow Hezbollah to operate against troops in the security zone," the military said at the time.
The IDF later said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in Nabatieh in response, including weapons storage facilities.

“Grey divorce” on the rise among the Dutch over-60s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:54:35 UTC
15:54:35 KST

“Grey divorce” on the rise among the Dutch over-60s
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of couples divorcing in the Netherlands is still falling, but a growing share of those who do split are over 60 – a trend sometimes called “grey divorce”.
Some 24,555 marriages ended in divorce in 2025, according to national statistics office CBS, down from 30,729 in 2018. The decline has been going for more than a decade. Fewer people are marrying in the first place, and those who do tend to stay together longer.
Older couples are the exception. Divorces among the under-60s have dropped since 2014, but among people over 60 they have gone up, and their share of all divorces has climbed from around 8% a decade ago to about 13% last year.
Hundreds of couples now divorce after 40 years or more together, including some who separate after a 50-year anniversary, which was almost unheard of at the turn of the century.
Relationship therapists link the shift to changing attitudes, with divorce more widely accepted than it was a generation ago, and to the moment when children leave home or retirement approaches and long-married partners find they have little left in common.
There is a knock-on effect on housing. Many older people who split up choose to live apart together rather than move in with a new partner, keeping two homes between them and freeing up fewer properties on an already tight market.

US attacks kill 12 in Iran as Tehran strikes bases in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:52:30 EEST
15:52:30 KST

The United States and Iran exchanged their largest attacks in weeks on Tuesday and Wednesday, with US forces striking sites across southern Iran and Tehran retaliating by firing missiles and drones towards US-linked military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and northern Iraq.
Iranian authorities also reported civilian deaths from the US operation, including five people killed when shrapnel struck a home hosting a wedding in southern Hormozgan province.
US Central Command said its September 1 operation targeted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps air defence systems, radar installations, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications infrastructure. It said the strikes followed Iranian attempts to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and US personnel in the region.
Iranian media reported attacks around Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island, Sirik, Konarak, Jask, Chabahar, Ahvaz and other locations close to the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian authorities said one strike near Kouhestak in Sirik County sent shrapnel into a residential property during a wedding reception. Iran's Health Ministry said five people died, including a child, while reports put the number of wounded at between 50 and 68.
Seven more people died and eight suffered injuries in US missile strikes on three locations in Khuzestan province, Iranian state media reported, citing deputy governor Valiollah Hayati.
Iran launched retaliatory attacks within hours.
The IRGC said ballistic missiles struck Camp Titin, a US Marine Corps training site near Jordan's Gulf of Aqaba, as well as Prince Hassan airbase. Tehran claimed the second attack hit hangars used for RQ-4 and MQ-9 drones and killed US personnel.
Those casualty claims remain disputed.
Jordan's armed forces said 13 Iranian ballistic missiles entered its airspace. Air defences intercepted 10, while three landed in remote areas. Jordan reported no deaths or injuries.
Iran also announced missile and drone attacks against US facilities in Erbil in Iraq's Kurdistan region. The IRGC said the strikes destroyed maintenance buildings, equipment warehouses and fuel storage facilities. US and Iraqi authorities had not confirmed those claims.
Bahrain said its air defences intercepted and destroyed Iranian drones after authorities issued repeated warnings telling residents to move to safe locations. Iran said it targeted radar installations and areas of Sheikh Isa airbase associated with US forces.
Kuwait also reported Iranian missiles and drones entering its airspace. Its military said air defences responded to the attacks.
Early Wednesday, the IRGC claimed that missile and drone strikes on Ali al-Salem airbase in Kuwait killed US personnel and damaged a drone hangar. Kuwait had previously reported no casualties.
Iranian commanders said further attacks would follow.
Colonel Ebrahim Zolfaghari, spokesman for Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters, said operations against US forces would continue "until they regret their crimes". IRGC political deputy General Yadollah Javani also warned Arab governments hosting American forces that bases used for attacks on Iran would face Iranian strikes.
US President Donald Trump issued his own threat after Washington's operation, saying Iran would face attacks at a "much harder and higher level" if Tehran retaliated.
Trump later rejected reports that the strikes sought to force Iran back into negotiations.
"I'm not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table," Trump wrote on Truth Social. He said Washington had "almost total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and questioned whether Iranian authorities would seek another agreement.
The latest attacks followed an exchange on August 31, when US forces struck Iran’s Larak Island and Tehran retaliated against US-linked military targets in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, ending a month-long pause in direct attacks.
The conflict began when the United States and Israel launched illegal attacks on Iran on February 28, 2026, in the middle of ongoing negotiations. A memorandum of understanding was signed on June 17, 2026, but it was soon undermined by U.S. violations of its commitments, leading to the breakdown of the agreement and a renewed escalation of hostilities. The Strait of Hormuz was open and free before the US/Israeli aggression.

Demerdzhiev: Bulgaria’s border security could serve as a model for the Entire EU

Ivan Demerdzhiev (L) and Hans Leijtens (R)
PHOTO mvr.bg
Font size
“The security of Bulgaria’s borders and the measures Bulgaria is implementing can serve as a model for the entire European Union”, Minister of Interior Ivan Demerdzhiev said during a meeting with Frontex Executive Director Hans Leijtens, the Ministry of Interior reported. As part of the joint operation “Bulgaria 2026,” 160 Frontex officers have been deployed along Bulgaria’s external borders.

Russia divide resurfaces as AfD leads in Saxony-Anhalt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:46:02 UTC
15:46:02 KST

Russia divide resurfaces as AfD leads in Saxony-Anhalt
NAUMBURG, Germany, Sept. 2 - For Rainer Huppenbauer, as for many in eastern Germany, decades of living with Soviet troops led to a familiarity that has shaped their attitudes to a fault line that has divided German politics since Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A wine merchant in the picturesque town of Naumburg, Huppenbauer says the experience had left many in the regions that made up the former communist German Democratic Republic with a feeling that Russia was not their natural enemy.
"Citizens in the GDR learned to live with the Russians. Because that is better than fighting with them," he says. "Not because they are pro-Russian, they simply don't want a politics that tells them every day how dangerous the Russians are."
With the approach of regional elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, the divide in attitudes towards Russia, which the government in Berlin has accused of being responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport, carrying out espionage and repeated undercover attacks on infrastructure, has again surfaced as a voting issue.
Opinion polls suggest the far-right AfD, an anti-immigrant party with strong support in the east that other parties accuse of being close to Moscow, could win power for the first time at state level.
The party has repeatedly called for an end to German support for Ukraine and a resumption of the energy agreements with Moscow that provided Germany with cheap oil and gas until supplies were abruptly shut off in 2022, when Russian troops attacked Kyiv.
Its programme calls for Russian language teaching to be expanded in schools and underlines the strong interest in "maintaining good relations with Russia, both economically and culturally."
"The current anti-Russian policy of the established parties, on the other hand, is not in Germany's interests," it says.
For Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition of conservatives and centre-left Social Democrats, such talk underlines accusations that an AfD-led government would favour Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom they accuse of waging a form of hybrid warfare against Germany.
Last year, the freshly sworn-in government ended decades of fiscal discipline to free up hundreds of billions of euros to rebuild Germany's armed forces in response to a perceived threat from Moscow.
FAMILIAR WORLD
In Naumburg, for decades tanks rattled over cobbled streets, Russian-speaking officers appeared in restaurants, and ordinary soldiers lived behind barracks walls.
Silke Satjukow, a professor of modern history at Halle-Wittenberg University, says the AfD's appeal in parts of eastern Germany lies in a familiar world people in the West never shared. "From the cradle to the grave, every child in the German Democratic Republic heard that the Soviet Union was 'the Friend'."
"Roughly as many Russian soldiers lived here as the local population. That means, around 30,000 soldiers," says Naumburg Mayor Armin Mueller, a member of Merz's CDU party.
He arrived in Naumburg as a young town planner shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, one of many western German professionals who headed east, drawn by the career opportunities that came with having skills the east lacked.
LOST JOBS — LOST IDENTITY?
Stefan Zimmerer, a Naumburg native born in 1967, fled to the West German embassy in Prague in autumn 1989. He returned months after the wall fell. Later he watched western Germans arrive to run institutions and companies in his home town while East Germans lost their jobs.
Zimmerer said many East Germans are sick of being labelled as Putin's friends, Nazis, or ungrateful AfD voters just because they feel that national politics has turned a blind eye to local problems. "You immediately get put into a box, people don't talk to each other anymore, and people don't even dare to bring up the problem anymore."
The memory of the collapsed East German economy also still looms: At the end of 1989, around 9.8 million of the GDR's population of 16 million had a job. Ten years later the number had been cut in half.
In Saxony-Anhalt, unemployment peaked at 22% in 2003. Today, it stands at 8%. More than 30 years after reunification, people in the East have a quarter of the wealth of West Germans, the 2026 Competitiveness Report East Germany shows.
Amid the current crises many East Germans do not trust the government in Berlin to protect the degree of prosperity they fought hard to build. They prefer detente with Russia, hoping to get back the cheap energy that helped them reach the standard of living they have now.
"Russia is in their minds, and the thinking goes: let's keep them close to us, do business with them, buy their oil and gas and everything will remain as it was (before the Russian invasion of Ukraine)," says wine merchant Huppenbauer. "And those who promise them that are the ones who get elected." REUTERS

Air defense downs 141 of 174 Russian drones; missile, UAV hits recorded at 16 locations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
09:43:22 EEST
15:43:22 KST

On Wednesday night, the Defense Forces of Ukraine neutralized 141 Russian drones, but hits by drones and missiles were recorded at 16 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"As of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 141 targets: 3 S8000 Banderol; 138 Russian UAVs of the Shahed type (including jet-powered), Herbera, and drones of other types," the report states.
In total, overnight into September 2 (from 18:00 on September 1), Russia attacked with two Iskander-M ballistic missiles, two Kh-59/69 guided air missiles, as well as 174 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (about half being jet-powered), S8000 Banderol, Herbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The downing of ballistic and air missiles was not reported.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, hits by Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 16 locations, as well as the fall of shot-down targets (debris) at four locations. In addition, part of the enemy strike means did not reach their targets, with information regarding them currently being clarified.
Thus, the effectiveness of air defense performance on drones alone amounted to about 81%, and on all air targets, given the lack of missiles for anti-ballistic air defense systems, 79.2%.
As reported, the previous massive strike launched by Russia against Ukraine occurred overnight into June 2, when 602 out of 656 drones and 40 out of 73 missiles were neutralized, with hits recorded at 38 locations. The most massive strike was launched by Russia over the course of May 13-14 using 1,428 strike UAVs, of which air defense neutralized 1,362, bringing air defense effectiveness against UAVs to 95.38%.
The highest percentage of neutralized drones and missiles was recorded overnight into July 9, when 718 out of 729 drones and missiles launched by the occupiers were neutralized, yielding an effectiveness of about 96.9%.

Hungary stalls Ukraine's EU accession talks again — Euractiv portal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:43:21 UTC
15:43:21 KST

BRUSSELS, September 2. /TASS/. Hungary has once again stalled the progress of negotiations on Ukraine and Moldova's accession to the European Union by suspending discussions on access to the single market and social policy, the Euractiv portal reported, citing sources.
According to them, Budapest refused to approve the opening of the second and third negotiating clusters, citing the requirement that Kiev first fulfill the agreement on the rights of ethnic Hungarians. The portal noted that the unanimous support of all 27 EU member states is required to open each stage of negotiations. Hungary had already raised similar concerns in July.
The EU accession negotiation process is divided into 33 sections (chapters), which are in turn grouped into six clusters. The start of negotiations sets no timeframe and does not guarantee EU admission. For instance, Montenegro, which could join the EU next year, has been negotiating for 14 years. Turkey formally remains a candidate and has been holding accession talks for nearly 21 years.

Turkey: Cargo ship missing after collision off Istanbul coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:42:00 UTC
15:42:00 KST

Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Turkey coast — authorities
September 2, 2026
Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday.
"We believe, and have more or less confirmed, that the Tugberk Imamoglu has sunk," Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told reporters in Istanbul.
Uraloglu said all 10 crew members aboard the vessel were Turkish nationals and that attempts to reach them by mobile phone had been unsuccessful.
"We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive," he added.
The bulk carrier Tugberk Imamoglu and the chemical tanker Alsu collided at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off the city's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement.
Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels are scouring the area.
The Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said that life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu, had been found floating on the surface.
"Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside," it added.
What else do we know about the missing ship?
The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish-flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea port of Eregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened.
According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled steel.
Authorities believe it sank in waters around 900 meters deep.
The 91-meter Turkish-flagged Alsu, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to the Aegean port of Aliaga. It was empty at the time of the collision and did not appear to have suffered any damage, the governor's office said.
The Sea of Marmara forms part of one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits.

Taiwan to expand offshore wind capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:41:37 UTC
15:41:37 KST

TAIWAN — Taiwan aims to add 15 to 18 GW of offshore wind capacity with government support, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Tuesday.
Cho made the remarks at a ceremony in Taichung marking the completion and start of operations for Orsted’s 920 MW Greater Changhua Offshore Wind Farms 2b and 4, per CNA.
Cho said Orsted is now the country’s second-largest foreign investor. He said the company’s Greater Changhua 1 and 2a wind farms generate enough clean electricity to meet the annual needs of about 1 million households, while the newly completed 2b and 4 projects are expected to supply enough for another 2 million households.
The new wind farms have 66 turbines rated at 14 MW each, with blades measuring 115 meters long, Cho explained, per Liberty Times. He said Taiwan now has 514 offshore wind turbines with a total installed capacity of 4.9 GW, ranking fifth globally.
Cho said the government’s strategy will focus on four areas: setting clear development targets, helping companies participate in international projects, promoting green finance, and streamlining across agencies.
Vice Economic Affairs Minister Lai Chien-hsin (賴建信) said concerns remain over whether Taiwan will have enough electricity to meet future demand, CNA reported. He said the Ministry of Economic Affairs has prepared a 10-year power supply plan covering supply chains, industry, and computing centers, and has raised its estimate for average annual electricity demand growth over the next decade to 2.5%.
The Greater Changhua 2b and 4 wind farms are located about 35 to 60 kilometers off Changhua County and use Siemens Gamesa 14-MW turbines. Offshore construction began in February last year with the final turbine being installed in January this year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Wednesday the government will prepare land and factories to help semiconductor and tech firms start operations faster, CNA reported.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of Semicon Taiwan, Cho said the Cabinet has instructed the economics ministry and science council to prepare land and factory facilities. Ready-to-use sites would allow investors to start operations with fewer delays, he said.
Cho said rapid advances in artificial intelligence are driving closer international cooperation in high tech. He said the country must remain part of that development as governments and companies invest in the next generation of technology.
More than 4,300 exhibitors from over 60 countries are taking part in Semicon Taiwan, Cho said. The US, European Union, UK, and other governments have also set up national pavilions, showing growing international interest in the semiconductor industry.
Semiconductor output reached about NT$6.7 trillion (US$209.1 billion) in 2025, up 22.7% from a year earlier, Cho said. Growth has exceeded expectations as demand for advanced chips and AI technology continues to rise, he added.
TSMC and other major international companies are investing heavily in advanced manufacturing, packaging, and memory technology, Cho said. The government also plans to strengthen the equipment and materials sectors to expand the industry's role in global supply chains.
Cho said continued investment by major companies shows confidence in the local technology sector. Their expansion could create further opportunities as the global semiconductor market continues to grow.
The government is also promoting 10 major AI infrastructure projects that Cho said will support the semiconductor industry's development. The projects aim to advance technology, strengthen international links, and encourage new AI applications.
Cho said the government will estimate how much electricity demand will rise as AI-related industries expand. It will work to provide enough power while preparing other resources needed for future investment.
The government will focus on land, energy, workers, and financing to support expansion, Cho said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Medical University Hospital said that it had become the first hospital in the country to fully implement an intelligent blood tube preparation system across all its nursing units.
The hospital said the system automates the preparation and labeling of blood collection tubes. The new process allows nurses to spend more time on patient care, reducing blood tube preparation time by 90.4%, per Storm Media.
TMUH began introducing the automated process in general wards in May and subsequently expanded it to intensive care units, the emergency department, and hemodialysis facilities. The system now covers all 18 nursing units, with 21 tube preparation machines installed.
In the past, after receiving a blood test order, nurses had to confirm the tests required and determine the appropriate number of tubes needed. The final step was manually attaching a label to each blood tube.
Under the new system, nurses can select an order at a nursing station or scan a barcode on a laboratory order. The system automatically determines the required tube type, dispenses the tubes, and applies the appropriate labels, reducing repetitive manual work and the need for nurses to make judgments about tube selection.
TMUH Nursing Department Director Lin Shu-chuan (林淑娟) said manual tube preparation could result in specimen rejection if the wrong tube was selected or a barcode was incorrectly positioned. Such errors can increase the risk of patients having to undergo another blood draw.
Since the system was introduced three months ago its utilization rate in general wards has reached 95.6%. The hospital said tests showed that preparing three blood collection tubes took an average of 83 seconds under the manual process, compared with just eight seconds using the automated system, per Storm Media.
Based on 24,965 tubes prepared, the hospital estimated that the system had saved about 520.1 hours of nursing work. Lin said the system's value extends beyond speed, as it is intended to improve specimen accuracy and patient safety.
For example, nurses can scan both a patient's wristband and the barcode on the specimen tube, and if the information does not match, the system prevents the process from proceeding, helping reduce human error. The system also links the hospital's medical, nursing, and laboratory information systems, creating an integrated process from specimen collection to testing.
TMUH Superintendent Shih Chun-ming (施俊明) said smart health care should not simply involve purchasing new machines but should address practical problems faced by nurses and other frontline workers. He said the true value lies in using technology to handle repetitive tasks so nurses can devote more time to clinical care and patient support.

Ukraine Requests to Purchase Patriot Missiles Using Funds From EU Loan
Ukraine has officially requested permission from the European Commission to purchase Patriot interceptor missiles using funds from a €90 billion ($98 billion) loan provided by the European Union, according to Suspilne on September 1.
Ukraine is asking for over €2 billion ($2.18 billion) to purchase these missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The European Commission previously received a list of military equipment from Ukraine detailing plans for the bulk of the remaining €6 billion ($6.54 billion) in the defense portion of the loan.
Most of those requested items involve equipment produced in Ukraine and the EU, primarily drones.
The request to purchase Patriot air defense missiles is a key element in Ukraine's plans to strengthen air defense and protect critical infrastructure amid Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Previously, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is seeking 300 additional Patriot interceptor missiles for the winter as it works to strengthen its air and missile defenses.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s Air Force has requested 360 Patriot missiles, but securing that quantity remains difficult given annual production levels.
Kyiv is therefore working with partner countries to identify additional supplies and hopes the United States could provide a small share of its existing stockpile.
On August 24, the European Commission approved a €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) defense support package for Ukraine to fund air defense systems, missiles, ammunition, and radars. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that the assistance was intended to help Ukraine protect its people and airspace amid intensifying Russian aerial attacks.
EU Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius noted that Ukraine had faced 376 missile strikes in the previous month alone, adding that the funds were provided through the EU's broader €90 billion ($105 billion) Ukraine Support Loan.

Julija still missing following the mudslides in Nepal
Julija Jakovicka (47), a Belgian-Latvian national, was on a group tour to Tibet and Nepal with 32 other people when disaster struck. In the border region, a tidal wave of mud, water and debris swept everything away. Since then, there has been no trace of the group of travellers.
“It is unclear exactly where Julija and her travelling companions were when the disaster struck, what happened to the buses, and whether or not the group had reached or crossed the border with Nepal,” say Julija’s family.
‘We are now trying to find out what information is missing. That is why we are appealing to anyone who knows Julija, who may have information about her or her travelling companions, or about the situation at the border, to contact us.’
Lived in Ghent for many years
The family wants to put a face to the name Julija and hopes to reach as many people as possible with her story.
‘Julija was born in Latvia on 16 October 1978, but she also holds Belgian nationality. She spent a significant part of her life in Ghent (East Flanders). She now lives in Frankfurt, Germany, where she works at the European Central Bank (ECB).’
‘Nevertheless, Julija still has strong ties with Flanders and Belgium. Her two sons, aged 16 and 19, still visit their grandmother in Flanders regularly. The eldest son is currently studying in Rotterdam.’
‘All we know is that Julija was travelling as part of a group tour organised by the Latvian travel agency Yantra.lv. According to our information, the group consisted of 33 people, mainly travellers from Latvia, along with some from Estonia and Lithuania.’
‘On 25 August, the group was staying at the Yuntian Intercontinental Hotel in Nagchu, Tibet. On 26 August, the day of the natural disaster, they left the hotel by coach at around 9 am local time, heading for the border with Nepal. Since then, there has been no sign of life from any of the 33 travellers.’
Any information is helpful
The family is particularly hoping to reach people who were in the area themselves on 26 August or who, through local, professional or personal contacts, have access to information that the family does not yet have.
"In particular, information may be important from travellers or emergency services personnel who were in the border area that day, people who saw the buses or members of the Yantra. lv group, travellers who used the same route or border crossing, people who took photographs or video footage in the area, people with contacts at local travel organisations, guides, emergency services, hospitals or authorities in Tibet, China or Nepal... “
‘Even information that seems unimportant at first glance can help to piece together the group’s final movements. Every photo, video, eyewitness account or local contact could potentially help to fill in a piece of the puzzle. Her two sons and the whole family are waiting in great uncertainty for news of their mum.’
Do you have any information, images or contacts that might help? If so, please contact the family directly via julijamissing@gmail.com.
The family asks people not to share unconfirmed information publicly on social media. Please pass on any tips directly, so that the information can be verified and, if relevant, passed on immediately to the relevant authorities. Every tip could be important.

EU: ‘Return hub’ plans in Rwanda and Uganda risk becoming ‘cruel black holes’ for human rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:38:33 UTC
15:38:33 KST

Ahead of the 4 September meeting between Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to discuss progress on plans to deport people to so-called “return hubs” in countries outside Europe where they may never have set foot, likely be to centres or facilities funded by EU member states, Eve Geddie, Director of the European Institutions Office of Amnesty International, said:
“By their very design, and wherever they may be located, ‘return hubs’ carry a risk of grave human rights violations, including arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment, and forced onward returns to countries of origin. There is a real danger that these locations will, in practice, become cruel black holes for human rights to outsource or offshore detention and deportation. Any responsible government should reject these plans outright.
“We are particularly alarmed that discussions are reportedly zeroing in on two countries with appalling human rights records: Uganda and Rwanda – despite ongoing conflict and political instability in the Great Lakes Region.
“These negotiations, and the EU’s broader so-called ‘migration diplomacy’ approach, are based on deep power asymmetries reflecting an unabashed attempt by the EU to shirk its migration responsibilities and shift them on to countries in the Global South that are already doing far more than Europe to receive refugees and with fewer resources.
“From the Italy-Albania deal and governments’ past attempts to outsource or offshore their migration policies, we already know that ‘return hubs’ will disproportionately harm racialized people. Following the shameful chants to ‘send them back’ heard in the European Parliament in June, governments across the political spectrum are now dancing to this same xenophobic and racist tune – willing to pursue an agenda to increase deportations at seemingly any cost. Amnesty International will continue to expose the harms and illegalities of these policies – and to resist them.”
Background
Amnesty International has repeatedly warned that ‘return hubs’ cannot be implemented in a human rights-compliant manner, given the severe risk of rights violations, as with all past attempts to outsource migration responsibilities.
While specific details have yet to be disclosed, there is a real danger that “return hubs” will in practice become deportation and detention sites involving automatic – and therefore arbitrary and unlawful – detention; refoulement, including in return hubs or through onward deportations; torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or punishment; and restrictions on access to due process and effective remedies, among other abuses.
Negotiations between these five EU member states are reported to be particularly advanced with Uganda and Rwanda, despite the well-documented human rights violations in both countries. There have also been reports of a planned centre in Uganda, which could become operational in 2027, that could accommodate up to 10,000 people.
The EU Return Regulation, which is yet to be formally adopted but will provide the legal basis for “return hubs” in EU law, states that these agreements may only be reached with countries where “international human rights standards and principles […] are respected.”
Amnesty International has long documented rights violations in Uganda, including repression, unlawful detention and deportations, and notably its extreme anti-LGBTQ+ law, which criminalizes consensual same-sex acts and carries the death penalty for the offence of ‘aggravated homosexuality’.
The Rwandan government and military control and closely support the M23 armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which has perpetrated serious abuses that may amount to war crimes. In its ruling in 2023, the UK Supreme Court found that Rwanda was not a safe third country for the UK to forcibly transfer people seeking asylum, given the country’s record of repression, restrictions on media and political freedoms, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment and torture. In September 2025, the European Parliament called on the European Commission to review assistance, including financial aid, to Rwandan public institutions involved in arbitrary detentions, torture or unfair trials.

As US seeks Gaza donor’s extradition, wife warns of ‘terrifying precedent’
Imprisoned in Spain, James ‘Fergie’ Chambers has donated some of his wealth to humanitarian projects in Gaza but is accused of aiding Hamas.
Madrid, Spain – A wealthy American donor to Palestinian causes who faces extradition from Spain to the United States over alleged financial support of Hamas is a victim of “political persecution”, his wife and lawyers have told Al Jazeera.
James “Fergie” Chambers was arrested on the Spanish island of Ibiza in July while searching for a school for his son with his wife, actress Stella Schnabel.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items

- list 2 of 4How a Swedish Palestinian minister raised controversy with Star of David

- list 4 of 4Israeli strikes on Gaza kill at least five, including children
US authorities have linked Chambers to the transfer of $7.5m to Tunisia and allege that the funds were ultimately used to provide financial support to the Palestinian armed group Hamas.
The indictment remains sealed, so the specific allegations against Chambers – who denies wrongdoing – are not yet known.
Chambers, heir to one of the richest families in the US, has supported a handful of humanitarian projects in Gaza with funds totalling more than $1m, a member of his legal team said shortly after his arrest.
The extradition effort is believed to be the first of its kind involving a US citizen accused of providing support to Hamas.
Chambers, who describes himself as a Marxist-Leninist, has been held in a Madrid jail for six weeks as Spanish authorities consider the US extradition request.
Schnabel, who is also an activist, said she was driving through the Balearic island of Ibiza with her husband to search for a school for their five-year-old son, as they were moving from Ireland to Spain, when he was arrested.
“Suddenly, several unmarked cars cut us off. Police officers got out of the cars and told us to get out of the car. I got out my phone, and they told me not to phone,” she told Al Jazeera. “They handcuffed Fergie. We said we loved each other, and he said, ‘Tell the kids I love them’. And they bundled him into a car, and he was gone. That was July 10. Over six weeks ago.”
Schnabel said US President Donald Trump’s administration was targeting her husband for being one of the largest donors to humanitarian projects in Gaza. This included supplying bread, water and medical care.
“He should be at home with his family, continuing his humanitarian work. Instead, he is facing political persecution because he has stood with the Palestinian people,” she said. “This sets a terrifying precedent for repression of the wider movement for a free Palestine, including precedent for the Trump administration exporting its repression far beyond the US borders to target the people of Europe.”
The US Department of Justice declined to comment when contacted by Al Jazeera.
‘We hope that Spain will not grant extradition’
The US sent the indictment and documentation to Spain last week, in time to meet the 45-day deadline after Chambers’s arrest in July.
Al Jazeera understands that the indictment is still sealed and has not been revealed to his defence team.
Spanish authorities must now assess the US request. Among the issues they may consider is whether the extradition would amount to political persecution, a circumstance that could provide grounds for refusing it.
Chambers comes from the family behind Atlanta-based Cox Communications. In 2023, he reached an agreement with his relatives under which his stake in the family business was bought back for approximately $250m, following a break with the family.
Since then, he has been funding dozens of projects in 20 countries, Schnabel has said.
On the central allegation about funding Hamas, Schnabel said this was a “trumped-up charge” for which the US has not provided a “shred of evidence”.
“My understanding is that the US appears to rely on the fact that he transferred $7.5m of his own funds from the US to Tunisia. The reality is that this money was transferred to Tunisia because we were living there, and for philanthropic activities, including supporting Club Africain [a football team],” Schnabel said.
“The money sponsored the club, helped to pay its debts and overdue salaries, rebuild its training centre and develop football fields for young people.”
The Tunisian side secured the league title in May.
Lawyers for Chambers have also pointed to his outspoken views on Israel and its genocidal war on Gaza.
In the week after the October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, Chambers posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’. There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for. No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done anything wrong. It’s simply genocide. Like it has been.”
In the wake of the 41-year-old’s arrest, FBI agents raided the rented property in Ibiza where Chambers had been staying, The Guardian reported.
Chambers is represented by Spanish human-rights lawyer Baltasar Garzon, who has argued that the case against his client is politically motivated and connected to his humanitarian work in Palestine.
“We request our client’s provisional release and to file all necessary legal actions with the courts,” he told Al Jazeera.
In 1998, Garzon sprang to international attention when he sought the extradition from London of the former Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet. He has also acted in human rights cases in Spain and Argentina.
“We hope that Spain will not grant extradition in what we consider to be a case of political persecution based on our client’s ideas and humanitarian aid to Palestine,” he added, referring to Chambers.

Drownings in Lake Cauma occurred after normal swimming hours
There have been two fatal accidents while swimming within three days at Lake Cauma in Flims in canton Graubünden. Mayor Christoph Schmidt says he is shocked, but does not want to hear any talk of a ban on swimming outside opening hours.
The latest incident took place on Sunday evening. At around 7:00 pm, a 27-year-old German man was trying to swim to a small island to rescue a friend when he himself got into difficulty. Despite rescue efforts, the young man died at the scene.
Just three days earlier, a 17-year-old tourist from the United Kingdom also had problems swimming and died that same evening in hospital.
The public bathing area at Lake Cauma is open every day during the summer season from 8:30 am to 5:00 pm, according to the Flims-Laax tourist board’s website.
“We are deeply shocked by the two tragic accidents that occurred in such quick succession at this much-loved and popular swimming lake. Both incidents occurred in the evening, after normal opening hours, when there is no guaranteed supervision in the water,” Schmidt told Keystone-ATS news agency.
+ A second young man drowns in same Swiss lake
The last tragic incident took place over ten years ago, in 2016. “Our thoughts are with the families of the victims, and we wish to express our deepest condolences to them for these tragic and painful events,” the mayor added.
Dangers often underestimated
Schmidt does not believe that Lake Cauma is currently particularly dangerous for swimmers. Indeed, it does not present any particular risks in terms of temperature or currents. However, it can generally be observed “that inexperienced swimmers repeatedly underestimate the dangers of open waters such as lakes”. In this regard, the mayor cites distances and temperature.
For Schmidt, “as with many other open bodies of water”, a ban on swimming outside opening hours is not currently under discussion, even following the fatal accidents. For some time now, however, information on the safety plan and bathing rules has been displayed within the bathing area. The safety and rescue plan for the lake and its implementation are refined each year in collaboration with the operator, “where appropriate, with the involvement of the relevant authorities”, the mayor added.

German Navy successfully tests Israeli LORA missile system in the North Atlantic
The German Navy has successfully completed a double test of Israel Aerospace Industries' LORA ballistic missile system, launching the weapon from an operational vessel in the North Atlantic
The German Navy conducted the classified test as part of its OPEX operational testing program, an initiative designed to support the "Marine 2035 and Beyond" program aimed at preparing the fleet for current and future security threats, IAI said in a statement. The missile, launched from a German Navy vessel equipped with the system's command and launcher carriage, successfully navigated its trajectory and struck its target with precision in both test scenarios, meeting all objectives.
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, inspector of the German Navy, called the test a historic achievement. "With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we have made naval history. I am extremely pleased with this achievement," Kaack said, according to Bild and a German Armed Forces Instagram post. "The system can be successfully deployed from our units, and its potential range surpasses anything we have previously known. For the protection of Germany and our allies, this test represents a new chapter in terms of deterrence and readiness at sea."
IAI Chairman Boaz Levy called the test "an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Ministry of Defense," noting it took place in Germany, "the country where the world's first ballistic missile was invented." He said the achievement builds on Israel's Arrow-3 missile defense system already stationed on German soil, further strengthening the countries' defense partnership.
IAI CEO Guy Bar Lev said the naval LORA system was "designed to provide precision strike capabilities at depth, even in challenging operational environments," calling it "one of the most advanced and operationally proven ballistic missile systems in the world."

LORA, which stands for "Long Range Attack," is an Israeli-developed short-range ballistic missile system delivered in a launch container for rapid deployment from naval vessels. According to Bild, two German frigates were deployed to waters between Ireland and Iceland for the test, with the missile system offering a range exceeding 500 kilometers (310 miles).
Suggested articles
IAI markets the system as capable of striking "strategic targets deep within enemy territory from mobile or maritime platforms," with the ability to destroy a detected target within ten minutes. The Israeli military has reportedly used the system, including an air-launched version, in strikes in Lebanon and against Iran.
The test comes as Germany moves to expand its long-range precision strike capabilities amid heightened concern over Russian aggression, following recent drone incidents including an attack on Leipzig Airport that Berlin has blamed on Russia. Germany is also finalizing a separate deal to acquire US Tomahawk missiles, with a range of up to 2,500 kilometers (1,553 miles), following an agreement reached on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara.

Estonia's defense minister's resignation sought in wake of national defense scandal

Estonia's defense minister's resignation sought in wake of national defense scandal
Pressure is mounting on Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur (Reform Party) to resign after the National Audit Office identified serious problems with financial management in the defense sector, with criticism now coming from both opposition and coalition politicians.
Social Democrat Raimond Kaljulaid said Pevkur had been a hardworking minister and a strong supporter of Ukraine but should consider stepping down voluntarily.
"If Hanno were to ask my opinion today, I would advise him to very seriously consider resigning as defense minister at the earliest opportunity and on his own initiative," Kaljulaid said. "The National Audit Office's repeated criticism, the confusion surrounding procurements and advance payments, and now a criminal investigation — it is simply too much."
Kaljulaid said Prime Minister Kristen Michal should appoint a nonpartisan defense expert with an impeccable reputation to lead the Ministry of Defense for the six months remaining until the elections.
Social Democratic Party leader Lauri Läänemets also called on Pevkur to resign, saying major problems identified at the ministry had remained unresolved for a year.
"We are spending a great deal of money on national defense, and the entire defense sector is under fire today. Hanno Pevkur has become a figure who, in a sense, is undermining trust in national defense," Läänemets told ETV morning show "Terevisioon."
Läänemets said that if Pevkur does not step down voluntarily, the issue could eventually lead to a no-confidence motion against him in the Riigikogu. Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu has also called for Pevkur's resignation.
Pressure on Pevkur increased further Wednesday when Toomas Uibo, chair of coalition party Eesti 200's parliamentary group, said he personally did not see how Pevkur could remain in office if media reports about defense procurement were accurate.
"This is not how things should or can be done in Estonia. I very much hope that the Reform Party makes decisions quickly and takes responsibility," Uibo said. "If the facts reported by the media are true, I personally don't see how the defense minister can continue in office."
The criticism follows a National Audit Office report that found numerous serious problems at institutions under the Ministry of Defense, which auditors said increased the risk of misuse of state funds and assets. Similar problems had been identified a year earlier.
Eesti Ekspress also reported that Estonia paid €70 million in advance to Indian suppliers as part of an effort to purchase artillery shells for Ukraine, despite the suppliers having never previously sold a shell. The promised materiel did not arrive, and the dispute is now in court.
The Prosecutor's Office has since opened a criminal investigation into circumstances covered by National Audit Office audits from this year and last year.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal has called a Cabinet meeting for early Thursday, asking Auditor General Janar Holm to provide an overview of accounting irregularities in the defense sector. Michal said he expects Pevkur, Commander of the Estonian Defense Forces Andrus Merilo, Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) Director General Elmar Vaher and Ministry of Defense Permanent Secretary Kaimo Kuusk to present a concrete plan for quickly resolving the problems.

Iceland said ‘No’ to EU membership talks. What does it mean?

Unknown Publisher

Icelanders voted to keep their stalled EU membership bid on ice, dealing a blow to Brussels' post-Ukraine enlargement drive. Watch the video!
On 29 August, a majority of Icelanders rejected reopening EU accession talks, frozen since 2013, turning down what the government called a "now or never" moment.
The result means no new negotiations with Brussels and no change to Iceland's existing ties: full access to the single market and Schengen area through the European Economic Area, but no seat in the European Parliament or vote in the Council. The referendum was legally advisory, but the government pledged to respect it, effectively shelving the question for years.
Iceland already adopts most EU law through the European Economic Area. Still, it retains unilateral control over its fishing waters, a legacy of the 1970s Cod Wars, which it was not willing to trade for shared quotas under Brussels' Common Fisheries Policy.

Expert: Health Insurance Fund cuts likely to lengthen waiting lists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Expert: Health Insurance Fund cuts likely to lengthen waiting lists
If the Health Insurance Fund (Tervisekassa) tries to reduce its expenses, it will likely have to do so by cutting services — which means longer waiting lists, says healthcare expert Andres Võrk.
On Friday, the Health Insurance Fund supervisory board approved the draft budget for next year, and Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller said the goal for the coming years is to bring the fund out of its financial crisis so that by 2030 the budget reaches balance — or even a surplus.
University of Tartu econometrics lecturer and healthcare expert Andres Võrk said that there is still little information about Health Insurance Fund's plans, and only one clear measure is known so far — postponing the pay rise for healthcare workers.
"It's clear that this immediately creates significant tension with healthcare workers, who have said during wage negotiations that salaries should rise at least at the pace of average wage growth, if not more," he said.
Võrk added that if the Ministry of Finance forecasts average wage growth of 5.6 percent this year and 4.7 percent next year, it is hard to see where such an increase could come from if it is not reflected in the price component of healthcare services.
"The minister suggested that Health Insurance Fund will not raise wages and that healthcare institutions should find internal buffers for pay increases. But considering that salaries make up a very large share of total costs — about half for hospitals and more than half for family‑doctor centers — finding such a buffer while other input prices rise is unlikely," Võrk said.
He noted that Health Insurance Fund can save costs not only by limiting price growth but also by reducing the number of services. But to assess this, more information is needed: how much the volume of services is expected to change, where reductions might occur, and how this would affect waiting lists.
Although Health Insurance Fund has said that access to healthcare services will not be reduced, Võrk said this may not be enough: the population is aging and demand for healthcare services is increasing. If the number of visits remains at the current level, waiting lists will grow.
"Both the minister and the head of Health Insurance Fund have emphasized the need for greater efficiency in the system — better care pathways. That is always important, whether money is abundant or scarce; efficiency must always be improved," Võrk said.
He explained that when money is lacking, hospitals are forced to become more efficient — but funding must be directed to areas where it creates the most added value.
"This may mean different choices between specialist care and primary care, or between different fields of specialist care — increasing funding in some areas more than others," Võrk said.
As a health economist, Võrk believes Health Insurance Fund should be much better staffed and have significantly stronger analytical capacity. While the fund is proud of its low administrative costs and efficient management, he said it should actually be a stronger negotiating partner for healthcare institutions when discussing prices and the value of services.
Confido CEO: Fund should act like an insurance company
Medical center Confido CEO and general surgeon Edvard Garder said that although little is known about the Health Insurance Fund's budget plans, in general it is certainly possible to achieve accounting balance. The question, however, is how unbalanced Estonia's healthcare system will be afterward.
"Tervisekassa cannot significantly influence its revenue side. Balance therefore means cuts. Budget lines can be renamed or new ones created, but the substance remains cuts," Garder said.
He noted that the think-tank Foresight Center has previously described the deficit as structural — meaning new annual cuts would be needed every year.
"Maintaining the same volume and quality of services without cuts would only be possible if operations were made more efficient. Given the current situation, I do not believe it is possible to achieve tens of millions in efficiency gains year after year when all input prices keep rising," Garder said.
Garder added that Estonia should abandon state‑planned pricing: Health Insurance Fund should not spend time calculating prices itself but should behave like an insurance company — which, in essence, it already is.
"Health Insurance Fund should purchase services based on quality and price from different providers, regardless of ownership form. The market will set the prices," Garder said.
He added that nothing currently forces hospitals within the hospital network development plan (HVA) to operate more efficiently or cheaply, whereas providers outside the HVA are forced to compete on price.
Minister Joller's promise that Health Insurance Fund's budget will reach balance — and hopefully even a surplus — by 2030 sounds very ambitious when stated publicly, Garder said.
"Of course I hope for the best for Estonian health care and I am very interested to see how this surplus will be achieved. But fundamentally, it is wrong to speak of Health Insurance Fund's budget balance as the goal. The goal should be a sustainable healthcare system as a whole, not simply 'Health Insurance Fund at zero by 2030'," Garder said.
He added that without major reforms — such as ownership‑neutral service purchasing or allowing funding to follow the patient to whichever provider they choose — he does not consider the goal realistic.
Health Insurance Fund costs surged after Covid
Võrk said that looking back at why Health Insurance Fund's costs have grown, the rapid surge occurred after the Covid pandemic. In 2023 and 2024, there were large pay increases for healthcare workers and rising input prices across the economy.
"Before Covid, in 2019, Health Insurance Fund's costs made up five percent of GDP; now they are six percent. One percentage point may seem small, but in reality that is nearly 20 percent growth," Võrk said. "Costs grew quickly, and everyone has gotten used to it."
But if the goal is to bring this share back down to pre‑Covid levels — where healthcare costs made up a smaller portion of the economy — the problem is that wages and input prices cannot be reduced. Expectations for the healthcare sector have risen.
"That is very hard to do. It seems the minister and Health Insurance Fund are trying to reduce the fund's role again, but this likely means cuts to services, because I do not believe healthcare workers would accept a decline in real wages," Võrk said.
He added that this means providers will offer fewer services for the price Health Insurance Fund pays and will find work elsewhere in the private sector — funded by individuals or companies. Movement from publicly funded to privately funded health care has increased in recent years.
Some service prices may contain 'air'
Võrk said that in terms of how much public funding goes to healthcare, Estonia is around the European average. Estonia spends 13 percent of public funds on health care, compared to 15 percent in Finland and 17 percent in Norway. This means Estonia does not value health care as highly as wealthier countries — but that is typical, he said: the richer a country becomes, the more it spends on health care.
He pointed out that some services funded by Health Insurance Fund may contain "air" — meaning prices may be higher than necessary. For example, laboratory service prices were cut by 15 percent last year because technological advances allowed a review. Next, diagnostic services such as radiology may be reviewed.
"Looking at the whole picture, hospitals' profits have decreased in recent years — they are not swimming in money. Some services with buffers, like lab or diagnostic services, help subsidize loss‑making services," Võrk explained. "If price lists are reviewed, everything should be reviewed."
How the changes will affect patients is not yet known, because details of how Health Insurance Fund plans to save costs are unclear. Võrk said the fund is right to emphasize that patients do not always need to see a specialist — often advice from a family doctor or nurse is enough, and e‑consultations are widely used.
But overall, as people live longer and have more illnesses, cutting the volume of services or allowing demand to grow faster than supply will lengthen waiting lists.
--
Editor: Karin Koppel, Argo Ideon

Germany news: Augsburg train station reopens after blast
Published September 2, 2026last updated September 2, 2026
What you need to know
- Minor injuries reported after object explodes near Augsburg train station
- Police are investigating 'criminal act' at power station near Cologne
- Germany is weighing further action against Russia after announcing it was behind the drone incident at Leipzig airport
Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Tuesday, September 1.
Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h
A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday.
The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes.
There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door.
The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main.
Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m.
According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train.
German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally.
"Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency.
"The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added.
Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete.
IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin
After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled.
The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.
Augsburg station reopens after police give all clear
Augsburg train station reopened after police sealed off the area while investigating an early morning blast that left two passers-by aged 17 and 18 with minor acoustic trauma.
According to the Bild tabloid, police said a hand grenade exploded outside a jewelry shop next to the station, causing minor damage to the facade. Police have not immediately confirmed the report of a grenade.
Police had completely shut down the station after a bomb sniffing dog uncovered a second "suspicious object," which turned out to be fragments of the grenade, Bild reported.
There was no further information available on suspects or a motive.
German FM says new EU Russia sanctions coming soon
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Wednesday said that the European Union is working on imposing more sanctions on Russian individuals in the coming weeks, a day after Germany said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport on August 4.
"Russia has escalated and must live with the consequences," Wadephul said at a gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland.
"Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said, without sharing further details on what the new measures would entail, other than they would target "a large number" of individuals.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said that the Leipzig incident had "all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism." adding that the EU was working on sanctions targeting 1,600 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military industry.
Officials had discovered a drone between Ukrainian cargo aircraft fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism, triggering speculation over who could have been responsible.
On Tuesday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that although the devices required "a high degree of technical expertise," the plan appears to have been carried out by "low-level" agents.
The ministers said the Russian consulate general in Bonn would be closed, along with the termination of the lease for the Russian House, a Russian cultural institution in the heart of Berlin.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected Germany's accusations and said the punitive measures are a "serious mistake."
WATCH: Germany blames Russia for attempted Leipzig drone attack
During a press conference on Tuesday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul disclosed intelligence findings about the incident in which an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig Airport last month.
Augsburg station closed due to 'suspicious object'
Police in Augsburg have said the city's main train station is now fully shut down as of 8:30 a.m. with rail service suspended, due to a "suspicious object," without sharing further details.
Earlier, one track had been operating as police investigated a blast from an unknown object earlier Wednesday morning.
Unidentified object explodes near Augsburg train station, injuring 2
An unidentified object exploded near a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg early Wednesday morning, with two people sustaining minor injuries due to acoustic trauma, police said.
Window panes were also reportedly damaged by the explosion, which occurred in a building passageway.
No information is yet available regarding the circumstances surrounding the incident.
Parts of the station were closed off as police continued investigating the scene. The State Criminal Police Office (LKA) is on the scene with an explosive-disposal robot, the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper reported.
Police first responded to the incident at around 5 a.m. local time.
Augsburg is a regional transport hub around 55 kilometers (35 miles) west of Munich.
Police label power station disruption in Bergheim a 'deliberate act'
Police are investigating a disruption at a power station in the town of Bergheim in western Germany, near Cologne.
On Tuesday evening, several power lines failed following a short circuit at the power station.
"Based on the current status of the investigation, we do not believe this was caused by a technical malfunction, but rather by a deliberate act, a criminal offense," a police spokesperson said on Wednesday morning.
The spokesperson did not initially provide any details regarding the damage or the actions of the alleged perpetrators.
Police said the incident on Tuesday evening did not cause a power outage to the surrounding area.
The incident comes as tensions are high after unknown individuals attempted to cause short circuits in extra-high-voltage power lines near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in the eastern state of Brandenburg on Tuesday morning.
Police found explosive devices near the plant are investigating the incident as an act of sabotage.
