Desalination crisis explained: what shut the plants, and could Israel run out of water?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:12:06 UTC
05:12:06 KST

A large share of Israel’s water now comes from seawater desalination, a field in which the country is considered a global pioneer. But since Saturday, most of Israel’s major Mediterranean desalination plants have been shut down because of unusually turbid seawater, forcing authorities to cut water supplies to farmers in the Negev and ask municipalities to stop watering public gardens.
For now, officials say household water supplies are not expected to be significantly affected, although disruptions have already been reported in some places, including Be'er Sheva.
So what caused the shutdown, how much water is Israel losing and why can microscopic algae disable some of the country’s most important infrastructure?
How much water does Israel use?
During a typical summer day, Israel consumes about 3.9 million cubic meters of water, including agricultural use.
The shutdown of the desalination plants created a potential shortfall of roughly 85,000 cubic meters per hour. In practice, cuts to agricultural water supplies amounted to about 300,000 cubic meters a day.
Danny Sofer, acting head of national water company Mekorot, said the system was forced to rely heavily on Israel’s natural water sources after five desalination plants stopped operating.
“Because five desalination plants stopped working, we activated our entire natural water system, which brings us to about 90% of our summer supply capacity,” he said.
“In winter, nobody would have noticed the problem, because consumption is about 50% of the summer level. In summer, we cannot fully overcome it.”
Which desalination plants shut down?
Israel operates six large Mediterranean desalination plants: Ashkelon, Palmachim, Sorek A, Sorek B, Ashdod and Hadera. Of those, only Hadera remained operational during the disruption. Israel also has a desalination plant in Eilat.
Sorek A and Sorek B briefly returned to operation Monday night before the Water Authority announced Tuesday morning that they had been shut down again. Energy Minister Eli Cohen later said Sorek A and Palmachim would be restarted.
What caused the shutdown?
A preliminary investigation by researchers at Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research points to a bloom of microscopic algae, apparently originating near the Nile Delta.
Satellite images showed large algal blooms in the area, while eastern Mediterranean currents can carry material northward and eastward from the Nile toward Israel.
“It would not be surprising if something that bloomed in the Nile Delta also reached southern Israel,” said Alon Zask, CEO of Israel Oceanographic and Limnological Research.
He noted that Ashkelon, Israel’s southernmost Mediterranean desalination plant, was the first to shut down, fitting that possible pattern.
The problem is that the algae are extremely small and may pass through the filters used at the entrances to desalination facilities.
Algal blooms are a natural phenomenon influenced by weather, sea currents and the amount of organic material in the water. They generally develop over time before collapsing, after which the organic matter they produce decomposes.
Scientists, however, cannot always determine why a particular bloom emerges at a specific place and time.
What kind of algae are they?
Prof. Tamar Guy-Haim of the National Institute of Oceanography said researchers believe the organisms belong to a group known as picophytoplankton.
“We are in the preliminary stages of characterizing the algae,” she said, adding that researchers are working with Prof. Edo Bar-Zeev of Ben-Gurion University.
“We believe it is probably cyanobacteria, small photosynthetic bacteria that are a natural part of the ecosystem and form the base of the food web.”
Researchers have not yet identified the exact species and are awaiting molecular test results.
The algae are not believed to be toxic through food or contact, and beaches have therefore remained open.
How does desalination actually work?
Desalination removes dissolved salts from water to produce water suitable for drinking, agriculture and other uses.
Modern Israeli plants largely rely on reverse osmosis. In the process, salty water is pushed at very high pressure through membranes that allow water molecules to pass while blocking salts.
About half of the seawater entering the system becomes desalinated water. The remainder becomes concentrated brine and is discharged back into the sea.
Technological advances in membrane performance and energy recovery have sharply lowered the cost of reverse osmosis, making it far more energy-efficient than older evaporation-based methods.
The Water Authority says water produced by Israel’s seawater desalination plants is of very high quality and must meet standards stricter than basic drinking-water requirements before entering the national system.
Who is being hit hardest?
For now, farmers in southern Israel are bearing the brunt of the shortage.
Growers were told to stop using desalinated water for irrigation, and some say their taps have effectively run dry.
Roy Yosef, a farmer from Be’er Milka who has grown tomatoes and cherry tomatoes for 15 years, warned that even a short interruption could destroy crops in the Nitzana region.
“Never before have they shut off agricultural water,” he said. “We are the main suppliers of tomatoes in Israel for the holidays.”
“Twenty-four hours without water can already cause irreversible damage. More than that? The entire crop dies.”
Doron Hevel, another Be’er Milka farmer who grows about 65 dunams of tomatoes and cherry tomatoes, described the situation as “a survival event.”
“We are at the peak of the season,” he said. “A medium-sized farm invests about NIS 2 million in the ground, and there will be no way to get that money back.”
Was Israel warned this could happen?
Yes.
A State Comptroller report published in November 2024 found that between 2007 and the end of 2023, there were 14 incidents in which seawater contamination forced desalination plants to stop production.
Shutdowns lasted anywhere from several hours to five days.
About 57% of the incidents were caused by microbial contamination, 29% by fuel and oil pollution and 14% by turbidity linked to storms and an earthquake.
The comptroller recommended that the Health Ministry conduct periodic surveys of algal toxins and other toxins released into the water, and develop a plan for coping with such events.
Can future shutdowns be prevented?
Experts say probably not completely.
Prof. Edo Bar-Zeev of Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research said Israel needs contingency systems capable of keeping water production running during exceptional events.
“In my opinion, it is impossible to completely prevent events like this,” he said. “What must be done is to prepare backup solutions in advance.”
He warned that the current episode could be a preview of a much more severe threat: a large oil spill.
“This event is only a teaser for similar events that could happen in the future, especially oil incidents,” Bar-Zeev said. “A major oil spill will happen. The only question is when.”
Such an event, he warned, could shut desalination plants for much longer, potentially for months.
“Oil reaching the desalination plants would be a tragedy,” he said. “There is currently no contingency plan for that scenario either. The current contingency plan is simply to take the switch at the desalination plants and turn it off.”

Japan Modifies ASM-3 Anti-Ship Missile to Destroy Air Targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:10:24 UTC
05:10:24 KST

Japan is likely to modify the ASM-3 supersonic anti-ship missile into an ultra-long-range air-to-air missile for intercepting aerial targets.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense announced its plans to procure air-to-air missiles for 2027 in a budget document.
Converting the anti-ship missile into an air-to-air interceptor is intended to create a means of countering long-range enemy aircraft — such as long-range radar detection aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, and strategic bombers.
Thanks to its ramjet engine, the upgraded air-to-air version of the missile will be capable of reaching an estimated range of 400-600 km.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries began developing the basic ASM-3 anti-ship missile in 2003 to replace the obsolete ASM-1 and ASM-2.
The development program lasted more than a decade, and in 2017, test launches from the decommissioned destroyer Shirane confirmed the new weapon’s performance characteristics.
However, the initial version of the missile, with a range of 200 km, never entered serial production because the Japanese Ministry of Defense deemed this range insufficient to penetrate modern naval air defense systems and demanded upgrades.
As a result, an improved version, the ASM-3A, was developed; by reducing weight and optimizing fuel consumption, its range was increased to 400 km or more.
In its basic anti-ship version, the ASM-3 is 6 meters long, has a body diameter of 350 mm, and a total launch weight of approximately 940 kg.
The missile is equipped with a penetrating high-explosive warhead weighing about 150 kg, designed to engage medium- and large-displacement surface ships.
The primary platform for the ASM-3 family of missiles is the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s F-2 fighter jets.
It should be noted that, starting in 2027, the Japanese Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radar missiles to counter Chinese air defense systems.

Tribunal alters gay ex-IAF man 'dismissal' to 'routine discharge'

Tribunal alters gay ex-IAF man 'dismissal' to 'routine discharge'
TNN / Sep 02, 2026, 01:39 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Instead of granting the discharge, IAF initiated a court of inquiry
NEW DELHI: The principal bench of Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) has converted the order of dismissal of a non-commissioned IAF officer, who confessed to being gay, into a routine discharge.The bench, headed by Justice Rajendra Menon and Justice Rasika Chaube, ruled that substituting dismissal with routine discharge prevents lasting career stigma for the ex-officer seeking employment outside the armed forces.The non-commissioned IAF officer, who had served about 10 and a half years, had applied for a compassionate premature discharge in 2024 to settle down with his partner, disclosing his relationship in an application.Instead of granting the discharge, IAF initiated a court of inquiry. The inquiry concluded he had breached discipline and risked national security by entering into a relationship with a foreigner. The court of inquiry also found him guilty of travelling abroad (Thailand and Sri Lanka) without permission. He was subsequently dismissed from service earlier this year.
He then approached AFT principal bench not to challenge IAF's disciplinary right, but to request "dismissal" be changed to a "discharge" so he could seek future civilian employment.
The bench held that while dismissal is warranted when rules are breached, exceptions must be considered in this case. "The respondents could have granted discharge to the applicant, but in the garb of maintaining discipline they dismissed him. The effect of both is identical inasmuch as the respondents do not want the service of the applicant."

Carney and Trump continue to trade barbs amid ongoing threats against Canadian sovereignty and economic disputes.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has reprimanded the United States for what he describes as a flippant approach to the ongoing trade dispute between the two countries.
On Tuesday, Carney hit back against a series of insults and disparaging remarks from US President Donald Trump and his officials, saying that talks can proceed once Washington takes a more serious approach to the issues at hand.

The Liberal Party leader’s remarks come as tensions flare once again between the US and Canada, which have historically had tight relations.

Carney also said Trump’s team attempted to push an asymmetrical deal that would damage Canada’s industries.
“Canada’s a sovereign state. We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals with,” Carney told reporters on Tuesday. He added, “Of course, we’re not going to accept those terms.”
The trade war between the two countries has prompted a surge of nationalism in Canada.
A June poll from the research firm Abacus Data found that national pride surged 12 points in two years, reaching 77 percent this year.
Carney has faced pressure not to yield to US demands. In addition to imposing steep tariffs, the Trump administration has also pushed Canada to cede its sovereignty and become a “51st state” within the US.
Trump has also taken symbolic actions designed to assert US dominance over the two countries’ shared border region. On August 27, the US president signed an executive order directing federal entities to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
“They are one of the worst countries in the world to deal with,” Trump said of Canada in a recent radio interview.
Other cabinet-level officials in the Trump administration have echoed Trump’s remarks disparaging Canada.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the news outlet CNBC that Canada’s economy is ill-equipped to handle a trade war with the US, and he blamed Carney for escalating the situation.
“Well, I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” Bessent said on Monday.
Of Carney, he added, “He came to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump agenda. He was 20 points behind in the polls. And then he started this. And it’s unfortunate that he’s not doing what’s best for the Canadian people.”
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, meanwhile, posted an image of two female Canadian cadets on social media, in an apparent effort to mock the country’s armed forces.
“This is real,” he wrote beneath the image of the two women, alongside an emoji of the Canadian flag.
Hegseth, a former TV host, has frequently castigated efforts to include women, LGBTQ people and racial minorities in the military as “woke” distractions from the US military’s core mission.
When reporters asked Carney to respond to such messages, he replied that such comments were “beneath” the officials’ office.
“Our plan has always been standing up for Canada, first and foremost, here at home,” Carney said.

‘Unbelievable’: how a tiny island in Canada appeared, vanished, and reappeared miles away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:06:49 UTC
05:06:49 KST

A thickly forested island appeared mysteriously on a western Canadian lake. Nearly 150 metres (500 feet) long and 75 metres (250 feet) wide, the land mass took local people and experts by surprise. It wasn’t on any maps or navigation charts.
One boater approached and took a video of the island, capturing nearly 100 trees undulating in the chop of the lake.
And then, within days, it disappeared.
On Monday, the island made its second appearance – nearly 20 miles from its location earlier in August – in stunning aquatic displacement that has left residents wondering how an entire island can seem to simply vanish.
The mystery has unfolded in the middle of Williston Lake, a long and narrow reservoir created after the W.A.C Bennett dam flooded the region in the early 1970s. At nearly 1,700 sq km (650 sqmiles) it is the largest body of freshwater in the westernmost province.
Bob Gammer, a spokesperson for BC Hydro, the government-owned utility that operates the reservoir and dam, said the island was “quite something and rather unbelievable” when he first saw the images.
“In the days of AI, you really needed another form of verification or evidence like a corroborating eyewitness account,” he said. “And soon, we got that.”
Satellite imagery confirmed the island was in fact real, and floating in the main body of the reservoir, roughly 60 miles west of the dam.
BC Hydro believes the island is the result of years of trees and plants growing largely undisturbed on the woody debris along sheltered sections of the reservoir’s shoreline.
Similar islands have shown up across the globe, including Wisconsin’s famed Forty Acre Bog. The giant, floating island on Lake Chippewa is knitted together by peat, mud, roots and trees.
Measuring roughly 12,000 sq metres (14,000 sq yards) in size, the British Columbia island is also bursting with life: birds and small animals are living among the mix of coniferous and broadleaf trees. Observers suspect the root system in the water hides some of the lake’s best fish.
Gammer likened the growing conditions to hydroponics and said: “Well-fed trees growing on a decaying food source with lots of water … they could grow pretty quick.”
The reservoir, he added, is higher than it has been in 14 years, as a result of high winter snowpacks and consistent summer rains that have raised water levels in the Peace River and the lake.
“Suddenly, there are all of the right conditions to potentially lift this kind of little island from where it was, and bring it out into open water,” he said.
Between sightings, the island may have drifted to shore. Its seeming disappearance “doesn’t mean it’s gone to the bottom of the reservoir”, Gammer previously told CBC. “It may have returned to a more sheltered area along the shoreline.”
BC Hydro doesn’t know how old the trees on the island are, but with the right conditions the forest could “just stay there for years” and grow. Local people speculated the trees could be decades old.
“It’s not like they’re just a bunch of little shrubs. This is an island with larger trees and it’s something you really have to wrap your mind around,” said Grammar. “It’s not an everyday thing. This is really really unusual.”
Rocky Avery, a friend of the boater and a longtime resident of the area who first posted the clip to social media to warn others about a possible hazard, said he would “totally jump on that island if I could”.
“It’s probably a bit shaky on the outer sections, but with those huge trees in the centre, I imagine someone could walk on it,” he said.
Gammer cautioned boaters from attempting to become the first to set foot on it, warning that video shows trees moving back and forth on a “delicate, thin layer of logs”, adding it is “very unsafe” and “very unstable”.
Avery’s social media posts about the island prompted a flurry of excitement and a seemingly inescapable nod to the current political situation in Canada. Recently, the US president, Donald Trump, chose to rename Lake Ontario after trade talks collapsed between the two countries. The announcement has prompted anger, frustration and mockery from the Canadian public.
“I’m surprised Trump hasn’t named [the island] and claimed it,” commented one user on Avery’s post.

Zelenskyy warns ‘Russian airspace will effectively be closing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:06:38 UTC
05:06:38 KST

The Ukrainian president warned airlines, insurers and foreign governments that the growing scale of Kyiv’s drone operations would make Russian airspace increasingly unsafe for aircraft.
Following almost a week of relentless Russian attacks on Kyiv and non-stop air raid alerts, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy issued a stark warning to international airlines and insurers: "Russian airspace will effectively be closing."
In his evening address on 1 September, Zelenskyy said the consequences of the war Moscow launched more than four years ago could no longer be confined to Ukrainian territory and that Kyiv's ever-growing drone operations would soon render Russian airspace unsafe.
“It was from Russia that the first missiles and the first drones came, and they crossed our country’s border from Russian airspace,” Zelenskyy said. “This escalation cannot and will not remain confined to Ukrainian territory.”
His warning was directed not only at Moscow but at airlines, insurers and foreign governments whose carriers continue to fly through Russian airspace and serve airports in Moscow, St Petersburg and other major cities.
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said.
Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine would not threaten civilian aircraft, but the sheer scale of Ukrainian UAV activity would have to be taken into account.
“Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such - not a single civilian aircraft,” he said. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.”
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing — the war started by Russia is closing its skies," he added.
Ukraine’s airspace has been closed to civilian aviation since 24 February 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
Russian civilian aviation, by contrast, has continued operating throughout the war, despite increasingly frequent disruptions and temporary airport closures during Ukrainian drone attacks.
Kyiv’s long-range operations have targeted military facilities and infrastructure supporting Moscow’s war effort, including airfields, missile units, oil refineries and other energy facilities.
Zelenskyy stressed that that would not change, saying Ukraine did not want innocent lives to be lost.
“We are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said, while calling on foreign ambassadors in both Kyiv and Moscow to relay the message to their governments.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry and other government agencies would provide international organisations with full information about the dangers in Russian airspace, he added.
Almost a week of attacks on Kyiv
Zelenskyy’s warning comes after almost a week of sustained Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities, with Moscow increasingly relying on jet-powered drones launched in repeated waves both day and night.
Kyiv and its surrounding region have been among the main targets, with repeated air-raid alerts disrupting transport, businesses and daily life across the capital.
The attacks point to a shift in Russian tactics. Rather than concentrating its largest attacks in massive overnight barrages of drones and missiles, Moscow has increasingly sent smaller waves of drones at intervals throughout the day, prolonging air-raid alerts and placing sustained pressure on Ukrainian air defences.
Officials in Kyiv said Russia was increasingly deploying jet-powered drones alongside ballistic missiles, presenting Ukrainian defences with a particularly difficult challenge.
Zelenskyy’s message is now that Russia can no longer expect the air war it has waged over Ukraine to stop at its own border.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," he said.

Large-scale tragedy in Nepal and Tibet: more than 1,000 dead, contact with 56 Ukrainians still unavailable
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
23:05:26 EEST
05:05:26 KST

Large-scale tragedy in Nepal and Tibet: more than 1,000 dead, contact with 56 Ukrainians still unavailable
Kyiv • UNN
The deaths of 1,066 people have been confirmed in Nepal and Tibet, and around 4,500 people are missing. Among them are 56 Ukrainian citizens.
The number of people killed as a result of the catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet has exceeded one thousand, while about 4,500 more are considered missing. Among those whose whereabouts have still not been established are 56 Ukrainian citizens, UNN reports, citing Reuters, The Guardian and Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
Amid the large number of unidentified victims, Nepal’s police are asking relatives of missing people to provide blood samples for DNA identification, as well as photographs. The search-and-rescue operation is continuing nearly a week later.
Details
According to the latest data from the Nepalese authorities, the death toll in the country has risen to 1,050. At least 16 more deaths have been confirmed in Tibet. The total number of confirmed victims of the natural disaster is at least 1,066 people. At the same time, the final scale of the tragedy cannot yet be determined. Thousands of people remain on missing-person lists, including local residents, hydroelectric power plant workers and hundreds of foreign tourists.
Rescue services continue to work in the areas worst affected by the torrent of water, ice, rocks and mud. The disaster destroyed roads and bridges, damaged energy infrastructure and effectively cut off some settlements from the outside world.
Hydropower facilities that were in the path of the disaster remain a separate problem. Rescuers are inspecting tunnels and other underground structures at hydroelectric power stations, where hundreds of workers may have been at the time of the disaster. Access to some tunnels is complicated by water, mud and debris. Drones and specialized equipment are being used to search for people. Foreign rescue and expert teams have also joined the operation.
Relatives of missing people asked to provide DNA
Due to the scale of the disaster and the condition of some of the bodies found, it is impossible to identify all the victims visually. In this regard, Nepal’s police appealed to relatives of missing people, asking them to provide blood samples to create DNA profiles, as well as photographs of the people being sought. The genetic data obtained will be compared with samples taken from unidentified victims.
Relatives who are outside Nepal are allowed to undergo the necessary analysis at an appropriate laboratory in their country and provide the results to Nepalese law enforcement agencies.
The need for DNA identification has become particularly urgent because of the large number of bodies found and the overloading of local morgues. Some unidentified victims have already had to be temporarily buried after forensic procedures were carried out, biological samples were collected and the data necessary for possible subsequent identification was recorded.
What is known about Ukrainians in Nepal
The situation remains particularly urgent for Ukraine because of the fate of 56 citizens whose whereabouts could not be established after the disaster.
According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as of August 31, the people in question belong to two tourist groups. One consisted of 48 Ukrainians, and the other of seven. In addition, another Ukrainian citizen who was traveling as part of an international tourist group is being sought.
At the same time, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs emphasized that no Ukrainians were included on the confirmed lists of those killed or injured. A lack of communication in itself does not mean that people have been affected: roads, power supply systems and communications networks have been seriously damaged in the disaster areas.
Ukrainian diplomats are currently working to establish the whereabouts of the citizens together with local authorities and the services involved in the search-and-rescue operation. The situation is complicated by the fact that some tourist routes passed through remote mountainous areas. Because of the destruction of infrastructure, rescuers can reach some locations only with the help of specialized equipment or aircraft.
What caused the disaster
The devastating flood occurred on August 26 in the Himalayas near the border between Nepal and Tibet.
According to experts' preliminary conclusions, the disaster was caused by a massive collapse of ice and rock. A huge mass of ice, rock and water rapidly surged down the mountain valleys and entered the river system. The flow turned into a powerful mixture of water, mud and debris that swept away structures and infrastructure along its path.
Initially, seismic instruments recorded a signal that could have resembled an earthquake. However, experts later concluded that the tremors were likely caused by the massive collapse itself, rather than by an earthquake that triggered it. Populated areas, roads, bridges, tourist infrastructure and energy facilities on both sides of the Nepal–Tibet border were affected.
Extent of the destruction
According to preliminary estimates, the flood left behind approximately 2.2 million tonnes of rock, debris and other sediment. Nepal's energy sector suffered significant damage. The disaster affected a number of hydropower plants and projects under construction. Overall, the damage may have affected around 10% of the country's generating capacity.
Dozens of bridges, residential buildings, schools, medical facilities and other infrastructure facilities were also destroyed or damaged.
In the worst-affected areas, the restoration of roads and electricity supplies is continuing in parallel with the search operation. Rescuers continue to inspect the debris, riverbanks and downstream areas where people may have been carried away.
Because thousands of people are still considered missing, the number of confirmed victims may change as search operations and the identification of recovered bodies continue.
Context
The disaster has once again drawn attention to the risks associated with the condition of glaciers in the Himalayas. Scientists warn that rising temperatures are contributing to ice melt, the degradation of permafrost and the instability of mountain slopes.
For Nepal, where a significant portion of the population and critical infrastructure is located in narrow mountain valleys, such events pose a particular danger. The current flood has already become one of the region's largest natural disasters in terms of the number of people killed and missing.
Recall
In Nepal, after the flood, 24 bodies were found in one house, including a child among the victims

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Koretskyi warns lawmakers of a $27 billion defense financing gap
Koretskyi told parliament on Tuesday that a government audit found Ukraine needs $30 billion from partners in 2026 if it fulfills its commitments, and faces a separate $27 billion shortfall in defense financing that it is asking allies to cover on an emergency basis. He named two drivers: the rising cost of the war, as Russia expands drone and missile production, and the fact that Ukraine’s Defense Ministry spent part of its second-half 2026 budget in the first half, leaving a gap.
“Without addressing these issues, without addressing the deficit, the state could find itself under significant financial risk. This is about supplying the defense forces, financing the social sphere, and paying wages,” Koretskyi said in parliament, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
He said the government still had to adopt 44 decisions – resolutions, orders, and other obligations – by Nov. 1. Of 26 bills pending in parliament, only 12 were on the agenda; the other 14 had not yet been included, he said, while the government itself had yet to submit 17 bills it had promised partners, which it now plans to file shortly.
Koretskyi Hints at Austerity Measures to Relieve $27B Budget Shortfall
Parliament rejects parcel tax bills for the second time this year
Lawmakers first declined to advance a related customs bill, No. 15460, which would have set the procedural mechanics – currency conversion rules, marketplace obligations, penalties – for ending the VAT exemption on parcels valued under €150 ($174). It drew 194 votes, short of the 226 needed, and was sent back for rework with 244 votes in favor, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
Parliament then rejected the core bill, No. 15112-d, along with six alternative versions, that would have ended the VAT exemption itself. The lead bill got 210 votes, also short of the 226-vote threshold.
“Dear colleagues, I’m sorry,” Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk said from the podium after the vote in parliament, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak of the Holos party told reporters the bill would only have taken effect in 2027, and that the Cabinet and State Customs Service had not yet begun developing the technical systems needed to enforce it, with no funding allocated in the state budget, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
The Finance Ministry had estimated the reform would bring roughly Hr. 10 billion ($224.6 million) into the state budget annually. Passage was a condition for Ukraine’s roughly $0.7 billion third IMF tranche and the €3.7 billion ($4.2 billion) second tranche of the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) Ukraine Support Loan. Under the IMF’s updated memorandum, the bill was due by the end of July – already a revision from an original March deadline. It is now the second time this year that a version of the reform has failed in parliament, after a related bill fell on May 26.
The rejected bills would have kept VAT exemptions in place for personal, non-commercial parcels under €45 ($52) sent between individuals, unaccompanied luggage under €150 ($174), and imports of drones and defense equipment.
A separate defeat threatens the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan
The same day, lawmakers also failed to approve the creation of an advisory group of experts to vet candidates for six vacant seats on the Accounting Chamber’s supervisory board, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
The nomination of experts to the Accounting Chamber’s board selection commission was a condition of the €3.7 billion ($4.2 billion) second tranche of the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan, due under the loan’s memorandum of understanding by August 2026 – a deadline that has now passed.

$100M Software Contract Will Streamline How Air Force Manages Aircrews
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:58 UTC
05:00:58 KST

The Air Force has issued a $100 million contract to combine its long-disjointed systems for managing aircrew readiness with software that is expected to reach initial operational capability next year, starting with the T-6A Texan II and the C-17 Globemaster III.
The new software, dubbed the Aerospace Readiness Enterprise System, will merge legacy training, scheduling, and readiness platforms, some of which continue to require manual inputs, which are used throughout major commands.
Once fully deployed, ARES will connect tens of thousands of personnel, cutting hours of flight scheduling into minutes while providing leaders with real-time tracking and automated paperwork, according to an Air Education and Training Command release.
Right now, the service relies on a swath of legacy software platforms like Patriot Excalibur, Puckboard, and the Graduate/Training Integration Management System, to track the different elements of aircrew readiness, scheduling, and other items—meaning leaders lack a comprehensive snapshot of readiness across the fleet.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center and AETC announced a collaborative effort to revamp the aircrew management process in an April release, saying the software factory Kessel Run would take the lead.
“Every pilot’s first impression of the Air Force is how we manage our aircrew, and we see an opportunity to modernize that experience,” Col. Brian Benton, then the AETC Command Integration Center lead, said in an April release. “ARES is our commitment to delivering a modern solution. With AETC accounting for approximately 45 percent of the Air Force’s flying hours and an enterprise user base of approximately 149,000 Airmen, getting this right is a top priority.”
Prototype testing began in earnest this past spring using both aircrew and non-aircrew operators from AETC, Air Combat Command, Air Mobility Command, and Air Force Global Strike Command. That phase concluded after about 90 days and was followed by user testing.
“We’re building a system that has to work for the Airmen on the flightline, at the speed of our operations,” said Col. Ryan Vetter, Benton’s successor, said in a June release. “By letting our pilots and schedulers test-drive ARES now, we ensure the warfighter’s voice is baked into the final product before we make any long-term commitments.”
The tool should smooth out kinks in legacy systems and speed up how aircrews are managed and deployed.
“ARES accelerates decision-making beyond basic scheduling by paving the way for predictive mission readiness, utilizing trend analysis and modeling for more accurate long-term timeline planning and risk analysis,” an AETC official told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“Streamlining flight operations into a single platform directly returns valuable time to squadron personnel,” the official added. “Currently, aircrews and schedulers must navigate several disconnected systems to build, deconflict, and finalize schedules.”
The Kessel Run-driven project awarded the contract to VivSoft Technologies, a 15-year-old company headquartered in Herndon, Va. VivSoft has supported USAF’s Platform One and, in 2024, nabbed a follow-on contract with the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center to integrate its ENBUILD accelerator within Platform One.
VivSoft representatives did not respond to a request for comment.
The company and Air Force are actively building an Artificial Intelligence-assisted Mission Engine to validate safety parameters during high-volume flying operations.
The mission engine is still in active development, but once fully fielded, the engine is designed to “automate the cross-referencing of pilot qualifications, currency requirements, and rest periods to flag potential safety violations instantly,” the AETC official said.
The official rollout begins at AETC in 2027 with beta testing involving aircrews for the T-6A Texan II and the C-17 Globemaster III, officials said. They’re planning to reach full operational capability by 2028 within AETC. Work on the contract is to conclude in 2030.
ACC has funded the project, working with Kessel Run and other major commands, including Air Force Special Operations Command, according to the April release.
“This effort represents a fundamental shift in how the Air Force approaches flight operations,” Benton said. “Developed on a modern Software-as-a-Service platform within the Air Force’s new Operations Enterprise Architecture, ARES is designed to provide a one-stop shop for an Airman’s entire career.”
Managing aircrew readiness has been an issue for years now. In 2016, the Government Accountability Office noted that USAF lacked an enterprise-level measure of pilot proficiency. The GAO again noted the findings four years later in its 2020 report on the Ready Aircrew Program.
At the time of the 2020 report, USAF responded with proposed fixes, including creating a common data architecture and aligning training with the National Defense Strategy.
ARES will integrate with the larger Air Resource Tool Enterprise Mission Information System. ARTEMIS is a combined master logbook and crew member human resources and medical record in one system and is in the process of fully replacing the 1990s-era Aviation Resource Management System, or ARMS.

Genetic evidence confirms ADHD symptoms cause poorer academic performance in kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:07 UTC
05:00:07 KST

Children who display more symptoms of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) tend to earn lower grades in school, and new research provides evidence that these symptoms directly cause poorer academic performance. By applying advanced genetic models to data from twins and siblings, scientists found that ADHD symptoms negatively affect grades, while grades do not appear to influence the severity of ADHD symptoms. The study was published in Behavior Genetics.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. These symptoms are highly heritable, meaning that the condition is strongly influenced by genetics. For years, scientists have observed that children with more ADHD symptoms tend to struggle academically. However, determining whether the symptoms directly cause poor school performance or if other shared factors are to blame has been a difficult task for researchers.
In medical science, the ideal setup for establishing cause and effect is a randomized controlled trial. But assigning children to experience mental health symptoms is ethically and practically impossible. To get around this, researchers often use a technique called Mendelian randomization. This method uses genetic variations as a stand-in for the exposure of interest, like ADHD. Because genes are assigned randomly at birth, they are less likely to be influenced by environmental factors that might confuse the results.
But Mendelian randomization has its own weaknesses. One major issue is horizontal pleiotropy, a scenario where a genetic variant influences the outcome through entirely different biological pathways, rather than just through the condition being studied. If a gene associated with ADHD also independently affects how a child learns, the results could be skewed. To address this problem, the authors of the current study combined genetic tools with data from twins and siblings. This approach allowed them to test the direction of the effect between ADHD symptoms and school grades while filtering out the noise of shared family environments and complex genetic overlap.
The research, led by Luis F. S. Castro-de-Araujo of Virginia Commonwealth University, utilized data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. This large-scale, long-term project tracks the development of thousands of children across the United States. For this analysis, the team focused on 1,523 twin and sibling pairs, as well as some individual children, during the third year of the study’s follow-up.
To measure ADHD symptoms, the researchers used a standard questionnaire called the Child Behavior Checklist, which was completed by the children’s caregivers. The caregivers also reported the children’s school grades from the previous year. Additionally, the researchers calculated polygenic risk scores for the participants. A polygenic risk score is a single number that estimates a person’s genetic likelihood of developing a specific trait based on millions of small genetic variants. In this case, the team calculated scores for both ADHD liability and educational attainment, focusing on a subsample of 1,071 children of European ancestry because the reference genetic data available was limited to that population.
The researchers fed these measures into a series of complex statistical models designed for twin data. The most advanced of these models allowed the team to look at causation in both directions at once. They could see if ADHD symptoms reduced grades and if low grades worsened ADHD symptoms, all while accounting for shared genetics, shared home environments, and horizontal pleiotropy.
The analysis provided evidence that ADHD symptoms have a direct, negative effect on a child’s school grades. When looking at the reverse direction, the researchers found that school grades did not have a statistically significant effect on ADHD symptoms. The team also tested whether these patterns differed between boys and girls. Despite ADHD being diagnosed more frequently in boys, the mathematical models showed that the negative effect of the symptoms on academic performance was consistent across both sexes.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that higher ADHD symptoms were associated with lower educational attainment across adolescence. In that earlier Dutch study, academic achievement was evaluated through secondary school educational track placement rather than caregiver-reported grades, but both studies point to similar academic hurdles for youth dealing with ADHD symptoms.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. First, the data for the third year of the study was collected during the COVID-19 pandemic. The disruptions to daily life and schooling during this period might have affected the grades reported by caregivers, potentially introducing extra noise into the data.
Another thing to keep in mind is the measurement of the symptoms themselves. The questionnaire completed by caregivers is a highly reliable research tool, but it is not the same as a formal clinical diagnosis of ADHD made by a medical professional.
The study’s reliance on genetic data from people of European ancestry also limits how broadly the findings can be applied. Because comprehensive genetic reference data for other populations is currently lacking, the researchers could only run their most advanced causal models on a specific subset of the participants. Future research will need to include diverse genetic data to ensure these findings apply to all populations. The authors also suggest that future studies track individual children over longer periods to see how symptom persistence influences academic performance as they grow older.
The study, “ADHD and Student Grades in Children from the ABCD Study®: A Twin and Siblings Study,” was authored by Luis F. S. Castro-de-Araujo, Daniel Zhou, Mei-Hsin Su, Sydney Kramer, Robert Loughnan, and Michael C. Neale.

The Diamond Moon and Other Astronomical Events To See in September 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

August set the bar high for stargazers, with two eclipses and the peak of the Perseids meteor shower. But it’s not time to put away your telescopes, with some lesser-known astronomical events set to arrive across the sky this month.
The Pleiades will appear next to the moon, Venus will reach its brightest point of the year, Neptune will be in its best position for spotting with a telescope, and as an encore to the Perseids, there will also be a smaller meteor shower.
Here are some dates worth marking on your calendar for the month to come.
Venus near Spica: September 1 and 2
September begins with an easy opportunity to spot two of the brightest objects in the night sky. Venus will appear near Spica, the most intense star in the constellation Virgo. Both objects will be visible to the naked eye.
The exact timing of Venus’ appearance is September 2 at 00:17 UTC. This means that, depending on the your location, the conjunction could occur in the afternoon or evening of September 1.
It should be easy to tell the two celestial objects apart. Venus will shine much more brightly, looking like a white dot that doesn’t twinkle as much as the stars. Spica will appear nearby as a considerably fainter bluish dot. The two will be approximately 1.5 degrees apart.
A handy trick is that 0.5 degrees in the sky is roughly the average diameter of a full moon. Therefore, once you find the brightest point in the sky—which will be Venus—you can find Spica about three moons away.
A Diamond Studded Moon: September 3
The moon will be accompanied by one of the most famous star clusters in the sky. On the night of September 3, it will appear approximately 1.1 degrees from the Pleiades—close enough to observe both objects in the same region. The moon will be about 59 percent illuminated, according to Star Walk’s calculations.
The Pleiades, also known as “the Seven Sisters” or M45, is a star cluster located in the constellation Taurus. Six or seven of its members are usually visible to the naked eye under good conditions, although the cluster contains hundreds of young stars. These stars were born at approximately the same time and remain gravitationally bound together.
The proximity to the waning moon offers a good opportunity for spotting them. To the naked eye, they will appear as a small group of bright points next to the moon, as if they were diamonds. Binoculars will allow you to make out many more. The encounter will happen again on September 30, when the two objects will once more be separated by just one degree.
A Modest Meteor Shower: September 9 and 10
September also has its own meteor shower. The Epsilon Perseids will peak September 9 and 10, producing up to eight meteors per hour.
The number of meteors is lower than that of the famous Perseids in August. However, this shower has one advantage: Its peak will occur just two days before the new moon, making the sky ideally dark for viewing.
Conditions will be especially favorable from the northern hemisphere, and, as with any meteor shower, it is recommended to find a dark location away from light pollution.
Venus at Its Brightest: September 22
Venus is usually one of the easiest objects to spot in the night sky, but toward the end of September it will shine even brighter. The planet will reach an apparent magnitude of approximately -4.8. By comparison, the full moon has a magnitude of -12.7, and Sirius—considered the brightest star in the sky—barely reaches -1.46.
Look for the planet after sunset, near the western horizon. Viewing conditions will be best from the southern hemisphere.
The Equinox: September 23
Unlike the other events on this list, the equinox isn’t something we can go out and observe directly. Instead, it’s an astronomical moment that marks a specific point in Earth’s orbit and, with it, the change of season.
The September equinox will occur on September 23 when the Sun crosses the equator as it moves southward. The event marks the astronomical beginning of fall in the northern hemisphere and spring in the southern hemisphere.
Neptune Is in the Neighborhood: September 26
Spotting Neptune is considerably more challenging than spotting other planets. The most distant planet in the solar system (sorry Pluto) is forecasted to reach opposition on September 26. This means that Earth will be approximately between Neptune and the Sun.
This positioning means Neptune will remain visible for much of the night and will be at one of its closest distances to our planet for the year. Therefore, September offers one of the best opportunities in 2026 to try to spot it.
It’s too faint to be seen with the naked eye. You’ll need a telescope and to know its position among the stars of Pisces. Even then, it will appear as a tiny bluish disk.
Harvest Moon: September 26
September will end with a particularly famous full moon. The full moon closest to the September equinox is traditionally called the Harvest Moon. The term does not describe a distinct physical phenomenon, nor does it mean that the moon will change color, size, or brightness. It’s a traditional name related to the harvests of the northern hemisphere.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

OpenAI Is About to Release Its First AI Model With ‘Critical’ Cyber Abilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

OpenAI announced Tuesday that its forthcoming AI model, Astra, is its first to reach the company’s threshold for what it calls “critical” cyber capabilities. OpenAI says it plans to publicly release a version of Astra “soon,” but will make the model’s advanced cyber capabilities available only to select partners in its Daybreak Blue early-access program at launch.
In a briefing with reporters, OpenAI safety and security leaders said the company has concluded that Astra reaches the critical cybersecurity capabilities outlined in its preparedness framework, which sets thresholds and protocols for when its AI models pose new levels of risk. The company says an AI model has reached its critical cyber threshold when it can independently find and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in real-world software. OpenAI leaders said the company has followed its procedure for this situation, which is to halt further development until appropriate safeguards and security measures can be implemented.
OpenAI previously said that it paused some training workloads related to the development of Astra and a future AI model for several weeks. Executives say the company has now resumed said work on Astra, and the future AI model, after putting additional safety and security controls in place. OpenAI says the multi-week pause was productive, and it is now confident that it can release Astra broadly in a safe way.
The announcement comes as Silicon Valley grapples with the advanced cybersecurity capabilities of cutting-edge AI models, and tries to assure users, lawmakers, and other companies that it can keep them under control. In July, OpenAI disclosed an incident in which agents running two of its models exploited vulnerabilities in what was supposed to be a siloed testing environment, gaining access to the internet and hacking the open source AI platform Hugging Face. (OpenAI notes that Astra was not one of the models involved in this case.)
Other AI companies, such as Anthropic and Meta, have disclosed similar incidents in recent weeks. On Monday, Anthropic also said it has paused some AI training workloads while it hardens its safety and security practices.
OpenAI says it’s implementing a multi-step approach to limit everyday users from accessing Astra’s advanced cyber capabilities, including a new “misalignment monitor.” If someone asks Astra to help them find an exploit in a real-world software system, for example, the model is supposed to refuse to answer. OpenAI says it has also made Astra more robust to jailbreaking attempts, and in tests it successfully refused unsafe queries at a significantly higher rate than previous models.
However, OpenAI notes in a blog post that its misalignment monitor may “occasionally flag legitimate activity as potential cyber misuse or unauthorized behavior, leading to it inadvertently being slowed, paused, or stopped.” OpenAI says the guardrail can be triggered in some cases even when a user is engaging in activities that don’t appear related to cybersecurity. When this happens, ChatGPT and Codex users may be asked to review the model’s action before proceeding, OpenAI said.
Partners in OpenAI’s Daybreak program—which includes digital infrastructure providers like Cisco, Cloudflare, and Palo Alto Networks—will get early access to a less restricted version of Astra with more robust cyber capabilities. The goal of the program is to ensure these companies can use advanced AI models like Astra to harden their defenses before similarly capable models are made broadly available. OpenAI leaders also said the company has been working closely with government partners to ensure they’re aware of Astra’s cyber skills and can get access to them.
Astra is not only capable of finding novel software vulnerabilities and developing ways to exploit them for hacking, but is also able to “chain” multiple exploits together, a technique used to bore deeper and deeper into a target system and gain access that wouldn’t be attainable using just one vulnerability.
According to figures from OpenAI, Astra outperforms industry leading AI models such as GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos on cybersecurity benchmarks such as ExploitBench, which Astra scored 100 percent on. However, these capabilities are broadly in line with the rising hacking abilities of AI models that OpenAI and Anthropic have been forecasting for months. In April, for example, Anthropic emphasized that Mythos Preview was able to autonomously develop exploit chains.
As the AI and cybersecurity industries have scrambled to adapt, though, many cybersecurity experts have emphasized that key digital security defenses and longstanding best practices are still durable. However, AI puts organizations and systems that haven’t fully implemented these protections at even more urgent risk.

Guinea-Bissau referendum nods to expansion of presidential powers

Guinea-Bissau referendum nods to expansion of presidential powers
The National Electoral Commission says 70 percent of voters cast their ballots in favour of the changes.
A referendum in Guinea-Bissau has approved a new constitution that will significantly increase the power of the president.
The National Electoral Commission said on Tuesday that 70 percent of votes cast last week were in favour of the changes, with the turnout at almost 60 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Guinea-Bissau sets election date following last year’s coup
- list 2 of 3One ‘party state’: Guinea dissolves main opposition parties
- list 3 of 3Guinea-Bissau votes on a stronger presidency: What’s at stake?
The referendum, proposed by the military government, which seized power in a coup in November last year, took place shortly ahead of a general election at the end of the year, which is aimed at returning the country to civilian rule.
However, the vote has been denounced by the main opposition party, PAIGC, and civil society groups, which argue that it threatens Guinea-Bissau’s transition back to democracy.
The military rulers say the changes are aimed at stabilising key state institutions ahead of December’s vote, when the presidency and parliamentary seats will be on the ballot.
Under the new rules, the president will be able to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and cabinet, which significantly weakens the country’s power-sharing system.
The president will also be able to create and abolish ministries and dissolve parliament under certain conditions. Currently, the prime minister oversees day-to-day affairs and is elected by parliament.
The number of parliamentary seats will also be reduced from 102 to 65, while the number of electoral constituencies will be cut by more than half, from 29 to 12.
Although the electoral commission reported a turnout of close to 60 percent of eligible voters, international news agencies had reported that polling stations were largely empty. PAIGC had called on people to boycott the referendum.
Critics accuse the military government of attempting to concentrate power, allowing the country’s rulers to reshape the political system in their favour ahead of the elections in December.
The fears are grounded in a rash of military takeovers in the region. West and Central Africa have seen nine coups since 2020, with military leaders insisting their actions were motivated by deteriorating security and the urge to protect democracy.

Russia’s Starlink rival falters as latest satellite batch stalls in low orbit, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:57:43 UTC
04:57:43 KST

The Rassvet communications satellites Moscow launched in July are likely to have shorter operational lifespans than planned because atmospheric drag increases at their current altitudes, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported.
Moscow accelerated Rassvet’s deployment after its forces lost unauthorized Starlink access in February. A complete network could support battlefield communications and remotely controlled strikes against Ukraine, but existing satellites provide only brief connectivity windows. The latest setback will likely delay continuous coverage, ISW assessed.
Russian forces had relied heavily on unauthorized Starlink terminals for frontline communications, drone operations, and command-and-control. Ukraine and SpaceX blocked them on 5 February, disrupting Russian communications and assaults across several sectors. A Russian-controlled network could reduce Moscow’s dependence on SpaceX and illicit supply chains for terminals.
None of the 16 satellites launched on 19 July had reached 550 kilometers as of 31 August, according to N2YO tracking data cited by ISW. Many remained between 300 and 400 kilometers, some were gradually losing altitude, and at least two were reportedly heading toward atmospheric reentry.
ISW identified 550 kilometers as the altitude reached by the successful first-batch satellites, while reporting 870 kilometers as Rassvet’s intended operational altitude. At lower altitudes, satellites must use more fuel to counter greater atmospheric drag, shortening their operating lives.
Of the 32 Rassvet satellites launched in 2026, only 12—all from the first batch launched on 24 March—reached sustainable altitudes. They remained at roughly 550 kilometers and provided two daily connectivity windows over Ukraine totaling up to 90 minutes, ISW reported.
Russia needs at least 200–300 working satellites for stable, round-the-clock coverage, presidential defense-technology adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov assessed. Bureau 1440 plans “dozens” more launches and “hundreds” more satellites, but Russia depends on the scarce, costly Soyuz-2.1b rocket.
Only six to eight Soyuz-2.1b launches of all types have occurred since 2022, limiting Russia to a maximum of 128 Rassvet satellites over four years at that rate, ISW assessed.
Ukraine struck the Progress Space Rocket Center, which builds Soyuz-type vehicles, on 14–15 August and attempted to strike Plesetsk Cosmodrome on 23 August, ISW noted. Both Rassvet batches launched from Plesetsk, showing Ukraine can threaten the rockets and launch infrastructure required to expand the constellation, the institute assessed.
What is Rassvet?
Rassvet, meaning “Dawn,” is a low-Earth-orbit broadband constellation developed by Bureau 1440 as Russia’s domestic alternative to Starlink. Its 5G-based satellites are intended to provide high-speed, low-latency internet independently of SpaceX.
Although initially designed for civilian communications, a mature network could provide Russian forces with battlefield connectivity, command-and-control links, and connections to long-range drones. Moscow aims to place 292 satellites in orbit by the end of 2027 and 924 by 2035.

Iran launches ‘decisive’ retaliation, fires missiles at US bases in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:53:27 UTC
04:53:27 KST

Iran said Tuesday evening it had launched what it described as a “decisive” retaliatory operation against U.S. targets while American strikes on Iranian territory were still underway.
Iranian reports said missiles were fired toward U.S. bases in Jordan and claimed an American MQ-9 military drone was shot down over Iran.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said U.S. forces had struck locations along Iran’s southern coast, including civilian sites, and that its forces had begun responding. In what it described as the first action of the retaliation, the IRGC said it had downed an MQ-9 drone.
Explosions were also heard in Eilat, following the launch of interceptors targeting Iranian missiles launched towards the city of Aqaba on the Israel-Jordan border. Residents of the city reported that they detected interceptors being launched from the city area towards Jordan.
In Jordan, authorities reported shortly before 11 p.m. that alerts had been sent to residents’ mobile phones, including in Aqaba, warning that they could be in danger. “The area where you are located may be exposed to falling debris. We ask you to remain calm and seek shelter in the nearest building or stay inside your vehicle,” the Jordanian warning said. According to reports, Jordanian air defense systems intercepted missiles in several parts of the country. Sirens sounded across Jordan at 11:15 p.m. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the target was the Tabaqin camp on the Gulf of Aqaba coast.
Jordan later said 13 ballistic missiles had been launched from Iran, with air defense systems intercepting 10 of them. The remaining three, according to the Jordanian military, exploded in areas “far from population centers.” At the same time, two U.S. officials told Reuters that there were no casualties among forces stationed there. Reuters noted that there was no official confirmation of an attack on a U.S. base in Bahrain.
The United States announced that the wave of strikes had ended at 1:33 a.m. “We struck IRGC targets, including air defense systems, radars, naval assets, facilities, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites,” U.S. Central Command said.
Explosions were reported at numerous locations across Iran, including the port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz, Qeshm Island inside the strait and the port city of Chabahar in southeastern Iran on the Gulf of Oman. Iranian reports also said Jiroft Airport in Kerman province, in the country’s southeast, had been struck. Explosions were also reported in Jask, another port city on the Gulf of Oman, as well as in Sirik on the Strait of Hormuz and nearby Minab. According to Iranian reports, four civilians attending a wedding were killed in the strike on Sirik. Iranian emergency services said another 50 people were wounded. Another strike was reported in Asaluyeh on the Persian Gulf coast, home to one of Iran’s main energy hubs.
Two Iranian sources told The New York Times that the strikes caused significant damage, without providing details. They said the targets hit included a military base in Bandar Abbas, the perimeter of the airport on Qeshm Island and additional targets in Sirik and Jask.
Minutes after the first reports of explosions, U.S. Central Command confirmed that the strikes were carried out by the United States and said they were aimed at various IRGC targets. “The strikes follow recent attempts by the IRGC to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. troops stationed in the region,” CENTCOM said.
Iran’s Tasnim News Agency, which is affiliated with the IRGC, meanwhile praised the missile fire. The agency said it was “one of the most extensive Iranian missile attacks against American bases and sites” in comparison with recent launches. “Iran warned that an attack by the American enemy would be answered. The important targets that were struck will be announced later,” the report said.
Following the renewed escalation, crude oil prices jumped about 5% on Tuesday to roughly $90 a barrel, while Brent crude futures surged about 7% to around $94.50. Natural gas prices also rose, with AFP reporting that European gas prices reached levels not seen since 2023.
About 90 minutes after the strikes began, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the United States was carrying out “large and powerful” attacks on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump said the strikes were retaliation for what he described as Iran’s failed attempt to lay sea mines in the strait and for the firing of eight missiles at a U.S. military base in Jordan, all of which he said were intercepted.
He warned that any further Iranian retaliation would trigger an attack at “a much harder and higher level,” adding that an even larger strike was still “waiting in the wings.”
“When it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote.
In an interview with Fox News, Trump issued a similar threat, saying: “If they respond, they will be hit at a much greater level. And if they do it again, they won’t be there.”
He described the Iranians as “crazy and stupid” and said the United States had also struck a radar installation that Tehran had been rebuilding.
“They tried to rebuild their radar because they can’t see anything,” Trump said. “We waited until it was almost completed, and then we hit it.”
Trump also expressed deep skepticism about the prospect of another agreement with Tehran, saying: “I think an agreement with them isn’t worth the paper it’s written on. We gave them many, many chances.”
At the same time, the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem warned Americans in the Middle East that the security situation remained volatile and could escalate unexpectedly, advising heightened vigilance and warning of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.
The embassy also warned that U.S. diplomatic facilities, including some outside the Middle East, had previously been targeted and that Iran and groups aligned with it could attack additional American interests overseas.
The latest confrontation comes as Trump has continued to signal that he wants to maintain economic pressure on Tehran rather than return to a prolonged war.
“This is very limited,” Trump told reporters Monday, while arguing that Iran remained under severe economic strain. “That doesn’t mean we won’t hit them. We’ll see what happens.”
Trump had already vowed Monday to “hit hard” after Iranian missile and drone attacks on U.S. bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates overnight Sunday.
Those attacks followed an earlier U.S. strike on missile launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Washington said the Larak strike was intended to prevent Iran from deploying naval mines in the strait and disrupting tanker traffic moving through the waterway as part of a U.S.-led effort to keep oil flowing out of the Persian Gulf and ease pressure on global prices.

New plan to tackle drug trafficking in Pacific as Australian cases soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
19:52:18 UTC
04:52:18 KST

New plan to tackle drug trafficking in Pacific as Australian cases soar
In short:
Australia has tipped $600 million into a new scheme to tackle drug smuggling in the Pacific.
More than 17 tonnes of illicit cocaine and methamphetamine have been seized in Australia so far this year.
What's next?
As part of the scheme, surveillance of the Pacific Ocean will be bolstered, helping authorities to intercept smuggling vessels and so-called narco subs.
The federal government has tipped $600 million into a new Pacific scheme designed to tackle the surge of drug smuggling into the region, including into Australia.
It comes as leaders grapple with increasingly sophisticated and determined criminal cartels trafficking cocaine and methamphetamines into the country.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced the investment at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau today, as leaders endorsed the Waqa Moana initiative aimed at bolstering surveillance of the vast Pacific Ocean and helping authorities to intercept smuggling vessels and so-called narco subs.
The new funding package, which will be spread over several years, will see Australia spend more on aerial surveillance across the Pacific, as well as additional training and support for police in the region.
The plan is also designed to help police across the Pacific region improve coordination to tackle the trade, while also bolstering Australian Federal Police cooperation with South and Central American countries in an attempt to target the source of the illegal drugs.
Drug smuggling in Pacific fuelled by Australian demand for illicit drugs
Australian and Pacific authorities have become increasingly concerned by the way the drug trade has contributed to social breakdown and police corruption in parts of the region, as well as its contribution to serious health problems like the HIV crisis in Fiji.
The government is also conscious that the drug smuggling trade ravaging some Pacific communities is being fed by Australia's appetite for illegal drugs, with smugglers keen to reach the lucrative markets of major cities such as Sydney, Brisbane and Melbourne.
Earlier this year, the ABC's Foreign Correspondent exposed how the trade was fuelling addiction and criminality across the region, while placing enormous pressure on police as they try to monitor vast swathes of ocean.
Mr Albanese said the Pacific was Australia's "home and family".
"That's why it's in Australia's interests to work with our Pacific partners to combat organised crime," he said.
"For the good of every country in the region, including our own, we need to work together to stamp out the illicit drug trade."
Earlier this year, Australian Federal Police declared the surge in drug smuggling a serious national security threat to both Australia and the region, with more than 17 tonnes of illicit cocaine and methamphetamine seized so far this year.
That is up from 5.5 tonnes in 2025.
Australia needs to ensure 'whole package' is delivered
Fiji's foreign minister, Sakiasi Raisevu Ditoka, said he hoped Pacific leaders would endorse the initiative.
"I believe that's what all the Pacific leaders would like," he said.
"It's such a huge problem for our communities, and hopefully we can all work together to get it fixed."
Analysts have raised questions as to whether the new commitments would be enough to pose a real threat to increasingly sophisticated and well-resourced syndicates running the illegal trade.
Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor of defence and security at the University of Western Australia, said enhancing ariel surveillance with extra planes, helicopters and drones would help authorities catch semi-submersible vessels trying to smuggle drugs.
"Uncrewed ariel vehicles or drones are very effective in the maritime domain at detecting things, especially when they are enabled by software like AI that can pick out small dots in the ocean," she said.
She said she believed Pacific Island nations would welcome the funds, particularly Fiji, which has become a transit point for large drug shipments trying to reach lucrative markets in Australia.
However, she said Australia needed to provide adequate training to ensure Pacific countries could operate the equipment the funding delivered.
"When you are providing capability to a country, whether a patrolled boat or aerial vehicle, it's important you provide the whole package to make sure it's effective," she said.
Drug smuggling to be on agenda at Pacific Islands Forum
The announcement comes as Pacific leaders prepare for their major meetings at the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau, with the plenary session today and a private retreat on Thursday.
The early stages of the gathering were disrupted by another diplomatic stoush; between China and Taiwan. Palau has given Taiwan a more prominent role at this year's meeting, as one of its three remaining Pacific allies.
China's envoy to the Pacific, Qian Bo, threatened that including Taiwan would have "consequences", while Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the "Taiwan authorities will only end up bringing humiliation upon themselves".
But Taiwan's foreign minister, Lin Chia-Lung, issued a sharp response on Tuesday, saying China was trying to "squeeze our international space and coerce our allies".
He also compared China to a guest at a party who acted like a host and created an unpleasant atmosphere for everyone.
"We should not make compromises because of China's bullying," he said.
