Ukraine reportedly asks to buy Patriot missiles using EU loan funds
Ukraine has submitted a request to the European Commission to purchase interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems using funds from the EU's €90 billion loan.
Source: Suspilne, citing its own sources
Details: Ukraine is seeking to spend more than €2 billion on Patriot missiles.
"The European Commission had previously received from Ukraine a list of weapons on which it plans to spend the bulk of the €6 billion remaining in the defence component of the loan. Most of the items concern equipment manufactured in Ukraine and the EU, primarily drones," Suspilne reported.
Patriot air defence systems use PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles of various modifications, which are capable, among other things, of shooting down ballistic missiles. In August 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the US would supply Ukraine with missiles for Patriot air defence systems every month. He also said that since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine had been receiving approximately three times fewer anti-ballistic missiles to defend the country.
The €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan programme provides for €30 billion in budget support and €60 billion for Ukraine's defence needs in 2026-2027. From this amount, €28.3 billion will be allocated to support Ukraine's defence industry in 2026.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that in June, the European Commission began disbursing €3.9 billion to Ukraine, the first instalment of an initial tranche of around €6 billion for the purchase of drones.

Ukrainian schools hear air-alert wails instead of the first-bell welcome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:31:29 UTC
03:31:29 KST

As Ukrainian schools open, students hear air raid sirens instead of the first bell
A boy stands near the site of a heavily damaged residential building following a Russian strike in Kyiv, Ukraine on Sept.1, 2026. (Vladyslav Musiienko / AFP via Getty Images)
Thousands of Ukrainian children mark a milestone on Sept. 1 by stepping into a new world of classrooms and learning, with the "first bell" ceremony traditionally marking this transition.
Yet this year, the "first bell" was forced underground as Russia pounded Kyiv with aerial attacks for the sixth consecutive day, as across the country, hundreds of thousands of pupils see their school life disrupted by Russia's full-scale war.
Nataliia Maievska, the director of a secondary school with an emphasis on bilingual studies, Lyceum No. 257 "Syniozernyi," in Kyiv's northwestern neighborhood, said it was a very bittersweet day.
While glad that her school was able to hold the ceremony in some capacity, she feels for the seven-year-old first-graders whose experience was tainted by the event.
Around 88 new students joined the lyceum's student body of around 1200.
"They will remember this. Because these are the moments that are remembered for a lifetime," said Maievska.
Lessons amid the sound of sirens
Just as the new students were settling into their classrooms, an air raid siren interrupted their first-ever lesson. Without panic, perhaps already used to the sound, the children took each other's hands and walked down to the underground shelter with their new class.
The loud wail of air-raid sirens, sounding more than 10 times a day, leaves the city paralyzed for up to 14 hours on some days.
Kyiv authorities announced on Aug. 31 that learning may need to start in a hybrid format to ensure maximum safety. Schools are told to prepare for all possible scenarios — from teaching in shelters to teaching completely remotely.
"It is impossible to provide full-fledged education for this school in the shelter today," said Maievska. While the school's shelter can accommodate all its students and staff, there is not enough space to fit hundreds of desks and boards to "imitate" a proper classroom atmosphere.
"Our children are already a little used to it, you can see it in their eyes."
The number of enrolled first-graders decreased by 10% compared to last year, according to Iryna Borzova, a member of the Ukrainian parliament's Youth and Sport Committee.
The lawmaker noted that while 2.2 million students are expected to learn in person, up to 800,000 children are likely to adopt a hybrid model, with lessons split between in-person attendance and online study.
About 200,000 students, mainly in the front-line regions, will have to study completely remotely, said Borzova.
For first-grade teacher Olena, this was an unusual first day of school. Instead of speaking to her students in front of the class, she was trying to keep the children safe in the shelter as an air alert interrupted their first-ever class.
However, she feels confident that these students will adapt.
"Our children are already a little used to it; you can see it in their eyes," says Olena.
Despite the sleepless nights, the constant threat of Russian attacks, and the difficult first day of school, Kyiv authorities estimate that almost 94% of first-year students attended school today.
Across the city, 412 schools started the school year. While most opened their doors physically, 11 of them had to experience the "first bell" fully online.
Much remains uncertain about the upcoming school year. Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine will enter its fifth year in a few months, but Ukrainians continue to adjust.
"There is nothing that can force us not to study, not to work, not to endure," added Maievska, looking at the year ahead with resolve.

Schools in at least nine Russian regions received bomb threats on the first day of class
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:30:50 UTC
03:30:50 KST

Anonymous bomb threats targeting schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and other institutions were received in at least nine Russian regions on Sept. 1, according to a count by The Insider. Incidents were reported in the Leningrad, Perm, Kemerovo, and Orenburg regions, along with Tatarstan, the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, and the Altai, Zabaykalsky, and Krasnoyarsk krais. Some institutions were evacuated, but as of the time of publication, no explosive devices had been reported found.
Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko claims that dozens of schools, kindergartens, hospitals, and other social facilities received threats. He called what happened an “information terrorist attack.” According to him, the “enemy” is trying to sow panic by disrupting Knowledge Day — the traditional first day of school on Sept. 1. Drozdenko did not specify, however, who exactly sent the messages or how he arrived at the conclusion that there was a single organizer behind the threats.
In Tatarstan, medical institutions under the regional Health Ministry began receiving anonymous emails starting at 8:00 a.m. The hospitals underwent a partial evacuation but returned to normal operations after inspection. In the Altai Krai, patients and staff were evacuated from the regional diagnostic center, and the anti-terrorism commission reported a wave of threats against social, administrative, and educational institutions.
Authorities in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug stated that after the buildings had been inspected none of the threats had proven to be actionable. Bomb threats against schools, kindergartens, and hospitals were also received in the Perm Krai, the Kemerovo and Orenburg regions, and the Zabaykalsky and Krasnoyarsk krais. There has still been no evidence presented publicly indicating that the geographically dispersed threats came from the same sender or group of senders.
Meanwhile, several museum venues in Moscow suspended operations. The Pushkin Museum announced a temporary closure and canceled tours for a period of four hours, the Museum of the East closed its main building until approximately 1:00 p.m., and the Museum of Moscow and all its branches stopped admitting visitors until 2:00 p.m. The ROSIZO branch on Petroverigsky Lane also suspended the exhibition “Art Behind Closed Doors: Leningrad Apartment Exhibitions of the 1960s–1980s.” The Pushkin Museum, the Museum of the East, and ROSIZO cited “technical reasons,” while the Museum of Moscow cited “reasons beyond our control.” None of the institutions officially linked the closures to the wave of bomb threats.
The mass sending of false threats has happened in Russia before. In February 2020, unknown individuals reported bomb threats against more than 1,500 sites in Moscow in a single day, including schools, hospitals, courts, and every metro station in the city’s network. No bombs were found, but around 8,000 people had to be evacuated.
Also in 2020, at the request of the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office, Roskomnadzor blocked access to Protonmail after the Federal Security Service (FSB) claimed its servers had been used to send threats to 830 sites. The FSB had previously blacklisted the Startmail service, which it claimed had been used to send more than 1,000 bomb threat emails targeting over 16,000 sites. Russian security agencies have not yet named the parties responsible for the current wave of messages.

LONDON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Britain's shop price inflation rose to a two-year high in August as higher energy, input and commodity costs fed through prices, data from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) showed Tuesday.
Shop prices rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating from 0.9 percent in July, according to the BRC.
Food inflation accelerated to 2.8 percent from 2.2 percent in July, while non-food rose to 0.9 percent from 0.2 percent.
"The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed," said Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the BRC.
"In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage," she said.
Dickinson said the months ahead will remain challenging for households, as rising bills put further pressure on budgets and retailers faced persistently high operating costs that limited their ability to absorb further increases without impacting investment, jobs and prices.
She called on the government to address business costs, including business rates, packaging costs and employment taxes, to support growth and help contain the cost of living. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Xi calls for SCO to strive for higher quality development, promote better global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
02:30:31 CST
03:30:31 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
BISHKEK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Tuesday that China is ready to work with all parties to continue to strive for higher quality development, and make the global governance system more just and equitable.
Xi made the remarks in his speeches at the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the "SCO Plus" meeting held in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
PUTTING DEVELOPMENT FIRST
This year marks the 25th founding anniversary of the SCO. Xi said that over the past 25 years, the most significant achievement of the organization has been its gradual transformation into a new type of regional cooperation organization that spans the largest geographical area, represents the largest population, and possesses enormous development potential in the world.
The SCO's most important experience for cooperation is that it has found the right way of coexistence featuring non-alliances, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party, while bringing countries in the region together to build a common home, he added.
At the crossroads concerning the future of humanity, the SCO should shoulder its historic responsibility and take the initiative in steering the course of history, he said.
Xi put forward a four-point proposal at the summit, calling on the SCO to stay committed to putting development and the people first, taking security as a key goal, and promoting dialogue and consultation.
The SCO, Xi said, should champion a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization, consolidate cooperation in traditional areas such as trade and investment, connectivity, energy and resources, and expand cooperation in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence (AI), digital economy, green industry and green mining.
China will develop an international AI application cooperation center with fellow SCO countries, establish a China-SCO port economic cooperation center in Tianjin, and implement 100 technological cooperation projects with other SCO countries in the next three years, he said.
The SCO should pursue coordinated measures to tackle traditional and non-traditional security threats, Xi said, adding that the organization must prevent external forces from interfering in internal affairs, endangering political security, and undermining regional stability.
China stands ready to work with all parties to act on the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, and support the early opening of the SCO's four security centers, so as to upgrade the capacity of member states in responding to security threats and challenges, Xi said.
According to Alexey Mukhin, director general of the Centre for Political Information in Moscow, the outcomes of the SCO summit demonstrated that all member states are focusing on development and security priorities, and working together to address threats and challenges and promote long-term development through effective mechanisms within the SCO framework.
This not only serves the common interests of all parties, but also contributes to improving regional and global governance, Mukhin said.
China stands ready to work with all parties to implement the Global Civilization Initiative, Xi said, adding that China will host SCO forums on innovation and sustainable development, on people-to-people friendship and on friendship cities, as well as establish a China-SCO basic education cooperation center.
The SCO should always advocate that all countries, regardless of their size, are equal, and that regional affairs should be discussed by all countries to bridge differences and build consensus, properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, and meet common challenges through multilateral collaboration, Xi said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
ADVANCING GLOBAL GOVERNANCE
At the "SCO Plus" meeting, Xi called on the SCO to shoulder the responsibility of the times and work together to advance a more just and equitable global governance system, as well as an equal and orderly multipolar world.
In his address, Xi noted that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible, and multipolarity, independent choice of development paths, and greater democracy in international relations are the right way forward.
Xi said that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power. As an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs, he said.
Xi said that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, in which sovereign equality and mutual respect should be upheld as fundamental principles, balance, order and the rule of law as essential requirements, multipolarism, dialogue and consultation as key pathways, and mutual benefit, win-win cooperation and universally beneficial and inclusive development as the way forward.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," Xi said.
China, as a major country, has set an example in this regard and played a leading role, said Seun Sam, a policy analyst at the Royal Academy of Cambodia.
"Major countries taking the lead in abiding by international law can have a demonstrative effect, help safeguard the sovereignty and interests of small countries like Cambodia, promote mutual trust among countries, and achieve peaceful coexistence," he said.
Xi called on countries to promote the common values of humanity, advance the rule of law in international relations, restore the authority and vitality of the United Nations, and improve the coordination and efficiency of global and regional multilateral mechanisms.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi said.
Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, said that with its deep experience in multilateral cooperation, the SCO has developed mature practices for transcending differences, building consensus and fostering cooperation.
It enables countries with different political systems, cultural traditions and interests to engage in equal dialogue and practical cooperation, precisely what is needed to build a more just and equitable global governance system, Ulmasov said.
Highlighting the role of the SCO, Xi put forward three proposals for the organization to advance common prosperity, promote the development and rise of the Global South, and guide the reform and improvement of global governance, to make greater contributions to an equal and orderly multipolar world.
As an important pillar of South-South cooperation, the SCO should carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the "SCO Plus" partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes, Xi said.
"Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said. ■
Chinese President Xi Jinping shakes hands with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. Xi attended the 26th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) held here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Wang Ye)

SAN FRANCISCO, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Apple Inc.'s leadership transition took effect Tuesday, with John Ternus succeeding Tim Cook as chief executive officer and Cook becoming executive chairman of the company's board of directors.
Apple's updated leadership page lists Ternus as CEO and a member of the board, while Cook is now listed as executive chair.
Apple announced the succession plan on April 20, saying the transition had been unanimously approved by its board and followed a long-term succession planning process. Cook remained CEO through the summer and worked closely with Ternus on the transition. As executive chairman, Cook will continue to assist with certain aspects of the company, including engagement with policymakers around the world.
Cook, who joined Apple in 1998, became CEO in 2011 and led the company for about 15 years. During his tenure, Apple introduced new product categories including Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro, as well as services ranging from iCloud and Apple Pay to Apple TV and Apple Music.
Apple said in April that under Cook's leadership, its market capitalization had grown from approximately 350 billion U.S. dollars to 4 trillion dollars, while annual revenue had risen from 108 billion dollars in fiscal 2011 to more than 416 billion dollars in fiscal 2025.
In a public letter to the Apple community, Cook reflected on his 15 years as CEO and said the transition was "not goodbye." He described Ternus as a brilliant engineer and thinker who had spent 25 years helping build Apple products.
Ternus joined Apple's product design team in 2001, became a vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and joined the executive team as senior vice president of Hardware Engineering in 2021.
He has overseen hardware engineering across a range of Apple products and played a key role in the introduction of iPad and AirPods, as well as multiple generations of iPhone, Mac and Apple Watch.
In his April statement, Ternus said he had spent almost his entire career at Apple, had worked under Steve Jobs and had Cook as his mentor. He pledged to lead the company according to the values and vision that have defined Apple for half a century. ■

BELGRADE, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- High-level representatives from across the Global South gathered in Belgrade on Tuesday to mark the 65th anniversary of the first conference of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), reaffirming support for multilateralism, sovereign equality and respect for international law amid heightened global tensions.
The commemorative meeting at the Palace of Serbia brought together more than 30 delegations, including representatives of the movement's current leadership Troika -- Azerbaijan, Uganda and Uzbekistan -- as well as countries with longstanding ties to NAM.
The meeting opened with addresses by Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic and Ugandan Vice President Jessica Alupo, who spoke on behalf of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, as Uganda currently chairs NAM.
Vucic described NAM as an important pillar of multilateralism and warned against what he described as selective approaches to international law.
Delivering Museveni's address, Alupo said the movement emerged in responseto the rigid ideological divisions and polarization of the Cold War and stressed the continuing importance of independent and balanced international cooperation.
She described NAM as "the correct response by sections of the people of the world to the narrow-mindedness that had emerged."
Several representatives from Africa, Asia and Latin America also emphasized themes of strategic autonomy and stronger cooperation among countries of the Global South.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama called for "positive neutrality" and proactive diplomatic engagement, urging Global South countries to translate their collective weight into concrete diplomatic results rather than align with competing power blocs.
Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud highlighted South-South cooperation and multilateralism in addressing transnational challenges, including terrorism and climate vulnerability.
Other participants included Angolan Foreign Minister Tete Antonio, Lebanese Defense Minister Michel Menassa, Indian Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju and Cuban First Deputy Foreign Minister Gerardo Penalver Portal.
The meeting came 65 years after the first NAM conference, held in Belgrade from Sept. 1 to 6, 1961, which brought together leaders of countries seeking to remain independent of the rival blocs of the Cold War.
Serbia, which is not a member of NAM but has observer status, has sought to preserve the diplomatic legacy of the 1961 conference and maintains relations with Global South countries. ■

UN report confirms Syria was building nuclear reactor during Assad rule
Syria’s Deir el-Zour site bombed by Israel in 2007 was an undeclared nuclear reactor under construction
Syria was constructing a nuclear reactor in Deir el-Zour under the leadership of ousted former president Bashar al-Assad, according to a UN report seen Tuesday by Associated Press.
Inspectors with the UN nuclear watchdog visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work that confirmed the existence of a long-suspected nuclear site, according to the confidential report circulated to member states.
Based on this visit, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported that it is “able to establish that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities as required under the NPT Safeguards Agreement”.
This information included a nuclear reactor under construction in Deir el-Zour, a fuel fabrication plant and another site used for fuel storage during the rule of Assad.
Under Assad, Syria was believed to have operated an extensive undeclared nuclear programme that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in eastern Deir el-Zour province. Following Assad’s ouster, the new government agreed to give IAEA inspectors access to suspected former nuclear sites.
The site in Deir el-Zour only became public knowledge after Israel launched air strikes in 2007 that destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it. Israel is believed to have its own undeclared atomic weapons programme that makes it the only country in the Middle East with nuclear bombs.

Health crisis looming as Gaza heads towards rainy season, warns WHO
Water quality in embattled Palestinian enclave already poor; flooding will exacerbate disease, threat to health, says UN agency.
The approach of winter and cold rains are set to worsen a public health crisis that already has a firm grip in the embattled Gaza Strip, the World Health Organization (WHO) has warned.
Recent water testing has shown there is a clear deterioration in the quality of water in the Palestinian enclave and diarrhea cases have surged, the United Nations health agency said on Tuesday, noting that the approach of winter threatens to exasperate the situation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 3 of 3Israeli strikes on Gaza kill at least five, including children
Much of Gaza has been destroyed during Israel’s genocidal war, and it remains under blockade, leaving much of its population without sufficient shelter and exposed to a lack of functioning infrastructure.
“Whilst we fail to provide people with the minimum quantities of water, water quality and water contamination remains a major issue,” said Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, the WHO’s representative in the Palestinian territories.
Potential flooding resulting from winter rains “will [send] the sewage, the waste and contaminated water into the pl000aces where people sleep, cook and care for their loved ones,” she warned.
Testing of approximately 6,700 water samples over the first eight months of 2026 indicated that “microbiological contamination almost tripled,” she told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Gaza.
Contamination increased from under six percent in January to over 18 percent in August, the tests showed.
Cases of acute diarrhea have almost doubled since March, jumping from around 27,000 cases to over 48,000, Van de Weerdt noted.
However, the WHO official insisted there is still time to prevent a public health disaster. She called for “unimpeded and expedited entry of humanitarian supplies”.
Materials needed for permanent shelter and sustainable provision of water and waste management are vital, she said. More laboratory supplies are urgently needed to help confirm the causes of disease and better respond to outbreaks.
Israel has been using water access as a “weapon” in Gaza, Doctors Without Borders declared in April. The group pointed to data from the United Nations, European Union and World Bank indicating that Israel had destroyed or damaged nearly 90 percent of water and sanitation infrastructure in the territory.

Vanuatu pushes France to accept ICJ jurisdiction in Pacific islands dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:21:32 UTC
03:21:32 KST

Vanuatu takes France to ICJ over Matthew and Hunter islands dispute
Vanuatu says French control of islands is a relic of colonial past, as France’s far right uses case as a political weapon.
The Pacific island nation of Vanuatu has filed an application with the International Court of Justice (ICJ) seeking sovereignty over two small Pacific islands controlled by France.
The Hague-based court said in a statement on Tuesday that Vanuatu’s application concerns sovereignty over Umaenupne, also known as Matthew Island, and Umaeneg/Leka, or Hunter Island.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Australia, PNG delay defence pact as China’s rise in Pacific region looms
- list 2 of 3First treaty to protect marine life in high seas to take effect in January
- list 3 of 3Australia, Papua New Guinea sign mutual defence treaty
The case seeks closure on a decades-old territorial dispute rooted in the region’s colonial history. Far-right parties in France are seeking to use the case as a political weapon.
The ICJ, also known as the World Court, will not immediately take up the case because France has not accepted the court’s compulsory jurisdiction over disputes with other states.
Vanuatu’s application has been sent to Paris to determine whether France agrees to let the court hear the case.
“No action will be taken in the proceedings unless and until France consents to the Court’s jurisdiction in the case,” the ICJ said.
The dispute has become part of a wider debate over France’s colonial legacy in the Pacific.
Vanuatu, jointly ruled by France and Britain until independence in 1980, argues that its decolonisation will not be complete until the islands are returned under its control.
The issue has also been seized upon by France’s far right, which has accused President Emmanuel Macron’s government of being prepared to surrender French territory, a claim Paris has repeatedly rejected.
Vanuatu has challenged French sovereignty over the islands since gaining independence, arguing that the colonial-era arrangement placing them under French control was made without consulting the Indigenous population.
Matthew and Hunter are uninhabited volcanic islands in the South Pacific, about 300 kilometres (190 miles) east of the French territory of New Caledonia and southeast of Vanuatu.
While the islands themselves are small, sovereignty affects control over surrounding waters, including fishing rights and access to seabed resources.
In 2025, France and Vanuatu agreed to new rounds of bilateral negotiations over the islands and their maritime boundaries after earlier talks in 2018 and 2019.
Earlier this year, Vanuatu said negotiations had reached an impasse and that it would take the dispute to an international court.
The ICJ, the United Nations’ highest court, deals with disputes between states and frequently rules on disagreements over land and maritime boundaries.

Zoologists stunned by Putin’s use of orcas hunting polar bears as a metaphor for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:19:25 UTC
03:19:25 KST

During a meeting with educators and college students on Aug. 29, Vladimir Putin spoke with Dmitry Balanchukov, a Chinese language teacher from the Belgorod Region who had won Russia’s Teacher of the Year award in 2025. Putin was interested in the teacher’s account of his trip to the North Pole, and the following exchange took place:
Putin: Was it interesting at the North Pole?
Balanchukov: Incredible.
Putin: Fascinating. Did you see any polar bears?
Balanchukov: Yes, of course. We saw two.
Putin: Two? Big ones?
Balanchukov: Huge.
Putin: Can you imagine there are orcas living nearby, and they eat these bears like small fry. They just attack in a pack and tear them apart. It’s all very interesting. That’s how the food chain works. Children need to be told about this too, so they understand what kind of world we live in and why we’re conducting the special military operation.
To call Putin’s account fascinating would be an understatement. No cases of orcas hunting polar bears have ever been documented.
As recently as July 2026, an article appeared in BBC Wildlife Magazine: “Can Any Animals Kill a Polar Bear?” by Melissa Hobson. The orca is named first among the six contenders, but as the article makes clear, the only “evidence” of such encounters has all been AI-generated:
“If any Arctic species was to try to take on a polar bear, killer whales might have a good chance of success. After all, orcas are extremely intelligent and are even known to hunt and kill blue whales.
There are different types of orcas, known as ecotypes, which have different characteristics. Bigg’s killer whales – also known as transient orcas – hunt mammals and are known to travel to the Arctic. These massive mammals can grow to more than eight metres and 6,600 kg (females reach around seven metres and 4700kg). Could they be a match for a polar bear (the very largest of which can sometimes grow to around 800kg but usually weigh between 350 and 600kg)?
Perhaps they could, but this is only speculation. There are no confirmed records of orcas hunting polar bears (although plenty of fake AI videos trying to spread this false news).
Similarly, there’s no documentation of polar bears hunting orcas. Nor is there scientific evidence of polar bears eating orca flesh – although that’s not to say that these scavengers wouldn’t tuck into the energy-dense blubber if they came across a killer whale carcass.
One reason we haven’t yet seen orcas and polar bears coming to blows could be because of their different habitats. Although both are found in the Arctic, polar bears spend most of their lives on sea ice while killer whales avoid the ice because they might get trapped.
Will climate change put the two in each other’s path more often – and who would come out the victor? That remains to be seen.”
The article’s author states that the only creature that can kill a polar bear is another polar bear — or a human.
Following Putin’s meeting with teachers, the independent Russian environmental outlet Kedr.media published an article titled “‘No one eats them’: Zoologists on Putin’s claim that orcas ‘eat polar bears like small fry.’” The resulting report cited the expert opinions of professional zoologists (all of whom chose to remain anonymous when discussing the president’s factual error). The article states:
“Contrary to the Russian president’s claims, orcas do not eat polar bears, Kedr learned upon speaking with two zoologists who specialize in marine mammals...
‘Absolutely no one preys on polar bears. They’re at the top of the food chain,’ one of the scientists told Kedr. ‘And so are orcas. The only thing they might theoretically compete over is that both polar bears and predatory orcas feed on seals.’
The zoologist notes that the two species could technically encounter each other, but the only hypothetical scenario in which an orca could eat a bear, or vice versa, is if one of the animals is already dead.
‘You could imagine an orca carcass washing up on shore and polar bears eating it. But that’s about it. Honestly, there is really nothing to comment on here, simply because there have been no cases of an orca attacking a bear,’ the zoologist says.
Scientists note that neither orcas nor polar bears have any natural predators, apart from humans.
‘The only enemy of the polar bear is humans — the human presence in the Arctic. And that really is a serious threat to the species’ survival. The same goes for orcas. People affect them by depleting their food sources — primarily fish — and through tourism. This year, once again, we’re seeing dozens of vessels chasing orcas off Kamchatka. So the human-caused threats they face really are shared,’ one of Kedr’s sources says.
Another scientist suggests that the president may have formed his impression of orcas and polar bears from AI-generated videos: ‘AI enthusiasts have churned out this kind of footage and dumped it online. They post a lot of similar nonsense — like orcas rescuing seals on their backs, or the other way around, fantastically pulling someone out of somewhere. There is similar content with other animals: lions and wolves living together as one pack, bears and other animals sleeping in the forest in an embrace. Seriously speaking, though — orcas, like all predators, prefer to attack prey they’re familiar with and know how to handle. That could be seals, walruses, or fish, depending on the group’s dietary specialization, which depends on the region where they live. But it’s not polar bears.’
Another zoologist with field experience notes on social media that orcas and polar bears use the same habitats, but there are no actual observations of them interacting. And theoretical speculation, the zoologist writes, should not be presented as fact — ‘not until there are observations in the wild.’”

The Guardian view on the global bond shock: Andy Burnham should take note | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:15:24 UTC
03:15:24 KST

“In the midst of every crisis lies great opportunity” is an aphorism attributed to Albert Einstein. It seems to be taken to heart by this White House. A global bond sell-off sparked by an inflationary shock emanating from the Gulf sees Donald Trump seeking to restrict plans by Japan – a longtime ally – to reduce dependence on an international system America dominates.
Japan, a successful exporter, has long done things its own way. For years Tokyo saw off the bond vigilantes despite running enormous deficits and a huge national debt. It demonstrated how a central bank could fund public spending and keep interest rates low if it wanted to. This economic model was refined by Shinzo Abe, Japan’s longest-serving prime minister. However, this week the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called time on Abenomics as his price for US help in stabilising Japan’s currency. Japan’s Sanae Takaichi, he indicated, should shrink her $2tn spending plans and raise rates. Abenomics did not suddenly become financially impossible. It became inconvenient to the issuer of the world’s reserve currency.
Kevin Warsh, Mr Trump’s handpicked chair of the US Federal Reserve, has made it clear that he will raise interest rates in response to inflationary pressures. Others will be expected to follow. In Japan’s case, Washington fears that a yen crisis could become a bond crisis. A disorderly rout could force Japan into ever larger currency interventions – and repeated appeals to Washington to help defend the yen. If such aid proved inadequate, Tokyo could end up defending its currency by dumping US treasury bonds – of which it has more than a trillion dollars worth – and put upward pressure on the very yields Mr Bessent is trying to contain. His demand that Tokyo raise rates and cut spending is not just about Japanese inflation. It is about trying to prevent Tokyo’s adjustment to the Iran shock being exported on to America’s balance sheet.
Mr Burnham’s first Commons speech as prime minister suggests an expansive programme to raise living standards and get growth through regional reindustrialisation. This, he says, rests on the “bedrock” of fiscal responsibility. Mr Burnham promises an activist state to deal with four decades of underinvestment and privatisation. But retaining Rachel Reeves’s fiscal framework leaves his investment plans hostage to interest rates, debt costs and feverish “headroom” speculation. Turmoil in global bond markets could derail his industrial strategy before it gets going.
Japan’s big bazooka spending programme was meant to do what Mr Burnham now says Britain must do on a smaller scale: use the state to rebuild productive capacity, reduce strategic dependence and build its export competitiveness. Tokyo has the fiscal firepower, a central bank able to dominate the sovereign bond market and trillions invested overseas. The UK government could mimic that and change its fiscal rules, its relationship to the Bank of England and the way investment is accounted for.
But Japan is Mr Burnham’s problem writ large. The war in Iran made it urgent to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. But the conflict’s inflationary shock makes that objective harder – though not impossible – to pursue. Mr Trump’s team is using its leverage over the yen to restrain Tokyo’s plan to make Japan resilient to external price spikes. Mr Burnham has been forewarned: the Gulf inflation shock wave bolsters the argument for economic independence while making the means of achieving it more difficult.

The Guardian view on loneliness: the decline in friendship leaves gen Z exposed | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:14:13 UTC
03:14:13 KST

Hope, Raye told a crowd at Reading festival on Saturday, was the theme of a set inspired by her second album. Having established through a show of hands that most of the audience had just done their GCSEs, and after recounting her own rocky road to stardom, the 28-year-old singer led a series of upbeat chants of “it’s gonna be all right”.
For anyone who thinks adolescence ought to be a time of optimism, it was a charming spectacle. But a new report from the Institute for Public Policy Research thinktank paints a much gloomier picture. Building on existing evidence of declining wellbeing, such as Alan Milburn’s report on young people who are not in education or work, the IPPR’s researchers found that 11- to 24-year-olds in England (gen Z and older members of gen Alpha) are increasingly lonely. They have fewer friends than young people in the past and are less contented with those they do have. One in 20 say that they have no friends at all. A series of interviews produced worrying evidence of their lack of confidence about the future.
They also spoke about problems with concentration that they associated with social media. When asked what they do in their spare time, the most common answer was “doomscrolling”. But while the authors point to “deference to unaccountable tech oligarchs” as one way in which politicians have let younger generations down, their analysis goes wider. It includes housing costs, a shortage of entry-level jobs, student debt, austerity and the Covid-19 pandemic. They conclude that the social contract with youth is broken and needs fixing.
This is a deliberately broad-brush study that focuses on what the 10 million 11- to 24-year-olds in England have in common. But it does not gloss over socioeconomic differences. The steepest falls in life satisfaction over the past decade have been in deprived areas; housing is a far more serious blockage on the route to independence for those without family wealth. Noting that the average deposit has risen to £78,000, the report states that “owning a home before your mid-30s has become close to an inherited trait”. With social housing all but impossible to access for most young adults, too many are either stuck with parents or in privately rented flats. Labour has already taken steps to boost the supply of new homes, but must do more to improve young people’s prospects. It is a national scandal that so many are locked out.
Adolescence is a complicated time of life, and there is an echo of Sigmund Freud’s idea of “ordinary unhappiness” in the report’s reference to the “ordinary challenges” of growing up. It is hard to leave school and parents, and decide what to do next. This is one reason why supportive peer relationships are so important, and why research on friendship is worthwhile.
But while gen Z and gen Alpha deserve attention, their problems should not be viewed in isolation. The weakening of the social fabric around them can be seen as part of a wider pattern that the IPPR rightly links to neoliberalism’s assault on collectivism. There is no single policy lever that can be pulled to mend the missing threads. But governments and councils are far from helpless. Housing, job-market reforms (including limits on AI in recruitment) and a stronger overall emphasis on generational fairness would all make the world a friendlier place for under-25s.

Poles eating more meat but drinking less alcohol
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:12:58 UTC
03:12:58 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poles are eating more meat but drinking less alcohol, continuing a long-term trend, the latest data from Statistics Poland (GUS) show.
The average person in Poland ate 82 kilograms of meat in 2025, which was 7.5% more than a year earlier. It also marks an increase of 15.7% since 2015 and 22.7% since 2005. Likewise, consumption of eggs rose 8.5% in 2025 to an average of 218 per person.
The increases have come amid rapidly rising incomes, which make such products more affordable. A separate GUS study earlier this year showed that the proportion of Poles who cannot afford to eat meat at least every other day fell from 8.2% in 2015 to 3% in 2025.
By contrast, vegetable consumption has changed little, with the average Pole eating 108 kg in 2025, compared with 107 kg a year earlier and 110 kg in 2005.
However, consumption of potatoes, a starchy staple of the Polish diet presented by GUS separately from other vegetables, has fallen sharply over the longer term, despite a slight increase last year. The average Pole ate 96.5 kg of potatoes in 2025, down 23.4% since 2005.
Meanwhile, alcohol consumption last year continued its recent decline. In 2025, the average Pole drank 81.7 litres of beer, down 4.9% from the previous year and 18.7% from the peak of 100.5 litres per person in 2018.
Likewise, consumption of spirits and liqueurs fell 5.9% year-on-year in 2025 to 3.2 litres per person. That was 13.5% down from a peak of 3.7 litres in 2019. In 2025, the amount of wine drunk per person, at 4.9 litres, fell even more, by 9.3% year-on-year.
However, alcohol consumption is still higher than it was two decades ago, with the average Pole drinking 28% more spirits and 1.2% more beer in 2025 than in 2005.
A 2023 study by ProVeg, an NGO, conducted in partnership with the University of Copenhagen and Ghent University, found that Poles were the most carnivorous among ten European countries surveyed.
Three quarters of Poles (74%) said they ate meat frequently, compared to an average of 62% across all countries. Italians and Spaniards (both 69%) were the next biggest meat eaters, while Germans (45%), Austrians (48%) and the Dutch (53%) were the least likely to eat meat frequently.
Meanwhile, 7% of people in Poland said they were either vegan (2%), meaning consuming no animal products at all, or vegetarian (5%), meaning they do not eat meat or fish. That was just below the European average of 8%.
In terms of what kinds of meat are favoured by Poles, GUS’s most recent such breakdown, from 2017, showed that pork was most popular, with the average Pole consuming 39.8 kg that year, followed by poultry (26.kg) and beef (2.3 kg).
Poland's first company to produce cultured meat – which is grown in a lab from animal cells without the need to raise and kill livestock – has received a state grant to support its work.
LabFarm this year presented a prototype of its chicken meatball https://t.co/pezABciGU6

Earlier this year, Poland’s current government, a coalition ranging from left to centre right, announced new rules intended to improve the quality and variety of school meals, including offering less meat.
From the start of the new school year, which began today, school canteens are expected to serve meat no more than twice a week, offer fish at least once per week, and offer a plant-based option at every meal.
They should also limit fried food to no more than twice a week, use seasonal and locally sourced products, and include fruit and vegetables with meals.
However, an attempt by the government to further raise taxes on alcoholic, sugary and sweet drinks was vetoed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki last December.

Ukraine does not threaten civil aviation, yet carriers flying to Moscow, St. Petersburg, or other major hubs must factor in the risk of drones in Russian skies, Zelensky said in an address posted to Telegram.
"Today we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports — Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous," he said.
"Although the Russian authorities do not report this as it should, the Russian sky will de facto be closed," he added.
At a press conference, Putin then accused Ukraine of "state terrorism" and said that Moscow could not negotiate with terrorists.
Russia's missile and drone attacks have closed Ukraine's airspace since beginning its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
This situation was brought about by Russia itself through the war it wages against Ukraine, Zelensky said.
The president pointed to Russia's attacks, including strikes on Sept. 1 that killed 12 people and injured another 21 in Ukraine's capital and Kyiv Oblast.
"This is purely Russian terror against civilians. Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has tried to block our ports, and due to Russian strikes on Ukraine, our skies are closed to civilian aviation," he added.
Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov welcomed Zelensky's announcement and condemned Russia's attacks, saying that "Ukraine will deliver a firm and proportionate response."
Zelensky also addressed ambassadors serving in Kyiv and Moscow, urging them to warn their governments as well as airlines serving destinations in Russia.
Ukrainian authorities would provide international bodies with full information about the hazards, according to Zelensky.
Kyiv will work with partners traveling to Russia, with Ukraine open to pausing strikes to ensure safe passage, as it did for CIA Director John Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow on Aug. 25, Zelensky said.

It is an important project for J&K and this bid will open investment in the Union Territory after a long time,” an official said Tuesday.

Its commercial inventory included 62 shops in the main commercial module, 38 spaces in Craft Bazaar, 11 kiosks, two food courts, a restaurant and 11 office spaces.But the dream never got off the ground. Most shops stayed shut. Buyers who acquired units did not open them. Weeds overran the premises, turning what was meant to be a bustling commercial hub into a near-deserted property.
Now, a fresh lease could mean a fresh start. The front and rear portions have been offered for development on a full-lease basis, with a multiplex and other commercial facilities proposed.The Sangarmaal auction also set the stage for another high-stakes property bid. At Batamaloo, about 6km away, roughly 70 kanals (8.75 acre) of bus-stand land has remained largely underused and vulnerable to encroachment. Srinagar Development Authority (SDA) is seeking to redevelop it for better use.Bidding opened at Rs 95 crore on Aug 27 and climbed to Rs 305 crore by evening, with Construction Engineers, another J&K consortium, emerging as highest bidder. Batamaloo is also being offered on a full-lease basis, with plans for shopping, office spaces and housing.

Meet Sean Parnell, Pentagon's Chief Spokesperson and a Contender to Succeed Army Secretary Driscoll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:08:59 UTC
03:08:59 KST

Prior to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitting his resignation Monday, Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had been suggested by some close to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as a potential replacement for the Senate-confirmed position.
The Hill reported last week that Parnell’s name was being floated, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the matter.
Asked about the reports, a senior Administration official told TIME: “Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”
News of Driscoll’s departure from the role he held for around 18 months came after months of reported tensions with Hegseth and turmoil within the department.
A person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation is quoted as telling media that for Army Secretary had recently “brought up concerns with the Administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible.”
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly did not address the tensions and fallout when approached by TIME, but instead emphasized that the United States Army is “more powerful than ever thanks to [Driscoll’s] work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War.”
Driscoll’s resignation is the latest in a series of high-profile departures within the Pentagon, following the April ouster of the Army’s top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, and the June departure of the lead commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue.
The firing of George was reportedly a source of contention between Driscoll and Hegseth.
Driscoll openly praised George, referring to him as “an amazing, transformational leader” whom he loved and respected during an April House Appropriations Committee Hearing. Driscoll told lawmakers that after George was fired, his family drove to the former general's house and gave him a hug.
Alongside the reported tensions, Hegseth has also come under serious scrutiny for the duration and mounting cost of the Iran war, which surpassed the six-month mark last week.
“I don’t have any confidence in him anymore. I think he’s all over the place—he’s accelerating the retirement or forcing out some of the most distinguished leaders in the DOD that we have,” Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said in July.
Meanwhile, under Parnell, the Department of Defense has imposed various restrictions limiting journalists’ access in the Pentagon.
In an unprecedented move in June, the department designated its press office a classified area.
“The Pentagon Press Office has been redesignated as a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility due to speechwriters from the Office of the Secretary of War sharing the facility,” said deputy Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez. “As a result, journalists will no longer be permitted to enter the office space. There’s nothing controversial about that.”
Now, with talk turning to who may replace Driscoll in the pivotal role of Army Secretary, Parnell's name continues to be floated. Notably, whoever is selected would need to be confirmed for the position by the Senate.
Here’s what to know about Parnell's military record, his past controversies, and more.
Parnell is an Afghanistan veteran who penned a memoir on his experience
Parnell arrived in Afghanistan in 2006 and during his 16-month deployment was awarded two Bronze stars and the Purple Heart. He was deployed alongside his platoon, nicknamed the Outlaws.
He returned home with shrapnel in his leg and a brain injury that had left him with vision problems.
Following retirement on medical grounds, he penned a 2012 war story memoir titled Outlaw Platoon, in partnership with author John R. Bruning, detailing his experiences in the region.
Parnell went on to become a senior advisor for the Concerned Veterans of America and is credited with playing a key role in the passage of the Mission Act in 2018 under President Donald Trump, with the goal of delivering care and support for U.S. veterans.
Parnell previously criticized Trump before becoming a staunch supporter
Parnell backed now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination where he faced off against Trump, who went on to win both the nomination and presidency.
According to Parnell, his support for Rubio, who at the time was a Senator in Florida, was cemented by his vocal backing of matters related to Veterans Affairs (VA).
“There are lots of strong options. But if fixing the VA, rebuilding our military, and doing right by our veterans is a top priority for you, then Senator Rubio should be your first and only choice,” Parnell said in a campaign press release.
In a separate interview, he described Rubio as a "unifying voice” who the country “desperately needs” and labeled him “my guy.”
By contrast, Parnell had called out Trump in 2015, referring to his criticism of the late Republican Sen. John McCain, a prisoner of war, as “the height of arrogance,” arguing that Trump had “no clue what our Vietnam POWs endured.”
However, Parnell had a change of heart once Trump took office, stating in a 2019 interview that the President had earned his respect “because he forces us to talk about issues. Political correctness doesn’t allow us to talk about them.”
At the 2020 Republican National Convention, Parnell further praised Trump, insisting he had “unleashed the economic might of this nation like no other President in our history.”
Parnell suspended his campaign for Senate amid abuse allegations
Parnell, after running unsuccessfully for the House in 2020, went on to launch a bid as the GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. He suspended his Trump-backed campaign in November 2021, after losing a fight for custody of his children to his then-estranged wife, who had accused him in court of abuse.
Laurie Snell had alleged that Parnell choked her and injured their children. Parnell vehemently denied the claims.
Snell also testified in court that Parnell had been unfaithful.
Following Trump’s announcement in February 2025 that Parnell was tapped to become chief spokesperson for the Pentagon, some media coverage saw the abuse allegations revisited.
If Parnell were put forward for a Senate-confirmed position in the future, the historical allegations could be brought up in his confirmation hearing.

Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:02:00 UTC
03:02:00 KST

Congo's Ebola caseload tops 6,000 as concerns grow
September 1, 2026
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, with confirmed infections now topping 6,000 and the death toll reaching 2,911, according to government figures.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, has spread to around 60 zones in six provinces, raising fears that the virus is outpacing efforts to contain it.
"Around 60 health zones are now affected, every week more are added to the list. And the same pattern is repeated everywhere: initially, there is resistance and denial, followed by gradual acceptance," DW correspondent Jonas Gerding reported from Bunia, the capital of the Ituri province, the epicenter of the latest Ebola outbreak in Congo.
"Unfortunately, a lot more people will die until this Ebola outbreak gets under control," he added.
Health experts have said the situation is particularly worrying in eastern Congo, where conflict and insecurity are making it harder for response teams to reach affected communities.
"This outbreak is the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic on record. It is growing faster and wider than the response to contain it, but it can be stopped," UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told journalists last week.
The United Nations has appealed for more funding as humanitarian agencies struggle to keep pace with the increasing number of cases.
"International attention, political focus and resources are still lagging behind the reality unfolding on the ground," Guterres said, warning that the world "must also overcome another virus — the virus of indifference."
Vaccination campaign gathers momentum
As researchers continue trials aimed at developing a licensed vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain, Congolese authorities have rolled out a vaccination campaign focused on front-line health workers.
The vaccine was originally developed for a different Ebola variant, but officials hope it will provide some protection against the current outbreak.
Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses had already arrived in the country.
"We will cover all the provinces that are around Ituri, moving in a ring towards the center of the outbreak, that is to say towards Ituri. But we have enough doses for all healthcare providers," he said on August 28.
Some health workers remain confident despite uncertainty over how effective the vaccine will be against the Bundibugyo strain.
"It is a vaccine that has already proven itself. We are talking about Ebola Bundibugyo, of Ugandan origin. But the vaccine that they want to administer to us was the vaccine that had succeeded for the Zaire type," said health worker Arnaud Batumbu.
"Since both cases involve a viral disease, I hope the vaccine will work for us now as well," he added.
Communities seek protection
Residents in hard-hit areas say they are ready to take the vaccine if it is properly explained to them.
"I will be ready to get vaccinated if only someone explains to me the importance of this vaccination," Clemency, a student in Tshopo province, told DW.
Others are calling for wider access. "Children need to be vaccinated too. They go back to school; there are many of them in class," said local resident Carine Lobwadji
Some community members also fear vaccine supplies may not be enough.
"I have learned that this is an insufficient quantity. I ask the authorities to add other doses for Tshopo and that we vaccinate everyone, especially those who will voluntarily agree, since some are afraid," said Onyeka Treasure, a photographer.
Violence hampers response
The latest outbreak is unfolding against a backdrop of violence and mass displacement in eastern DRC, complicating efforts to stop transmission.
Ebola response teams have reported attacks while carrying out their work, including during operations to safely handle Ebola-related deaths.
"We demand greater security so we can operate in the field and do our work without endangering our lives," Floribert Magene, a member of an Ebola response team, told The Associated Press on Monday after an attack in Ituri province.
Magene said his team was assaulted near Mambasa while responding to a call to secure a body.
Economic toll grows
Beyond the health emergency, the outbreak is worsening economic hardship for many families.
Schools have reopened in towns such as Bukavu and Bunia, but many parents are struggling to afford basic school supplies.
Stationery shop owner Furaha Mpangu Esperance told DW that demand has collapsed as families prioritize food and other essentials.
"In any case, it doesn't work. The situation is serious because there are no customers. We have even lowered the prices but there is no one to buy. Before, we even sold 10 boxes, 20 boxes a day. Today not even three boxes, not even two! The situation is critical," he said.
To reduce disruption to education, the government has proposed radio-based learning for children unable to attend school.
"For us, it's a double objective: to ensure that children continue to go to school, despite the epidemic, and to ensure that distance learning is the device that will help them," Education Minister Raissa Malu told DW.
Teachers, however, say many areas lack the infrastructure needed for effective distance learning.
"We, the teachers, are ready, but we don't have the tools. In sensitive areas, even picking up frequencies is quite a problem," said Patrick Girinegi, president of the Ituri teachers' inter-union alliance. "The first-grade children can't read, nor do the parents. Several schools don't have printers or computers. How will it go?"
Many students and parents would rather see classrooms remain open with stronger health measures in place.
"It's easy for me to understand when it's my teacher himself who explains it to me. Saying that the child stays at home to listen to the radio, I don't think it's going to work. We [must] find ways to go to school without contaminating ourselves," said Viviane Tshipamba, vice-president of the Ituri children's committee.
Despite the challenges, health authorities point to a positive sign: more than 1,360 people have recovered from Ebola so far. For many Congolese, those recoveries offer hope that with stronger support, increased vaccination rates and improved security, the outbreak can still be brought under control.
Marcus Loika, Gaston Mukendi and Mitima Delachance contributed to this article.

German politician wants to send Taurus missiles to Ukraine after Russian drone attack in Leipzig airport

Wolfgang Kubicki, chair of Germany’s pro-business liberal Free Democratic Party (FDP), proposed that Berlin summon Russia’s ambassador and use the prospect of Taurus missiles for Ukraine as leverage against further hybrid attacks during an appearance on German broadcaster ntv.
Kubicki’s proposal does not change German policy. The FDP has no seats in the Bundestag, Germany’s federal parliament, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out supplying the missiles. However, it recasts military aid to Ukraine as a potential cost Moscow would face for hybrid attacks inside Germany. Berlin has since formally blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle operation that prompted his remarks.
Kubicki said “a reasonable person” would tell the ambassador that Germany had so far withheld Taurus missiles. If the hybrid threat continued, Berlin should do everything possible to ensure Ukraine received the weapons it needed to defend itself against Russia, he added.
Taurus, the weapon Kubicki spoke about, is a German-Swedish cruise missile launched from military aircraft, with a range exceeding 500 kilometers. Ukraine has sought it for years to strike military targets far behind Russian lines.
Germany refused to supply Taurus missiles in 2025 while funding hundreds of Ukrainian-made long-range systems. Merz again ruled out a transfer in March, arguing that Ukrainian weapons were more effective.
Leipzig sharpens Germany’s hybrid-war debate
Germany formally blamed Russia on 1 September for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and said it would close the Russian consulate in Bonn and terminate the agreement under which the Russian House cultural center operates in Berlin, DW reported. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cited evidence from German and allied intelligence services, as well as investigations across Europe. Russia has denied involvement.
The operation that prompted Kubicki’s warning involved an explosives-laden drone that struck the wing of a Ukrainian Antonov An-124 heavy cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August but failed to detonate, Die Zeit reported. The airport handles civilian freight and NATO logistics, while Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines uses it as a base.
Investigators later found evidence that three drones were involved and discovered about 50 grams of suspected military explosive near the runways.

Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:01:07 UTC
03:01:07 KST

The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks.
The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out.
A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said.
Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”
He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said.
The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, supported Germany’s move and the new round of European sanctions, saying: “These hybrid attacks are multiplying in Europe. They cannot go unanswered.
“In the face of this escalation, we must be united, determined, and strengthen our support for Ukraine. France will continue to play its full part.”
Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, said: “The security of our allies is the security of us all. Attempts to intimidate us or to drive a wedge between allies will not succeed: hybrid actions against any one of us are a matter of concern for all of us, and will be met with a united response.”
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said: “Attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence – and it will fail. Our support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s aggression is unshakeable.”
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, called the sanctions “another mistake,” suggesting the restrictions were aimed at currying favour with voters.
“I think it’s another mistake, a serious one,” Putin said during a press conference broadcast by the Russian state news agency Tass. “And in my view it clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people.”
The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building.
A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones.
New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said.
Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection.
The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed.
The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin.
Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”.
Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack.
It marks the lowest point in decades for relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which had already plunged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
This weekend will see a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point.
The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible.
The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600g of explosives and was discovered in the security area of the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.
The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday.
Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network.
Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil”.
Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other.

US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll has officially resigned after months of alleged tension with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, ending an 18-month tenure that included a high-profile role in the US efforts to advance peace negotiations over Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Citing an anonymous US official on Monday, Aug. 31, CBS News reported that Driscoll submitted his resignation after speaking to US President Donald Trump about the current state of the Army. The White House separately confirmed his resignation.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told CBS News.
“The US Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief [Trump himself] and Secretary of War [Pete Hegseth],” she continued, citing Driscoll’s military readiness, as well as his involvement in Russia-Ukraine negotiations.
Friction with Hegseth
Driscoll’s departure followed months of friction with Hegseth over the Army’s leadership and current modernization efforts.
The possibility of his exit was first reported by The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), while CBS News separately reported on Aug. 22 that Driscoll was considering leaving by the end of the year.
The tensions reportedly intensified after Hegseth ousted General Randy George, a close friend of Driscoll’s, from his role as Army chief of staff in April, asking him to take early retirement.
Koretskyi Hints at Austerity Measures to Relieve $27B Budget Shortfall
General Christopher Donahue, then commander of US Army Europe and Africa, also filed for retirement.
Both George and Donahue supported the Unmanned Assault Battalion, a unit established in 2025 to study drone warfare, including lessons from Ukraine. The army later began planning to phase out the battalion amid friction between officers who backed it and acting Army Chief of Staff, General Christopher LaNeve, CBS News reported.
Driscoll and George had also promoted the Army Transformation Initiative, which emphasized greater use of unmanned systems.
A source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Driscoll raised concerns with the Trump administration over the transformation effort and the removal of senior officers involved in it.
Role in Ukraine peace effort
On Nov. 19, 2025, Driscoll traveled to Kyiv with two four-star generals, where he met with President Volodymyr Zelensky, alongside other Ukrainian officials and defense-industry representatives as part of efforts to revive stalled diplomacy between Kyiv and Moscow.
The visit took place as Zelensky traveled to Turkey for discussions with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
The White House opted to involve Driscoll because it reportedly believed Moscow might be more open to military-brokered talks, particularly after previous diplomatic efforts produced little progress in the stalled negotiations.
Driscoll held talks with Russian officials in Abu Dhabi, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on Nov. 24, 2025, as Washington revised its Ukraine peace proposal from 28 points to 19. According to several US media outlets, he was also expected to meet Ukrainian officials during the visit.
Ukraine had repeatedly called for an immediate ceasefire during three rounds of talks held in Istanbul in May, June, and July 2025.
Russia, however, refused the ceasefire proposals, and instead issued demands that included the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from four regions, an end to Western military assistance, and limits on Ukraine’s mobilization and martial law.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war remain ongoing, although Moscow has yet to agree to a ceasefire or engage on terms acceptable to Kyiv.
Russia rejects peace proposals
Citing Kremlin-linked sources, Bloomberg reported on Aug. 26 that Russia was considering escalating attacks on Ukraine after concluding that peace negotiations have “reached a dead end.”
According to the sources, all attempts at negotiations have effectively collapsed, leaving Ukraine and Russia with virtually no progress.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov announced on Aug. 29 that peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine are currently on a “deep pause” as Russian forces press their offensive in eastern Ukraine.
Moscow increasingly viewed Ukrainian strikes as attacks by NATO, because alliance members are supplying Kyiv with weapons and intelligence, Bloomberg reported.Around the same time, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow, to allegedly deter Russia from escalation against NATO’s eastern flank.
On Monday, Zelensky said Kyiv and Washington are discussing a possible visit by senior US envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner. “This trip would be very useful for working out decisions toward peace,” Zelensky said.
