John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:36:33 UTC
02:36:33 KST

John Ternus succeeds Tim Cook as Apple CEO after 15 years
Apple gears up for innovation under Ternus before a new product launch event that could include foldable phones.
John Ternus has officially taken over as the chief executive officer of Apple, succeeding Tim Cook, who ended a 15-year tenure leading the tech giant.
Ternus, who took the helm on Tuesday, had been serving as the senior vice president for hardware engineering at the Cupertino, California-based company since 2021.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Apple regains top spot as world’s most valuable company
- list 2 of 4US stocks near record high, oil falls as Trump claims Iran talks under way
- list 3 of 4Telegram says Apple suspension followed content norms violation by one user
- list 4 of 4Google Maps renames Lake Ontario after Trump’s decree on ‘Lake America’
When Apple announced the transition in April, the company said that Cook will move into the role of executive chairman.
Ternus is an old hand at the company. He joined Apple’s product design team in 2001 and climbed the ranks. He was appointed vice president of hardware engineering in 2013 and was promoted in 2021 to the senior vice president role that he has now moved up from.
A graduate of the University of Pennsylvania, Ternus had previously worked on virtual reality headsets at a company called Virtual Research Systems.
Since joining Apple, Ternus has overseen the launch of a range of its most well-known product lines, including the iPad and AirPods.
Given Ternus’s background in hardware engineering, analysts saw his appointment as a sign that the company, best known for its iPhone, is pushing to double down on innovation across its device portfolio.
“The appointment of Ternus is Apple’s subtle way of [doubling down] on hardware innovation as a core strategy. It doesn’t refute the Tim Cook era; it marks a new stage in Apple’s history by intertwining AI with hardware, rather than treating AI as a standalone product,” Babak Hafezi, professor of international business at American University, told Al Jazeera.
Ternus’s task
Ternus is set to hit the ground running in the new role. On September 9, Apple is expected to unveil its latest iPhone as well as a foldable device, a new product in its lineup. The foldable phone market, although still niche, is a growing segment of the consumer phone sector that is currently dominated by Samsung, which launched it in 2019.
Analysts forecast that Apple will make headway quickly. Apple is expected to ship 17 million foldable iPhones and reach 40 percent of the market share by the end of next year, according to IDC research, a tech intelligence firm.
Apple is also slated to launch a new version of Siri, its personal assistant, with the newest version of its iOS software planned for release this month. It is intended to be more conversational and provide more personalised content for individual users, including scanning personal emails and text messages.
In a news statement announcing the new feature, the company used the example of using Siri “to find a restaurant recommendation a friend messaged them about, surface a hotel confirmation number from an old email”.
Ternus comes into his new role at a time that Apple has been criticised for a slower rollout in the generative AI space, falling behind companies like OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, and Anthropic, the maker of Claude.
However, Aleksandar Tomic, associate dean for strategy, innovation, and technology at Boston College, argues that focusing on its core products could help Apple lead the AI boom in the long run.
“To use a metaphor, there were people during the gold rush mining for gold, and then there were those selling the picks and shovels for the prospectors. Apple has really stayed in the picks-and-shovels lane,” Tomic said.
“They have not done any kind of data centre, industrial-grade chips, but they have developed their own chips that they put into the Macs and MacBook Pros that allow people to run local LLMs [Large Language Models] and so on. The iPhone becomes kind of an AI access engine.”
In June, analysts at Morgan Stanley expressed concern that Apple may struggle with an AI Siri rollout because its older phones lack the capability to run advanced AI features.
This comes as Apple also faces supply chain strains. In June, the company raised the price on some MacBooks and iPads as the cost of computer memory increased due to AI companies driving up demand for chips and servers.
It also has to walk a tightrope between Washington, DC’s trade war with China, where it has a huge market and major supply chain, even as it has attempted in the last few years to diversify some of that to India and Vietnam. Apple has announced plans to invest billions of dollars in the US, and President Donald Trump wants the company to make its iPhones there.
For investors, Cook is a tough act to follow. Under his leadership, the company’s stock jumped 2,258 percent. Apple’s stock has grown steadily over the last year, too. It is up more than 37 percent since this time last year, and more than 16 percent since the beginning of 2026.
On Tuesday, the company’s stock rose by 2.2 percent in midday trading as Ternus took over his new role.

EU vows to maintain pressure on Iran despite growing criticism of alignment with Washington
TEHRAN — The European Union has pledged to continue working with the United States, the G7 and other international partners to maintain economic and political pressure on Iran, in a move that highlights what critics describe as Brussels’ growing alignment with Washington’s Iran policy despite its earlier calls for restraint and diplomacy.
In a statement issued ahead of this week’s G20 meeting, the EU said it would support efforts aimed at ensuring that Iran, as it described the situation, “ceases its destabilizing activities and engages in peace negotiations in good faith.”
The bloc also endorsed the use of additional economic pressure, including measures linked to the US-led “Operation Economic Outcast,” which Washington has presented as part of its campaign to intensify economic pressure on Tehran.
“The EU will continue to work closely with the United States and other G7 and international partners to maintain pressure on Iran and contribute to de-escalation and regional stability,” the statement said.
The EU’s position reflects a significant evolution in Europe’s approach to the conflict. At the beginning of the US-Israeli war against Iran, several European governments publicly stressed that they had not participated in the attacks and called for diplomacy and restraint. European officials also expressed concern that the conflict could escalate into a wider regional war with serious consequences for energy supplies, trade and migration.
A report by the Council on Foreign Relations noted that the US launched its military operation with little or no consultation with its European allies, leaving European governments divided over the use of force and the extent to which they should support Washington.
Germany, France and Britain initially resisted direct involvement in the US military campaign. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, for example, questioned whether Washington had a convincing plan for achieving its objectives and said European governments had not been consulted before the operation began.
However, European governments have gradually moved closer to Washington’s position, particularly through sanctions and political pressure on Tehran.
 
  
Europe’s shifting position raises questions over policy effectiveness
The shift has prompted criticism from analysts who argue that Europe is repeating a pattern of failed policies by attempting to exert pressure on Iran while lacking an independent diplomatic strategy capable of influencing the course of the conflict.
Sophia Besch of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace argued in April that Europe should avoid simply “falling in line” with Washington and instead develop a strategy that allows it to engage with the conflict independently. She noted that the United States had gone to war with Iran without consulting European governments, while the Trump administration subsequently criticized European allies for failing to provide sufficient support.
A separate analysis by Poland’s Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) said European governments had acknowledged that they lacked effective instruments to exert pressure on Tehran or control its actions. It also warned that European governments were concerned that the US-Israeli military campaign lacked a realistic long-term plan and could produce further destabilization, with economic and migration consequences for Europe itself.
These assessments raise questions over the effectiveness of a European strategy increasingly centered on sanctions and coordination with Washington. Rather than creating an independent European diplomatic channel, Brussels appears to be moving toward greater synchronization with the US pressure campaign, even as the costs of the conflict increasingly affect European economies.
The economic consequences are particularly significant. The ongoing conflict around the Strait of Hormuz has disrupted energy markets and contributed to higher oil and gas prices. European Central Bank policymaker Olli Rehn has warned that the prolonged conflict could keep inflation in the eurozone above the ECB’s target, with eurozone inflation reaching 3.3 percent in August.
Pressure from Washington and the limits of European autonomy
The European shift has also taken place under sustained pressure from the Trump administration. Washington has repeatedly demanded greater European support for its war against Iran, while criticizing European countries for refusing to provide direct military assistance.
In the early stages of the conflict, European governments rejected calls to participate directly in efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. France, for example, said it would not take part in operations to open or “liberate” the waterway under the circumstances at the time.
Washington’s pressure nevertheless continued. US officials accused European allies of failing to meet what they considered their responsibilities, while President Donald Trump repeatedly demanded greater assistance from NATO members.
The evolution of Europe’s position therefore illustrates what critics describe as a broader failure of EU foreign policy: Brussels has sought to preserve its transatlantic relationship while simultaneously presenting itself as an independent diplomatic actor, but the Iran conflict has exposed the limits of that approach.
Brookings analysts have described Europe’s initial approach to the war as a serious miscalculation, arguing that many European governments hoped a short conflict might lead to political change in Iran. They concluded that this expectation proved mistaken and that the war exposed Europe’s weaknesses in dealing with the crisis.
The criticism comes as the United States itself faces growing questions over the effectiveness of its Iran strategy. A recent Council on Foreign Relations assessment said the US war had failed to produce the quick victory predicted by Trump and that Washington now faced a situation in which it had few good options.
Reuters has similarly reported that, six months into the conflict, the war had developed into a costly stalemate, with Iran’s government remaining in place despite severe economic pressure and a US naval blockade that has sharply constrained Iranian oil exports.
Against this backdrop, the EU’s decision to maintain pressure on Tehran risks tying Europe more closely to a US strategy whose stated objectives have yet to be fully achieved.
For Iran, the latest European statement is likely to be viewed as further evidence that the EU has moved away from its earlier emphasis on diplomacy and toward alignment with Washington’s coercive approach.
For Europe, meanwhile, the central question is increasingly whether following Washington’s pressure campaign can deliver the stability the EU says it seeks — or whether it will instead deepen the economic and geopolitical costs of a conflict over which European governments have limited influence.

In Keir Starmer’s north London constituency, full of pretty pubs and elegant townhouses, few tears were being shed at the news of his departure as its MP.
One man nursing a pint outside a pub in Kentish Town simply remarked “good” when informed his MP had quit. He added: “I thought he was very nice before he became prime minister; I met him a few times. But he messed the country up and screwed over pensioners.”
Annie, a 30-year-old doctor having a coffee and pastry on a bench near the tube station, said: “I think everyone here wanted him to leave. He’s had a rough time of it, sure, but we have all had enough of him.”
Dominic Ford, a 75-year-old pensioner reading a book outside the Parakeet pub, was more sympathetic. “I think he’s sensible. It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,” he said. “He’s a very nice, honest guy, and he was very visible around here. We used to see him going to the Arsenal with his son. He was a good local MP, and very honest. I felt very sorry for him when he resigned as prime minister.”
On a quiet street among rows of pastel-coloured terrace houses is the Pineapple, Starmer’s favourite pub. It is out of the way of the high street, and the former prime minister is frequently seen there drinking a pint.
He may have become tired of his pub visits being documented in various newspapers, because when the Guardian visited and asked regulars what they thought about him stepping down, the bar staff firmly said that questions about Starmer were not allowed. Perhaps this commitment to discretion is why he has referred to the pub as his “church” and “the best pub in land”.
Starmer announced his departure as prime minister in June after several unpopular choices including making Peter Mandelson, a friend of Jeffrey Epstein, ambassador to the US. On Tuesday, Starmer told the Camden New Journal he wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”.
Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the seat.
Laura Hyland, a 67-year-old artist, said she was pleased Starmer was stepping down and that she welcomed the prospect of a byelection. “He gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive. Arresting people for holding signs saying ‘I support Palestine Action’ was disgraceful.”
Anita, 52, was doing her shopping on the high street. She also welcomed Starmer standing down, and said: “I can’t stand him. He was completely useless and I am glad he stood down.”
The former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Theresa May both committed to serving out a term as an MP for their constituencies after losing a general election.
Sunak is still representing his North Yorkshire constituency, now Richmond and Northallerton, two years after Starmer taunted him about whether he would be moving to California to work in tech. Lewis Galloway, 43, who works in marketing, said he would have liked to see the same from Starmer.
“It’s a shame that he’s standing down,” he said. “There was something nice about Theresa May and Rishi Sunak when they stood down and still worked for their constituents from the backbenches. It is a real shame to lose him from this form of public service so prematurely.”

China Focus: Restoring road access to mudslide-hit border port remains top priority
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
01:35:11 CST
02:35:11 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 1, 2026 shows a road emergency repair site in Gyirong County, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. The damaged section of G216 national highway leading to the Gyirong Port in Gyirong County was reduced to only 700 meters by around 6 p.m. on Tuesday. Restoring road access to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port remains the top priority as rescue efforts continue, according to Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters and acting mayor of Xigaze City, where Gyirong County locates. Nearly 700 personnel are involved in the effort to reopen the G216 national highway leading to the port on the China-Nepal border, according to the official. (Xinhua/Jiang Fan)
GYIRONG, Xizang, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Restoring road access to the mudslide-hit Gyirong Port remains the top priority as rescue efforts continue in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, a local official said Tuesday.
Nearly 700 personnel are involved in the effort to repair the G216 national highway leading to the port on the China-Nepal border, according to Norbu Tsering, deputy head of the emergency rescue headquarters and acting mayor of Xigaze City.
Drone footage seen by Xinhua reporters showed that by around 6 p.m. Tuesday, crews had repaired the highway on a limited basis, allowing search and rescue vehicles access to within some 700 meters of the port.
The final stretch of the highway to Gyirong Port was severely damaged by the mudslide, cutting off road access and hampering rescue operations in the disaster area.
While road repairs continue, rescuers have spent four consecutive days searching a 0.7-square-kilometer area around the border gate using life detectors and other equipment, Norbu Tsering said.
Heavy rainfall is expected over the next two days, while supplies and additional personnel are being airlifted into the core disaster area to sustain rescue operations.
The mudslide, caused by an ice-rock avalanche in Nepal, hit Gyirong Port on Aug. 26, claiming 16 lives and leaving 546 others missing at the border port as of 6 p.m. Saturday, according to the regional government's latest update.
More than 2,000 personnel have joined the search and rescue operations, including those from the People's Liberation Army (PLA), the People's Armed Police Force and China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise.
The PLA Western Theater Command's air force deployed drones on Tuesday to monitor changes in high-risk areas, providing information to support disaster response and coordination of rescue operations.
A unit of the People's Armed Police Force used machinery in coordinated operations to level an open work area covering several hundred square meters, creating space for emergency support personnel and resources to be positioned closer to the disaster zone.
A medical and epidemic prevention team provided medical and psychological support and disinfected affected areas. The team is also working to meet the basic medical and epidemic prevention needs of rescue workers and disaster-affected residents.
Following the mudslide, China's meteorological authorities have launched coordinated sky-ground observation for Gyirong Port, employing satellites, weather radars and ground-based stations to support weather monitoring and forecasting services in the affected areas, according to the China Meteorological Administration on Tuesday.
To address challenges posed for meteorological monitoring and forecasting due to complex terrain in the areas, the administration has coordinated the use of observation equipment, including Fengyun meteorological satellites, in key areas such as the disaster zone, barrier lake areas, upstream catchment zones and downstream river banks.
As of 5 p.m. Tuesday, telecom operators in Xizang had restored one base station and added 12 emergency base stations in areas affected by the mudslide, ensuring uninterrupted communications for emergency command, rescue operations and supply coordination.
After the disaster, telecom operators dispatched repair teams and activated all-operator emergency mode and 5G roaming services to improve coverage in the border area.
The barrier lake above the Gyirong Port has been fully drained and risks associated with it are now under control, according to an assessment by a team of experts on Tuesday.
Earlier radar surveys put the barrier lake's area at about 0.1 square kilometers with up to 2.2 million cubic meters of water. Rescue workers closely monitored water inflows and changes in the dam through on-site observation, video surveillance and slope-monitoring radar.
The charity federation of Xigaze has issued a public notice on donation channels for disaster relief, accepting bank transfers and on-site donations.
Meanwhile, China has dispatched the second batch of emergency humanitarian aid for Nepal, including water purification and lighting equipment, genetic testing devices and drones. ■

LONDON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Britain's long-term government bond yields rose sharply on Tuesday, with the 30-year gilt yield climbing to around 5.9 percent, its highest level since 1998, as a global bond sell-off combined with higher energy prices and renewed concerns over inflation and public finances.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt rose to around 5.25 percent at one point, its highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis, before closing at 5.21 percent. The 30-year gilt yield later ended the session at 5.85 percent.
The moves came amid a broader sell-off in global bond markets, with government bond yields also rising in the United States, Germany and Japan.
Market analysts said renewed tensions in the Middle East had pushed up international energy prices, reviving concerns that inflation could remain elevated for longer and prompting investors to reassess the outlook for monetary policy in major economies.
Bond markets have also been weighed down by concerns over high public debt and substantial government borrowing needs in several major economies, as investors demand higher returns to hold longer-dated debt.
In Britain, domestic inflation and fiscal concerns have added to the pressure on gilts.
Data released by the British Retail Consortium on Tuesday showed that shop prices rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating from 0.9 percent in July and marking the fastest increase in more than two years.
Food prices increased 2.8 percent, while non-food prices rose 0.9 percent. The industry body said higher energy, raw material and commodity costs were increasingly being passed on to consumers.
Britain's fiscal position has also remained under close market scrutiny. Data from the Office for National Statistics showed that public sector net borrowing stood at 1.8 billion pounds (2.4 billion U.S. dollars) in July, 700 million pounds higher than a year earlier.
From April to July, cumulative public sector net borrowing reached 56.7 billion pounds, 6 billion pounds lower than the same period last year but still 2.3 billion pounds above the level forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility.
The British government is due to present a new budget on Oct. 28. Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is seeking to roll out a series of measures aimed at boosting investment and easing cost-of-living pressures.
Market participants are widely concerned that higher gilt yields could further increase the government's financing and debt-servicing costs, adding to the challenge of balancing additional spending with efforts to keep the public finances on a sustainable path. ■

SCO adopts declaration on nuclear safety partnership
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
01:34:50 CST
02:34:50 KST

BISHKEK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) adopted on Tuesday a declaration on enhancing multilateral partnership for nuclear safety and security.
In the declaration, the SCO member states confirmed that a country bears full responsibility for its nuclear security, and that the responsibility for nuclear safety lies with the operator of the nuclear facility and the state in which the facility is located.
Member states said they are deeply concerned about the illegal trafficking of nuclear materials and other radioactive substances, the threats to nuclear facilities and infrastructure (including computer security), and the risks of nuclear terrorism.
They, in the declaration, also strongly condemned any attacks on or threats of attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, deeming such acts a violation of international law, and called for refraining from such actions, which pose a threat to international peace and security.
The members considered it necessary to take effective measures to prevent nuclear and radiological emergencies and ensure the physical security of nuclear materials and other radioactive materials, as well as related facilities, according to the document.
They also called for strengthening the domestic control mechanism for nuclear materials and other radioactive substances, boosting joint education, scientific research and technology projects, expanding cooperation and conducting exchanges on advanced practices and experiences in the field of safe operation of nuclear facilities.
The member states also agreed to conduct exercises and training among their respective competent authorities, strengthen early warning systems and, where necessary, share technical data, forecasting models and analytical information in real time, while ensuring the security and confidentiality of sensitive information. ■

8,800-year-old mining workshop uncovered in SE Türkiye
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-02
01:34:42 CST
02:34:42 KST

ANKARA, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- A mining workshop dating back about 8,800 to 8,900 years has been unearthed in southeastern Türkiye, Turkish Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said on Tuesday.
In a post on social media platform X, Ersoy said the workshop, covering around 5 square meters and dated to 6900-6800 BC, was found at Cayonu Mound in the Ergani district of Diyarbakir Province.
Excavations uncovered raw and semi-processed malachite, processed malachite samples, copper beads, copper objects, and a stone-paved work area within the workshop.
"The new discovery reveals the earliest production technologies in human history," said Ersoy.
Cayonu Mound is a 12,000-year-old Neolithic site that witnessed the transition from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to settled life, agriculture, and animal husbandry. ■

Peru declares state of emergency in 893 districts over El Nino rain threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:34:15 UTC
02:34:15 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Peru declared a 60-day state of emergency in 893 districts across 22 regions and Callao over the threat of intense rainfall linked to El Nino, local media reported Tuesday.
The measure was established through Supreme Decree No. 124-2026-PCM, published Tuesday in the official government gazette El Peruano, according to Peru21 media outlet.
The declaration covers districts in 22 regions, including La Libertad, Lambayeque, Piura, Tumbes, Lima and Ica, as well as the Constitutional Province of Callao.
The decree is based on technical reports from Peru’s National Meteorology and Hydrology Service, National Center for Disaster Risk Estimation, Prevention and Reduction, National Civil Defense Institute and the commission studying El Nino.
Authorities warned that continued Coastal El Nino conditions and the development of El Nino in the central equatorial Pacific could contribute to intense rainfall.
The emergency declaration will allow regional and local governments to implement immediate measures to reduce risks and carry out response and rehabilitation efforts during the 60-day period.
The National Civil Defense Institute will coordinate and monitor the measures with regional and local authorities and government ministries.
The measures will be financed through the institutional budgets of the entities involved and will not require additional funding from the national Treasury, according to the decree.
Authorities warned last week that El Nino could put about 1.2 million people at risk, particularly in areas vulnerable to flooding and landslides.
Northern agricultural regions are among the areas considered most exposed to the phenomenon.
El Nino involves abnormal warming of Pacific Ocean waters and can cause intense rainfall and flooding in parts of Peru.

Schools across the Democratic Republic of Congo reopened Tuesday for a new academic year, according to Education Minister Raissa Malu, despite rising Ebola cases.
The school year began across the country, including in areas affected by the Ebola outbreak, Malu told reporters in Kinshasa.
“Some parts of our country continue to face insecurity and conflict, while others face the health risk linked to the Ebola virus disease,” she said.
“But our duty remains the same — to make schools work wherever possible and to preserve the right to education wherever circumstances make the situation more difficult,” she added.
Malu said face-to-face teaching would continue in areas where health conditions permit.
“Where health conditions allow, teaching will continue face-to-face, in compliance with the recommended preventive measures,” she said.

Confirmed Ebola cases in the current outbreak have reached 6,100, including 2,950 deaths, according to a Health Ministry update Tuesday.
Ituri remains the epicenter of the outbreak.
About 31 million students are expected to attend school across the country this academic year.

Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:34:06 UTC
02:34:06 KST

Russia is sending jet-powered drones against Ukrainian cities in growing numbers—no longer only the Iranian Shahed-238 it fields as the Geran-3, but the newer, faster Geran-4 and Geran-5. The fear everyone voices is their speed, but speed breaks the cheap layer, not the missiles.
Ukraine's expensive air-defense missiles already routinely shoot down cruise missiles, and to them, a fast drone is just one more target. The strain falls on the cheap layer instead—the interceptor drones Ukraine built to down thousands of Shaheds a month for a few thousand dollars each, a fraction of a missile's price.
Those were designed to catch slow drones, and against jet speed, they struggle. If that layer breaks, the cost of defending Ukraine's skies climbs—and the Defense Ministry has already started paying to keep it from breaking.
The shift is not marginal, and it continues to accelerate. Russia had sent more than 2,500 jet-powered Shaheds against Ukraine by 30 August, against roughly 1,500 in July, informal presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov wrote—the drones, he noted, were launched practically straight from the factory. Russia fired roughly 1,400 jet-powered drones since the start of 2026 to June, and air defenses recorded about 180 in all of 2025, Colonel Oleksandr Zaruba of Ukraine's State Research Institute said.
A record month, and the weapon built to beat it
Ukrainian interceptor drones destroyed more than 33,000 Russian drones of all types in March 2026—roughly double the February total and a record for the cheapest layer of Ukraine's air defense, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said.
Russia sent Shaheds—cheap, propeller-driven, long-range, lumbering in at about 185 kilometers per hour (115 mph)—in mass raids meant to swamp Ukraine's defenses. Ukraine adapted, with mobile fire teams, electronic warfare, and layered engagement, then added interceptor drones that destroy incoming drones for a fraction of a surface-to-air missile's cost.
As Ukraine got better at catching propeller drones, Russia reached for speed—jet-powered versions that fly more than three times faster than the Shaheds Ukraine spent three years learning to intercept.
By August, Ukraine's military intelligence said Russia had stopped building the Geran-3 and shifted to the newer jets, producing roughly 3,000 of them a month.
Conventional air defense already handles this
The worry centers on velocity: a jet drone flies several times faster than a propeller-driven or electric one, reducing the time defenders have to detect, identify, and hit it. But the fear aims at the wrong place, said Oleksii Kolesnyk, director of the Ukrainian firm Reactive Drones.
"A jet-powered UAV is, in many ways, similar to a cruise missile. For conventional air defense, jet-powered drones are simply another aerial target," he told Euromaidan Press.
Ukraine's surface-to-air systems routinely intercept cruise missiles. A fast drone is standard work for them—though Zelenskyy said in late August that the jets are the hardest to intercept, and that combat aircraft now mainly protect against them.
The strain lands on the interceptor drones
An interceptor drone, unlike a ground-launched missile, has to chase its target down and ram it, which worked against slow Shaheds. Against something near cruise-missile speed, the geometry breaks.
The problem exists almost only for interceptor drones, Kolesnyk said—they were never designed for these speeds. At jet velocities, guidance, target tracking, and the final homing onto the target all hit technical ceilings, and faster interceptors alone will not fix it.
"New technical solutions will be needed," he said.
Interceptor drones are why Ukraine can answer mass raids without firing a missile worth hundreds of thousands of dollars at each incoming drone. Break that math, and the affordability of Ukraine's whole air defense shifts.
The Defense Ministry's answer
Through the defense-tech accelerator Brave1, Ukraine backed 12 technologies under the EU4UA Defence Tech grant program, offering up to €150,000 each for high-speed interceptors capable of reaching 450 kilometers per hour (about 280 mph) or more.
Ukraine is testing four new drone interceptors as Russia floods its skies with faster Gerans
That push has since produced candidates. By late August, Ukraine had four interceptor systems built to run down the jets, all already in field testing, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said, and the Alexa Spatium had entered service. Ukraine now wants to bring them up to standard and build them in the thousands.
Not a revolution, but an evolution with a long history
Colonel Oleksandr Saienko, a former Ukrainian brigade commander, rejected the idea that any of this is new.
"This is better described as an evolution of unmanned systems rather than a completely new stage of warfare," he said.
Trending Now
Jet drones long predate this war. "The first jet-powered UAVs appeared back in the 1970s," he said, pointing to Soviet reconnaissance drones beginning with the Tu-143 and continuing with the Tu-141 and Tu-243—platforms Ukraine itself later flew in the Donbas war and the full-scale invasion. What has changed is scale, and the problem the drones now solve: arriving before the defender can react.
Ukrainian intelligence: Russia’s new jet-powered Geran-4 attack drone runs on Chinese turbojets
Saienko's warning points past the engine.
"The decisive advantage will not belong to whoever simply has a jet engine. It will belong to whoever integrates these platforms into an effective reconnaissance-strike system, protects them against electronic warfare, manufactures them at scale, and keeps costs manageable," he said.
His frame is the kill chain—detect, identify, decide, engage—and every gain in speed compresses that cycle. "If a target is flying at 500 to 700 kilometers per hour, even a delay of several dozen seconds may make interception impossible," he said, adding: "Radars must see sooner, command systems must classify automatically, and operators get less time—until automation becomes a requirement."
Why hasn't every drone gone jet-powered
Speed solves one problem and creates several. "They are simply another category of strike UAV," Kolesnyk said.
Compact turbojets are expensive and hard to source for smaller drones. Bigger airframes have to be reinforced to take the loads and vibration, which adds weight and cost. Fuel burn climbs far above that of the electric or piston drones built for endurance, and higher speed leaves less room for navigation errors.
So, jet drones fill a niche rather than taking over the whole strike fleet. "They are most effective at ranges of roughly 200 to 600 kilometers," Kolesnyk said—fast strikes on high-value or time-sensitive targets, where getting there quickly matters more than flying cheaply or far.
Russia unleashes its Geran-5 air defense killer on Ukraine, equipped with British Raspberry Pi microcomputer tracker
Ukraine didn't drop first-person-view (FPV) drones when fiber-optic ones arrived, and jam-resistant drones didn't replace the rest. Each capability added a layer rather than erasing the previous one. Saienko expects the same. "The emergence of jet aviation did not eliminate piston-engine aircraft. The same principle applies," he said. Cheap propeller drones are ideal for mass attacks, while jet platforms handle speed.
The next fight is over reaction time
Jet drones force defenders to decide faster, and that is the harder demand. A slow propeller drone is a wasteful target for an expensive missile. A cruise missile demands an instant answer. A jet drone sits in between—and an operator has to sort which weapon meets which target in seconds, while holding scarce interceptors back for the worst threats. Every misjudgment costs something.
"The challenge is no longer only interception—it is detecting, identifying, and assigning the target quickly enough," Saienko said.
Both experts reach the same conclusion from opposite ends: Kolesnyk through the technical limits of the interceptor drone, Saienko through the entire defensive network. Both land on automation—AI-driven target recognition, distributed sensors, and fast data sharing to shrink the gap between spotting a target and hitting it. The winner won't necessarily fly the fastest aircraft. It will process information faster than its opponent.
Over four days at the end of August, Russia fired about 800 jet drones at Ukraine, Ukraine's president said—a type most of Ukraine's cheap interceptors still cannot catch. And the problem won't stay Ukraine's alone. Drones from the same broad Shahed family have already strayed into NATO airspace and turned up in other wars. The interception race Ukraine is running now is one everyone will eventually run.

US military not adapting fast enough says former General
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:30:47 BST
02:30:47 KST

The United States has not yet developed the new concept of warfare required to exploit advances in artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and other emerging technologies, General David Petraeus has warned, calling for extensive changes to American force structures, training, procurement and military institutions.
Speaking at the House of Lords on 1 September, the former commander of US and coalition forces in Iraq and Afghanistan said technological superiority alone would not provide a lasting military advantage. While describing the American innovation sector as the most dynamic in the world, Petraeus argued that US defence institutions are not changing rapidly enough to exploit the technologies being developed.
He said: “The United States confronts a somewhat different challenge. Our innovation ecosystem remains the most dynamic in the world. Advances in artificial intelligence, software, autonomous systems, advanced manufacturing, and other emerging technologies continue at extraordinary speed.”
Petraeus added: “Our challenge is therefore not principally one of technological innovation. It is one of transforming our military institutions rapidly enough to exploit that innovation.”
He told peers that the United States was already investing heavily in emerging military capabilities, but argued that purchasing increasingly advanced equipment without corresponding changes to military organisations would not be sufficient.
Petraeus said: “The United States is investing heavily in emerging capabilities, and those investments are necessary—though not nearly sufficient. No nation will secure enduring strategic advantage simply by purchasing better technology. And the United States has not yet developed the revolutionary new concept of warfare this moment requires, much less begun the vast resulting changes in force structure, organization, training, leader education, procurement, and personnel.”
He compared the scale of the changes he believes are now required with reforms undertaken by the US military during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Petraeus recalled that in 2006 the Army and Marine Corps developed new counterinsurgency doctrine, reorganised forces, changed training and professional military education, accelerated acquisition, adjusted personnel policies and introduced systems for rapidly capturing and distributing operational lessons.
He said: “Those reforms were significant. But they were modest compared with what is required now. The challenge before us is of an altogether different order—and greater urgency. It calls for swift and revolutionary institutional transformation.”
Petraeus said every major defence institution would need to be considered against the demands of a new concept of warfare. He identified force organisation, leadership education, formation training, procurement, engagement with industry, recruitment of technological expertise and the exploitation of operational lessons among the areas requiring simultaneous change.
He said: “Every major defense institution must be reconsidered through the lens of the new concept of warfare. How we organize forces, educate leaders, train formations, procure capabilities, engage industry, cultivate technological talent, and capture and exploit operational lessons will all have to evolve together.”
Part of that process would involve reconsidering established force structures and equipment whose roles are being affected by surveillance, precision strike and unmanned systems. Petraeus said political leaders would have to challenge established assumptions while military leaders reconsider organisations that had served successfully for generations.
He said: “None of this will be easy. Political leaders will have to challenge long-established assumptions; military leaders will have to rethink organizations and force structures that have served successfully for generations; acquisition systems will have to operate at the pace of technological change; and industrial capacity, innovation, education, and national resilience will all have to be treated as elements of national security.”
Petraeus also warned of resistance to the changes, saying: “Powerful institutional, industrial, and legislative constituencies will resist changes that threaten established structures, priorities, and interests.”
The former CIA director said the starting point should be a new concept for conducting warfare rather than simply another cycle of equipment procurement. “Our first priority, therefore, should not simply be to acquire new technologies, critically important though that is. Our first priority should be to develop an entirely new concept of warfare. Only then can we identify the institutional changes required to execute it successfully.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Egypt on Tuesday for a rare two-day visit, as Beijing and Cairo seek to protect their economic interests and strengthen coordination amid the fallout from the months-long Middle East war.
Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, were welcomed at the airport by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and his wife, along with an Egyptian folk dance performance.
The visit comes as China and Egypt face potential US sanctions over financial and economic ties to Iran. Washington has threatened expanded measures against countries and institutions supporting Tehran, potentially affecting Chinese and Egyptian banks.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has positioned itself as a neutral player in the conflict and repeatedly called for a lasting ceasefire. Egypt, meanwhile, has urged restraint as the regional conflict threatens its security and trade interests.
Beijing looks to deepen regional influence

Analysts say Beijing sees Cairo as an important regional partner because of Egypt’s diplomatic role in mediating between Israel and Palestinian groups and its relationships with both Washington and other Middle Eastern powers.
“China sees Cairo as a strategic power broker,” said Gamal Salama, a political science professor at Egypt’s Suez University.
Egypt’s ties with Washington and regional actors give Beijing “political access and diplomatic leverage” in a region where China wants a greater role, Salama said.
Both China and Egypt support an independent Palestinian state as part of a two-state solution.
Xi said he looked forward to “renewing the friendship” with Sisi and working with him to establish a new blueprint for deepening their comprehensive strategic partnership, in an editorial published by Egyptian media Tuesday.
Trade and investment at the heart of visit
The visit marks 70 years of diplomatic relations between China and Egypt and comes as economic ties continue to expand.
China’s trade surplus with Egypt reached $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
The two countries are expected to sign agreements covering artificial intelligence, transport, energy and investment in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, Egyptian media reported.
Beijing has also strengthened military ties with Cairo. The Chinese and Egyptian air forces conducted joint exercises in August featuring China’s J-16 fighter jet.
For Egypt, closer ties with China could provide additional investment and technology while allowing Cairo to preserve its longstanding relationship with Washington.
“What Egypt is seeking is strategic autonomy: not breaking with Washington, not aligning completely with Beijing, but creating enough room to pursue its own national interests,” Salama said.
The visit also comes ahead of an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump later this month, as Beijing seeks to reinforce relationships with US-friendly countries across the region.

Which American weapon — and how — caused the Lamerd massacre on the first day of the attack on Iran?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:28:57 UTC
02:28:57 KST

Which American weapon — and how — caused the Lamerd massacre on the first day of the attack on Iran?
TEHRAN — The apparent first combat use of a new US precision missile during the war against Iran has raised fresh concerns over the potential impact of advanced American weapons on civilian populations, with an investigation by Airwars finding evidence that the munition scattered lethal fragments across an area far wider than its publicly advertised fragmentation radius.
An Airwars analysis of three apparent Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) attacks in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd on February 28, the first day of the US-Israeli attacks on Iran, found that one strike produced visible damage extending at least 170 meters from the estimated point of detonation. Civilians were reportedly killed at distances of up to more than 50 meters from the explosion.
According to the investigation, the attacks killed at least 21 civilians, including at least seven children and two women, while as many as 170 others were injured.
The findings are particularly significant because the PrSM is designed not simply to destroy a target through a conventional blast, but to detonate shortly before reaching the ground and disperse tens of thousands of metal pellets in a 360-degree pattern.
The weapon's fragmentation mechanism means that people, buildings and vehicles within its lethal or damaging range can be struck by high-velocity projectiles even if they are not located directly at the point of impact.
Airwars said the distinctive pattern left by the munition was visible across streets, buildings and vehicles in Lamerd. Rather than the large crater normally associated with many conventional missile strikes, the aftermath showed thousands of small impact marks consistent with the dispersal of fragmentation pellets.
A weapon designed for long-range precision
The PrSM is manufactured by Lockheed Martin and is launched from the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, or HIMARS. The company says the missile can strike targets at ranges of up to 500 kilometers, making it a significantly longer-range weapon than earlier systems employing similar fragmentation technology.
Each missile is reportedly capable of carrying approximately 180,000 pellets, although key technical details, including the exact size of its warhead and the distance its fragments can travel, have not been publicly disclosed.
The missile appears to be an evolution of the Alternate Warhead version of the US Guided Multiple Launch Rocket System. That weapon also disperses large numbers of pellets but has a reported range of about 70 kilometers, less than one-sixth that of the PrSM.
The apparent use of the PrSM in Iran therefore represents more than the deployment of another battlefield weapon. It demonstrates the extension of a fragmentation-based strike capability to considerably greater distances, while raising questions about how such a weapon can be employed safely in or near populated areas.
Airwars said neither the US Department of War nor Lockheed Martin has publicly specified the PrSM's fragmentation or lethal radius. By contrast, promotional material produced by Lockheed Martin appears to indicate a maximum fragmentation radius of roughly 50 meters. The damage documented in Lamerd was therefore more extensive than the radius suggested by the promotional material analyzed by Airwars.
Michael Meier, a former Special Assistant to the US Army Judge Advocate General for the Law of Armed Conflict, warned that the weapon's use in densely populated locations could create an inherent risk to civilians.
 
 “You would be hard pressed to find a reason to use the PrSM in a densely populated area,” Meier said, adding that if the lethality radius were around 100 meters, civilian casualties would be inevitable.
Three strikes in less than a minute
Airwars reconstructed the sequence of events using CCTV footage, images published by Iranian media and testimonies collected by journalists who visited the affected locations.
The investigation identified three separate strikes over a distance of roughly 550 meters in the Shahrak Isar and Tal-e Khandagh residential neighborhoods and at the Shahid Naimi sports hall. The strikes reportedly occurred within approximately 31 seconds.
The first strike hit Shahrak Isar at approximately 17:37:46. Airwars identified damage extending almost 80 meters from the estimated impact point. Masoumeh Monfared and her son, Abedin Gharibdoos, were reportedly killed outside their home, around 40 meters from the estimated epicenter.
Ten seconds later, another missile reportedly struck the Tal-e Khandagh neighborhood. Two-year-old Avina Barzegar was killed while playing in the yard of her home. A memorial marker identifies the location, which Airwars estimated to be approximately 50 meters from the missile's estimated point of detonation. The investigation identified observable pellet damage extending at least that far.
The third strike hit the Shahid Naimi sports hall at approximately 17:38:17. At least seven civilians were reportedly killed, most of them children.
Among the victims was 12-year-old Ilya Khatami, who was reportedly struck while attempting to flee after playing football. Another boy, Abdul Mosavar Rahmani, and football coach Mahmoud Najafi were also killed. Two teenage girls, Helma Ahmadizadeh and Elham Zaeri, were reportedly killed inside the sports center while practicing volleyball.
The investigation also identified damage at a learning center approximately 170 meters from the sports hall strike. Airwars described this as the furthest documented damage associated with the three attacks, although it cautioned that the actual radius could have been greater because of limitations in the available imagery.
Dispute over responsibility
The US military has denied responsibility for the Lamerd strikes. US Central Command argued that CCTV footage was consistent with the dimensions and silhouette of an Iranian Hoveyzeh cruise missile.
However, damage analysis cited by Airwars from The New York Times challenged that assessment. Experts consulted in that analysis reportedly concluded that the pattern of destruction was inconsistent with a Hoveyzeh missile and instead identified the weapons as PrSMs, making the Lamerd attacks the missile's likely first known combat use.
The distinction is important because the physical evidence left at the sites corresponds to the PrSM's known operating concept. The missile reportedly detonates 15 to 20 meters above the ground, distributing fragments over a broad area rather than producing a single large crater.
Airwars also found no reports indicating that militants were killed or military infrastructure was struck at the three locations. An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps compound is located north of the sports hall, but the investigation found no evidence that it was the target of the attacks.
Meier stressed that the legality of a strike depends on assessing the military target, the anticipated effects of the weapon and whether expected civilian harm would be excessive in relation to the anticipated military advantage.
He also questioned the apparent military rationale of the strike, noting that the IRGC compound remained standing and therefore asking whether it could have been considered a sufficiently high-value target to justify the potential effects of the weapon.
A weapon likely to shape future conflicts
The controversy surrounding the PrSM comes as the United States moves to substantially expand production of the weapon.
In July, the US Department of War announced an $8.4 billion contract with Lockheed Martin to accelerate PrSM production. Britain subsequently announced a deal to acquire the missiles as well.
The scale of investment suggests that the missile is expected to become an increasingly important component of US and allied long-range strike capabilities.
Yet the Lamerd strikes have placed a critical question at the center of the debate: whether a weapon capable of dispersing enormous numbers of lethal fragments across a wide area can be reliably employed in environments where civilian populations and military targets exist in close proximity.
For Iran, the findings add to concerns over the civilian consequences of the US-Israeli military campaign. Beyond the immediate casualties, they raise broader questions about the growing use of long-range precision weapons whose effects can extend considerably beyond their intended points of impact.
The central concern is therefore not simply the range or accuracy of the PrSM, but the consequences of deploying a highly destructive fragmentation weapon in populated areas. As the United States and its allies invest heavily in expanding such capabilities, the experience in Lamerd could become an important case in assessing whether claims of precision and deep-strike capability adequately account for the risks borne by civilians on the ground.

Ryanair's Boeing 737 comes with retractable onboard stairs that cut costs and turnaround times, but an Italian safety study has linked them to hundreds of passenger falls since 2021.
Ryanair's Boeing 737 hides a hazard just outside the cabin door: its retractable onboard stairs.
Passengers who have used them have faced a significantly higher risk of falling than those using stairs provided by airports. That is the conclusion of a study by Italy's National Agency for Flight Safety (ANSV), published in August 2026.
The study analysed falls reported in Italy during boarding and disembarkation between 2023 and 2025. Of 104 incidents, 85 involved passengers who used the forward integrated stairs of Boeing 737 aircraft, accounting for 82% of cases, according to Corriere della Sera.
The scale of the figures is even clearer when set against total passenger numbers. Over the same period the Irish airline carried around 27% of all passengers in Italy. The other carriers, which make up the remaining 73%, recorded 19 falls between them.
The trend is not confined to Italy. Since 2021 Ryanair has registered 489 falls on stairs, 360 of them, or 73%, on the Boeing 737's integrated stairway. According to ANSV, that is three times as many falls as those recorded on airport stairways.
To track and analyse the incidents, ANSV used the ECCAIRS system, the digital platform run by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). The system collects and analyses aviation safety data from EU countries.
Why the stairs are riskier
For disembarkation, airlines often hire mobile stairs from airports. Ryanair's Boeing 737 instead has the option of an integrated system that can be deployed while parked, allowing passengers to disembark without airport handlers. This cuts disembarkation times and ground-service costs.
The integrated stairway has 12 steps, about 61 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres high, with a tread depth of 25 centimetres and an inclination of 35 degrees.
ANSV's investigation found the dimensions "are at the limits for step height and steepness" compared with those used by airport operators, "who have lower steps and, usually, a less pronounced inclination, and platforms and treads that are considerably larger."
It also notes that the first step of the stairway is asymmetrical for passengers on the way down because of the shape of the fuselage in relation to the step.
According to Ireland's air accident investigation unit (AAIU), EU regulations do not impose requirements on the size of integrated stairs because they are not deemed critical to flight operations.
ANSV's study began with three incidents in Genoa, Venice and Bologna, in which three people suffered "serious injuries".
In Genoa on 22 March 2025, one person was taken by ambulance to hospital after a fall that occurred "most likely due to the inattention of the passenger," according to ANSV's reports.
Two days later in Venice, another passenger suffered serious injuries after falling from the integrated stairs. According to staff, the passenger was carrying two suitcases and was not holding the handrail. In the Bologna incident, the passenger also fell while carrying two bags.
After these incidents, Ryanair updated its disembarkation protocol, and since 23 July cabin crew have been repeating the warning to use the handrail also in the language of the country of origin and destination.
The problem with the integrated stairs on the Boeing 737 had already been examined by the aviation safety agencies of Ireland and Spain (CIAIAC) after falls in 2021 in Dublin and in 2024 in Alicante.
Following those incidents, the Spanish agency urged Boeing to redesign the stairway, reducing its steepness and increasing the surface area of the steps. CIAIAC also called on Ryanair to abandon use of the integrated system and rely solely on stairs provided by airport operators.
No investigation carried out so far has concluded that the system is defective. ANSV has endorsed the Spanish recommendations to Boeing and Ryanair, while attributing the falls to human factors such as inattention and failure to use the handrail.

Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:23:15 UTC
02:23:15 KST

Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.
Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.
“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.
Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland.
Serhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.
For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.
Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.
Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.
“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.
She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”
Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.
Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline.
Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.
Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.
Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.
On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.
In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.
Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

Reuters: Venezuela to hand oil fields run by Chinese, Russian firms to U.S.-backed operator
The American company North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) will take control of several oil fields in Venezuela that were previously operated by several Chinese companies and one Russian firm, two U.S. officials told Reuters.
NABEP will receive a total of 14 oil production contracts in Venezuela. It will exercise operational control, while the U.S. government will hold rights to a 35% stake in the company, along with “preferential access” to 20% of the oil produced, at cost.
In August, U.S. President Donald Trump said Washington and Caracas had struck the “biggest oil deal in history.” Under the deal, the U.S. will gain access to some 64 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves. As a result, U.S. officials said, Venezuela will be able to attract about $100 billion in private investment, which will help rebuild the country’s economy.

In Nepal's Tragedy, a Warning for a Warming World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
17:20:00 UTC
02:20:00 KST

On Aug. 26, a landslide and a glacier collapse in the Himalayas sent an avalanche of water, rock and soil cascading down the Trishuli River valley, which sits on the border between the northern Rasuwa district of Nepal and Gyirong County in Tibet. The flood moved with overwhelming force and terrifying speed, sweeping away homes, schools, shops, vehicles, and people.
A week later, the reports are bleak: more 1,000 people have died in Nepal and Tibet and around 4,500 people remain missing. Some of the bodies carried away by the deluge were found hundreds of miles downstream in India. Rescue workers are still fighting to reach survivors. At least 900 workers remain missing from several hydropower projects along the Trishuli River, which runs through several remote, mountainous districts of Nepal. Hundreds of workers are believed to be trapped inside the tunnels in the hydropower projects.
A final accounting of lives lost is expected to be in thousands. In the Chitwan district of southern Nepal, some 120 miles from the mountain valleys where the glacial fury first struck, officials have buried nearly 200 unidentified bodies in a forested area because of a lack of morgue space. Mass burials have also started in a forest outside Kathmandu, the capital. DNA samples have been collected so the bodies can be identified later.
Families are still waiting outside hospitals in Kathmandu, the capital, for news of their loved ones. “Even if it’s just their bodies, at least we’d know,” Dil Kumari Masrangi Magar, a woman from Udaypur district in southeastern Nepal, told me outside Kathmandu’s Teaching Hospital. Magar was searching for her missing brother-in-law and a nephew, and had pasted their photos on a hospital wall already covered with images of the dead and names of the missing.
Many others were coming to terms with their loss after recognizing identifying details in photographs of the dead. Among them was Kesari Tamang, a woman, whose brother Sankha Budha Tamang ran a hotel in Betrawati town in central Nepal. He had been swept away by the flood and a body matching his description had been recovered 100 miles downstream in Kapilvastu. The family was travelling there to identify him. “If we start early tomorrow, we will reach there in about 10-11 hours,” Tamang told me. Another relative let out a deep sigh and said, “If it’s not him, we will just come back,” he said. “but it looks like it is him.”
The obliteration of the Gyirong port building on the Nepal-China border on the morning of Aug. 26, by a wave of mud and boulders, rising as high as 80 meters, has become a globally recognized image of the disaster’s scale and ferocity.
The landscape of loss in Nepal
The catastrophic floods have caused an estimated damage of $8 billion, according Nepal’s Finance Ministry. But the concentrated nature of this disaster, confined to a commercially important river valley, means the impact will be much greater. Fifteen hydropower plants—ten operational and five under construction—with a combined capacity of 753 megawatts have been affected by the floods. Roughly 11% of Nepal’s total power generation capacity has been knocked out. Multiple transmission lines and substations have been destroyed, severely crippling the country’s electrical infrastructure. Preliminary estimates by the Independent Power Producers’ Association Nepal put the damage to the hydropower plants at up to $230 million, a figure expected to rise.
More than 40 bridges have been destroyed or damaged, and 25 miles of vital roadways have been erased from the map, or buried under thick mud, cutting off remote mountain communities and compounding the rescue effort. At the same time, 69 schools have been damaged or destroyed, affecting 19,000 children, according to the charity Save The Children. At least 65,000 people have been directly affected.
Much of the downstream death toll was the result of poor planning and weak enforcement of zoning laws, which allowed settlements to be built along riverbanks. Yet nothing could have saved the hydropower plants, which Nepal needs both to wean itself off fossil fuels and to sustain its energy exports. Melting glaciers, a consequence of global warming, combined with high seismic activity, make the Himalayas a hotspot for catastrophic disaster risk downstream.
This is also a lesson for other vulnerable river valleys in Nepal. Four major hydropower plants backed by Indian investments sit in the Arun River basin, directly below Makalu, the world’s fifth highest mountain, at 8,463m, in eastern Nepal. The basin also lies downstream from the Tibetan region of China, where dozens of glacial lakes have swollen in size and could burst at any time. The Arun sits just across the border from the Indian state of Sikkim, where a $1 billion, 1,200-megawatt dam, the Teesta III, was wiped out by a glacial lake outburst in October 2023.
The Annapurna massif towers above the Marsyangdi River in Nepal, which flows through a valley next to the Langtang Lirung mountain where the glacier melted last week. Five cascade hydropower projects—operational and under construction—have been built on the Marsyangdi River. These sit directly beneath the Thulagi Glacial Lake, which has expanded in recent years because of global warming and is held back by a fragile moraine dam.
The science behind the flood
In the immediate aftermath, as is often the case with disasters, there was much speculation. A smaller flood struck the same river last year, caused by a glacier collapse in Tibet, leading many to assume this one had originated in from the same glacier. Online commentators quickly rushed to question why Chinese authorities had not sounded an alarm early on.
But it turned out to be an ice-rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung, a mountain in northern Nepal near the border with Tibet. At first, many linked the flood to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake near the Tibetan border. But the U.S. Geological Survey later revised that account, determining that the avalanche had triggered the earthquake, at 8:37 a.m. that morning in Nepal, not long before the floods.
Satellite photos now reveal a distinct 0.9 mile-wide break in a hanging glacier at 16,400 feet, on the north face of Langtang Lirung, a 23,733-foot mountain in Nepal. Some scientists argue, however, that this was not a simple glacial calving but rather a bedrock failure, likely caused by melting permafrost seeping into a pre-existing fissure. This bedrock fracture sent a mix of rock and ice plunging more than 3,280 feet onto the flatter glacier below. The immense friction and kinetic energy from the drop melted much of the ice, producing collapse so vast that it triggered a localized magnitude 5.2 tremor.
The ice and rocks bulldozed surrounding debris down to the monsoon-swollen Lhende Khola and swept nine miles downstream to the Rasuwagadi border checkpoint between Nepal and China, sending a wall of mud and boulders racing down the Trishuli River into Nepal. Geologists estimate the avalanche displaced up to 200 million cubic meters of debris, making it the largest rock-ice event ever recorded.
A challenge and an opportunity for Balendra Shah
On Sept. 8, 2025 Gen Z in Nepal erupted in protests, which faced violent reprisals from then government, and forced its resignation. In the national election in March, Balendra Shah, a 35-year-old former rapper and independent politician won a major victory and was elected Prime Minister of the country. As the one-year anniversary of the protests approaches, my colleagues and I were planning to take stock of the protests, the reprisals, the election of the new government and its performance in the first six months in power.
The Aug. 26 flood is their biggest test yet. But the sheer scale of the Nepal-Tibet flood would have overwhelmed even the most well-equipped governments, as evidenced by the fact that it took the Chinese authorities three days to reach the disaster site. These are some of the most remote and extremely rugged mountain settlements in a geopolitically sensitive border region.
The Nepal government has deployed 19,000 security personnel and mobilized 16 helicopters in search and rescue operations, and more than 11,000 people have been rescued so far. Although news initially spread of the government refusing international assistance immediately after the floods, it reversed course later, requesting specialized technical personnel and equipment, especially to rescue workers trapped inside hydropower tunnels and to conduct DNA tests of unidentified bodies and remains.
Once the rescue phase and immediate relief efforts conclude, attention should shift to long-term rehabilitation and resettlement for survivors. Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund has collected nearly $33 million in its domestic bank accounts, alongside more than $1.8 million in foreign currency accounts. International donors—through individual country pledges, multinational contributions, and local nonprofit relief efforts—have pledged over $200 million in combined emergency financial aid, potential loans, and dedicated reconstruction funds, alongside significant technical assistance.
How these funds and this assistance are managed and distributed, and whether affected families on the ground actually receive support, could set this government apart from its predecessors. This unprecedented flood, regardless of its colossal toll, also offers Prime Minister Shah and his government, an opportunity to demonstrate a proactive approach to search and rescue, rehabilitation, and a preparedness strategy for the future.

Unidentified individuals damaged the Janswalde Thermal Power Plant in Brandenburg, Germany, by using explosive devices.

The Janschwalde thermal power plant is one of the largest power plants in Brandenburg.

Russia doubles LNG shadow fleet in a year to boost gas exports – Bloomberg
