Xi calls on SCO to work toward more just, equitable global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
23:47:05 CST
00:47:05 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping delivers an important speech during the "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Sept. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhai Jianlan)
BISHKEK, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday called on the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) to shoulder the responsibility of the times and work together to advance a more just and equitable global governance.
Xi made the remarks in his speech at the "SCO Plus" meeting in the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek.
"The meeting today focuses on strengthening the role of the United Nations and building a multipolar world, and it demonstrates SCO's commitment to reforming and improving global governance as required by our times," Xi said.
"Currently, major changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the globe. Hegemonism, unilateralism and protectionism are resurging against historical trends. Nevertheless, the overwhelming majority of the world do not condone power politics, conflict and confrontation, or isolation and backwardness," he added.
What they want instead, Xi said, is to hold a place on the world stage through national development and international cooperation.
Xi noted that in recent years, the rise of the Global South is driving a profound shift in the international balance of power, adding that the trend toward a multipolar world is irreversible.
"What kind of multipolarity does the world need? How are countries going to take part in and promote it? The international community should build consensus and make the right choice that can stand the test of practice and history," Xi said.
Noting that as a responsible major country, China advocates for an equal and orderly multipolar world, Xi said sovereign equality and mutual respect are fundamental principles; balance, order and the rule of law are inherent requirements; multilateralism, dialogue and consultation are essential pathways; mutual benefit, win-win and inclusiveness are the way forward for development.
"We should ensure equal rights, equal opportunities and equal rules for all countries, regardless of their size, strength and wealth," Xi said, adding that "as an important part of a multipolar world and a key driving force behind it, the Global South countries ought to have greater representation and voice in international affairs."
He called on various parties to promote the common values of humanity, reject double standards, exceptionalism, foreign interference, bullying and the law of the jungle, and advance the rule of law in international relations.
"Major countries in particular should take the lead in observing international norms and honoring the rule of law, and work together to tackle global challenges," he added.
Xi also said that world affairs should be discussed by all, and international norms should be set by all.
"The authority and vitality of the United Nations need to be restored. Multilateral mechanisms, global and regional, should enhance their coordination and improve their efficiency," he said.
"We should focus on the development agenda, uphold openness and cooperation, and bridge the digital and AI divides, so that technological revolution and development achievements can benefit all nations," Xi added.
Xi noted that after a 25-year journey, the SCO has successfully set a stellar example in conducting relations among big countries, among neighbors, and among countries of different sizes.
The SCO, Xi said, has successfully brought together half of the world's population and a quarter of the global economy, generating strong driving forces for development, adding that a more united and vibrant SCO is fully capable of making greater contributions to a multipolar world.
"It is important that SCO member states and partners ride the trend of history and shoulder the responsibility of our times. Let us take the people-centered and action-oriented approach, jointly advocate an equal and orderly multipolar world, make global governance more just and equitable, and build a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said.
To further enhance the SCO's role, Xi called for advancing common prosperity in the vast continent straddling Asia and Europe with the SCO Strength.
"We should continue to leverage our strengths, unlock our potential, and connect the multiple growth poles across the continent through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation. We should empower each other, help each other succeed, and work together to create new opportunities and promote shared prosperity," Xi said.
"We should promote the development and rise of the Global South through the SCO Wisdom," Xi said, calling on various parties to "carry forward the Shanghai Spirit, strengthen and expand the SCO Plus partnerships, and jointly speak up for peace, foster synergy for development, build bridges for cooperation, and pave the way for win-win outcomes."
Xi also proposed that the SCO countries should guide the reform and improvement of global governance through the SCO Action.
"We should stay committed to building partnerships rather than alliances, and engaging in dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
Xi also called for sticking to the principle of "planning together, building together and benefiting together" to encourage equal participation in global governance by all countries and ensure all will benefit from it. ■

Britain's summer 2026 warmest on record: provisional statistics
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
23:47:01 CST
00:47:01 KST

LONDON, Sept. 1 (Xinhua) -- The summer of 2026 was provisionally the warmest on record in Britain, the Met Office said Tuesday.
Britain recorded an average mean temperature of 16.5 degrees Celsius over the meteorological summer, the highest in records dating back to 1884. The figure surpassed the previous record of 16.1 degrees Celsius set in 2025.
The five warmest British summers have all occurred since 2003, according to the Met Office, the national weather service.
The season began with Britain's second warmest June on record, followed by its second warmest July. Although unsettled weather in late August moderated temperatures, persistent warmth across the three months was enough to set a new seasonal record.
Daily temperatures peaked at 38.1 degrees Celsius at Kew Gardens in London on Aug. 13. In total, 54 Met Office weather stations broke their all-time daily maximum temperature records during the summer.
Dr Amy Doherty, who leads the National Climate Information Center at the Met Office, said these records are now breaking with increasing frequency, reflecting the influence of human-induced climate change on the temperatures being experienced in Britain.
A rapid attribution study by Met Office scientists has shown the record-breaking summer was made around 130 times more likely because of human-induced climate change.
Dr Mark McCarthy, head of climate attribution at the Met Office, said the summer was an example of extremes expected to occur more frequently because of human-induced climate change.
The summer was also notably dry and sunny. Britain had its third driest July on record. Late-August rain kept seasonal rainfall totals away from national records, though rainfall remained below average.
Britain also had its sixth sunniest summer on record, with 621.9 hours of sunshine.
Met Office climate scientist Dr James Pope said the summer of 2026 would be around average for Britain in a world 2.5 to 3 degrees Celsius warmer than the pre-industrial period. He added that the season's dry conditions were also consistent with projections that British summers will become hotter and drier as the climate warms. ■

Les datacenters énergivores se développent en Europe, la résistance aussi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:44:37 UTC
00:44:37 KST

KRONSTORF, Autriche — Un village paisible niché dans les contreforts des Alpes pourrait bientôt consommer plus d’électricité que l’ensemble des foyers viennois.
Tout cela, c’est grâce à Google.
Le géant américain construit le premier centre de données hyperscale d’Autriche à la périphérie de la petite commune de Kronstorf, située à deux heures de route de la capitale. A terme, ce site pourrait consommer l’équivalent de 7% de la demande actuelle en électricité du pays.
Advertisement
Une résistance croissante pourrait toutefois venir contrecarrer les ambitions de l’entreprise. Un groupe d’opposants locaux — inquiets de la consommation énergétique vorace du centre de données et méfiants face à la mainmise d’un mastodonte américain de la tech — se bat pour empêcher son extension.
“Nous voulons vraiment leur donner du fil à retordre”, assume Harald Müllner, un expert en informatique originaire de Linz, une ville voisine, et qui a cofondé un collectif local regroupant des scientifiques, des artistes et des militants opposés au centre de données. “Ils doivent comprendre que ça ne convient pas à la population.”
Leurs manifestations et leurs pétitions contre les projets de Google reflètent une tendance observée de l’autre côté de l’Atlantique, où les démocrates surfent sur une vague croissante de rejet à l’égard des centres de données à l’approche des élections de mi-mandat américaines de cette année. Le président Donald Trump, quant à lui, a pris le parti des Big Tech, affirmant lundi dans un post sur son réseau social que les communautés s’opposant aux datacenters “finiront par être arriérées et pauvres”.
En Europe, des militants s’attaquent à des projets en France, tandis qu’en Italie, les habitants manifestent contre certains projets. En Irlande, où les centres de données consomment déjà un cinquième de l’électricité totale, les opposants ont tenté — sans succès — d’en faire bloquer la construction devant les tribunaux.
Mais jusqu’à présent, les inquiétudes suscitées par les centres de données en Europe se sont heurtées à la crainte des gouvernements de voir le continent prendre du retard par rapport aux Etats-Unis et à la Chine dans la course à l’intelligence artificielle.
“Nous ne pouvons pas réclamer une plus grande souveraineté européenne en matière d’IA, tout en dressant sans cesse de nouveaux obstacles qui entravent l’infrastructure même sur laquelle elle repose”, a déclaré Elisabeth Zehetner, secrétaire d’Etat autrichienne à l’Energie, à propos des demandes visant à renforcer la réglementation des centres de données de grande envergure, comme celui de Kronstorf.
Advertisement
L’Union européenne prévoit de tripler la capacité de ses datacenters d’ici 2035. Bruxelles et les gouvernements nationaux se sont engagés à lever les obstacles réglementaires qui freinent l’essor de l’intelligence artificielle, tout en affirmant que celle-ci peut être soutenable.
Les militants autrichiens demeurent sceptiques. “Un centre de données hyperscale n’est pas durable par nature. Il est tout simplement gigantesque”, estime Christina Gruber, écologiste spécialiste des eaux douces qui milite contre le datacenter de Kronstorf.
“Il y a tellement de facteurs : la conversion des terres arables, cette soif extrême d’énergie, la consommation d’eau”, poursuit-elle. “Et la question bien plus importante qui plane sur tout cela est tout simplement : ‘Dans quel but ? Est-ce que ça en vaut la peine ?’”
Des libellules et une grenouille
Lorsque Harald Müllner et Christina Gruber se garent devant l’immense chantier par une journée caniculaire du mois d’août, un flot ininterrompu de camions sort par le portail principal, transportant les débris déblayés par une douzaine de pelleteuses.
Un étang situé à l’entrée du chantier, destiné à servir de refuge à la faune sauvage, a été surnommé le “biotope Google”. | Zia Weise/POLITICO
Des grues dominent une salle de serveurs à moitié achevée. Des piles de panneaux métalliques, de barres d’armature et de tuyaux en béton cuisent au soleil. Un peu plus loin sur la route, là où l’Enns se jette dans le Danube, des stations de pompage sont prêtes à prélever l’eau de refroidissement destinée au nouveau centre de données.
Le nom de Google n’apparaît nulle part. Le seul indice laissant supposer que le géant américain est à l’origine de la poussière qui s’envole au-dessus de l’autoroute voisine est un petit panneau “défense d’entrer” accroché à la clôture, aux couleurs emblématiques de l’entreprise.
Advertisement
Pourtant, Google est partout. Lorsque les travaux ont débuté en avril, les élus locaux ont célébré l’événement avec un Bundt cake, connu localement sous le nom de “gugelhupf”, rebaptisé “Googlhupf” pour l’occasion. Les habitants appellent la forêt située en face du chantier, que l’entreprise a aidé à planter, la “forêt Google” ; un petit étang près de l’entrée, une très grande flaque d’eau abritant une poignée de libellules et une grenouille solitaire, a été surnommé le “biotope Google”.
Le géant américain affirme prendre des mesures pour compenser l’impact environnemental de ce centre de données. L’entreprise va recouvrir le toit du bâtiment de panneaux solaires et créer un fonds destiné à améliorer l’écosystème fluvial local, détaille Michiel Sallaets, responsable de la communication en Europe chez Google pour les infrastructures techniques.
“Greenwashing”, réplique Harald Müllner.
Les deux militants s’inquiètent pour l’Enns, qui assurera à la fois le refroidissement du centre de données et recevra les eaux usées réchauffées. “Tout rejet d’eau chaude altère l’habitat et cause un stress supplémentaire aux espèces qui y vivent”, pointe Christina Gruber.
Google affirme qu’il n’y a aucune raison de s’inquiéter. “Les rapports d’experts indépendants réalisés dans le cadre de la procédure d’autorisation montrent également que l’impact du centre de données sur la température de l’Enns est négligeable”, assure Michiel Sallaets.
Ce qui irrite les militants, c’est que, malgré les répercussions potentielles, la loi autrichienne ne prévoit pas que le projet de datacenter fasse l’objet d’une étude d’impact environnemental exhaustive.
Advertisement
“Il faut modifier la loi”, plaide Christina Gruber. La construction d’une éolienne nécessite une étude d’impact environnemental, alors que les centres de données en sont exemptés, compare-t-elle.
Google “a fait toutes les procédures requises”, souligne Michiel Sallaets. L’entreprise “se comportera en voisin bon et transparent”, promet-il.
Une infrastructure très gourmande en énergie
La principale préoccupation des opposants toutefois concerne l’énergie.
Un poste électrique situé à proximité du chantier est en cours d’agrandissement afin de répondre aux besoins considérables en électricité du centre de données. | Zia Weise/POLITICO
La première phase du projet prévoit une demande en électricité de 150 mégawatts par heure, qui passerait à 500 si Google décidait d’agrandir le site. Les datacenters fonctionnant 24 heures sur 24, le site devrait consommer 1,31 térawattheure au cours de la première phase, d’après Austrian Power Gridutrichien et le gestionnaire de réseau d’électricité de Haute-Autriche.
Ce chiffre s’élève à 4,4 térawattheures dans le cadre des projets d’extension. L’ensemble des foyers de Vienne, une ville de 2 millions d’habitants, consomme environ 3,4 térawattheures.
Advertisement
Contrairement aux Etats-Unis, où de nombreuses entreprises ont installé sur place des générateurs fonctionnant aux énergies fossiles, le centre de données de Kronstorf est raccordé au réseau électrique national. L’Autriche est alimentée à près de 90% par des énergies renouvelables — une raison centrale pour laquelle Google a choisi cet emplacement, l’entreprise ayant pour objectif de faire fonctionner ses datacenters à l’électricité verte d’ici 2030.
Mais les opposants craignent que la production d’énergie renouvelable en Autriche ne soit pas en mesure de suivre le rythme. Le pays dépend en effet de l’énergie hydroélectrique, qui est vulnérable à la sécheresse. Au cours de cet été sec, la production hydroélectrique a chuté de près d’un tiers.
Compte tenu du changement climatique, “ça ne va pas s’améliorer”, anticipe Harald Müllner. “Nous observons une tendance parallèle : nous consommons davantage d’électricité tout en en produisant moins.”
Les locaux craignent également que le centre de données n’entraîne une hausse des prix de l’électricité, comme cela s’est produit en Irlande et aux Etats-Unis, ajoute Christina Gruber.
Il y a un risque de hausse des prix si l’Autriche ne compense pas les besoins énergétiques du centre de données par des énergies renouvelables supplémentaires, selon Christoph Dolna-Gruber, expert à l’Austrian Energy Agency, qui conseille le gouvernement et les compagnies d’électricité.
“Lorsque la demande augmente, mais que l’offre ne parvient pas à suivre, le prix de l’électricité augmente naturellement lui aussi”, explique-t-il, tout en précisant que l’intégration étroite de l’Autriche au marché européen de l’énergie rend difficile toute estimation de l’ampleur de cette hausse.
Advertisement
Bien qu’il soit raccordé au réseau électrique autrichien, qui produit une énergie propre, le datacenter de Kronstorf ne sera pas neutre en carbone : les plans de Google prévoient l’installation d’énormes générateurs diesel pour assurer son fonctionnement en cas de coupure de courant. Bien que cela soit rare en Autriche, ces générateurs doivent être mis en marche régulièrement pour des essais, remarque Christoph Dolna-Gruber.
Idéalement, le gouvernement devrait exiger des exploitants de centres de données qu’ils contribuent au développement des énergies propres, estime-t-il.
Dans une déclaration adressée à POLITICO, le ministère autrichien de l’Energie et de l’Economie a assuré que le réseau électrique était en mesure de prendre en charge ce nouveau datacenter. “En principe, a-t-il ajouté, l’expansion des centres de données doit aller de pair avec le développement des énergies renouvelables, des réseaux à haute capacité, des systèmes de stockage et de la flexibilité.”
L’Europe d’abord
Il y a une autre raison pour laquelle les militants autrichiens s’opposent au datacenter de Kronstorf : Google est une entreprise américaine.
Si vous effectuiez une recherche sur Google pour savoir où construire un centre de données en Autriche, imagine Harald Müllner, la périphérie de Kronstorf figurerait parmi les premiers résultats : une plaine idéale pour la construction, de l’eau de rivière disponible pour le refroidissement du site et un immense poste électrique juste à côté.
Alors pourquoi, demande-t-il, ce projet n’a-t-il pas au moins été confié à une entreprise européenne ? “Les Américains prennent les meilleurs emplacements, et nous devons ensuite construire des lignes électriques vers des sites moins attractifs, déplore Harald Müllner. Nous les avons laissés faire.”
Advertisement
Google affirme que son projet permettra de créer une centaine d’emplois. Mais les militants soutiennent que le centre de données réinjectera ses bénéfices aux Etats-Unis et ne profitera pas à l’économie locale.
“Ils utilisent notre énergie. Mais nous ne savons tout simplement pas où vont les recettes”, soulève Harald Müllner.
Le ministère autrichien de l’Economie a souligné que des entreprises telles que Google “peuvent apporter une contribution importante à la région grâce à leurs investissements, aux contrats passés avec des entreprises locales et à leurs infrastructures de pointe en matière de cloud et d’intelligence artificielle”.
Si les questions relatives à l’énergie et à l’environnement doivent être “examinées avec soin”, a ajouté le ministère, “un rejet systématique de ces projets n’est pas justifié”.
Les travaux à Kronstorf étant déjà bien avancés, Christina Gruber estime qu’il n’est pas réaliste d’essayer de mettre fin au projet dans son ensemble. Elle et Harald Müllner concentrent leurs efforts sur l’extension — la deuxième phase qui triplerait la consommation énergétique du centre de données.
Elle espère que leur action servira d’avertissement aux autres géants américains de la tech. Les militants se préparent déjà à lutter contre de nouveaux projets dans l’est du pays.
“Une chose que nous avons déjà accomplie, conclut-elle, c’est que cela ne sera pas aussi facile pour les suivants.”
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

We must not allow Ukraine to be left alone with the aggressor --- Tusk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:44:00 UTC
00:44:00 KST

We must not allow Ukraine to be left alone with the aggressor --- Tusk
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this during commemorative events at Westerplatte in Gdańsk marking the 87th anniversary of the outbreak of World War II, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“The most important lesson of Westerplatte is that the victim of aggression must never again be left alone,” Tusk stressed.
Tusk emphasized that the main lesson of Westerplatte should be the need for solidarity and the readiness of the free world to confront aggression together.
87 years after the outbreak of World War II, evil has once again found itself on Europe’s borders, he said.
“People are dying again — by the thousands and hundreds of thousands. Children are dying under bombs again. And this is happening right next door, in Ukraine,” Tusk stressed.
He urged Western countries to help Ukraine withstand the war against Russia.
“From Westerplatte, we loudly call on the entire free world: stand in solidarity. Today, we must help Ukraine withstand this war. We cannot repeat the mistakes of the past; Munich cannot happen again [a reference to the 1938 Munich Agreement — Ed.]. This ugly, helpless and powerless policy of concessions to evil must not happen again,” the Polish prime minister said.
He stressed that no one can deny the obvious truth that Russia is the aggressor that launched yet another horrific war, and that the West must therefore act decisively.
“It is the responsibility of the entire West to say: Ukraine’s fate will soon be our fate as well. Here, at Westerplatte, we must say this out loud: the coming months, this autumn and the winter ahead, could be decisive not only for Ukraine’s independence, but also for the security of Poland and the entire free world,” he said.
He also drew a parallel between the isolation of the Polish troops at Westerplatte in 1939 and Ukraine’s situation today.
“If we say today, ‘it’s only Ukraine,’ then someone in a few months, a year or two, will again say, ‘it’s only Poland,’” the Polish prime minister said.
Tusk also stressed that NATO cannot remain an “alliance on paper” and that Europe and the United States must demonstrate genuine solidarity in the face of threats.
The Polish prime minister separately drew attention to Russia’s current hybrid activities in Europe. According to him, Poland and a number of other European countries have already faced sabotage, subversive acts and provocations.
“Poland is the victim of many provocations. We most likely had acts of sabotage again several dozen hours ago, arson attacks,” he said.
According to Tusk, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Poland, Romania, Denmark and, more recently, Germany have also faced sabotage, subversive acts and provocations.
Tusk called on European countries and the United States to recognize the common nature of this threat.
“It may happen that Germans, French, Italians and Spaniards — all nations without exception and all leaders of the free world — will understand that in the face of evil, no one can be left alone,” the Polish prime minister said.
Tusk also noted that Poland must rely not only on the heroism of its military, but also on its own strength, genuine alliances and the resilience of its society.
Westerplatte is known as one of the symbols of the outbreak of World War II: on September 1, 1939, the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish military garrison on the Westerplatte peninsula in Gdańsk.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Poland has extended the buffer security zone along the Polish-Belarusian border from September 1 through November 29, 2026.

Japan, South Korea, and the New Logic of Nuclear Energy Security in Northeast Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:44:00 UTC
00:44:00 KST

After the 2011 accident at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Plant, Japan stopped all nuclear power production. Today, the country is restarting reactors, rewriting its energy law, and recasting nuclear power as a pillar of national and regional security rather than a liability to be managed. South Korea, its neighbor and rival in reactor exports, is moving along a parallel track, despite a change of government that briefly appeared to threaten the opposite.
Together, the two countries are reshaping the nuclear politics of Northeast Asia and doing so increasingly in concert with Washington, as energy policy folds into the broader architecture of trilateral security cooperation.
The unresolved question behind both countries’ restarts is what to do with the spent fuel piling up at reactor sites. I explored one effort to solve that issue earlier this month in a visit to Japan’s Horonobe Underground Research Laboratory. There, hundreds of meters below the surface, engineers are testing whether the geological disposal methods every nuclear country is counting on actually hold up over time. Horonobe is a research site, however, not a repository, and Japan still has no designated location for permanent waste disposal. That gap has not slowed the political momentum above ground.
Before 2011, nuclear power supplied roughly 30 percent of Japan’s electricity. After the meltdown at Fukushima Daiichi, every commercial reactor in the country was taken offline, and public opinion turned sharply against nuclear power. What followed was over a decade of dependence on imported liquefied natural gas and coal, at a cost Japan, which imports about 90 percent of its primary energy, could not sustain indefinitely, especially as global gas markets tightened after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The return to nuclear power began in earnest with Prime Minister Kishida Fumio’s Green Transformation (GX) policy, launched in 2022. The GX Basic Policy, approved by the Cabinet in February 2023, explicitly committed the government to restarting reactors already cleared by regulators and to building next-generation designs.
The Seventh Strategic Energy Plan, approved by the Cabinet in February 2025 along with the accompanying GX2040 Vision, cemented nuclear power’s return as government policy rather than a temporary emergency measure. In early 2026, that policy produced its most tangible result yet: the restart of Unit 6 at Tokyo Electric Power Company’s Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, the world’s largest nuclear facility by capacity. Perhaps more pointedly, it’s run by the operator directly responsible for Fukushima Daiichi. Such a restart would have been politically unthinkable a decade ago.
The motivation is obvious. New public funding for data center and semiconductor facilities, worth over a trillion yen, requires that the electricity used come entirely from renewable or nuclear sources. That sends an unambiguous signal that Tokyo now considers nuclear energy to be indispensable to industrial policy, not just decarbonization.
South Korea is moving along a similar trajectory, even if it once looked to be headed in a different direction. President Lee Jae-myung took office in June 2025 after having campaigned on skepticism toward nuclear power. Lee argued that the technology was inherently dangerous and that the country’s reactor-heavy generation mix needed re-examining in favor of renewables. Seven months later, confronted with polling showing strong public support for nuclear energy and with surging electricity demand from an AI-driven data center boom, his government reversed course.
Seoul confirmed it would proceed with two new large reactors under the 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand, which targets a nuclear share of nearly 32 percent by 2030 and over 35 percent by 2038. In August 2026, Lee’s government went further, naming small modular reactors and nuclear fusion among seven technologies it wants to establish as future growth engines for the South Korean economy.
Korean reactor technology is already competitive with Western vendors. Around the same time Lee took office, Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power signed a contract to build two APR-1000 reactors in Dukovany, Czechia, a deal worth roughly $18.6 billion. The company has since signed cooperation agreements covering nuclear development in the Philippines, small-reactors studies with Singapore, and full fuel-cycle cooperation with France’s Orano. South Korea, which imports roughly 90 percent of its own energy needs and around 30 percent of its low-enriched uranium from Russia, is treating nuclear exports and domestic energy security as two sides of the same policy.
In July 2026, nuclear energy became an area of interest for trilateral cooperation between the United States and its two East Asian Allies. Japan, South Korea, and the United States agreed to jointly develop and export small modular reactors across the Indo-Pacific, explicitly extending their trilateral security partnership into commercial nuclear cooperation.
With Russia and China as the only realistic nuclear vendors for many developing countries, Washington has a clear interest in ensuring that Japan and South Korea enter the race. It would benefit Washington if its two Northeast Asian allies, rather than Beijing or Moscow, become the default suppliers of reactor technology to the rest of the region.
For Tokyo and Seoul, folding nuclear commerce into the trilateral security relationship also offers insurance against the awkward fact that both countries’ export ambitions still run through Washington’s non-proliferation rules and, in South Korea’s case, the 123 Agreement governing nuclear cooperation with the United States.
Japan’s own export potential remains constrained precisely because its domestic restart is still incomplete. Barely a handful of reactors are back online out of the roughly three dozen that existed before 2011. That leaves South Korea, for now, as the more credible reactor exporter of the two.
What the restart narrative tends to leave out is that neither country has solved the problem I found researchers still puzzling over at Horonobe: Japan has no operating deep geological repository and no site formally designated to host one. That means the used fuel accumulating at reactor sites, including at the restarted Kashiwazaki-Kariwa plant, has nowhere permanent to go. South Korea faces the same problem, with domestic opposition to any proposed storage site consistently more intense than opposition to reactors themselves.
That gap matters for the trilateral SMR push, too. Exporting reactor technology to Southeast Asia or the Pacific Islands without a credible regional answer on waste management invites the same criticism that has dogged nuclear power at home in both countries: that the industry is better at building political consensus for new construction than for dealing with what construction leaves behind.
For now, Northeast Asia’s nuclear revival is a story about energy security, industrial competitiveness, and alignment with Washington against Chinese and Russian reactor diplomacy. But underneath all these developments lurks the unanswered question of what to do with the increasing amounts of nuclear waste. That may end up mattering as much to the region’s energy future as any restart or export deal announced so far.

Novartis halts clinical trials following patient deaths

Novartis halts clinical trials following patient deaths
At the end of August, Novartis halted several clinical trials of experimental cell therapies for autoimmune diseases in the fields of immunology and neuroscience, following the deaths of three patients.
The Basel-based pharmaceutical giant confirmed the news to the AWP news agency, which had initially been reported by the US newspaper The Wall Street Journal (WSJ), stating that the decision to suspend the programmes in question “follows the reporting of three cases of immune effector cell-associated haemophagocytic syndromes, the complications of which proved fatal”.
More
AI’s next pharma challenge: tackling costly and risky clinical trials
The experimental treatment, known as rapcabtagene autoleucel (or rap-cel), is based on a cell therapy known as CAR-T, which genetically modifies a patient’s white blood cells to induce them to destroy defective cells. Death due to an immune reaction is a known risk associated with this type of therapeutic approach, and the WSJ noted that the US competitor Bristol-Myers Squibb had previously suspended similar trials as a precautionary measure.
Novartis was, however, keen to emphasise that the rap-cel programme in oncology is in no way affected by the suspension. The company is now carefully evaluating the data that has emerged to determine the next steps.

Kyiv preparing to relocate 200,000 residents in case of prolonged blackouts
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
18:41:00 EEST
00:41:00 KST

Kyiv preparing to relocate 200,000 residents in case of prolonged blackouts
The authorities in Kyiv are getting temporary accommodation ready in case of prolonged winter blackouts. Over 200,000 Kyiv residents have been put on relocation lists, and 2,000 have consented to move temporarily.
Source: Suspilne
Details: More than 200,000 Kyiv residents who may find it difficult to remain at home without electricity and heating have been placed on temporary relocation lists. So far, 2,000 people have given consent to relocation.
They are primarily people with reduced mobility, people with disabilities, and families with children with disabilities.
The Kyiv City State Administration has stressed that relocation is voluntary. Residents must give consent to be moved if prolonged outages of heating and electricity would make it unsafe for them to stay in their homes or leave them unable to meet their basic needs independently.
Kyiv Deputy Mayor Maryna Khonda said the city changed its approach to working with such residents after last winter.
"The main task is to assign social workers to specific buildings so that if necessary they have people's contact details and can call them immediately, rather than relying on announcements during a crisis," she stressed.
The city is already identifying sites where people on the lists could stay temporarily in the event of prolonged outages. Possible options include boarding houses, sanatoriums, hospitals and hotels.
"One such centre has 60 beds ready at the moment. It has separate rooms for men and women, as well as rooms for families. Residents will be provided with bedlinen, personal hygiene products and three meals a day," Suspilne reported.
The city is also working separately to increase the number of places available for families with children.
The Kyiv City State Administration says Kyiv is home to more than 16,000 children with disabilities, over 160,000 adults with disabilities, and around 26,000 people who live alone. These groups may need extra help if prolonged power and heating outages make it unsafe for them to remain at home.
Specialised vehicles will be used to take people to their temporary accommodation. District branches of the Red Cross may also be involved if necessary.
However, the city has not yet published a final list of facilities capable of accommodating all the people on the lists, Suspilne noted.
Background: Ekonomichna Pravda previously learned that the authorities in Kyiv were compiling lists of residents with reduced mobility who may need to be moved to temporary accommodation in the event of prolonged heating outages caused by Russian attacks.

Religious Zionism chairman Bezalel Smotrich and Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin reached an agreement Tuesday to run together in the upcoming election, in a move aimed at improving their chances of crossing the electoral threshold and entering the Knesset.
Under the agreement, Feiglin will receive the No. 2 position on Smotrich’s slate, as well as the eighth, 10th and 11th places. The latter positions are currently considered unlikely to win seats.

If Winter agrees to join, he would be offered the No. 2 position, pushing Feiglin down to third place. Winter is also expected to receive additional spots in the top 10 for candidates associated with him.
Even in that scenario, however, Feiglin is expected under the current agreement to retain two positions in the slate’s top 10.

Germany says Russia behind attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Germany blames Russia for attempted airport drone attack
September 2, 2026
The German government said on Tuesday that it held Russia "responsible" for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.
"The federal government concludes that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig," said Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt at a press conference in Berlin .
Leipzig airport attack: What has Germany said?
"The means used — such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine," added Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.
He said the attack fit the pattern of a "long series of destabilization operations" against Europe.
Authorities discovered a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism on the evening of August 4 in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft and believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby.
Last week, German media reported a third drone, also loaded with explosives, had also been discovered at the airport.
German federal prosecutors described the incident as a "serious attack on Germany's transport and logistics infrastructure."
"Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday.
"We do not view Leipzig as an isolated incident, but rather see it in the context of other hybrid actions," he continued. "We assume that Germany will be the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia."
How will Germany respond?
Dobrindt insisted that Germany is "not at war" but that it is "a daily target of hybrid warfare."
Therefore, he said, Germany would respond to the hybrid attack in Leipzig in a "proportionate and measured, yet resolute manner."
Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany's response would be coordinated closely with European Union and NATO partners.
"We are tightening entry controls for Russian nationals" and Berlin would propose the listing of more Russian individuals for European Union sanctions, Wadephul said, as the Russian ambassador to Berlin was summoned.
In addition to a strengthening of internal security, he also announced additional measures including the closure of the Russian consulate in the western city of Bonn from September 18 and the rescinding of a contract enabling the operation of the "Russian House," a Russian cultural center in Berlin.
"Our message to the Russian leadership is clear," Germany's top diplomat said. "We are sticking to our security course. The attack on Leipzig shows that this is necessary. We will not allow our social cohesion to be divided by Russian attacks. We remain ready to react along with our partners when the protection of our population demands it."
Finally, he said that Germany would continue to support Ukraine in its "defensive battle against Russian aggression."
How have NATO and the EU responded?
"NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig on 14 August," said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, adding that the alliance would continue strengthening its ability to deter and defend its allies against threats.
"Russia's attempts to intimidate us, to undermine our unity and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and will fail," he added.
"The German government has taken strong measures and the message is clear: hybrid attacks will not go without a clear response," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
"We are united in our resolve to stand against Russian aggression," she continued. "We will deter anyone who seeks to undermine our freedom and security. Russia is seeking to sow distrust and fear among our societies. But it will fail. And we will stand by Ukraine for as long as it takes."
The European Union's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said earlier on Tuesday that it was "clear" that Russia was involved in the drone incident, but declined to comment further until Germany had identified those it believes were responsible,
Kallas said Russia was becoming increasingly provocative, raising the question of what could be done to deter Moscow from escalating tensions any further.
How have Russia and Ukraine responded?
Russia's President Vladimir Putin rejected Berlin’s allegations, claiming Germany's leadership was attempting use the incident to deflect from their own failings and dissatisfaction among voters with "the need to counter an aggressive Russia."
Putin also claimed Russia was being set up.
"But where is the proof? Well, the proof has been planted," Putin told reporters in the early hours of Wednesday in Kyrgyzstan.
Ukraine meanwhile, welcomed Berlin's measures against Russia following the failed drone attack at Leipzig airport.
Ukrainian Ambassador to Germany Oleksii Makeiev praised Berlin's response late on Tuesday.
"I welcome Germany's resolute response to the Russian attack in Leipzig," Makeiev wrote on social media platform X.
Kyiv has been in close contact with Berlin to secure critical infrastructure against drones, a coordinated approach against Russia's "shadow fleet" and further sanctions against Moscow, he said.

Turkish entrepreneur turns discarded mussel shells into artificial reefs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:37:16 UTC
00:37:16 KST

Turkish entrepreneur Nermin Sena Ozger is turning discarded mussel shells into artificial reefs in western Türkiye, recycling organic waste while creating new habitats for marine life.
Ozger, a diving instructor, industrial designer and entrepreneur, grew up closely connected to the sea in Izmir’s Foca district.
As part of her master’s degree, completed at Izmir University of Economics in 2019, she researched ways to enhance underwater experiences.
During her doctoral studies at Yasar University, completed in 2026, Ozger focused on using discarded mussel shells in artificial reefs.
Her project was titled “Towards Symbiocentric Artificial Reef Design: An Application-Based Study Through Bio-Reef.”
Ozger established a company at Teknopark Izmir within the Izmir Institute of Technology and further developed the project with support from the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye (TUBITAK) Individual Young Entrepreneur Program and the UN Industrial Development Organization's Global Cleantech Innovation Program (GCIP).
She began collecting discarded shells from businesses selling stuffed mussels and mussel-export processing facilities.
After upcycling about 3 tons of mussel shells in the initial phase, she produced four artificial reef prototypes.
The prototypes were purchased by IZDENIZ AS, a subsidiary of Izmir Metropolitan Municipality, and installed at Telgraf Bay in Seferihisar’s Sigacik neighborhood.
The reefs are periodically inspected by divers to monitor their contribution to the marine ecosystem. An Anadolu photojournalist accompanied the team underwater and documented marine life developing around them.
Ozger told Anadolu that while working on artificial reef design, she realized mussel shells could be transformed into a water-resistant material.
After being satisfied with the first prototypes, the team applied for the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye’s 1707 Order-Based Research and Development Project program.
Ozger said artificial reefs around the world are predominantly made of concrete, but her team wanted to remove discarded mussel shells from the waste stream and reuse them.
“It is estimated that more than 40 tons of mussel shells are thrown away every month in the Aegean Region,” she said.
“When we combine the ideas of reducing this 40 tons of waste, transforming this waste into habitats as it is reduced, and turning these habitats into tourism attractions, we focused on mussel shells with the idea of bringing what comes from the local sea back to the sea,” she added.
Ozger said artificial reefs are designed to support underwater life and create habitats in areas where marine life has declined.
Marine life began developing on the prototypes more quickly than on concrete reefs, she said, with algae growth attracting other species.
“The most striking point about these prototypes we placed underwater is that, compared with their main competitor, concrete reefs, life begins to develop on them more quickly,” Ozger said.
“In particular, we observe that herbivorous organisms, what we call algae, begin to develop faster. This means that other marine creatures living around the reefs are also being attracted to the area in greater numbers,” she added.
Ozger said Telgraf Bay was selected for the first prototypes because of its potential for diving tourism.
During the latest inspection dive, the team spotted an octopus inside one of the reef’s cavities, which Ozger described as a significant milestone.
“For the first time, we saw an octopus inside one of the cavities of our prototypes,” she said.
“This is actually a historic milestone for us, this octopus den we observed today. It had decorated the space, and there were clear signs that it had truly settled there,” she added.
The team also observed small fish using the reefs for shelter and protection.
“We witnessed in particular that black bream, rainbow wrasse and Mediterranean rainbow wrasse were using these reefs like a shield,” Ozger said.
“We recorded videos and took photographs of these moments. This is a very encouraging and hopeful development for us,” she added.
Ozger said 35 more artificial reefs would be installed at Telgraf Bay under the project.
The aim is to reduce waste while turning the area into a new attraction for divers and underwater photographers, she said.

Premier Carney says Canada 'never' had trade deal with US, door to future talks still open
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:35:50 UTC
00:35:50 KST

Merve Aydogan
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that his government "never" believed it had secured a trade deal with the US, even as talks continued until the negotiations ultimately broke down.
Speaking to reporters in Ottawa after his Liberal Party swept all three federal by-elections held on Monday, Carney said the collapse stemmed from "an accumulation of issues, each of them serious enough" to block a deal on its own.
He pointed to unresolved concerns over the French language and Quebec culture, restrictions Washington sought to place on Canada's ability to pursue trade agreements with other countries, and terms that would have locked Canada into an "uncompetitive" position in key industries, particularly automobiles.
Asked for specifics on the restrictions Washington had sought, Carney said any broad limits on manufacturing sectors would affect virtually every country Canada trades with or is negotiating with, from ASEAN members to India, the Philippines, Thailand and the Mercosur bloc.
"Canada is a sovereign state," he said, adding that Ottawa "will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals."
Saying that the broader issue was Washington's approach, Carney described it as treating core Canadian industries as though they "would be subsidiaries effectively of the United States industries" or would be "gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out," an outcome he said Ottawa would not accept.
He called the position misguided, arguing that "the United States auto industry is made stronger by the Canadian and the Mexican auto industries," especially at a time of major change in the sector.
Despite the breakdown, Carney left the door open to renewed talks.
"We never viewed that we had that deal, and it diverged towards the end. At some point, maybe it'll converge again," he said.
On the by-election results, Carney said voters had shown clear trust in his government, giving it "more than 50%" support in every riding, and described Canadians as united and ready to buy domestically and travel within the country.
He also cited economic gains, saying job growth is running "four times the rate of the United States," foreign direct investment has hit its highest level in two decades, and non-US exports are on pace to double amid the strongest quarterly growth in the G7.
Asked about US officials mocking Canada's military, Carney said such conduct was "beneath their office." He also denied that Ontario Premier Doug Ford played any role in derailing the talks, saying trade decisions rest solely with the federal government and Cabinet.

The Hindu rituals of death, cremation, prayer and final farewell have been overwhelmed by the scale of the disaster.
Nepal has begun burying the victims of the devastating flood that hit the mountainous country last week in mass graves after taking DNA samples.
Nepal has begun burying victims of last week’s devastating flood in mass graves after taking DNA samples.
Nepalese authorities said on Tuesday that 1,003 bodies had been recovered, with 3,916 people still listed as missing, following the massive surge of freezing water, rocks and debris that tore down Himalayan valleys on August 26.
The deadly wave was triggered by a high-altitude glacial collapse, and then carved a path of destruction through the country.
At a mass burial ground in Chitwan district, the Hindu rituals of death, cremation, prayer and final farewell have been overwhelmed by the scale of the disaster, as authorities bury unidentified bodies after DNA sampling because there are too many to store or identify individually.
Police using a drone to search for survivors said on Tuesday they had found 24 bodies in a single house in Nuwakot district. At least 17 bodies have been recovered from rivers far downstream in India.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah has described the catastrophe as “unimaginable and heartbreaking”.

Hungary demands protection of its national minority in exchange for opening EU negotiating clusters for Ukraine – sources

Source: European Pravda, citing its own sources in the EU
Details: Hungary is demanding that Ukraine make progress in fulfilling its commitments towards the Hungarian minority before Budapest unblocks the opening of the clusters.
Diplomatic sources in the Council of the EU told European Pravda that during a discussion of plans to open clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine and Moldova, the Hungarian representative said Budapest is ready to move forward – but only if Ukraine takes steps towards fulfilling a bilateral agreement on protecting the rights of national minorities.
Until then, the Hungarian side said, there will be no progress on opening the clusters.
Background:
- At a meeting of the Working Party on Enlargement and Countries Negotiating Accession to the EU (COELA) on 1 September, Hungary again refused to approve the screening results for clusters 2 and 3 for Ukraine.
- An earlier attempt to approve the screening results on 22 July 2026 also failed because of Hungary's position. Budapest was prepared to give the green light only to progress on cluster 3 and only for Moldova.
- The sixth negotiating cluster, External Relations, was opened for Ukraine in Brussels on 14 July. Taras Kachka, then Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European and Euro-Atlantic integration, said the opening of the remaining four clusters would not be postponed until after the summer.
- Hungary had previously blocked the opening of clusters 2-6 for Ukraine at the technical level, but later agreed to lift its veto on cluster 6.

U.S. Withdraws Another 200 Troops from Nigeria After Destroying “Islamic State” Strongholds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:33:19 UTC
00:33:19 KST

The United States has started withdrawing approximately 200 service members from combat units stationed in Nigeria.
The New York Times reported on this latest reduction in the U.S. military contingent, citing official sources within the U.S. Department of Defense.
This decision marks the second troop withdrawal in the last two months following a large-scale deployment of forces in this Central African country.
The U.S. presence in the region increased significantly late last winter, when the U.S. deployed more than a hundred troops for training missions.
Subsequently, the Pentagon deployed full-fledged combat units to directly participate in eliminating strongholds of the “Islamic State” terrorist group.
A key element of the operation was the participation of operators from U.S. Navy SEAL Team 6, who conducted combat operations in the Lake Chad region.
A series of joint attacks in May resulted in the elimination of Abu Bilal al-Minouki, who was considered the second most influential leader of the “Islamic State” in the region.
In addition to the special operations forces, soldiers from the 503rd Parachute Regiment of the U.S. Army’s 173rd Mobile Brigade Combat Team were deployed to the mission.
U.S. paratroopers trained Nigerian ground forces in the country’s northeast in several key areas of modern combat.
The training programs covered small-unit tactics, providing first aid in combat conditions, neutralizing explosive devices, and using unmanned aerial vehicles.
Despite the reduction in the size of the combat component, a portion of the U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) contingent remains in the country.
U.S. service members remaining in Nigeria will focus on continuing training programs for local security forces and sharing intelligence.

German power grid hit in suspected sabotage as Russia tensions mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:32:23 UTC
00:32:23 KST

Germany on Tuesday formally accused Russia of carrying out an explosive-drone attack at Leipzig airport last month and announced the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin in response.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the August 4 incident fit Russia’s pattern of “hybrid operations,” adding that the German government had “come to the conclusion that Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack.”
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the Russian consulate in Bonn would be ordered to close from September 18, along with the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
“There is no overreaction on our part, but there is a response when we are attacked,” Wadephul said earlier Tuesday. “Russia must understand that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always ready for negotiations, but under no circumstances will be deterred.”
The accusation came nearly a month after an explosive drone was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft at Leipzig airport. The plane was carrying military ammunition, and German authorities suspect the drone failed to detonate only because of a technical malfunction.
The discovery forced departures and arrivals at the airport, one of Germany’s major cargo hubs, to be halted temporarily and flights to be diverted. Authorities later said a DHL aircraft redirected to Hanover reported being struck by an unidentified object about 400 meters from Leipzig airport, raising suspicion that a second drone may have been involved.
Russia has not yet responded to Germany’s formal accusation. The Russian Embassy in Berlin previously dismissed allegations of Russian involvement as a “fabricated provocation” and part of what it called a “new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany.”
The announcement came on the same day German authorities opened a separate investigation into suspected sabotage of power infrastructure in Brandenburg, although officials have not linked that incident to Russia.
The damage occurred at a substation in Turnow-Preilack near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power station, which has a capacity of about 1,500 megawatts and is Germany’s fourth-largest coal plant.
Police said they were alerted at around 8 a.m. and found at least one unexploded incendiary device at the scene. Damage to several power lines caused a brief outage before electricity was fully restored.
German media reported that improvised explosive devices and components resembling homemade rockets or pyrotechnics were found at the site. Bild reported that at least one explosion occurred, although a police spokeswoman stressed: “We are not talking about rockets here.”
The Märkische Allgemeine Zeitung, citing security and industry sources, said emergency crews found several components for devices carrying explosives and that the substation may have been struck more than once. Investigators were examining whether the attackers intended to trigger a wider blackout.
The site is considered particularly sensitive because electricity generated at Jänschwalde passes through the substation before entering the transmission grid.
There is currently no indication who carried out the Brandenburg attack. While European governments have accused Moscow of conducting sabotage and disruption operations as part of a wider campaign against countries supporting Ukraine, Germany has also experienced domestic attacks on energy infrastructure.
Earlier this year, far-left anarchists damaged Berlin’s electricity network, leaving neighborhoods in the southwest of the capital without power for several days during freezing weather. The Volcano Group claimed responsibility for that attack and has also been suspected of carrying out an arson attack that disrupted production at Tesla’s Berlin-area factory in 2024.
The Leipzig case comes amid a broader wave of unexplained drone activity over civilian airports and strategic sites across Europe. Intelligence officials have increasingly assessed that Russian agencies may be behind some of the incidents, with the aim of disrupting transport, spreading fear and weakening European support for Ukraine.
Some German officials have argued that such incidents should no longer be described merely as “hybrid” operations. Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, a German member of the European Parliament who chairs its security and defense committee, has called them “real attacks.”
Separately, Polish authorities said Tuesday that deliberate sabotage was likely behind a fire at a WB Electronics facility in Skarżysko-Kamienna, a plant that produces drones used by the Ukrainian military.
“Everything points to this being an act of sabotage,” Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said.
Polish prosecutors are also examining whether foreign intelligence services were involved in the blaze, which caused damage estimated at about 15 million zlotys, roughly $4 million.

Jehovah's Witnesses say six believers sentenced in Russia on evidence from 'bereaved' informant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Jehovah's Witnesses say six believers sentenced in Russia on evidence from 'bereaved' informant
LONDON, Sept 1 - Six Jehovah's Witnesses have been convicted of "extremist" activity in Russia after being entrapped by an informant of the FSB security service who posed as a bereaved woman seeking comfort in religion, a spokesperson for the faith group said on Tuesday.
Two of the accused, Zaur Murtuzov and Darya Petrochenko, were sentenced last week to five years each in a penal colony. Four other women received compulsory labour sentences of up to four years.
The Jehovah's Witnesses are a Christian movement known for door-to-door evangelism and a literal approach to studying the Bible. Russia banned them in 2017 as an "extremist organisation".
The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2022 that the ban was unlawful. It has been similarly condemned by the U.N. Human Rights Committee.
Jarrod Lopes, a New York-based spokesperson, said the latest case was based on testimony from a woman who had infiltrated the group in 2022 after picking up a card in a cemetery that contained the message "There is Hope" and gave contact information.
The woman said she had suffered a bereavement and expressed interest in the Bible. Over the next two years she cultivated the group of believers, secretly recording conversations with them and delivering them to the FSB, Lopes said.
He said the exploitation of the group's kindness to a stranger proved "how wrong it is to criminalize a faith that makes people good neighbors".
Before being sentenced, Petrochenko told the court that she was innocent, did not regret her actions and had not lost her faith in people.
"I genuinely wanted to support a person who had supposedly lost a loved one. I asked nothing of her, nor did I offer her anything... I caused no harm to her or to the constitutional order," she said.
According to the Jehovah's Witnesses, the FSB has frequently used informants to infiltrate prayer cells and make secret recordings in order to obtain evidence for prosecutions.
Lopes said 174 Witnesses — 159 men and 15 women — are currently in prison in Russia. REUTERS

Qatar accuses Israel of exploiting regional conflicts to impose new realities in Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria.
Qatar is holding talks with Oman and Pakistan to de-escalate tensions in the region, the country’s Foreign Ministry has said, after a recent flare-up in fighting between the US and Iran.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari warned on Tuesday against normalising the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, where the war between Iran and the US has seen shipping in the waterway grind almost to a halt.

Last week, Russia said British military facilities in Ukraine "and beyond" could be targeted in response to Kyiv’s use of UK missiles to strike Russia.
In response to a question regarding Israel-Palestine, Burnham recalled his previous statement that they needed to “look again at the approach that we'd taken.”
"We've seen the really quite worrying statement about the E1 (West Bank settlement) extension and the settlements there, and the fast-track tender process, which I think would lead to decisions being made before the Israeli election," he said.
Burnham warned that could "imperil, if not end, the two-state solution," adding these matters are urgent and they do need to be confronted.
“I believe we will be updating the House soon on those matters.”
The prime minister also touched on a written statement issued by his office while he was speaking in parliament, which expressed "full solidarity" with Germany after what he called Russia’s "egregious and reckless attack" at Leipzig Airport last month.
He added: “It is a very, a very serious development, and it requires the most intense European cooperation in response.”
Citing an announcement by the UK weather agency earlier Tuesday that summer 2026 was provisionally the warmest ever recorded in the country, Burnham said: “I can confirm to the House that I will attend COP 31 in Türkiye in November.”
COP31 Summit will be held in the southwestern Turkish city of Antalya on Nov. 9-20.
Burnham also noted that he will thank French President Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday in London for the cooperation that has enabled the UK to prevent over 48,000 migrants from crossing the English Channel.
Turning to his early release scheme, he said that anyone convicted of manslaughter, death by dangerous driving or indecent assault will now not see any change to their prison term.
The UK’s Conservative Party warned Monday that Burnham’s early-release scheme could result in dangerous prisoners being freed as the government seeks to ease prison overcrowding.
The scheme was introduced after the prison system came close to running out of capacity in the summer of 2024, with fewer than 100 spaces remaining. An updated version of the scheme is due to take effect on Oct. 1.

Greenland's ice sheet shrinks for 30th year in a row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:24:11 UTC
00:24:11 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Greenland's large ice sheet shrank for the 30th year in a row, broadcaster KNR reported Tuesday.
The Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS) announced that the ice sheet that covers about 80% of Greenland's area shrank in size for the 30th year in a row.
The ice sheet had reportedly been shrinking since 1995/1996, thus not considered a short-term fluctuation.
GEUS described the phenomenon as a "climate signal."
GEUS researcher Signe Hillerup Larsen said the 30 years of consecutive melting was "not at all" a "surprise," but stressed the need to follow the development.
"It's important because the melting of the ice sheet contributes to global sea level. The more ice that melts from the ice sheet, the more the seas rise," she explained.
KNR reported that Greenland's melting season ends in August, while the mass loss is calculated from September to August. The ice sheet reportedly lost a total of around 173 billion tons of ice in the past year.
"We expect the ice to continue to melt for many years to come, when we look at the general trends in the climate, and that it will get warmer," Larsen also said.

MVRDV to stack colorful WOMA housing around fornasetti mosaic plaza in miami
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:22:18 UTC
00:22:18 KST

In Miami’s Wynwood Norte, MVRDV has broken a 163-residence mixed-use building into a stack of differently scaled blocks, which gives WOMA the appearance of several buildings gathered across one site. The development marks Ecuador-based Uribe Schwarzkopf’s first project in the United States and occupies the former home of a coffee roasting company.
Across the exterior, deep red and green sections sit beside blue or sandy volumes, while recessed windows and shifting grids give each piece its own rhythm. The fragmented massing responds to a neighborhood still defined largely by smaller buildings, thus keeping the project legible from the sidewalk even as it rises well above them.
The visual history of Wynwood enters the architecture through a textile-inspired facade that refers to the area’s former identity as Miami’s Fashion District. MVRDV also draws on the street art for which the neighborhood has become famous, and uses color and graphic surface treatment across the stacked blocks.
Across the residential floors, the unit mix extends from micro-units and studios to larger apartments, with a limited group of duplex atelier residences designed by MVRDVforUribe Schwarzkopfaround live-work use. Double-height windows open these ateliers toward the exterior, giving artists and designers room to work while allowing studio or exhibition space to register from the street. A single penthouse crowns the building with a private terrace, while the remaining homes are distributed through the stacked volumes instead of concentrating in one continuous tower.
Setbacks between the blocks create planted terraces and pockets of outdoor space throughout the building, with larger shared amenities placed higher up. A semi-Olympic pool sits on the rooftop beside landscaped garden lounges, while a wellness terrace and fitness studio occupy another communal zone. The amenities appear between and above the colored volumes, so the shared areas read as part of the stepped massing instead of a single deck placed on top.
WOMA will bring 163 residences to a former coffee roasting site in Wynwood Norte
fornasetti mosaics lead into the public plaza
At the center of the project, a publicly accessible plaza opens between the building volumes and connects back to the street through broad stairs. Bisazza glass mosaics cover the stair surfaces with Fornasetti’s recurring hand motifs ‘MANI’, turning the approach into one of WOMA’s most graphic moments. Retail edges the plaza, with offices opening from the same level, and the renderings show planting tucked beneath the overhanging residential blocks to create shade around the shared space.
The studio of Bolivian-born fashion designer Rosita Hurtado will sit alongside this plaza, which is planned to host exhibitions and fashion shows as part of the mixed-use program. Kobi Karp serves as associate architect, bringing local Miami experience to the project, while a planned Brightline station in Wynwood Norte could eventually add another connection beyond the immediate neighborhood.

Ireland in talks to join British-led naval alliance
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
16:21:08 BST
00:21:08 KST

High-level talks between British and Irish defence officials have begun on Ireland joining the Joint Expeditionary Force, the ten-nation grouping led by Britain, according to The Journal.
Niall O’Connor reports that the Irish government has directed the Department of Defence to progress the plan, and that Ireland will initially work as an observer.
Dublin would not join the core elements of the force but a wider grouping known as JEF+, according to the report, which says Ireland has ruled out participation in what it describes as the more offensive core elements.
Sources told the outlet the arrangement is seen as an opportunity for practical cooperation with like-minded partners on shared security challenges, complementing Ireland’s engagement at European Union level. The key, The Journal reports, is that Ireland would draw on the force’s maritime security apparatus to respond to hybrid threats such as drone incursions.
Military sources quoted in the report were candid about what Ireland brings. Given the limits of Irish naval capability, the report says, membership would essentially amount to a watching brief, though it would also offer capability building along with information and intelligence sharing. The meetings are examining what practical benefit Ireland can draw from the other nations.
Who is JEF?
The Joint Expeditionary Force brings together Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. It was established in 2014 and operates outside the NATO command structure while being designed to complement it.
The First Sea Lord set out the argument for its existence in an interview published last week. General Sir Gwyn Jenkins said the force brings unique freedoms and permissions because it does not require consensus among all ten nations to act, giving political flexibility to respond in a crisis earlier than NATO might be able to mobilise, given the higher bar of consensus the alliance requires. He said NATO commanders welcome it for exactly that reason, because it gives them choice and options in the early stage of a crisis.
That structure is what makes an Irish association possible at all. Ireland is not a NATO member and its policy of military neutrality would make accession difficult, but the JEF is not a treaty alliance with a mutual defence clause, which leaves room for arrangements of the kind now under discussion.
The force is currently running Lion Protector 26, which began on 3 August and continues to 12 October across Northern Europe, the North Atlantic and the Baltic Sea region. Its opening activity involved escorting vessels carrying allied military equipment into Latvian ports and moving it inland.
Why Ireland is moving
Ireland’s National Maritime Security Strategy, published in February, stated that securing Irish waters will require broader international relationships, with Minister for Defence Helen McEntee saying at the time that the State should not be afraid to work with Britain on security matters.
The undersea infrastructure question sits behind much of this. A substantial share of transatlantic data cables pass through or near Irish waters, and Russian vessels have been observed loitering over cable routes on multiple occasions. Ireland’s defence spending is the lowest in the European Union at around 0.2 per cent of gross domestic product, and the Naval Service has struggled with crewing shortages that have left ships alongside.
The First Sea Lord described the Russian undersea programme in blunt terms in the same interview, saying of the organisation Moscow presents as a deep sea research directorate: “Let’s not kid ourselves. It’s not a research agency. It is an independently funded arm of the Russian state, whose sole purpose is to pursue the destruction of critical underwater infrastructure.”
He also said that allies are struggling to contain very capable Russian submarines.
Cooperation already under way
Practical cooperation is running ahead of any formal arrangement. A Royal Navy warship and a Merlin helicopter are operating in the Irish Sea this week providing air defence for the meetings of EU defence and foreign ministers in County Wicklow, at Irish request, with the ship required to remain outside Irish territorial waters on constitutional grounds.
The French air defence frigate Aquitaine performed a similar role off Dublin and County Cork in July.
British involvement in Irish security has drawn political comment at Westminster, with the Conservative MP John Cooper writing to the Defence Secretary last week to complain about the offshore restriction and accusing Ireland of freeloading on defence.

Jerusalem schools strike after Israel enforces curriculum and bans teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-01
15:19:46 UTC
00:19:46 KST

Jerusalem schools strike after Israel enforces curriculum and bans teachers
Private and Christian schools in East Jerusalem have declared an open-ended strike, protesting sudden Israeli permit blockades for West Bank educators and a systematic push to replace the Palestinian curriculum.
The academic year in occupied East Jerusalem began on Tuesday with an open-ended strike by teachers at private and Christian schools after Israeli meddling in students’ curriculum.
All new first and seventh-grade classes at East Jerusalem’s Palestinian-majority municipal schools have been told to exclusively use the Israeli curriculum this year.
Entry permits for West Bank teachers to teach in East Jerusalem schools have also been blocked by Israel, according to Haaretz.
It means that one-in-three Palestinian students in occupied East Jerusalem, more than 45,000 in total, will be enrolled in the Israeli educational programme, a nearly fourfold increase over six years ago.
Jerusalem Governorate spokesman Marouf al-Rifai described the forced integration of Israeli curriculum into Palestinian schools as a cultural and educational crime.
“The adherence of Jerusalem’s people, teachers, and students to the Palestinian curriculum is not merely an adherence to a textbook, but rather a defense of memory, identity, history, and the right to determine the national narrative,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
Israeli forces recently seized educational compounds formerly operated by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA, in the Shu’fat refugee camp and Kafr Aqab, to be replaced with Israeli-administered facilities.
Hamas official Haroun Nasser el-Din issued a statement saying that “the school, the book, and awareness are basic pillars in the battle of Jerusalem”. East Jerusalem and the West Bank have been illegally occupied by Israel since 1967.
“The Palestinian identity in Jerusalem is deeper than to be erased by imposed curricula or the occupation’s procedures and its arrogant policies,” he added.
The permit crisis
Palestinian schools in East Jerusalem have already suffered a severe staffing shortage due to Israel effectively blocking teachers from the West Bank from reaching the city’s schools. The General Secretariat for Christian Educational Institutions in Jerusalem announced an indefinite strike in response to the crisis.
“We were surprised, unfortunately once again, by the non-renewal of entry permits for more than 70 teachers and employees from our educational, administrative, and support cadres, in a sudden manner and without prior warning, which hindered their access to their schools and directly affected their readiness for the opening of the school year,” the body said in a statement.
“The absence of this large number of cadres affects various aspects of school work, educational, administrative, and health, in addition to cleaning services and security and safety procedures, which makes it impossible to guarantee a safe and stable start for our students.”
Sylvia Amer, deputy director for academic and administrative affairs at College des Freres Jerusalem, said that the abrupt reversal of dozens of permits just 10 days before schools were due to open forced the suspension of classes.
“The sudden ban came after they had previously confirmed to us in June that all permits would be available for all members of our teaching and administrative staff and employees,” Amer said.
“If this reality continues, it will gradually lead to affecting the independence of schools and their educational and cultural identity”.
Systematic extortion tactics
The staffing crisis at East Jerusalem schools has been worsened by recent Israeli legislation targeting Palestinian schools.
A Knesset law passed earlier this year prohibits the employment of teachers holding academic degrees from Palestinian Authority institutions within the Israeli educational system.
This effectively targets the core of East Jerusalem’s teaching workforce, where approximately 60 percent of the 6,700 Arab educators hold Palestinian degrees, according to the Haaretz report.
Mike Bassam Farraj, general director of Greek Orthodox Patriarchate Schools, told Al Jazeera that the permit denials and legislative hurdles act as a systematic pressure campaign.
“It serves as a systematic pressure method practised on Christian schools in Jerusalem and private schools in general, aiming to reduce the numbers of employees and teachers coming from the West Bank,” Farraj noted.
Israeli authorities have also weaponised budgetary allocations to coerce institutions, he added.
“In reality, there are continuous financial temptations – so as not to use the word ‘blackmail’ – based on the equation: ‘Adopt the Israeli Bagrut curriculum and take whatever budgets you wish,’ where they then grant you much broader spaces and capabilities,” Farraj explained.
To counter this academic siege, Farraj detailed their reliance on the judiciary.
“As for some other professions, we are forced to engage in legal confrontations and relentless follow-ups before responsible and governmental authorities,” he explained.
“The matter often reaches – as in the specialisation of human medicine, for example – obtaining decisions from the Supreme Court to extract and prove the right of our graduates to obtain professional practice certificates according to their specialisations, whether in medicine or law or others.”
